The Four Great Kings, the gods of the Realm of the Four Great Kings, the Trāyastriṃśa gods, the Yāma gods, the Tuṣita gods, the Nirmāṇarati gods, the Paranirmitavaśavartin gods, the Brahmakāyika gods, the Brahmapurohita gods, the Brahmapārṣadya gods, the Mahābrahman gods, the Ābhāsvara gods, the Śubha gods, the Parīttaśubha gods, the Apramāṇaśubha gods, the Śubhakṛtsna gods, and the Apramāṇavṛha gods become joyful, thinking, "We shall come to be."

The gods of Great Fruit (*Bṛhatphala*), the gods of the Unfallen (*Avṛha*), the gods Free from Heat (*Atapa*), the gods of Good Appearance (*Sudṛśa*), the gods of Good Vision (*Sudarśana*), and the gods of the Ultimate (*Akaniṣṭha*) [do not engage] in sexual union with the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva; indeed, he remains a celibate practitioner (*brahmacārī*). For the sake of establishing sentient beings in awakening, and not for the sake of fettering them, he unites with phenomena; in this way, he makes his vow.

"From the first production of the thought of awakening onward, one must be a practitioner of celibacy (brahmacārin) and not a non-practitioner of celibacy. Why is that? For indeed, for one who indulges in sensual desires, even rebirth in the Brahma-world becomes an obstacle; what need is there to mention the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening? Therefore, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, having gone forth, should realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening as a practitioner of celibacy, and not as a non-practitioner of celibacy."

When this had been said, the venerable Śāradvatīputra addressed the Blessed One as follows: "But, Blessed One, must a bodhisattva mahāsattva necessarily have a mother, a father, a wife, a son, and a daughter? The Blessed One replied: "Śāradvatīputra, for some bodhisattva mahāsattvas, there must necessarily be a mother and a father; there must be a wife, a son, and a daughter."

Some must necessarily have mothers, fathers, wives, sons, and daughters; however, Śāradvatīputra, there are some bodhisattva mahāsattvas who, from the very first production of the thought of awakening, undertake the practice of celibacy and remain perpetually youthful until they fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Furthermore, some bodhisattva mahāsattvas, through skill in means (*upāyakauśalya*), while enjoying the five strands of sensual pleasure for the sake of maturing sentient beings, go forth from the midst of the city and realize unexcelled, perfect enlightenment. On the other hand, some bodhisattva mahāsattvas, having attained the profound perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) and being free from the afflictions of desire, teach the non-enjoyment of the strands of sensual pleasure for the sake of maturing sentient beings, yet they do not enjoy them themselves.

"It is just as if, Śāradvatīputra, a skilled illusionist or an illusionist’s apprentice, well-trained in the knowledge of the application of illusory arts, were to manifest the five strands of sensual pleasure and display himself as one who is enjoying, playing, and diverting himself with those five strands of sensual pleasure. What do you think, Śāradvatīputra? Would that illusionist or illusionist’s apprentice have actually consumed those five strands of sensual pleasure? "Certainly not, Blessed One. The Blessed One said:

In the same way, Śāradvatīputra, bodhisattva mahāsattvas who are well-trained in the Mahāyāna and have attained the dwelling in the illusory nature of phenomena (māyopama-dharmatā-vihāra), through the power of great compassion, teach the enjoyment of the qualities of sensual pleasure for the sake of ripening those beings to be trained who are free from all afflictions; yet they do not enjoy the qualities of sensual pleasure, nor do they dwell together with them, nor are they afflicted by them.

In many ways, Śāradvatīputra, bodhisattvas mahāsattvas speak in praise of sensual pleasures; yet sensual pleasures are ablaze, sensual pleasures are murderers, sensual pleasures are adversaries, sensual pleasures are enemies, sensual pleasures are like a blazing torch, and sensual pleasures are like the fruit of the *kimpāka* tree.

Sensual pleasures are like the edge of a sword; sensual pleasures are like a pit of glowing coals; sensual pleasures are like poisoned food; sensual pleasures are like a fishhook; sensual pleasures are like a well of delusion. In this way, Śāradvatīputra, bodhisattva mahāsattvas thoroughly understand sensual pleasures. For the sake of maturing those beings who lack skill in means, and for the sake of separating them from the five strands of sensual pleasure, they display the five strands of sensual pleasure.

They do not become intoxicated by those [sensual pleasures], nor do they resolve upon evil deeds for the sake of desire or on account of desire. When this had been said, the venerable Śāradvatīputra addressed the Blessed One as follows: "But how, Blessed One, should a bodhisattva mahāsattva course in the perfection of wisdom? The Blessed One replied: "In this regard, Śāradvatīputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while coursing in the perfection of wisdom, does not perceive a bodhisattva."

He does not perceive even the conduct of a bodhisattva; he does not perceive the perfection of wisdom; he does not perceive even the name "perfection of wisdom. He does not perceive that "he practices," nor does he perceive that "he does not practice. He does not perceive form; he does not perceive feeling; he does not perceive perception; he does not perceive mental formations; he does not perceive consciousness.

For what reason? Because, Śāradvatīputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva is empty by his very nature; thus, the name "bodhisattva" is empty of the name "bodhisattva. For what reason? This is its very nature. Thus, form is not made empty by emptiness, nor is emptiness other than form; form itself is emptiness, and emptiness itself is form.

Feeling is not empty because of emptiness; emptiness is not other than feeling. Feeling itself is emptiness, and emptiness itself is feeling. Perception is not empty because of emptiness; emptiness is not other than perception. Perception itself is emptiness, and emptiness itself is perception. Volitional formations are not empty because of emptiness; emptiness is not other than volitional formations. Volitional formations themselves are emptiness, and emptiness itself is volitional formations. Consciousness is not empty because of emptiness; emptiness is not other than consciousness. Consciousness itself is emptiness, and emptiness itself is consciousness.

For what reason? Because this so-called "bodhisattva" is merely a name; this so-called "emptiness" is merely a name; this so-called "form" is merely a name; this so-called "feeling" is merely a name; this so-called "perception" is merely a name; these so-called "volitional formations" are merely names; and this so-called "consciousness" is merely a name.

For form is like an illusion, sensation is like an illusion, perception is like an illusion, mental formations are like an illusion, and consciousness is like an illusion. An illusion is a mere name; it does not abide in a location, nor does it abide in a specific place. It is non-existent, unproduced, equal to the false, a deceptive appearance, devoid of intrinsic nature. And that which lacks intrinsic nature is non-arising and non-ceasing.

There is no fixed place, no decrease, no increase, no affliction, and no purification. Practicing in this way, a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not perceive the arising of any dharma, nor does he perceive its cessation; he does not perceive a fixed place, nor does he perceive decrease, nor does he perceive increase, nor does he perceive affliction, nor does he perceive purification. He does not perceive form, nor does he perceive feeling.

He does not perceive perception; he does not perceive mental formations; he does not perceive consciousness. Even that which is called "awakening" or "bodhisattva," he does not perceive that either. Why is that? Because it is a phenomenon consisting of the engagement with artificial names, a phenomenon consisting of the engagement with artificial names.

These are conceptualized and designated by adventitious names that are falsely imagined, and through such conventional usage, they are clung to; yet, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive nor apprehend any phenomena, and not perceiving them and not apprehending them—

He does not conceive [them] and does not adhere [to them]. Furthermore, Śāradvatīputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in the perfection of wisdom should investigate in this way: "That which is called 'bodhisattva' is a mere name; that which is called 'awakening' (bodhi) is a mere name; that which is called 'Buddha' is a mere name; that which is called 'perfection of wisdom' is a mere name; and that which is called 'practicing in the perfection of wisdom' is a mere name."

"This which is called 'form' is a mere name; this which is called 'feeling' is a mere name; this which is called 'perception' is a mere name; this which is called 'volitional formations' is a mere name; this which is called 'consciousness' is a mere name. For example, Śāradvatīputra, the term 'self' is used in conventional discourse, yet when sought for according to reality, it is not to be found."

A "sentient being" (sattva) is conventionally designated as such, yet when sought for according to reality, it is not apprehended. A "living soul" (jīva) is conventionally designated as such, yet when sought for according to reality, it is not apprehended, on account of the emptiness of non-apprehension. A "nourisher" (poṣa) is conventionally designated as such, yet when sought for according to reality, it is not apprehended. A "person" (puruṣa) is conventionally designated as such, yet when sought for according to reality, it is not apprehended.

A "person" (pudgala) is conventionally designated as a "person," yet when sought for according to reality, it is not apprehended. A "human being" (manuja) is conventionally designated as a "human being," yet when sought for according to reality, it is not apprehended. A "young man" (mānava) is conventionally designated as a "young man," yet when sought for according to reality, it is not apprehended. An "agent" (kārāpaka) is conventionally designated as an "agent," yet when sought for according to reality, it is not apprehended.

"One who feels" (vedaka) is a conventional designation, yet when thoroughly sought as it truly is, he is not found. "One who experiences" (vedayitṛka) is a conventional designation, yet when thoroughly sought as it truly is, he is not found. "One who arouses" (utthāpaka) is a conventional designation...

And when that which is called "the arouser" is sought for as it really is, it is not apprehended; when that which is called "the knower" is sought for as it really is, it is not apprehended; and when that which is called "the seer" is sought for as it really is, it is not apprehended.

That which is conventionally designated as "the toucher" is not found when sought for according to reality; just as that which is conventionally designated as "the cognizer" is not found when sought for according to reality, by virtue of the emptiness of non-apprehension.

To the extent that things are conventionally designated by mere names and signs, even so, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva courses in the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive a bodhisattva; he does not perceive a Buddha; he does not perceive the perfection of wisdom. He does not perceive form; he does not perceive feeling; he does not perceive perception; he does not perceive mental formations; he does not perceive consciousness.

Even that name by which one is conventionally designated, he does not perceive as a real entity. Practicing in this way, the bodhisattva mahāsattva, while practicing the perfection of wisdom, surpasses all other forms of wisdom—up to and including the wisdom of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas—with the exception of the wisdom of a Tathāgata, by virtue of the emptiness of non-apprehension (*anupalambha-śūnyatā*). Why is that? Because he does not perceive nor apprehend even that [wisdom] by which he might become attached.

Śāradvatīputra, practicing in this way, a bodhisattva mahāsattva courses in the perfection of wisdom. Śāradvatīputra, suppose this Jambudvīpa were completely filled with monks like Maudgalyāyana, just as a thicket of reeds, or a thicket of rushes, or a thicket of bamboo, or a thicket of sugarcane, or a field of rice, or a field of sesame seeds.

The wisdom of those [shravakas] does not approach even a hundredth part of the wisdom of a bodhisattva mahasattva practicing the perfection of wisdom; it does not approach even a thousandth part; it does not approach even a hundred-thousandth part; it does not approach even a ten-millionth (koṭī) part; it does not approach even a hundred-ten-millionth part; it does not approach even a thousand-ten-millionth part; it does not approach even a hundred-thousand-ten-millionth part; it does not approach even a ten-million-niyuta part.

It does not approach even a hundred-thousandth part of it, nor a ten-thousand-millionth part, nor a hundred-thousand-ten-thousand-millionth part; it does not admit of any number, nor any fraction, nor any calculation, nor any comparison, nor any likeness. For what reason? Because, Śāradvatīputra, whatever wisdom belongs to a bodhisattva mahāsattva is for the sake of the final nirvāṇa of all sentient beings.

It is present, but not so for all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas. Furthermore, Śāradvatīputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, the wisdom cultivated by him in a single day stands surpassing the wisdom of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas. Let alone, Śāradvatīputra, Jambudvīpa filled with monks such as yourself and Maudgalyāyana.

If, Śāradvatīputra, this trichiliocosm were filled with monks such as yourselves, their wisdom would not approach even a hundredth part of the wisdom of a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom; it would not approach even a thousandth part, nor a hundred-thousandth part, nor a ten-millionth part, nor a hundred-ten-millionth part, nor even a thousand-ten-millionth part.

It does not approach even a hundred-thousandth part; it does not approach even a ten-millionth part (*koṭīniyuta*); it does not approach even a hundred-ten-millionth part; it does not approach even a thousand-ten-millionth part; it does not approach even a hundred-thousand-ten-millionth part. It does not admit of any number, nor any fraction, nor any calculation, nor any comparison, nor any resemblance; it is beyond all measure.

"Let alone, Śāradvatīputra, a trichiliocosm world-system. If, Śāradvatīputra, world-systems in the eastern direction as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges were filled with monks like Maudgalyāyana, Śāradvatīputra, their wisdom would not approach even a hundredth part, nor even a thousandth part, of the wisdom of a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom that has been cultivated for a single day."

It does not approach even a hundred-thousandth part; it does not approach even a ten-millionth part; it does not approach even a hundred-ten-millionth part; it does not approach even a thousand-ten-millionth part; it does not approach even a hundred-thousand-ten-millionth part; it does not approach even a ten-billionth part; it does not approach even a hundred-billionth part; it does not approach even a thousand-billionth part; it does not approach even a hundred-thousand-billionth part.

It does not admit of being reckoned as a number, nor as a fraction, nor as a calculation, nor as a comparison, nor as a likeness; it cannot even be approached by a fraction thereof. Let alone, Śāradvatīputra, world-systems in the eastern direction as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā, filled with monks like Maudgalyāyana, Śāradvatīputra. If, Śāradvatīputra, there were [world-systems] in the southern direction as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā...

Śāradvatīputra, suppose world-systems were completely filled with monks like Maudgalyāyana; the wisdom of all those monks would not approach even a hundredth part, nor a thousandth part, nor a hundred-thousandth part, nor a ten-millionth part, nor a hundred-ten-millionth part, nor a thousand-ten-millionth part of the wisdom of a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom for a single day.

It does not approach even a hundred-thousandth part of it; it does not approach even a ten-millionth part; it does not approach even a hundred-ten-millionth part; it does not approach even a thousand-ten-millionth part; it does not approach even a hundred-thousand-ten-millionth part. It does not admit of any number, nor any fraction, nor any calculation, nor any comparison, nor any likeness; it cannot even be endured as a point of reference.
Let alone, Śāradvatīputra, world-systems in the southern direction as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā being filled with monks like Maudgalyāyana, Śāradvatīputra.

If, Śāradvatīputra, world-systems in the western direction as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā were filled with monks like Maudgalyāyana, Śāradvatīputra, the wisdom of those monks would not approach even a hundredth part, nor a thousandth part, nor a hundred-thousandth part, nor a ten-millionth part of the wisdom of a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom for a single day.

It does not approach even a hundred-millionth part; it does not approach even a thousand-millionth part; it does not approach even a hundred-thousand-millionth part; it does not approach even a niyuta-of-millions part; it does not approach even a hundred-niyuta-of-millions part; it does not approach even a thousand-niyuta-of-millions part; it does not approach even a hundred-thousand-niyuta-of-millions part.

It does not approach a fraction, nor does it approach a part, nor does it approach a count, nor does it approach a comparison, nor does it even admit of a likeness. Let alone, Śāradvatīputra, world-systems in the western direction as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā; suppose, Śāradvatīputra, that they were filled with monks equal to Maudgalyāyana.

Śāradvatīputra, if the world-systems in the northern direction were as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā, and if they were filled with monks like Maudgalyāyana, Śāradvatīputra, the wisdom of those monks would not approach even a hundredth part, nor a thousandth part, nor a hundred-thousandth part, nor a ten-millionth part of the wisdom of a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom for a single day.

It does not approach even a hundred-millionth part; it does not approach even a ten-thousand-millionth part; it does not approach even a billion-millionth part; it does not approach even a hundred-billion-millionth part. It does not approach even a ten-trillion-millionth part; it does not approach even a hundred-trillion-millionth part; it does not approach even a thousand-trillion-millionth part; it does not approach even a hundred-thousand-trillion-millionth part.

It does not admit of being numbered, nor does it admit of being expressed as a fraction, nor does it admit of being calculated, nor does it admit of being compared, nor does it even bear comparison by way of analogy. Let alone, Śāradvatīputra, world-systems in the northern direction as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā, filled with monks like Maudgalyāyana, Śāradvatīputra.

If, Śāradvatīputra, world-systems in the northeastern direction as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā were filled with monks like Maudgalyāyana, Śāradvatīputra, the wisdom of those [monks] would not equal even a hundredth part of the wisdom of a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom that has been cultivated for a single day.

It does not approach even a thousandth part; it does not approach even a hundred-thousandth part; it does not approach even a ten-millionth part; it does not approach even a hundred-ten-millionth part; it does not approach even a thousand-ten-millionth part; it does not approach even a hundred-thousand-ten-millionth part; it does not approach even a ten-billionth part; it does not approach even a hundred-billionth part; it does not approach even a thousand-billionth part.

It does not approach even a hundred-thousand-billionth part; it does not admit of any number, nor any fraction, nor any calculation, nor any comparison, nor any likeness—it is simply incomparable. Let alone, Śāradvatīputra, world-systems in the northeastern direction as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā, were they to be filled, Śāradvatīputra, with monks equal to Maudgalyāyana.

If, Śāradvatīputra, world-systems in the southeastern direction as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā were filled with monks like Maudgalyāyana, Śāradvatīputra, their wisdom would not approach even a hundredth part, nor a thousandth part, nor even a hundred-thousandth part of the wisdom of a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom for a single day.

It does not approach even a ten-millionth part, it does not approach even a hundred-ten-millionth part, it does not approach even a thousand-ten-millionth part, it does not approach even a hundred-thousand-ten-millionth part, it does not approach even a niyuta-ten-millionth part, it does not approach even a hundred-niyuta-ten-millionth part, it does not approach even a thousand-niyuta-ten-millionth part, nor does it approach even a hundred-thousand-niyuta-ten-millionth part.

It does not admit of being numbered, it does not admit of being reckoned as a fraction, it does not admit of being calculated, it does not admit of being compared, nor can it even be approached by analogy. Let alone, Śāradvatīputra, world-systems in the southeastern direction equal in number to the sands of the river Gaṅgā, were they to be filled [with such beings].

Śāradvatīputra, by monks such as Maudgalyāyana; if, Śāradvatīputra, the world-systems in the southwestern direction were filled with monks such as Maudgalyāyana, equal in number to the sands of the river Gaṅgā—Śāradvatīputra, whatever wisdom they possess does not approach even a hundredth part, nor even a thousandth part, of the wisdom of a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom that has been cultivated for a single day.

It does not approach even a hundred-thousandth part; it does not approach even a ten-millionth part; it does not approach even a hundred-ten-millionth part; it does not approach even a thousand-ten-millionth part; it does not approach even a hundred-thousand-ten-millionth part; it does not approach even a ten-million-niyuta part; it does not approach even a hundred-ten-million-niyuta part; it does not approach even a thousand-ten-million-niyuta part; it does not approach even a hundred-thousand-ten-million-niyuta part.

It does not admit of being numbered, it does not admit of being reckoned as a fraction, it does not admit of being calculated, it does not admit of being compared, nor can it even be approached by analogy. Let alone, Śāradvatīputra, world-systems in the southwestern direction as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā, filled with monks like Maudgalyāyana, Śāradvatīputra.

If, Śāradvatīputra, world-systems in the northwestern direction were as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā and were filled with monks like Maudgalyāyana, Śāradvatīputra, the wisdom of all those monks would not approach even a hundredth part, nor a thousandth part, nor even a hundred-thousandth part of the wisdom of a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom that has been cultivated for a single day.

It does not approach even a ten-millionth part, nor a hundred-ten-millionth part, nor a thousand-ten-millionth part, nor a hundred-thousand-ten-millionth part, nor a niyuta-ten-millionth part, nor a hundred-niyuta-ten-millionth part, nor a thousand-niyuta-ten-millionth part, nor a hundred-thousand-niyuta-ten-millionth part; it does not admit of calculation, nor a fraction, nor counting, nor comparison, nor even a resemblance—it cannot bear comparison.
Let alone, Śāradvatīputra, world-systems in the northwestern direction as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā, filled with monks like Maudgalyāyana, Śāradvatīputra.

Śāradvatīputra, if worlds in the direction below were as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā and were completely filled with monks like Śāradvatīputra and Maudgalyāyana, their combined wisdom would not approach even a hundredth part, nor a thousandth part, nor a hundred-thousandth part, nor even a ten-millionth part of the wisdom of a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom for a single day.

It does not approach even a hundredth part of it; it does not approach even a thousandth part of it; it does not approach even a hundred-thousandth part of it; it does not approach even a ten-millionth (koṭī) part of it; it does not approach even a hundred-ten-millionth part of it; it does not approach even a thousand-ten-millionth part of it; it does not approach even a hundred-thousand-ten-millionth part of it; it does not approach any number, nor any fraction, nor any calculation, nor any comparison.

It does not approach even a fraction of it, nor can it bear comparison. Let alone, Śāradvatīputra, world-systems in the downward direction as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges being filled with monks like Maudgalyāyana; even if, Śāradvatīputra, world-systems in the upward direction were as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges and were completely filled with monks like Maudgalyāyana, their wisdom would [not equal] that of a bodhisattva.

The wisdom cultivated by a Mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom for even a single day does not approach even a hundredth part of [the wisdom of others]; it does not approach a thousandth part; it does not approach a hundred-thousandth part; it does not approach a ten-millionth part; it does not approach a hundred-ten-millionth part; it does not approach a thousand-ten-millionth part; it does not approach a hundred-thousand-ten-millionth part; it does not approach a ten-million-billionth part.

It does not approach even a hundred-thousandth part of a billionth; it does not approach even a thousandth part of a billionth; it does not approach even a hundred-thousandth part of a hundred-billionth. It does not admit of any number, nor any fraction, nor any calculation, nor any comparison, nor even any resemblance whatsoever.

Śāradvatīputra said: "Blessed One, this wisdom of the Blessed One’s disciples—the wisdom of a stream-enterer, a once-returner, a non-returner, an arhat, as well as that of a pratyekabuddha, a bodhisattva, and a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksambuddha—all these wisdoms are undifferentiated. They are without distinction, empty, secluded, of the nature of non-arising, and empty of intrinsic nature. Furthermore, Blessed One, there is no differentiation in that which is undifferentiated, secluded, unarisen, and empty of intrinsic nature."

Or rather, no distinction whatsoever is perceived. How then, Blessed One, is it that this wisdom of a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom—which has been cultivated for even a single day—surpasses the wisdom of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas? The Blessed One replied:

What do you think, Śāradvatīputra? For what purpose is the wisdom of a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom present for even a single day—[the wisdom] of one practicing the knowledge of the aspects of the path while acting for the benefit of all sentient beings through all modes [sarvākāraiḥ], having fully awakened to all phenomena through all modes, so that all sentient beings may be led to final nirvana?

"In that case, has the wisdom of all the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas been established by means of that task? He replied, "Certainly not, Blessed One. The Blessed One said, "What do you think, Śāradvatīputra? Do all the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas think thus: 'Having realized unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, we must lead all sentient beings to final nirvāṇa in the realm of nirvāṇa without remainder'? He replied, "Certainly not, Blessed One."

The Blessed One said: "Therefore, Śāradvatīputra, by this method also you should understand this: whatever wisdom belongs to all the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, when compared to the wisdom of a bodhisattva mahāsattva, this wisdom of all the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas does not approach even a hundredth part of it; it does not approach even a thousandth part; it does not approach even a hundred-thousandth part; it does not approach even a ten-millionth part; it does not approach even a hundred-ten-millionth part."

It does not approach even a thousandth part; it does not approach even a hundred-thousandth part; it does not approach even a ten-millionth part; it does not approach even a hundred-ten-millionth part; it does not approach even a billionth part; it does not approach even a ten-billionth part; it does not approach even a hundred-billionth part; it does not approach even a trillionth part. It does not admit of calculation, nor a fraction, nor enumeration, nor comparison, nor even a resemblance.

It is so. What do you think, Śāradvatīputra? Do all the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas ever think: "Having practiced the six perfections, having matured sentient beings, having purified the buddha-field, and having fulfilled the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha"?

"Having fulfilled [the perfections] and awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, I shall lead immeasurable, incalculable, and infinite sentient beings to final nirvana. He replied, "Certainly not, Blessed One. The Blessed One said:

Furthermore, Śāradvatīputra, it occurs to the bodhisattva mahāsattva: "Having practiced the six perfections, having ripened sentient beings, having purified the buddha-field, having fulfilled the powers of a Tathāgata, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, and having awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, [I shall liberate] immeasurable, incalculable, and infinite sentient beings."

They should be brought to final nirvāṇa. For example, Śāradvatīputra, it does not occur to a firefly, a species of living being, "May I illuminate Jambudvīpa with my light; may Jambudvīpa be filled by my light. In the very same way, Śāradvatīputra, it does not occur to any of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.

"Having practiced the six perfections, having matured sentient beings, having purified the buddha-field, having fulfilled the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, and having awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, I shall lead immeasurable, incalculable, and infinite sentient beings to final nirvāṇa."
It is just as if, Śāradvatīputra, the orb of the sun, rising up, pervades all of Jambudvīpa with its radiance and makes all of Jambudvīpa manifest with its light.

In the same way, Śāradvatīputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the six perfections brings sentient beings to maturity, purifies a buddha-field, fulfills the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; having realized unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, he leads immeasurable, incalculable, and infinite sentient beings to final nirvana.

When this had been said, the venerable Śāradvatīputra addressed the Blessed One as follows: "Blessed One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having transcended all the levels of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, reach the level of an irreversible bodhisattva and purify the bodhisattva path? When this had been said, the Blessed One addressed the venerable Śāradvatīputra as follows:

"In this regard, Śāradvatīputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, starting from the first production of the thought of awakening, while practicing the six perfections and abiding in phenomena that are empty, signless, and wishless, transcends the levels of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas and attains the level of an irreversible bodhisattva. Śāradvatīputra asked: "Abiding on which level does a bodhisattva mahāsattva become worthy of offerings (dakṣiṇīya) by all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas?"

The Blessed One said: "Śāradvatīputra, from the first production of the thought of awakening onwards, as a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the six perfections until he sits upon the seat of awakening—in this interval, he is to be called the one worthy of offerings for all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas. For what reason? Because, Śāradvatīputra, it is by depending on the bodhisattva mahāsattva that the manifestation of all wholesome dharmas occurs in the world."

Namely, there is the appearance in the world of the ten paths of wholesome action; there is the appearance in the world of the five precepts; and [there is the appearance] of the *poṣadha* rite endowed with eight factors.

The manifestation of the four dhyānas occurs in the world; the manifestation of the four immeasurables occurs in the world; the manifestation of the four formless attainments occurs in the world; the manifestation of the five supernormal knowledges occurs in the world; the manifestation of the six recollections occurs in the world; and the manifestation of the perfection of generosity occurs in the world.
The perfection of ethical discipline appears in the world; the perfection of patience appears in the world; the perfection of vigor appears in the world.

The perfection of meditation appears in the world; the perfection of wisdom appears in the world; the emptiness of the internal appears in the world; the emptiness of the external appears in the world; the emptiness of the internal and external appears in the world; the emptiness of emptiness appears in the world; the great emptiness appears in the world.

The emptiness of the ultimate appears in the world; the emptiness of the conditioned appears in the world; the emptiness of the unconditioned appears in the world; the emptiness of the absolute appears in the world; the emptiness of that which has no beginning or end appears in the world; the emptiness of non-dispersal appears in the world; the emptiness of intrinsic nature appears in the world.

The emptiness of all phenomena appears in the world; the emptiness of specific characteristics appears in the world; the emptiness of non-apprehension appears in the world; the emptiness of non-existence appears in the world; the emptiness of intrinsic nature appears in the world; the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence appears in the world; and the four foundations of mindfulness appear in the world.

The appearance of the four right efforts occurs in the world; the appearance of the four bases of psychic power occurs in the world; the appearance of the five faculties occurs in the world; the appearance of the five powers occurs in the world; the appearance of the seven factors of enlightenment occurs in the world; the appearance of the noble eightfold path occurs in the world; and the appearance of the four noble truths occurs in the world.

The manifestation of the eight liberations occurs in the world; the manifestation of the nine successive meditative attainments occurs in the world; the manifestation of the gateways to liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—occurs in the world; [and] the manifestation of all meditative concentrations occurs in the world.

There is an appearance; there is the appearance in the world of all the gateways of dhāraṇīs. There is the appearance in the world of the ten powers of a Tathāgata. There is the appearance in the world of the four grounds of self-confidence. There is the appearance in the world of the four analytical knowledges. There is the appearance in the world of great loving-kindness. There is the appearance in the world of great compassion.

The eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha appear in the world; Śāradvatīputra, it is through the appearance of such virtuous dharmas as these that the great kṣatriya clans are known in the world, the great brahmin clans are known, the great householder clans are known, and the gods of the Four Great Kings are known.

The Trāyastriṃśa gods are known; the Yāma gods are known; the Tuṣita gods are known; the Nirmāṇarati gods are known; the Paranirmitavaśavartin gods are known; the Brahmakāyika gods are known; the Brahmapurohita gods are known; the Brahmapārṣadya gods are known; the Mahābrahmā gods are known; the Ābhā gods are known.

The gods of Limited Radiance are known; the gods of Immeasurable Radiance are known; the gods of Utmost Radiance are known; the Pure gods are known; the gods of Limited Purity are known; the gods of Immeasurable Purity are known; the gods of Universal Purity are known; the Great gods are known; the gods of Limited Greatness are known; the gods of Immeasurable Greatness are known; the gods of Vast Fruit are known.

The Avṛha gods are known; the Atapa gods are known; the Sudṛśa gods are known; the Sudarśana gods are known; the Akaniṣṭha gods are known; the Ākāśānantyāyatana gods are known; the Vijñānānantyāyatana gods...

The gods of the sphere of nothingness are discerned; the gods of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception are discerned; the stream-enterers are discerned; the once-returners are discerned; the non-returners are discerned; the arhats are discerned; the pratyekabuddhas are discerned; the bodhisattvas, mahāsattvas, are discerned; and the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksambuddhas are discerned. He said:

"But further, Blessed One, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva purify the sacrificial gift? The Blessed One said: "In a certain sense, Śāradvatīputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva purifies the sacrificial gift."

For what reason? Because, Śāradvatīputra, the offerings of a bodhisattva mahāsattva are utterly pure. For this reason, Śāradvatīputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva as a donor is the donor of many wholesome qualities; namely, of the ten paths of wholesome action, the five bases of training, the fast of the eightfold limbs, the four meditative absorptions (dhyānas), the four immeasurables (apramāṇas), and the four formless attainments (ārūpyasamāpattis).

of the five superknowledges (*pañcābhijñā*), the six recollections (*ṣaḍanusmṛti*), the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*), the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*), the perfection of patience (*kṣāntipāramitā*), the perfection of vigor (*vīryapāramitā*), the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*), the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), internal emptiness (*adhyātmaśūnyatā*), external emptiness (*bahirdhāśūnyatā*), internal-and-external emptiness (*adhyātmabahirdhāśūnyatā*), the emptiness of emptiness (*śūnyatāśūnyatā*), great emptiness (*mahāśūnyatā*), the emptiness of the ultimate (*paramārthaśūnyatā*), the emptiness of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtaśūnyatā*), the emptiness of unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtaśūnyatā*), the emptiness of the absolute limit (*atyantaśūnyatā*), and the emptiness of that which has no beginning or end (*anavarāgraśūnyatā*).

of the emptiness of non-dispersal, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of specific characteristics, the emptiness of the unapprehendable, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of self-nature, the emptiness of the self-nature of non-existence, and of the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of miraculous power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the noble eightfold path.

[He spoke] of the path, of the four noble truths, of the eight liberations, of the nine successive meditative attainments, of the gateways to liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—of the gateways to the dhāraṇīs, of the ten powers of a Tathāgata, of the four grounds of self-confidence, of the four analytical knowledges, of great loving-kindness, of great compassion, and of the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha. He said:

"How should a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when engaged [in practice], be said to be 'engaged in the perfection of wisdom'? The Blessed One replied: "In this regard, Śāradvatīputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who is engaged in the emptiness of form should be said to be 'engaged'; one who is engaged in the emptiness of feeling should be said to be 'engaged'; one who is engaged in the emptiness of perception should be said to be 'engaged'; one who is engaged in the emptiness of formations should be said to be 'engaged'."

One who is engaged in the emptiness of consciousness should be said to be "engaged. One who is engaged in the emptiness of the eye should be said to be "engaged. One who is engaged in the emptiness of the ear should be said to be "engaged. One who is engaged in the emptiness of the nose should be said to be "engaged. One who is engaged in the emptiness of the tongue should be said to be "engaged. One who is engaged in the emptiness of the body should be said to be "engaged. One who is engaged in the emptiness of the mind should be said to be "engaged."

One who is engaged in the emptiness of form should be said to be "engaged. One who is engaged in the emptiness of sound should be said to be "engaged. One who is engaged in the emptiness of odor should be said to be "engaged. One who is engaged in the emptiness of taste should be said to be "engaged. One who is engaged in the emptiness of tangibles should be said to be "engaged. One who is engaged in the emptiness of phenomena should be said to be "engaged. One who is engaged in the emptiness of the eye-element should be said to be "engaged."

One who is engaged in the emptiness of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) should be said to be "engaged. One who is engaged in the emptiness of the eye-consciousness realm (*cakṣurvijñānadhātu*) should be said to be "engaged. One who is engaged in the emptiness of the ear realm (*śrotradhātu*) should be said to be "engaged. One who is engaged in the emptiness of the sound realm (*śabdadhātu*) should be said to be "engaged. One who is engaged in the emptiness of the ear-consciousness realm (*śrotravijñānadhātu*) should be said to be "engaged. One who is engaged in the emptiness of the nose realm (*ghrāṇadhātu*) should be said to be "engaged. [And one who is engaged] in the emptiness of the odor realm (*gandhadhātu*)...

He should be called "engaged, engaged. He should be called "engaged, engaged" in the emptiness of the nose-consciousness element. He should be called "engaged, engaged" in the emptiness of the tongue element. He should be called "engaged, engaged" in the emptiness of the taste element. He should be called "engaged, engaged" in the emptiness of the tongue-consciousness element. He should be called "engaged, engaged" in the emptiness of the body element. He should be called "engaged, engaged" in the emptiness of the tactile-object element.

One who is engaged in the emptiness of the body-consciousness element should be said to be "engaged. One who is engaged in the emptiness of the mind element should be said to be "engaged. One who is engaged in the emptiness of the phenomena element should be said to be "engaged. One who is engaged in the emptiness of the mind-consciousness element should be said to be "engaged. One who is engaged in the emptiness of suffering should be said to be "engaged. One who is engaged in the emptiness of its origin should be said to be "engaged. One who is engaged in the emptiness of its cessation should be said to be "engaged."

One who is engaged in the emptiness of the path should be said to be "engaged. One who is engaged in the emptiness of ignorance should be said to be "engaged. One who is engaged in the emptiness of formative forces should be said to be "engaged. One who is engaged in the emptiness of consciousness should be said to be "engaged. One who is engaged in the emptiness of name-and-form should be said to be "engaged. One who is engaged in the emptiness of the six sense bases should be said to be "engaged. One who is engaged in the emptiness of contact should be said to be "engaged."

One who is engaged in the emptiness of sensation should be said to be engaged; one who is engaged in the emptiness of craving should be said to be engaged; one who is engaged in the emptiness of grasping should be said to be engaged; one who is engaged in the emptiness of existence should be said to be engaged; one who is engaged in the emptiness of birth should be said to be engaged; one who is engaged in the emptiness of aging and death should be said to be engaged.

One who is engaged in the emptiness of all phenomena (sarvadharma-śūnyatā) should be called "engaged. Some phenomena belong to the category of conceptualization—both conditioned and unconditioned; one who is engaged in the emptiness of all these phenomena should be called "engaged. Furthermore, Śāradvatīputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) should be called "engaged" when engaged in the emptiness of intrinsic nature (prakṛti-śūnyatā). It is indeed thus, Śāradvatīputra.

A bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in the perfection of wisdom, when engaged with these seven kinds of emptiness, is to be called "engaged. Indeed, Śāradvatīputra, a bodhisattva practicing in the perfection of wisdom through these seven kinds of emptiness is neither to be called "engaged" nor "disengaged."

For what reason? Because he does not perceive form as either conjoined or unconjoined; he does not perceive feeling as either conjoined or unconjoined; he does not perceive perception as either conjoined or unconjoined; he does not perceive mental formations as either conjoined or unconjoined. Nor...

He does not perceive consciousness as either conjoined or disjoined; he does not perceive form as having the nature of arising or the nature of cessation. He does not perceive feeling as having the nature of arising or the nature of cessation. He does not perceive perception as having the nature of arising or the nature of cessation. He does not perceive volitional formations as having the nature of arising or the nature of cessation.

One does not perceive consciousness as having the nature of arising or the nature of cessation. One does not perceive form as having the nature of affliction or the nature of purification. One does not perceive feeling as having the nature of affliction or the nature of purification. One does not perceive perception as having the nature of affliction or the nature of purification. One does not perceive mental formations as having the nature of affliction or the nature of purification.

One does not perceive consciousness as having the nature of affliction or the nature of purification. One does not perceive that form comes together with feeling; one does not perceive that feeling comes together with form. One does not perceive that feeling comes together with perception; one does not perceive that perception comes together with feeling. One does not perceive that perception comes together with mental formations.

He does not perceive that formations come together with perception; he does not perceive that formations come together with consciousness; he does not perceive that consciousness comes together with formations. Why is that? Because, by virtue of the emptiness of intrinsic nature, no dharma whatsoever comes together with any other dharma, nor departs from it, nor is joined with it, nor is disjoined from it.

Śāradvatīputra, that which is emptiness is not form; for the emptiness of form does not form. That which is the emptiness of feeling is not feeling; for the emptiness of feeling does not feel. That which is the emptiness of perception is not perception; for the emptiness of perception...

That which is the emptiness of formations does not perceive them, for those are not the formations; indeed, that which is the emptiness of formations does not perform any formative activity. That which is the emptiness of consciousness is not that consciousness, for that which is the emptiness of consciousness does not cognize. Why is that? Because, Śāradvatīputra, form is not one thing and emptiness another, nor is emptiness one thing and form another. Form itself is emptiness, and emptiness itself is form. Feeling is not one thing and emptiness another.

Emptiness is not other than feeling, and feeling is indeed emptiness; emptiness is indeed feeling. Emptiness is not other than perception, and perception is not other than emptiness; emptiness is indeed perception, and perception is indeed emptiness. Formations are not other than emptiness, and emptiness is not other than formations; formations are indeed emptiness, and emptiness is indeed formations. Consciousness is not other than emptiness, and emptiness is not other than consciousness.

Consciousness itself is emptiness, and emptiness itself is consciousness. Śāradvatīputra, that which is emptiness does not arise and does not cease; it is not defiled and is not purified; it does not diminish and does not increase; it is not past, not future, and not present. That which does not arise and does not cease, which is not defiled and is not purified, which does not diminish and does not increase, and which is not past, future, or present—in that, there is no form, no feeling, no perception, and no...

There are no volitional formations, nor consciousness; therein there is no eye, no ear, no nose, no tongue, no body, and no mind. Therein there is no form, no sound, no odor, no taste, no tangible object, and no mental phenomena. Therein there is no earth element, no water element, no fire element, no wind element, no space element, and no consciousness element. Therein there is no eye-element, no form-element, and no eye-consciousness-element.

Therein, there is no ear element, no sound element, and no ear-consciousness element; therein, there is no nose element, no odor element, and no nose-consciousness element; therein, there is no tongue element, no taste element, and no tongue-consciousness element; [and] no body element and no tangible-object element.

There is no body-consciousness element; therein there is no mind-element, no phenomena-element, and no mind-consciousness element. Therein there is no ignorance, nor the cessation of ignorance; therein there are no volitional formations, nor the cessation of volitional formations; therein there is no consciousness, nor the cessation of consciousness; therein there is no name-and-form, nor the cessation of name-and-form; therein there is no sixfold sense-base, nor the cessation of the sixfold sense-base; therein there is no contact, nor the cessation of contact; therein there is no feeling, nor the cessation of feeling; therein there is no craving...

Therein is no cessation of craving, nor therein is there grasping; no cessation of grasping, nor therein is there becoming; no cessation of becoming, nor therein is there birth; no cessation of birth, nor therein is there aging and death; nor therein is there the cessation of aging and death. Therein is no suffering, nor the full comprehension of suffering; therein is no origin, nor the abandonment of the origin; therein is no cessation, nor the realization of cessation; therein is no path, nor the cultivation of the path; therein is no attainment, nor is there clear realization.

Therein, there are no stream-enterers and no fruit of stream-entry; therein, there are no once-returners and no fruit of once-returning; therein, there are no non-returners and no fruit of non-returning; therein, there are no arhats and no fruit of arhatship; therein, there are no pratyekabuddhas and no pratyekabodhi; therein, there are no bodhisattvas and no knowledge of the aspects of the path; therein, there is no Buddha and no awakening.

In this way, Śāradvatīputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom should be said to be "engaged. Practicing thus in the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive form as either engaged or disengaged; he does not perceive feeling as either engaged or disengaged; he does not perceive perception as either engaged or disengaged; he does not perceive mental formations as either engaged or disengaged.

He does not perceive consciousness as either engaged or disengaged. Thus, practicing in the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive the eye as either engaged or disengaged; he does not perceive the ear as either engaged or disengaged; he does not perceive the nose as either engaged or disengaged.

He does not perceive the tongue as either engaged or disengaged; he does not perceive the body as either engaged or disengaged; he does not perceive the mind as either engaged or disengaged. Thus, practicing in the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive form as either engaged or disengaged; he does not perceive sound as either engaged or disengaged; he does not perceive odor as either engaged or disengaged.

He does not perceive taste as either engaged or disengaged; he does not perceive tangibles as either engaged or disengaged; he does not perceive mental phenomena (*dharma*) as either engaged or disengaged. Thus, practicing in the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), he does not perceive the eye-element as either engaged or disengaged; he does not perceive the form-element as either engaged or disengaged.

Practicing thus in the perfection of wisdom, one does not perceive the eye-consciousness element as either conjoined or disjoined; likewise, one does not perceive the ear element as either conjoined or disjoined; one does not perceive the sound element as either conjoined or disjoined; nor does one perceive the ear-consciousness element as either conjoined or disjoined.

Thus, practicing in the perfection of wisdom, one does not perceive the nose-element as either engaged or disengaged; one does not perceive the odor-element as either engaged or disengaged; one does not perceive the nose-consciousness-element as either engaged or disengaged. Practicing thus in the perfection of wisdom, one does not perceive the tongue-element as either engaged or disengaged.

He does not perceive the taste-element as either conjoined or unconjoined; he does not perceive the tongue-consciousness-element as either conjoined or unconjoined; he does not perceive the body-element as either conjoined or unconjoined; nor does he perceive the tangible-object-element as either conjoined...

Or he does not perceive it as "engaged," nor does he perceive it as "disengaged" with respect to the body-consciousness element; he does not perceive it as "engaged" or "disengaged" with respect to the mind element; he does not perceive it as "engaged" or "disengaged" with respect to the phenomena element; nor does he perceive it as "engaged" or "disengaged" with respect to the mind-consciousness element.

Practicing thus in the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive the earth element as either engaged or disengaged; he does not perceive the water element as either engaged or disengaged; he does not perceive the fire element as either engaged or disengaged; he does not perceive the air element as either engaged or disengaged; he does not perceive the space element as either engaged or disengaged.

He does not perceive the element of consciousness as either conjoined or unconjoined; practicing thus in the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive ignorance as either conjoined or unconjoined. He does not perceive formative forces as either conjoined or unconjoined; he does not perceive consciousness as either conjoined or unconjoined; he does not perceive name-and-form as either conjoined or unconjoined.

He does not perceive the six sense bases as either engaged or disengaged; he does not perceive contact as either engaged or disengaged; he does not perceive feeling as either engaged or disengaged; he does not perceive craving as either engaged or disengaged; he does not perceive grasping as either engaged or disengaged; he does not perceive becoming as either engaged or disengaged.

He does not perceive birth as either conjoined or unconjoined; he does not perceive old age and death as either conjoined or unconjoined. Practicing thus in the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive the perfection of generosity as either conjoined or unconjoined. Nor...

For he does not perceive non-repudiation emptiness itself. Not perceiving it, how could he join non-repudiation emptiness with omniscience, or disjoin them? He does not join natural emptiness with omniscience, nor does he disjoin them; for he does not perceive natural emptiness itself. Not perceiving it, how could he join natural emptiness with omniscience, or disjoin them?

He does not join the emptiness of all phenomena with omniscience, nor does he disjoin them; for he does not even perceive the emptiness of all phenomena itself. Not perceiving it, how could he join or disjoin the emptiness of non-apprehension with omniscience? He neither joins nor disjoins the emptiness of non-existence with omniscience.

He does not join the emptiness of intrinsic nature with omniscience, nor does he separate them; for he does not even perceive the emptiness of intrinsic nature.

He does not perceive it. Not perceiving it, how could he join or disjoin the emptiness of intrinsic nature with omniscience? He does not dissociate them, for he does not even perceive the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*). Not perceiving them [as real], how could he join or disjoin the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha with omniscience? Śāradvatīputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who practices in this manner is to be called "engaged in the perfection of wisdom."

Furthermore, Śāradvatīputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not associate the Buddha with omniscience, nor does he dissociate him from it; he does not associate omniscience with the Buddha, nor does he dissociate it from him. Not perceiving them, how could one join awakening with omniscience, or omniscience with awakening, or separate them?
It is in this way, Śāradvatīputra, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva is said to be "engaged in the perfection of wisdom."

It is not appropriate to say that old age and death are substantial, nor that they are weak; it is not appropriate to say that the perfection of generosity is substantial, nor that it is weak; it is not appropriate to say that the perfection of ethical discipline is substantial, nor that it is weak; it is not appropriate to say that the perfection of patience is substantial, nor that it is weak; it is not appropriate to say that the perfection of vigor is substantial, nor that it is weak; it is not appropriate to say that the perfection of meditative concentration is substantial, nor that it is weak; it is not appropriate to say that the perfection of wisdom is substantial, nor that it is weak.

It is not appropriate to say that internal emptiness is powerful or weak; it is not appropriate to say that external emptiness is powerful or weak; it is not appropriate to say that internal and external emptiness is powerful or weak; it is not appropriate to say that the emptiness of emptiness is powerful.

It is not tenable that it is "not weak. It is not tenable that Great Emptiness is "powerful" or "not weak. It is not tenable that Ultimate Emptiness is "powerful" or "not weak. It is not tenable that Conditioned Emptiness is "powerful" or "not weak. It is not tenable that Unconditioned Emptiness is "powerful" or "not weak. It is not tenable that Absolute Emptiness is "powerful" or "not weak. It is not tenable that Emptiness without Beginning or End is "powerful" or "not weak."

It is not appropriate to say that the emptiness of non-dispersal is powerful or weak; it is not appropriate to say that the emptiness of intrinsic nature is powerful or weak; it is not appropriate to say that the emptiness of all phenomena is powerful or weak; it is not appropriate to say that the emptiness of specific characteristics is powerful or weak; it is not appropriate to say that the emptiness of non-apprehension is powerful or weak; it is not appropriate to say that the emptiness of non-existence is powerful or weak.

It is not tenable that the emptiness of intrinsic nature is substantial nor that it is weak; it is not tenable that the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence is substantial nor that it is weak. It is not tenable that the applications of mindfulness are substantial nor that they are weak; it is not tenable that the right efforts are substantial nor that they are weak; it is not tenable that the bases of psychic power are substantial...

It is not tenable that they are weak; it is not tenable that the faculties are substantial or that they are weak; it is not tenable that the powers are substantial or that they are weak; it is not tenable that the factors of enlightenment are substantial or that they are weak; it is not tenable that the noble eightfold path is substantial or that it is weak; it is not tenable that the noble truths are substantial or that they are weak; it is not tenable that the meditative absorptions are substantial or that they are weak.

It is not appropriate to say that the immeasurables are substantial or that they are weak. It is not appropriate to say that the formless attainments are substantial or that they are weak. It is not appropriate to say that the eight liberations are substantial or that they are weak. It is not appropriate to say that the nine successive meditative attainments are substantial or that they are weak. It is not appropriate to say that emptiness is substantial or that it is weak. It is appropriate to say that they are weak; yet it is not appropriate to say that the signless (*animitta*) is substantial, nor is it appropriate to say that it is weak. It is not appropriate to say that the wishless (*apraṇihita*) is substantial, nor is it appropriate to say that it is weak. It is not appropriate to say that the superknowledges (*abhijñā*) are substantial, nor is it appropriate to say that they are weak. It is not appropriate to say that the gateways of mnemonic formulas (*dhāraṇīmukha*) are substantial, nor is it appropriate to say that they are weak. It is not appropriate to say that the four analytical knowledges (pratisaṃvid) are substantial nor that they are weak; it is not appropriate to say that great loving-kindness (mahāmaitrī) is substantial nor that it is weak; it is not appropriate to say that great compassion (mahākaruṇā) is substantial nor that it is weak; it is not appropriate to say that the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (āveṇikabuddhadharma) are substantial nor that they are weak; it is not appropriate to say that the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpattiphala) is substantial nor that it is weak; it is not appropriate to say that the fruit of once-returning (sakṛdāgāmiphala) is substantial nor that it is weak.

It is not appropriate to say that the fruit of the once-returner is essential or that it is weak; it is not appropriate to say that arhatship is essential or that it is weak; it is not appropriate to say that pratyekabuddha-enlightenment is essential or that it is weak; it is not appropriate to say that the knowledge of the aspects of the path is essential or that it is weak; it is not appropriate to say that the knowledge of all aspects is essential or that it is weak. Śāradvatīputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in this manner should be said to be "engaged in the perfection of wisdom."

Furthermore, Śāradvatīputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, it is neither appropriate nor inappropriate to say that form exists or does not exist; it is neither joined nor disjoined [to such a view]. It is neither appropriate nor inappropriate to say that feeling exists or does not exist; it is neither joined nor disjoined [to such a view]. It is neither appropriate nor inappropriate to say that perception exists or does not exist; it is neither joined nor disjoined [to such a view]. It is neither appropriate nor inappropriate to say that volitional formations exist...

It is neither appropriate nor inappropriate to say that it does not exist; it is neither appropriate nor inappropriate to say that consciousness exists or does not exist; it is neither appropriate nor inappropriate to say that the eye exists or does not exist; it is neither appropriate nor inappropriate to say that the ear exists or does not exist; it is neither appropriate nor inappropriate to say that the nose exists or does not exist; it is neither appropriate nor inappropriate to say that the tongue exists or does not exist; it is neither appropriate nor inappropriate to say that the body exists or does not exist.

It is neither appropriate nor inappropriate to say that the mind exists or does not exist; it is neither appropriate nor inappropriate to say that form exists or does not exist; it is neither appropriate nor inappropriate to say that sound exists or does not exist; it is neither appropriate nor inappropriate to say that odor exists or does not exist; it is neither appropriate nor inappropriate to say that taste exists or does not exist; it is neither appropriate nor inappropriate to say that tangibility exists or does not exist.

It is neither appropriate nor inappropriate to say that phenomena exist or do not exist. It is neither appropriate nor inappropriate to say that eye-consciousness exists or does not exist. It is neither appropriate nor inappropriate to say that ear-consciousness exists or does not exist. It is neither appropriate nor inappropriate to say that tongue-consciousness exists or does not exist. It is neither appropriate nor inappropriate to say that there is no tongue-contact, nor that it does not exist; it is neither appropriate nor inappropriate to say that there is no body-contact, nor that it does not exist; it is neither appropriate nor inappropriate to say that there is no mind-contact, nor that it does not exist. It is neither appropriate nor inappropriate to say that there is no feeling conditioned by eye-contact, nor that it does not exist; it is neither appropriate nor inappropriate to say that there is no feeling conditioned by ear-contact, nor that it does not exist.

It is neither appropriate nor inappropriate to say that feeling conditioned by nose-contact exists or does not exist; it is neither appropriate nor inappropriate to say that feeling conditioned by tongue-contact exists or does not exist; it is neither appropriate nor inappropriate to say that feeling conditioned by body-contact exists or does not exist; it is neither appropriate nor inappropriate to say that feeling conditioned by mind-contact exists or does not exist; it is neither appropriate nor inappropriate to say that the earth element exists or does not exist.

It is neither appropriate nor inappropriate to say that the water element exists or does not exist; it is neither appropriate nor inappropriate to say that the fire element exists or does not exist; it is neither appropriate nor inappropriate to say that the wind element exists or does not exist; it is neither appropriate nor inappropriate to say that the space element exists or does not exist; it is neither appropriate nor inappropriate to say that the consciousness element exists or does not exist; it is neither appropriate nor inappropriate to say that ignorance exists or does not exist.

It is neither appropriate nor inappropriate to say that the formative forces (*saṃskāra*) exist or do not exist; it is neither appropriate nor inappropriate to say that consciousness (*vijñāna*) exists or does not exist; it is neither appropriate nor inappropriate to say that name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) exists or does not exist; it is neither appropriate nor inappropriate to say that the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) exist or do not exist; it is neither appropriate nor inappropriate to say that contact (*sparśa*) exists or does not exist; it is neither appropriate nor inappropriate to say that feeling (*vedanā*) exists or does not exist;
it is neither appropriate nor inappropriate to say that craving (*tṛṣṇā*) exists or does not exist; it is neither appropriate nor inappropriate to say that grasping (*upādāna*) exists...

It is neither appropriate nor inappropriate to say that "it does not exist. It is neither appropriate nor inappropriate to say that "existence exists" or "it does not exist. It is neither appropriate nor inappropriate to say that "birth exists" or "it does not exist. It is neither appropriate nor inappropriate to say that "aging and death exist" or "they do not exist. It is neither appropriate nor inappropriate to say that "the perfection of ethical discipline exists" or "it does not exist."

It is not appropriate to say that the perfection of patience exists, nor is it appropriate to say that it does not exist; it is neither conjoined nor disjoined. It is not appropriate to say that the perfection of meditation exists, nor is it appropriate to say that it does not exist; it is neither conjoined nor disjoined. It is not tenable that the emptiness of own-characteristics exists, nor is it tenable that it does not exist; it is neither joined with nor dissociated from [existence or non-existence]. It is not tenable that the emptiness of the unapprehendable exists, nor is it tenable that it does not exist; it is neither joined with nor dissociated from [existence or non-existence]. It is not tenable that the emptiness of non-existence exists, nor is it tenable that it does not exist; it is neither joined with nor dissociated from [existence or non-existence]. It is not tenable that the emptiness of own-being exists, nor is it tenable that it does not exist; it is neither joined with nor dissociated from [existence or non-existence]. It is not tenable that the emptiness of the own-being of non-existence exists, nor is it tenable that it does not exist; it is neither joined with nor dissociated from [existence or non-existence].

It is neither appropriate nor inappropriate to say that the applications of mindfulness do not exist or that they do not not exist; it is neither appropriate nor inappropriate to say that the right efforts do not exist or that they do not not exist; it is neither appropriate nor inappropriate to say that the bases of psychic power do not exist or that they do not not exist; it is neither appropriate nor inappropriate to say that the faculties do not exist or that they do not not exist; it is neither appropriate nor inappropriate to say that the powers do not exist or that they do not not exist; it is neither appropriate nor inappropriate to say that the factors of enlightenment do not exist or that they do not not exist.

It is neither appropriate nor inappropriate to say that the noble eightfold path exists or does not exist; it is neither appropriate nor inappropriate to say that the noble truths exist or do not exist; it is neither appropriate nor inappropriate to say that the meditative absorptions exist or do not exist; it is neither appropriate nor inappropriate to say that the immeasurables exist or do not exist; it is neither appropriate nor inappropriate to say that the formless attainments exist or do not exist; it is neither appropriate nor inappropriate to say that the eight liberations exist or do not exist.

It is neither appropriate nor inappropriate to say that the nine successive meditative attainments exist or do not exist; it is neither appropriate nor inappropriate to say that the gateways to liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—exist or do not exist; it is neither appropriate nor inappropriate to say that the superknowledges exist or do not exist.

It is not applicable nor non-applicable that the concentrations exist or do not exist; it is not applicable nor non-applicable that the gateways of dhāraṇī exist or do not exist; it is not applicable nor non-applicable that the ten powers of a Tathāgata exist or do not exist; it is not applicable nor non-applicable that the four fearlessnesses exist or do not exist; it is not applicable nor non-applicable that the four analytical knowledges exist or do not exist.

It is not appropriate to say that great loving-kindness exists, nor is it appropriate to say that it does not exist; it is neither conjoined nor disjoined. It is not appropriate to say that great compassion exists, nor is it appropriate to say that it does not exist; it is neither conjoined nor disjoined.
