The Blessed One replied: "Śāradvatīputra, whatever is the divine eye of the gods belonging to the retinue of the Four Great Kings, that the bodhisattva fully knows. Whatever is the divine eye of the Trāyastriṃśa gods, that the bodhisattva fully knows. Whatever is the divine eye of the Yāma gods, that the bodhisattva fully knows."
The Bodhisattva understands that divine eye of the Tuṣita gods, as well as that of the Nirmāṇarati gods.

The Bodhisattva understands the divine eye of the gods; the Bodhisattva understands that divine eye of the Paranirmitavaśavartin gods; the Bodhisattva understands that divine eye of the Brahmakāyika gods; the Bodhisattva understands that divine eye of the Brahmapurohita gods; the Bodhisattva understands that divine eye of the Brahmapārṣadya gods.

The Bodhisattva understands the divine eye of the Mahābrahmā deities; the Bodhisattva understands the divine eye of the Ābhā deities; the Bodhisattva understands the divine eye of the Parīttābhā deities; the Bodhisattva understands the divine eye of the Apramāṇābhā deities; the Bodhisattva understands the divine eye of the Ābhāsvara deities.

The divine eye of the Śubha devas, that the bodhisattva understands; the divine eye of the Parīttaśubha devas, that the bodhisattva understands; the divine eye of the Apramāṇaśubha devas, that the bodhisattva understands; the divine eye of the Śubhakṛtsna devas, that the bodhisattva understands; the divine eye of the Bṛhat devas, that the bodhisattva understands.

The divine eye of the Parīttabṛha devas, that the bodhisattva understands; the divine eye of the Apramāṇabṛha devas, that the bodhisattva understands; the divine eye of the Bṛhatphala devas, that the bodhisattva understands; the divine eye of the Avṛha devas, that the bodhisattva understands; the divine eye of the Atapa devas, that the bodhisattva understands.

The divine eye of the Sudṛśa gods, that the bodhisattva understands; the divine eye of the Sudarśana gods, that the bodhisattva understands; the divine eye of the Akaniṣṭha gods, that the bodhisattva understands.

Furthermore, Śāradvatīputra, as for the divine eye of a bodhisattva mahāsattva, the gods of the Four Great Kings do not know it; the divine eye of a bodhisattva mahāsattva, the Trāyastriṃśa gods do not know it; the divine eye of a bodhisattva mahāsattva, the Yāma gods do not know it.

The divine eye of the bodhisattva mahāsattva is not known by the Tuṣita gods; the divine eye of the bodhisattva mahāsattva is not known by the Nirmāṇarati gods; the divine eye of the bodhisattva mahāsattva is not known by the Paranirmitavaśavartin gods; the divine eye of the bodhisattva mahāsattva is not known by the Brahmakāyika gods.

That divine eye of the bodhisattva mahāsattva which the Brahmapurohita gods do not know; that divine eye of the bodhisattva mahāsattva which the Brahmapārṣadya gods do not know; that divine eye of the bodhisattva mahāsattva which the Mahābrahmā gods do not know; that divine eye of the bodhisattva mahāsattva which the Ābhā gods do not know.

That divine eye of the bodhisattva mahāsattva which the gods of Limited Light do not know; that divine eye of the bodhisattva mahāsattva which the gods of Immeasurable Light do not know; that divine eye of the bodhisattva mahāsattva which the gods of Utmost Purity do not know; that divine eye of the bodhisattva mahāsattva which the Śubha gods do not know.

That divine eye of the bodhisattva mahāsattva which the Parīttābha gods do not know; that divine eye of the bodhisattva mahāsattva which the Apramāṇābha gods do not know; that divine eye of the bodhisattva mahāsattva which the Śubhakṛtsna gods do not know; that divine eye of the bodhisattva mahāsattva which the Bṛhatphala gods do not know.

That divine eye of the bodhisattva mahāsattva which the Parīttabṛhat devas do not know; that divine eye of the bodhisattva mahāsattva which the Apramāṇa-bṛhat devas do not know; that divine eye of the bodhisattva mahāsattva which the Avṛhatphala devas do not know; that divine eye of the bodhisattva mahāsattva which the Avṛha devas do not know.

That divine eye of the bodhisattva mahāsattva which the Atapa gods do not know; that divine eye of the bodhisattva mahāsattva which the Sudṛśa gods do not know; that divine eye of the bodhisattva mahāsattva which the Sudarśana gods do not know; that divine eye of the bodhisattva mahāsattva which the Akaniṣṭha gods do not know.

Endowed with that divine eye, the bodhisattva mahāsattva perceives the passing away and rebirth of beings in world systems in the eastern direction as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges; endowed with that divine eye, the bodhisattva mahāsattva perceives the passing away and rebirth of beings in world systems in the southern direction as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges.

Endowed with that divine eye, the bodhisattva mahāsattva perceives the passing away and rebirth of beings in world systems in the western direction as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges. Endowed with that divine eye, the bodhisattva mahāsattva perceives the passing away and rebirth of beings in world systems in the northern direction as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges.

Endowed with which divine eye, the bodhisattva mahāsattva perceives the passing away and rebirth of beings in world systems as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges in the northeastern direction; endowed with which divine eye, the bodhisattva mahāsattva perceives the passing away and rebirth of beings in world systems as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges in the southeastern direction.

He knows: by means of that divine eye with which the bodhisattva mahāsattva is endowed, he knows the passing away and rebirth of beings in world systems as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā in the southwestern direction; by means of that divine eye with which the bodhisattva mahāsattva is endowed, he knows the passing away and rebirth of beings in world systems as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā in the northwestern direction.

Endowed with which divine eye, the bodhisattva mahāsattva perceives the death and rebirth of beings in world-systems in the downward direction as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges; endowed with which divine eye, the bodhisattva mahāsattva perceives the death and rebirth of beings in world-systems in the upward direction as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges—this, Śāradvatīputra, is the purification of the divine eye of the bodhisattva mahāsattva.

He asked: "Blessed One, what is the purification of the wisdom-eye of a bodhisattva mahāsattva? The Blessed One replied: "Śāradvatīputra, it is that eye endowed with which a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not perceive any phenomenon—whether conditioned or unconditioned, wholesome or unwholesome, faulty or faultless, afflicted or unafflicted, mundane or supramundane, or with-outflows or without-outflows."
By means of which eye of wisdom no phenomenon whatsoever remains unseen, unheard, or unknown—this, Śāradvatīputra, is the purification of the eye of wisdom of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.

[Śāradvatīputra] asked: "What is the purification of the Dharma-eye of a bodhisattva mahāsattva? The Blessed One replied: "In this regard, Śāradvatīputra, with the Dharma-eye, a bodhisattva mahāsattva understands: 'This person is a follower by faith; this person is a follower by dharma; this person dwells in emptiness. For this person, the five faculties will arise through the gateway of the liberation of emptiness; by means of the five faculties, he will enter the concentration of immediate succession (ānantarya-samādhi).'"

By means of the immediate concentration (*ānantarya-samādhi*), he will produce the knowledge and vision of liberation (*vimukti-jñānadarśana*). Through that knowledge and vision of liberation, he will abandon the three fetters (*saṃyojana*): the view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*), doubt (*vicikitsā*), and adherence to rites and rituals (*śīla-vrata-parāmarśa*). This person is called a stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*). Having attained the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*), he effects the attenuation of sensual desire and ill-will; this person is a once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmī*).

By means of that very path cultivated to a superior degree, he will attain the abandonment of sensual desire and ill-will; this person is a non-returner (*anāgāmī*). By means of that very same path cultivated to a superior degree, he will abandon attachment to the realm of form, attachment to the formless realm, ignorance, pride, and restlessness; this person is an arhat. This is one who dwells in the signless (*ānimitta*). For this person, the five faculties will arise through the gate of liberation that is the signless.

By means of the five faculties, he will enter the immediate concentration (*ānantarya-samādhi*); by means of the immediate concentration, he will produce the knowledge and vision of liberation (*vimukti-jñāna-darśana*). He will produce the knowledge of liberation; by means of the knowledge and vision of liberation, he will abandon the three fetters: the view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*), doubt (*vicikitsā*), and adherence to rules and observances (*śīla-vrata-parāmarśa*). This person is called a stream-enterer (*śrotāpanna*).

Having attained the path of cultivation, this person will attenuate sensual desire and ill-will; such a person is a once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmī*). By means of that very same path, when cultivated to a superior degree, he will achieve the abandonment of sensual desire and ill-will; such a person is a non-returner (*anāgāmī*). By means of that very same path, when cultivated to a superior degree, he will abandon attachment to the realm of form, attachment to the formless realm, ignorance, pride, and restlessness; such a person is an arhat.

This dweller in the wishless state—through this wishless gate of liberation—will give rise to the five faculties. By means of the five faculties, they will enter the uninterrupted concentration (*ānantarya-samādhi*). Through the uninterrupted concentration, they will produce the knowledge and vision of liberation (*vimukti-jñāna-darśana*). Through the knowledge and vision of liberation, [they will realize] the three...

He will abandon the fetters: the view of a self-identity, doubt, and the adherence to rules and rituals; this person is called a stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*). Having attained the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), he will thin out sensual desire and ill-will; this person is a once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmī*). By means of that very same path, when it has been cultivated to a superior degree, he will reach the abandonment of sensual desire and ill-will; this person is a non-returner (*anāgāmī*).

By means of that very path, cultivated to a superior degree, he will abandon attachment to the realm of form, attachment to the formless realm, ignorance, pride, and restlessness; this person is an Arhat. Śāradvatīputra, this is the purification of the Dharma-eye of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.

Furthermore, Śāradvatīputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva knows that whatever has the nature of arising, all that has the nature of cessation; having understood this, he attains the five faculties beginning with faith. This, Śāradvatīputra, is the purification of the Dharma-eye of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.

Furthermore, Śāradvatīputra, with the Dharma-eye, a bodhisattva mahāsattva knows: "This bodhisattva mahāsattva who has first produced the thought of awakening practices the perfection of generosity; he practices the perfection of ethical discipline; he practices the perfection of patience; he practices the perfection of vigor; he practices the perfection of meditative concentration; he practices the perfection of wisdom."

Then, endowed with the faculty of faith and the faculty of vigor, and through skill in means, he will intentionally take on a physical existence. By the apprehension of roots of goodness, this bodhisattva mahāsattva will be reborn in great kṣatriya families, he will be reborn in great brāhmaṇa families, he will be reborn in great householder families; he will be reborn among the gods of the Four Great Kings, and he will be reborn among the Trāyastriṃśa gods.

They will be reborn among the Yāma gods; they will be reborn among the Tuṣita gods; they will be reborn among the Nirmāṇarati gods; they will be reborn among the Paranirmitavaśavartin gods. There, he...

Abiding therein, he will bring sentient beings to maturity and attend to them with every provision for happiness; he will purify a buddha-field and please, honor, revere, respect, and worship the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksambuddhas; and he will not fall into the level of a Śrāvaka or the level of a Pratyekabuddha.

This bodhisattva mahāsattva does not turn back until he has fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. Śāradvatīputra, this too is the completely pure Dharma-eye of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.

Furthermore, Śāradvatīputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva knows: "This bodhisattva mahāsattva has been prophesied for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; this one has not been prophesied. This one is fixed; this one is unfixed. These will receive a prophecy; these will not receive a prophecy. These are irreversible and have attained the [spiritual] faculties; these are not irreversible and have not attained the faculties. The higher knowledges of this one are perfected; those of this one are not perfected."

This bodhisattva mahāsattva, having gone to world-systems in the eastern direction as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges with his fully perfected supernormal powers, pleases the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas; he attends upon them, honors them, reveres them, respects them, and worships them. Having gone to world-systems in the southern direction as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges, he pleases the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas; he attends upon them and honors them.

He honors, respects, and worships them; having gone to world-systems in the western direction as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges, he pleases the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones, and attends upon them; he honors, respects, and worships them. Having gone to world-systems in the northern direction as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges, he pleases the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones, and attends upon them.

He honors, reveres, respects, and worships them. Having gone to world-systems in the northeastern direction as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges, he pleases the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas; he attends upon them, honors, reveres, respects, and worships them. Having gone to world-systems in the southeastern direction as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges, he pleases the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas; he attends upon them.

He honors, reveres, respects, and worships them. Having gone to world-systems in the southwestern direction as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā, he pleases the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas; he attends upon them, honors, reveres, respects, and worships them. Having gone to world-systems in the northwestern direction as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā, he pleases the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas; he attends upon them.

He honors, reveres, respects, and worships them. Having gone to world-systems in the downward direction as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges, he pleases the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones; he attends upon them, honors, respects, and worships them. Having gone to world-systems in the upward direction as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges, he pleases the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones; he attends upon them, honors, respects, and worships them.

"This one will attain the superknowledges; this one will not attain them. This one has attained patient acceptance; this one has not attained patient acceptance. This one has attained the faculties; this one has not attained the faculties. The buddha-field of this bodhisattva mahāsattva will be completely pure; the buddha-field of this bodhisattva mahāsattva will not be completely pure."

"This bodhisattva mahāsattva has great vows; this one does not have great vows. By this one, sentient beings have been brought to maturity; by this one, sentient beings have not been brought to maturity.

The Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, in world-systems throughout the ten directions as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges, speak the praises of this bodhisattva mahāsattva; they do not speak the praises of that one. These bodhisattva mahāsattvas stand in the presence of the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones."

They will be thus: "These do not abide among non-beings. "The lifespan of this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, once he has attained awakening, will be immeasurable"; "his [lifespan] will be limited. "His radiance, his renown, and his community of monks will be immeasurable"; "his [radiance, renown, and community] will be limited. "This Bodhisattva, having become an unsurpassed, perfectly awakened Buddha, will have a community of Bodhisattvas"; "he will not have one. "This one will practice what is difficult to perform; this one will not practice it."

"This one is in his final existence; this one is not in his final existence. This one will sit at the seat of awakening; this one will not sit there. Mara will be the adversary of these bodhisattva mahāsattvas; he will not be the adversary of those. In this way, Śāradvatīputra, is the perfectly pure Dharma-eye of the bodhisattva mahāsattvas.

He asked: "Furthermore, Blessed One, what is the completely pure Buddha-eye of a bodhisattva mahāsattva? The Blessed One replied: "Śāradvatīputra, it is when a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having entered the adamantine-like samādhi of the unsurpassed mind of awakening, attains the knowledge of all aspects (sarvākārajñatā). He becomes endowed with the ten powers of a Tathāgata; he becomes endowed with the four grounds of self-confidence (vaiśāradya)."

He is endowed with the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; he is endowed with great loving-kindness; he is endowed with great compassion; he is endowed with great sympathetic joy; he is endowed with great equanimity; and he is endowed with the unobstructed liberation of a Buddha.

That is his eye, by which eye no thing whatsoever remains unseen, unheard, unthought, or unknown by the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva. Śāradvatīputra, this is the perfectly pure Buddha-eye of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who has fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

In this way, Śāradvatīputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to purify and obtain the five eyes should apply himself to the six perfections. Why is that? Because, Śāradvatīputra, within the six perfections are included all wholesome dharmas, as well as all the dharmas of the śrāvakas and all the dharmas of the pratyekabuddhas.

Śāradvatīputra, those who would speak correctly of what is called "the gathering of all wholesome dharmas" would speak correctly of the perfection of wisdom. Why is that? Śāradvatīputra, this perfection of wisdom is the mother of these five eyes; and having trained in these five eyes, bodhisattva mahāsattvas fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Śāradvatīputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices this perfection of wisdom, he attains the perfection of the superknowledges (*abhijñā*). He experiences manifold kinds of miraculous power (*ṛddhividhi*): having been one, he becomes many; having been many, he becomes one. He appears and he also experiences disappearance.

He passes through walls, through enclosures, and even through mountains with his body as if they were not there; just as if he were moving cross-legged through the air. Just as a bird [flies] upon the earth, he emerges from it without sinking. Just as one moves through water, he travels by way of walking even on what is not water. Just as on the earth, he emits smoke and even blazes forth, like a great mass of fire.

Even these two, the sun and the moon, so possessed of great miraculous power (*maharddhika*), so possessed of great majesty (*mahānubhāva*), and so renowned for great authority (*maheśākhya*), he touches with his hand and brings under his control as far as the Brahma-world with his body; yet by that miraculous power he does not become conceited. For he does not perceive any such accomplishment by which he might become conceited, because of the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*) and because of the non-arising of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvānutpādatā*). He does not even give rise to a volition regarding miraculous power or the manifestation of miraculous power, except for the mental attention (*manasikāra*) directed toward omniscience (*sarvajñatā*).

In this way, Śāradvatīputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in the perfection of wisdom realizes the superknowledge of the direct manifestation of the modes of psychic power. With the divine ear-element, purified and surpassing that of humans, he hears both kinds of sounds, namely, those that are divine and those that are human. Yet, by means of that divine ear-element, he does not conceive the thought, "I hear sounds."

For he does not perceive the ear or sounds, by reason of their emptiness of intrinsic nature and their non-arising of intrinsic nature. He does not even produce volition regarding the divine ear-element, except for the mental engagement with omniscience. In this way, Śāradvatīputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in the perfection of wisdom accomplishes the superknowledge of realizing the divine ear-element.

With his own mind, he understands the minds of other beings and other individuals as they truly are. He understands a mind with passion as "a mind with passion," understanding it as it truly is; he understands a mind free from passion as "a mind free from passion," understanding it as it truly is. He understands a mind with hatred as "a mind with hatred," understanding it as it truly is; he understands a mind free from hatred as "a mind free from hatred," understanding it as it truly is.

He understands, as it truly is, a mind with delusion as "a mind with delusion"; he understands, as it truly is, a mind free from delusion as "a mind free from delusion"; he understands, as it truly is, a mind with craving as "a mind with craving."

He understands, as it truly is, a mind free from craving as "a mind free from craving. He understands, as it truly is, a mind with clinging as "a mind with clinging. He understands, as it truly is, a mind without clinging as "a mind without clinging. He understands, as it truly is, a distracted mind as "a distracted mind. He understands, as it truly is, a limited mind as "a limited mind."

He understands, as it truly is, an expansive mind as "an expansive mind"; he understands, as it truly is, a vast mind as "a vast mind"; he understands, as it truly is, an immeasurable mind as "an immeasurable mind"; he understands, as it truly is, a concentrated mind as "a concentrated mind"; and he understands, as it truly is, an unconcentrated mind as "an unconcentrated mind."

One understands, as it truly is, a secluded mind as "a secluded mind"; one understands, as it truly is, an unsecluded mind as "an unsecluded mind"; one understands, as it truly is, a mind with outflows as "a mind with outflows"; one understands, as it truly is, a mind without outflows as "a mind without outflows"; and one understands, as it truly is, a mind with blemishes as "a mind with blemishes."

He understands, as it truly is, a mind free from blemish as "a mind free from blemish. He understands, as it truly is, a surpassable mind as "a surpassable mind. He understands, as it truly is, an unsurpassable mind as "an unsurpassable mind. And by means of that knowledge of others' minds, he does not conceive pride; for that mind is no-mind, by virtue of its inconceivability. He does not conceive pride, thinking, "I understand this."

For in that way, he does not apprehend that mind by which he might conceive [of it], based on its emptiness of intrinsic nature, based on its isolation from intrinsic nature, and based on its non-arising of intrinsic nature. He does not even give rise to the volition of knowing the mind; he does not give rise to the volition of accomplishing the knowledge of the mind, except for the mental engagement with omniscience (*sarvajñatā*). Thus...

Indeed, Śāradvatīputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom brings forth the knowledge of the superknowledge that directly realizes the mental activities of all sentient beings. He brings forth the knowledge of the superknowledge that directly realizes the recollection of various kinds of former existences. He recollects even a single thought, up to recollecting a hundred thoughts; he recollects even a single day, up to recollecting two hundred days.

He recollects even one month, up to and including a hundred months; he recollects even one year, up to and including a hundred years; he recollects even one eon (*kalpa*), up to and including a hundred eons; he recollects even many hundreds of eons; he recollects even many thousands of eons; he recollects even many hundreds of thousands of eons;
he recollects even many hundreds of thousands of *niyutas* of *koṭīs* of eons.

"In this regard, he recollects his manifold former abodes with their aspects, details, and specific characteristics—both his own and those of others—thinking: 'I had such a name, such a clan, such a birth, such food, such a lifespan, and such a limit to my life; having passed away from there, I was reborn here; and so on, until: having passed away from there, I was reborn here. Yet, by means of that superknowledge of the realization of the recollection of former abodes, he does not become conceited."

For that knowledge is non-knowledge by virtue of its inconceivability; he does not conceive, "I know this," because he does not apprehend that very knowledge by which he might so conceive, due to the emptiness of intrinsic nature, the isolation from intrinsic nature, and the non-arising of intrinsic nature. He does not even give rise to volition, except through the mental engagement with omniscience by means of the knowledge of recollection.

In this way, Śāradvatīputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in the perfection of wisdom brings forth the knowledge of the superknowledge that realizes the recollection of former abodes. With the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, he beholds sentient beings passing away.

He discerns beings as they are being reborn—whether beautiful or ugly, lowly or exalted, fortunate or unfortunate—according to their karma. He knows: "These worthy beings were possessed of misconduct of body, possessed of misconduct of speech, and possessed of misconduct of mind; they were revilers of the noble ones and held wrong views. Because of that cause and by reason of that condition, upon the breakup of the body, they have been reborn in states of deprivation, in miserable destinies, in perdition, in the hells."

Furthermore, these venerable ones, being endowed with good conduct of body, endowed with good conduct of speech, and endowed with good conduct of mind; not revilers of the noble ones, possessing right view—by reason of that, by condition of that, at the breaking up of the body, they are reborn in a happy destination, in the heavenly world, among the gods. Thus, throughout the ten directions, in all world-systems, in the world bounded by the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*) and extending to the limits of the realm of space (*ākāśadhātu*), he perceives as it really is the passing away and rebirth of beings belonging to the six realms of existence.

He understands it, yet he does not conceive pride on account of it; for that eye is a non-eye by virtue of its inconceivability. He does not conceive, "I see," because he does not perceive that very eye by which he might conceive such, by virtue of the emptiness of intrinsic nature, the isolation of intrinsic nature, and the non-arising of intrinsic nature. He does not even give rise to the thought of a divine eye.

He does not produce the volition for the accomplishment of the divine eye, except through the mental engagement with the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*). In this way, Śāradvatīputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) accomplishes the superknowledge (*abhijñā*) of the realization of the divine eye; yet he does not reach the level of a śrāvaka or the level of a pratyekabuddha. He does not perceive any dharma whatsoever that fully awakens to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Having attained the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*) by means of that supernormal knowledge (*abhijñā*), he effects the abandonment of all afflictions along with their underlying tendencies and residual impressions; yet, he does not conceive pride on account of that supernormal knowledge of the realization of the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣaya-jñāna*).

For that knowledge is non-knowledge and is inconceivable; it does not conceive, "I know. For he does not apprehend that very superknowledge of the realization of the knowledge of the exhaustion of the outflows (*āsravakṣayajñānasākṣātkriyābhijñā*), by which he might conceive [such a thought]. This is on account of the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvaśūnyatā*), on account of the isolation of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvaviviktatā*), and on account of the non-arising of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvānutpādatā*). He does not even produce the volition toward the knowledge of the exhaustion of the outflows.

He does not form the intention to accomplish the superknowledge of the realization of the destruction of the outflows (*āśravakṣayasākṣātkriyābhijñājñāna*), except through the mental engagement with the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*). In this way, Śāradvatīputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in the perfection of wisdom accomplishes the superknowledge of the realization of the destruction of the outflows. Furthermore, Śāradvatīputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in the perfection of wisdom fulfills the six superknowledges (*ṣadabhijñā*).

They increase toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment. Śāradvatīputra, there are bodhisattva mahāsattvas who, practicing the perfection of wisdom and abiding in the perfection of generosity, purify the path to the knowledge of all aspects, by means of a mind that is not grasping, based upon absolute emptiness.

Śāradvatīputra, there are bodhisattva mahāsattvas who, practicing the perfection of wisdom and abiding in the perfection of ethical discipline, purify the path to the knowledge of all aspects by means of absolute emptiness, on account of the non-existence of both transgression and non-transgression.

Śāradvatīputra, there are bodhisattva mahāsattvas who, practicing the perfection of wisdom and abiding in the perfection of patience, purify the path to the knowledge of all aspects by means of absolute emptiness, on account of imperturbability.

Śāradvatīputra, there are bodhisattva mahāsattvas who, practicing in the perfection of wisdom and established in the perfection of vigor, purify the path to all-aspect omniscience by means of absolute emptiness, through the non-laxity of physical and mental vigor. Śāradvatīputra, there are bodhisattva mahāsattvas who, practicing in the perfection of wisdom, [established] in the perfection of meditative concentration...

Abiding [in this], they purify the path to omniscience by means of absolute emptiness, based on a state of non-distraction of mind. Śāradvatīputra, there are bodhisattva mahāsattvas who, practicing the perfection of wisdom and abiding in the perfection of wisdom, purify the path to omniscience by means of absolute emptiness, based on the non-apprehension of a mind characterized by poor wisdom.

In this way, Śāradvatīputra, bodhisattva mahāsattvas practicing the perfection of wisdom, abiding in the six perfections, purify the path to the knowledge of all aspects by means of absolute emptiness, based on the state of neither coming nor going, and based on non-appropriation. Generosity is designated based on appropriation; ethical discipline is designated based on impurity; patience is designated based on agitation.

Vigor is designated in dependence upon laziness; meditative concentration is designated in dependence upon lack of concentration; wisdom is designated in dependence upon poor wisdom. He does not think, "I have crossed over," nor does he think, "I have not crossed over. He does not think, "I am a giver," nor does he think, "I am not a giver. He does not think, "I am virtuous," nor does he think, "I am immoral. He does not think, "I am endowed with patience," nor does he think, "I am angry."

One does not conceive the thought, "I am one who has initiated vigor"; one does not conceive the thought, "I am lazy. One does not conceive the thought, "I am concentrated"; one does not conceive the thought, "I am unconcentrated. One does not conceive the thought, "I am wise"; one does not conceive the thought, "I am unwise. One does not conceive the thought, "I am reviled"; one does not conceive the thought, "I am praised. One does not conceive the thought, "I am honored"; one does not conceive the thought, "I am dishonored. Why is that?
Because, Śāradvatīputra, non-arising does not conceive the thought, "I am reviled," nor does it conceive the thought, "I am praised," nor does it conceive the thought, "I am honored."

He thinks; or he thinks, "I am being treated with disrespect. Why is that? Because the perfection of wisdom completely cuts off all otherness. Śāradvatīputra, whatever qualities belong to a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom here, those do not exist among the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas. Fulfilling these qualities, he brings sentient beings to maturity, purifies the buddha-field, and attains the knowledge of all aspects.

Furthermore, Śāradvatīputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he generates a mind of equanimity toward all sentient beings. Having generated a mind of equanimity toward all sentient beings, he attains the equality of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-samatā*). Having attained the equality of all phenomena, he establishes all sentient beings in that equality of all phenomena.

In this very life, he becomes dear and pleasing to the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones; he becomes dear and pleasing to all bodhisattvas, all śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas. Wherever he is reborn, in each of those places he never sees with his eyes forms that are unpleasant, nor does he hear with his ears sounds that are unpleasant, nor does he smell with his nose odors that are unpleasant.

He does not taste unpleasant tastes with the tongue; he does not touch unpleasant tactile objects with the body; he does not cognize unpleasant mental phenomena with the mind. In this way, Śāradvatīputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not fall away from unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Furthermore, while this exposition of the perfection of wisdom was being taught, three hundred monks covered the Blessed One with the robes they were wearing. [They did so] for the sake of unexcelled...

They generated the mind set upon perfect enlightenment. Then, at that moment, the Blessed One manifested a smile. Thereupon, the Venerable Ānanda rose from his seat, draped his upper robe over one shoulder, placed his right knee upon the ground, and bowing with palms joined toward the Blessed One, addressed him thus: "Blessed One, what is the cause, what is the condition for manifesting this smile?"

"Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones do not manifest a smile without cause or condition. When this was said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the Venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, these three hundred monks, in the sixty-first aeon, shall arise in the world as Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones named Mahāketu."

In the eon known as Tārakopama, when they have passed away from here, these very beings will be reborn in the buddha-field of the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Akṣobhya. And sixty thousand sons of the gods belonging to the realm of desire (kāmāvacara) will resolve their minds upon unexcelled perfect enlightenment; they will please the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Maitreya and will practice the holy life right there.

And that Tathāgata Maitreya will grant them the prophecy of their unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment. Then, through the power of the Buddha, at that moment those four assemblies, while remaining seated, beheld a thousand Buddhas in the eastern direction; they beheld a thousand Buddhas in the southern direction; they beheld a thousand Buddhas in the western direction; and they beheld a thousand Buddhas in the northern direction.

In the northeastern direction, they saw a thousand Buddhas; in the southeastern direction, they saw a thousand Buddhas; in the southwestern direction, they saw a thousand Buddhas; in the northwestern direction, they saw a thousand Buddhas; in the downward direction, they saw a thousand Buddhas; and in the upward direction, they saw a thousand Buddhas—and yet, they did not [perceive] those arrays of qualities of the Buddha-fields.

There, in this Sahā world-system, they beheld those arrays of qualities of the Buddha-fields belonging to those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, in those various world-systems. Then, ten thousand beings from that assembly made a vow: "We shall perform such actions that, by virtue of those performed deeds, we shall be reborn in these Buddha-fields. Thereupon, the Blessed One, knowing the intention of those sons of good family, manifested a smile.

Then the Venerable Ānanda rose from his seat, draped his upper robe over one shoulder, placed his right knee upon the ground, and bowing with palms joined toward the Blessed One, addressed the Blessed One as follows: "Blessed One, what is the cause, what is the condition for manifesting this smile? For Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, do not manifest a smile without a cause or a condition. The Blessed One said: "Ānanda, do you see these ten thousand living beings? He replied: "I see them, Blessed One."

"I see them, Blessed One. The Blessed One said: "Ānanda, these ten thousand beings, having passed away from here, will be reborn in those Buddha-fields. They shall never be separated from Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksambuddhas. After that, there will appear in the world Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksambuddhas named Vyūharāja."

Then the venerable Śāradvatīputra, the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, the venerable Subhūti, the venerable Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra, and the venerable Mahākāśyapa—these and many other well-known monks, as well as bodhisattvas mahāsattvas, and monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen, said this to the Blessed One: "This is a great perfection, O Blessed One, for bodhisattvas mahāsattvas, namely, the perfection of wisdom."

“O Bhagavān, this perfection of wisdom is the noble perfection of the bodhisattvas, the mahāsattvas; O Bhagavān, this perfection of wisdom is the foremost perfection of the bodhisattvas, the mahāsattvas; O Bhagavān, this perfection of wisdom is the distinguished perfection of the bodhisattvas, the mahāsattvas.”

That is to say, the perfection of wisdom. O Blessed One, this is the excellent perfection of the bodhisattvas, the mahāsattvas—namely, the perfection of wisdom. O Blessed One, this is the most eminent perfection of the bodhisattvas, the mahāsattvas—namely, the perfection of wisdom. O Blessed One, this is the sublime perfection of the bodhisattvas, the mahāsattvas—namely, the perfection of wisdom.

“O Blessed One, this perfection of wisdom is the unsurpassed perfection of the bodhisattvas, the mahāsattvas; O Blessed One, this perfection of wisdom is the peerless perfection of the bodhisattvas, the mahāsattvas; O Blessed One, this perfection of wisdom is the unequaled perfection of the bodhisattvas, the mahāsattvas; O Blessed One, this perfection of wisdom is the perfection of those equal to the unequaled of the bodhisattvas, the mahāsattvas.”

“O Bhagavān, this perfection of the bodhisattva mahāsattvas is peerless; that is to say, the perfection of wisdom. O Bhagavān, this perfection of the bodhisattva mahāsattvas is incomparable; that is to say, the perfection of wisdom. O Bhagavān, this perfection of the bodhisattva mahāsattvas is like space; that is to say, the perfection of wisdom. O Bhagavān, this perfection of the bodhisattva mahāsattvas is the perfection of the emptiness of intrinsic characteristics; that is to say, the perfection of wisdom.”

"Blessed One, this perfection of the emptiness of all phenomena is the perfection of wisdom of the bodhisattvas, the mahāsattvas. Blessed One, this perfection of the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence is the perfection of wisdom of the bodhisattvas, the mahāsattvas. Blessed One, this perfection of the fulfillment of all qualities is the perfection of wisdom of the bodhisattvas, the mahāsattvas."

“Blessed One, this perfection of wisdom is endowed with all virtues for the Bodhisattvas, the Mahāsattvas; that is to say, it is the perfection of wisdom. Blessed One, this perfection of wisdom is invincible for the Bodhisattvas, the Mahāsattvas; that is to say, it is the perfection of wisdom.
For herein, Blessed One, by the Bodhisattvas, the Mahāsattvas, who course in this perfection of wisdom...”

The incomparable gift has been given, is being given, and will be given; by that, the incomparable perfection of giving has been fulfilled, is being fulfilled, and will be fulfilled. By that, an incomparable physical form has been attained, is being attained, and will be attained. By that, they have become, are becoming, and will become possessors of the incomparable Dharma, namely, of unexcelled perfect enlightenment.

In this regard, Blessed One, by those bodhisattvas mahāsattvas who have practiced, are practicing, and will practice the perfection of wisdom, an unequaled morality has been observed, is being observed, and will be observed. By that, the unequaled perfection of morality has been fulfilled, is being fulfilled, and will be fulfilled. By that, an unequaled physical form has been attained, is being attained, and will be attained. By that, they have become, are becoming, and will become possessors of the unequaled Dharma, namely, unsurpassed perfect enlightenment.

In this regard, Blessed One, by bodhisattva mahāsattvas practicing in this perfection of wisdom, incomparable patience has been cultivated, is being cultivated, and will be cultivated. By that, the incomparable perfection of patience has been fulfilled, is being fulfilled, and will be fulfilled. By that, an incomparable attainment of selfhood has been obtained, is being obtained, and will be obtained. By that, they have become, are becoming, and will become possessors of the incomparable Dharma, namely, of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

In this regard, Blessed One, by those bodhisattvas mahāsattvas who have practiced, are practicing, or will practice in this perfection of wisdom, incomparable vigor has been initiated, is being initiated, and will be initiated. By that, the incomparable perfection of vigor has been fulfilled, is being fulfilled, and will be fulfilled. By that, an incomparable physical form has been attained, is being attained, and will be attained. By that, they have become, are becoming, and will become possessors of the incomparable Dharma; that is to say, of unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

In this regard, Blessed One, by Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas practicing in this perfection of wisdom, unequaled meditations have been produced, are being produced, and will be produced. By that, the unequaled perfection of meditation has been fulfilled, is being fulfilled, and will be fulfilled. By that, an unequaled physical form has been attained, is being attained, and will be attained. By that, they have become, are becoming, and will become possessors of the unequaled Dharma, namely, of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

In this regard, Blessed One, by Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas practicing in this perfection of wisdom, incomparable wisdom has been cultivated, is being cultivated, and will be cultivated. By that, the incomparable perfection of wisdom has been fulfilled, is being fulfilled, and will be fulfilled. By that, an incomparable physical form has been attained, is being attained, and will be attained. By that, they have become, are becoming, and will become possessors of the incomparable Dharma, namely, of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Right here, Blessed One, while practicing in this perfection of wisdom, he became a recipient of form that is unequaled and peerless; he became a recipient of feeling that is unequaled and peerless; he became a recipient of perception that is unequaled and peerless; he became a recipient of volitional formations that are unequaled and peerless; he became a recipient of consciousness that is unequaled and peerless. Having fully awakened to an enlightenment that is unequaled and peerless, he has set in motion the wheel of Dharma that is unequaled and peerless.

The Buddhas, the Blessed Ones of the past, while practicing in this very perfection of wisdom, became attainers of the unequaled form; they became attainers of the unequaled feeling; they became attainers of the unequaled perception; they became attainers of the unequaled volitional formations; they became attainers of the unequaled consciousness. Having fully awakened to the unequaled enlightenment, they set in motion the unequaled wheel of Dharma.

Future Buddhas, Blessed Ones, as they practice right here in this perfection of wisdom, will become attainers of incomparable form; they will become attainers of incomparable feeling; they will become attainers of incomparable perception; they will become attainers of incomparable formations; they will become attainers of incomparable consciousness. Having fully awakened to incomparable enlightenment, they will turn the incomparable wheel of Dharma.

The Buddhas, the Blessed Ones of the present, while coursing in this very perfection of wisdom, become attainers of incomparable form; they become attainers of incomparable feeling; they become attainers of incomparable perception; they become attainers of incomparable volitional formations; they become attainers of incomparable consciousness. Having fully awakened to incomparable enlightenment, they shall turn the incomparable wheel of Dharma.

Therefore, Blessed One, bodhisattva mahāsattvas who wish to reach the further shore of all dharmas should apply themselves to the perfection of wisdom. Those bodhisattva mahāsattvas who practice this perfection of wisdom, Blessed One, are worthy of homage by the world with its gods, humans, and asuras.

When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to those many great śrāvakas and those bodhisattva mahāsattvas: "So it is, noble sons, so it is, just as you say. Those bodhisattva mahāsattvas who course here in the perfection of wisdom are to be honored by the world with its gods, humans, and asuras."

For what reason? Because, sons of good family, it is by depending on the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva that the appearance of the world of humans occurs in the world; the appearance of the world of gods occurs in the world; the appearance of great kṣatriya clans occurs in the world; the appearance of great brāhmaṇa clans occurs in the world; and the appearance of great householder clans occurs in the world.

There is the arising of beings; there is the appearance in the world of universal monarchs (*cakravartin*); there is the appearance in the world of the gods of the Four Great Kings (*cāturmahārājakāyika*); there is the appearance in the world of the gods of the Thirty-three (*trāyastriṃśa*); there is the appearance in the world of the Yāma gods; there is the appearance in the world of the Tuṣita gods; and there is the appearance in the world of the gods who delight in emanations (*nirmāṇarati*).

There is an appearance in the world of the Paranirmitavaśavartin gods; there is an appearance in the world of the Brahmakāyika gods; there is an appearance in the world of the Brahmapurohita gods; there is an appearance in the world of the Brahmapārṣadya gods; there is an appearance in the world of the Mahābrahman gods; and there is an appearance in the world of the Ābhā gods.

The appearance of the Parīttābha (Limited Light) gods occurs in their world; the appearance of the Apramāṇābha (Immeasurable Light) gods occurs in their world; the appearance of the Ābhāsvara (Radiant) gods occurs in their world; the appearance of the Śubha (Pure) gods occurs in their world; the appearance of the Parīttaśubha (Limited Purity) gods occurs in their world; the appearance of the Apramāṇaśubha (Immeasurable Purity) gods occurs in their world; and the appearance of the Śubhakṛtsna (Universal Purity) gods occurs in their world.

There is an appearance in the world of the Bṛhat devas; there is an appearance in the world of the Parīttabṛhat devas; there is an appearance in the world of the Apramāṇabṛhat devas; there is an appearance in the world of the Bṛhatphala devas; there is an appearance in the world of the Avṛha devas; there is an appearance in the world of the Atapa devas; there is an appearance in the world of the Sudṛśa devas.

The appearance of the Sudarśana gods occurs in the world; the appearance of the Akaniṣṭha gods occurs in the world; the appearance of stream-enterers occurs in the world; the appearance of once-returners occurs in the world.

The appearance of non-returners occurs in the world; the appearance of arhats occurs in the world; the appearance of pratyekabuddhas occurs in the world; the appearance of bodhisattva mahāsattvas occurs in the world; and the appearance of Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas occurs in the world.

For it is by depending on the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, O sons of good family, that there appears in the world the manifestation of food, drink, vehicles, clothing, beds, seats, shelters, and livelihoods; as well as gems, pearls, conchs, crystals, corals, silver, and gold. Furthermore, O sons of good family, whatever sources of happiness for sentient beings there may be—whether divine or human, and even the bliss of liberation—all that, O sons of good family, comes about by depending on the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva.

For what reason? O sons of good family, it is because a bodhisattva, while practicing the conduct of a bodhisattva, abides in the six perfections; he himself gives gifts and encourages others to give gifts; he himself guards morality and encourages others in morality; he himself cultivates patience and encourages others in patience; and he himself exerts vigor and encourages others in vigor.

He himself generates the meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*) and enjoins others to the meditative concentrations; he himself cultivates wisdom (*prajñā*) and enjoins others to the cultivation of wisdom. It is by relying upon the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva that sentient beings practice the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*). While practicing these six perfections, those sentient beings attain both mundane and supramundane prosperities.
Therefore, noble sons, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva is one who has set out for the welfare and happiness of all sentient beings.
Then, at that time, the Blessed One extended his tongue-faculty from his mouth and pervaded this great trichiliocosm.
Then, indeed, from that tongue-faculty, rays of light of many colors and various hues issued forth.

Having emitted it, they pervaded world-systems in the eastern direction, as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges, with a great radiance; they pervaded world-systems in the southern direction, as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges, with a great radiance; they pervaded world-systems in the western direction, as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges, with a great radiance; and they pervaded world-systems in the northern direction, as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges, with a great radiance.

Those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, replied:

Then those bodhisattva mahāsattvas said this to those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones: "In that regard, O Blessed One, we shall go to see, pay homage to, and attend upon the Blessed One Śākyamuni, the Tathāgata, Arhat, and Samyaksaṃbuddha; and to see those bodhisattva mahāsattvas gathered from the ten directions; and to hear this perfection of wisdom."

Those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, spoke thus: "Noble sons, do now whatever you deem to be the right time. Then those Bodhisattvas, Mahāsattvas, having bowed their heads at the feet of those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksambuddhas from the ten directions, and having circumambulated them seven times, took up various kinds of parasols, banners, and flags; flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, ointments, powders, and robes; and gold and silver flowers, and with great [reverence]...

Accompanied by the music of cymbals, drums, and various instruments, they approached the Blessed One, Śākyamuni, the Tathāgata, Arhat, and Samyaksaṃbuddha. Then the gods of the Four Great Kings, the Trāyastriṃśas, the Yāmas, the Tuṣitas, the Nirmāṇaratis, the Paranirmitavaśavartins, the Brahmakāyikas, the Brahmapurohitas, the Brahmapārṣadyas, the Mahābrahmaṇas, the Ābhās, the Parīttābhas, the Apramāṇābhas, the Ābhāsvaras, the Śubhas, the Parīttaśubhas, and the Apramāṇaśubhas [all arrived].

The Śubhakṛtsna, Vṛha, Parīttavṛha, Apramāṇavṛha, and Bṛhatphala deities; and the Śuddhāvāsa deities—the Avṛha, Atapa, Sudṛśa, Sudarśana, and Akaniṣṭha—taking divine flowers, garlands, ointments, incense, and powders, as well as divine blue lotuses, red lotuses, white lotuses, and divine Māndārava, Mahāmāndārava, Keśara, and Tamālapattra blossoms, approached the place where the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, Arhat, and Samyaksaṃbuddha Śākyamuni was staying.

Then those bodhisattva mahāsattvas and those gods scattered, strewed, and showered down upon the Blessed One Śākyamuni, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, flowers, garlands, perfumes, ointments, powders, robes, parasols, banners, and flags. Then those flowers and other offerings, having risen into the air above, remained in this great trichiliocosm world-system in the form of a mass of flowers.

It was square, with four pillars, well-proportioned in its divisions, delightful, and pleasing to the mind. Then, from that assembly, hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of living beings rose from their seats, bowed with palms joined toward the Blessed One, and said this to the Blessed One: "O Blessed One, may we also in a future time become recipients of such qualities as those of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksambuddha."

"In this very way, the Saṅgha of Śrāvakas is my retinue; and in this way we teach the Dharma in the assembly, just as the Tathāgata teaches the Dharma at present. Then the Blessed One, knowing their resolute intention, and knowing their patience regarding the non-arising, non-ceasing, non-conditioning, and non-manifestation of all phenomena, manifested a smile.

Then the Venerable Ānanda rose from his seat, draped his upper robe over one shoulder, placed his right knee upon the ground, and bowing with palms joined toward the Blessed One, addressed the Blessed One as follows: "What, O Blessed One, is the cause, what is the condition for manifesting a smile? For Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, do not manifest a smile without cause or without condition. The Blessed One said:

"Ānanda, from this assembly, hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of living beings have attained the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). And these, in the future..."
"In sixty-eight *koṭis* of eons, there will appear in the world Tathāgatas, Arhats, perfectly enlightened Buddhas named Bodhyaṅgapuṣpa during the Puṣpākara eon.
Thus ends the first chapter of the *Śatasāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā*.
Now begins the second chapter.

Then the Blessed One addressed the venerable Subhūti: "May it be inspired in you, Subhūti, to deliver a discourse on the Dharma concerning the perfection of wisdom of the bodhisattvas, the mahāsattvas—how bodhisattvas, the mahāsattvas, shall set forth in the perfection of wisdom."

Then, this thought occurred to those bodhisattva mahāsattvas, those great śrāvakas, and those sons of the gods: "How is it that the venerable Subhūti, by means of what empowerment of the power of wisdom and eloquence, will teach the perfection of wisdom to the bodhisattva mahāsattvas? Or is it rather through the majestic power of the Buddha?"

Then, through the power of the Buddha, the venerable Subhūti, knowing with his own mind the thoughts in the minds of those bodhisattva mahāsattvas, those great śrāvakas, and those sons of the gods, addressed the venerable Śāradvatīputra: "Venerable Śāradvatīputra, whatever the disciples of the Blessed One speak, utter, or proclaim—all that is the personal effort (*puruṣakāra*) of the Tathāgata."

And whatever Dharma has been taught by the Tathāgata, all of it is not in contradiction with the nature of phenomena (dharmatā). Therefore, those sons of good family, training in that teaching of the Dharma, directly realize that very nature of phenomena.

"Śāradvatīputra, it is the Tathāgata himself who, through the application of skillful means, will teach the perfection of wisdom to the bodhisattva mahāsattvas. In this matter, venerable Śāradvatīputra, it is not within the domain of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas to teach the perfection of wisdom to the bodhisattva mahāsattvas. Then the venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One: "Bodhisattvas..."

“O Blessed One, it is said ‘Great Beings. Of which dharma is this a designation—namely, ‘bodhisattva’ or ‘perfection of wisdom’? O Blessed One, I do not perceive that dharma, namely, ‘bodhisattva’ or ‘perfection of wisdom’.”

"Therefore, Blessed One, since I do not perceive that Bodhisattva, nor that Perfection of Wisdom, nor that name 'Bodhisattva,' which Bodhisattva shall I instruct and admonish in which Perfection of Wisdom? When this was said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the Venerable Subhūti: "Subhūti, these are mere names: namely, the Perfection of Wisdom, the Bodhisattva, and the name 'Bodhisattva'."

And that name is not apprehended internally, nor externally, nor in between the two. Subhūti, it is just as, for example, the name "sentient being, sentient being" is a mere designation; and whatever is a designated phenomenon has neither arising nor cessation, except that it is conventionally expressed by means of mere names and symbols. And that name is not apprehended internally, nor externally, nor in between the two.

Subhūti, it is just as, for example, with the name "living being," "living being": that name is a mere designation. And whatever is a designated phenomenon has neither arising nor cessation, except that it is conventionally expressed by means of mere names and symbols. Furthermore, that name is not found internally, nor externally, nor in between the two.

Subhūti, it is just as if there were a being, a being—by name; yet that is merely a designation, a phenomenon of designation. It has neither arising nor cessation, except that it is conventionally expressed by means of mere names and conventions. And that name is not found internally, nor externally, nor in between the two.

Subhūti, it is just as if there were a person named "Person"—that name is merely a designation, and that which is a designated phenomenon has neither arising nor cessation, except that it is conventionally expressed by means of mere conceptualization and linguistic convention. Furthermore, that name is not found internally, nor externally, nor in between the two. Subhūti, it is just as if there were a man named "Man"—that name is merely a designation.

And whatever is a designated phenomenon (*prajñaptidharma*), it has neither arising nor cessation; it is merely expressed by way of a name and convention. And whatever is a designated phenomenon, it has neither arising nor cessation; it is merely expressed by way of a name and convention.

And that name is not apprehended internally, nor externally, nor in between the two. Subhūti, it is just as with the name "human being," "human being": that name is merely a designation. And whatever is a designated phenomenon has neither arising nor cessation, except that it is conventionally expressed by means of mere conceptualization and linguistic convention. And that name is not apprehended internally, nor externally, nor in between the two.

Subhūti, it is just as, for example, with the name "young man," young man"—that name is merely a designation, and that which is a designated phenomenon has neither arising nor cessation, except that it is conventionally expressed by means of mere names and conventions. Furthermore, that name is not apprehended internally, nor externally, nor in between the two. Subhūti, it is just as, for example, with the name "agent," agent.

That which is called "name" is merely a designation; and as for that designated phenomenon, it has neither arising nor cessation, except that it is conventionally expressed by means of mere conceptualization and linguistic agreement. Subhūti, it is just as if there were someone called "the maker" or "the one who causes to make. That name is merely a designation, and whatever is a designated phenomenon has neither arising nor cessation; it is only by way of mere conceptualization and convention that it is expressed in common usage. Furthermore, that name is not found internally, nor externally, nor in between the two.

Subhūti, it is just as if there were something called "the arouser," the so-called "arouser. That name is a mere designation, and as for that which is a designated phenomenon, it has neither arising nor cessation; it is merely expressed by way of conventional terminology and mental labeling. Furthermore, that name is not found internally, nor externally, nor in between the two. Subhūti, it is just like the term "the arouser."

That which is called "name" is merely a designation, and that which is a designated phenomenon has neither arising nor cessation; it is only by way of mere conceptualization and convention that it is expressed in common usage. And that which is a designated phenomenon (prajñaptidharma) has neither arising nor cessation; it is merely expressed through the medium of names and conventions. Furthermore, that name is not found internally, nor externally, nor in between the two. Subhūti, it is just as with the name "seer," "seer"—that name is a mere designation. And that name is not apprehended internally, nor externally, nor in between the two. In the very same way, Subhūti, whatever is the perfection of wisdom, whatever is the bodhisattva, and whatever is the name "bodhisattva"—all this is merely a designation. And as for that which is a designated phenomenon (*prajñaptidharma*), it has neither arising nor cessation; it is only by means of mere conceptualization and convention (*saṃjñāsaṅketa*) that it is expressed in common usage. And that name is not apprehended internally, nor externally, nor in between the two.

Subhūti, it is just as if this internal personal existence called "form," and so on up to [the other aggregates], were merely a designation of phenomena (dharmaprajñaptimātra); and of that designation of phenomena there is neither arising nor ceasing, except as a mere matter of conventional terminology and linguistic convention.

It is conventionally designated; yet that is perceived neither internally, nor externally, nor in between the two. Subhūti, it is just as with this so-called "internal feeling"—up to and including all such things—it is merely a designation of phenomena (*dharmaprajñaptimātra*). And of that designation of phenomena, there is neither arising nor cessation, except that it is conventionally expressed by means of mere names and conventions. That name is perceived neither internally, nor externally, nor in between the two.

Subhūti, it is just as with that which is called "internal perception": it is merely a designation for phenomena (*dharmaprajñaptimātra*). Of that designation for phenomena, there is neither arising nor cessation; it is only by means of mere conceptual designation and linguistic convention (*saṃjñāsaṅketamātra*) that it is expressed. And that name is not found internally, nor externally, nor in between the two.

Subhūti, it is just as with these so-called "internal formations"—to whatever extent they exist, they are merely a designation of phenomena (*dharmaprajñaptimātra*). Of that designation of phenomena, there is neither arising nor cessation, except that it is conventionally expressed by means of mere names and symbols.
