Furthermore, that name is not apprehended internally, nor externally, nor in between the two. Subhūti, "taste" is likewise merely a designation of phenomena; and for this designation of phenomena, there is neither arising nor cessation; it is merely expressed by way of a name and convention, namely, "taste."

And that name is not apprehended internally, nor externally, nor in between the two. Subhūti, "contact" is merely a designation for phenomena; and of that designation for phenomena there is neither arising nor cessation, except that it is conventionally expressed by means of mere names and conventions, namely, "contact. And that name is not apprehended internally, nor externally, nor in between the two.

"Subhūti, that which is called 'Dharma' is merely a designation for a dharma; and of that designation for a dharma, there is neither arising nor cessation, except that it is conventionally expressed by means of mere names and signs—namely, 'Dharma. And that name is not apprehended internally, nor externally, nor in between the two."

"Subhūti, that which is called the 'eye-element' (cakṣurdhātu) is merely a designation for phenomena (dharmaprajñaptimātra). And of that designation for phenomena, there is neither arising nor cessation; it is only by way of mere conceptualization and convention that it is expressed, namely, as the 'eye-element. Furthermore, that name is not apprehended internally, nor externally, nor in between the two."

"Subhūti, what is called the 'form realm' (rūpadhātu) is merely a designation for phenomena (dharmaprajñaptimātra). And of that designation for phenomena, there is neither arising nor cessation; it is only by way of mere conceptualization and convention that it is expressed as 'the form realm. Furthermore, that name is not found internally, nor externally, nor in between the two."

"Subhūti, the so-called 'eye-consciousness element' is merely a designation for phenomena; and of that designation for phenomena, there is neither arising nor cessation, except that it is conventionally expressed by means of mere names and signs, namely, 'the eye-consciousness element. And that name is not apprehended internally, nor externally, nor in between the two. Subhūti, the so-called 'ear-element'... [and so on].

In this way, this is merely a designation of phenomena (*dharmaprajñaptimātra*). Of that designation of phenomena, there is neither arising nor cessation; it is only by means of mere conceptualization and convention (*saṃjñāsaṅketamātra*) that it is expressed as "the ear-element" (*śrotradhātu*). And that name is not apprehended internally, nor externally, nor in between the two.

Subhūti, the so-called "sound-element" is merely a designation for a phenomenon; and of that designation for a phenomenon, there is neither arising nor ceasing, except that it is conventionally expressed by means of mere names and symbols, namely, "the sound-element. Furthermore, that name is not apprehended internally, nor externally, nor in between the two.

"Subhūti, the auditory consciousness element is merely a designation of phenomena; it neither arises nor ceases, except that it is conventionally expressed by means of a mere name and sign, namely, 'the auditory consciousness element. And that name is not apprehended internally, nor externally, nor in between the two."

"Subhūti, that which is called the 'olfactory element' (ghrāṇadhātu) is merely a designation for phenomena (dharmaprajñaptimātra). And of that designation for phenomena, there is neither arising nor cessation; it is only by way of mere conceptualization and convention that it is expressed as 'the olfactory element. Furthermore, that name is not apprehended internally, nor externally, nor in between the two."

"Subhūti, that which is called the 'odor-element' is merely a designation for a phenomenon; and of that designation for a phenomenon there is neither arising nor cessation, except that it is conventionally expressed by means of mere names and symbols, namely, 'odor-element. And that name is not apprehended internally, nor externally, nor in between the two."

"O Subhūti, that which is called the 'olfactory consciousness element' is merely a designation for phenomena; and of that designation for phenomena there is neither arising nor cessation, except that it is conventionally expressed by means of mere names and symbols, namely, 'olfactory consciousness element. And that name is not apprehended internally, nor externally, nor in between the two."

Subhūti, that which is called the "tongue-element" is merely a designation for phenomena; and of that designation for phenomena there is neither arising nor cessation, except that it is conventionally expressed by means of mere names and conventions, namely, "the tongue-element. And that name—

It is not found internally, nor externally, nor in between the two. This so-called "taste-element" (rasa-dhātu) is a mere designation; and for this designation of phenomena (dharma-prajñapti), there is neither arising nor ceasing, except that it is conventionally expressed by means of mere names and symbols as "the taste-element. Furthermore, that name is not found internally, nor externally, nor in between the two.

"Subhūti, that which is called the tongue-consciousness element is merely a designation for phenomena; and of that designation for phenomena there is neither arising nor ceasing, except that it is conventionally expressed by means of mere names and conventions, namely, 'the tongue-consciousness element. And that name is not apprehended internally, nor externally, nor in between the two."

"Subhūti, that which is called the 'body-element' (kāyadhātu) is merely a designation for phenomena; and of that designation for phenomena, there is neither arising nor ceasing, except that it is conventionally expressed by means of mere names and symbols, namely, 'the body-element. Furthermore, that name is not apprehended internally, nor externally, nor in between the two."

"Subhūti, that which is called the 'tangible element' (spraṣṭavyadhātu) is merely a designation of phenomena (dharmaprajñaptimātra). And of that designation of phenomena, there is neither arising nor ceasing; it is only by way of mere conceptualization and convention that it is expressed as 'the tangible element. Furthermore, that name is not found internally, nor externally, nor in between the two."

"Subhūti, that which is called the 'body-consciousness element' is merely a designation for a dharma; and of that designation for a dharma there is neither arising nor cessation, except that it is conventionally expressed by means of mere names and signs, namely, 'the body-consciousness element. And that name is not apprehended internally, nor externally, nor in between the two."

"Subhūti, the mind-element (*manodhātu*) is merely a designation of phenomena (*dharmaprajñaptimātra*); and of that designation of phenomena there is neither arising nor cessation, except that it is conventionally expressed by means of mere names and conventions, namely, 'the mind-element. And that name is not found internally, nor externally, nor in between the two. Subhūti, the phenomenon-element (*dharmadhātu*) is merely a designation of phenomena; and of that designation of phenomena there is neither arising nor cessation, except that it is [conventionally expressed] by means of mere names and conventions."

It is conventionally designated as "the realm of phenomena" (*dharmadhātu*). Yet that name is not apprehended internally, nor externally, nor in between the two. Subhūti, the so-called "realm of mental consciousness" (*manovijñānadhātu*) is merely a designation for phenomena; and of that designation for phenomena, there is neither arising nor cessation, except that it is conventionally expressed by means of mere conceptualization and linguistic convention—that is to say, as "the realm of mental consciousness."

And that name is not apprehended internally, nor externally, nor in between the two. In the very same way, Subhūti, that which is called "perfection of wisdom," "bodhisattva," or "the name of a bodhisattva"—all this is merely a designation of phenomena (*dharmaprajñaptimātra*). There is neither arising nor ceasing for that designation of phenomena, other than its being conventionally expressed through mere names and symbols as "perfection of wisdom," "bodhisattva," or "the name of a bodhisattva."

And that name is not apprehended internally, nor externally, nor in between the two. Subhūti, it is just as, for example, the internal personal body is designated by the mere name "person"; it is designated by the name "head-bones," it is designated by the name "neck-bones," it is designated by the name "shoulder-bones," it is designated as "back-bones," it is designated as "rib-bones," and it is designated by the name "hip-bones."

It is designated by the name "thigh bones"; it is designated by the name "shank bones"; it is designated by the name "foot bones. This is merely a conventional designation of phenomena (*dharmaprajñaptimātra*); and of that conventional designation of phenomena, there is neither arising nor cessation, except that it is designated by mere names and conventions. It is designated by the name "head bones," and it is designated by the name "neck bones."

There are what are called the bones of the arms, what are called the bones of the back, what are called the bones of the sides, what are called the bones of the hips, what are called the bones of the thighs, and what are called the bones of the shanks; yet that name is not found internally, nor externally, nor in between the two.

In the same way, Subhūti, that which is called "perfection of wisdom," "bodhisattva," or "the name of a bodhisattva"—all this is merely a designation of phenomena (*dharmaprajñaptimātra*). And of that designation of phenomena, there is neither arising nor cessation, except that it is conventionally expressed by means of mere names and conventions. Furthermore, that name is not apprehended internally, nor externally, nor in between the two.

Subhūti, it is just as if these external things—grass, wood, branches, leaves, and foliage—all of which are designated by various names: there is neither arising nor ceasing for them, except that they are conventionally expressed merely by means of names and designations. And those names are not found internally, nor externally, nor in between the two.

In the same way, Subhūti, that which is called "perfection of wisdom," "bodhisattva," or "the name of a bodhisattva"—all this is merely a designation of phenomena (*dharmaprajñaptimātra*). And of that designation of phenomena there is neither arising nor ceasing, except that it is conventionally expressed by means of mere names and symbols. Furthermore, that name is not found internally, nor externally, nor in between the two.
Subhūti, it is just as, for example, only the mere name of the past Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, remains; and that name is not apprehended internally, nor externally, nor in between the two.

Subhūti, it is just as, for example, a dream, an echo, an optical illusion, a magical creation, a mirage, the moon in water, or a phantom created by a Tathāgata—all these phenomena are mere designations. And regarding that designation of phenomena, there is neither arising nor ceasing, except that they are conventionally expressed by means of mere names and symbols. Furthermore, that name is not found internally, nor externally, nor in between the two. In the very same way, Subhūti, all these things—what is called "perfection of wisdom," what is called a "bodhisattva," and what is called the "name of a bodhisattva"—are likewise [mere designations].

All phenomena are mere designations; and as for that designation of phenomena, there is neither arising nor cessation, except that they are conventionally expressed by means of mere names and symbols. Furthermore, that name is not found internally, nor externally, nor in between the two. In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom should train in the designation of names and symbols, and in the designation of phenomena.

In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in the perfection of wisdom does not perceive form as permanent; he does not perceive form as impermanent; he does not perceive form as pleasant; he does not perceive form as painful; he does not perceive form as self; he does not perceive form as non-self; he does not perceive form as peaceful.

He does not perceive form as being non-peaceful; he does not perceive form as being empty; he does not perceive form as being non-empty; he does not perceive form as having signs; he does not perceive form as being signless; he does not perceive form as being with aspiration; he does not perceive form as being without aspiration; he does not perceive form as being conditioned.

One does not perceive that form is unconditioned; one does not perceive that form is affliction; one does not perceive that form is non-affliction; one does not perceive that form is purification; one does not perceive that form is arising; one does not perceive that form is cessation; one does not perceive that form is secluded; one does not perceive that form is non-secluded.

He does not perceive form as being wholesome; he does not perceive form as being unwholesome. He does not perceive form as being blameworthy; he does not perceive form as being blameless. He does not perceive form as being with-outflows; he does not perceive form as being without-outflows. He does not perceive form as being defiled; he does not perceive form as being undefiled. He does not perceive form as being mundane.
One does not perceive that what is called "form" is supramundane; one does not perceive that what is called "form" is saṃsāra; one does not perceive that what is called "form" is nirvāṇa.

One does not perceive feeling as permanent; one does not perceive feeling as impermanent. One does not perceive feeling as pleasant; one does not perceive feeling as painful. One does not perceive feeling as self; one does not perceive feeling as non-self. One does not perceive feeling as peaceful; one does not perceive feeling as unpeaceful.

He does not perceive feeling as being empty; he does not perceive feeling as being non-empty. He does not perceive feeling as having signs; he does not perceive feeling as being signless. He does not perceive feeling as being with aspiration; he does not perceive feeling as being without aspiration. He does not perceive feeling as being conditioned; he does not perceive feeling as being unconditioned.
He does not perceive feeling as defilement; he does not perceive feeling as purification; he does not perceive feeling as arising.

He does not perceive feeling as "cessation. He does not perceive feeling as "secluded. He does not perceive feeling as "not secluded. He does not perceive feeling as "wholesome. He does not perceive feeling as "unwholesome. He does not perceive feeling as "blameworthy. He does not perceive feeling as "blameless. He does not perceive feeling as "with outflows."

He does not perceive feeling as being with outflows; he does not perceive feeling as being defiled; he does not perceive feeling as being free from defilement. He does not perceive feeling as being mundane; he does not perceive feeling as being supramundane. He does not perceive feeling as being saṃsāra; he does not perceive feeling as being nirvāṇa.

One does not perceive perception as permanent; one does not perceive perception as impermanent. One does not perceive perception as pleasant; one does not perceive perception as painful. One does not perceive perception as self; one does not perceive perception as non-self. One does not perceive perception as peaceful; one does not perceive perception as unpeaceful.

He does not perceive the name "perception" as empty; he does not perceive the name "perception" as non-empty. He does not perceive the name "perception" as having signs; he does not perceive the name "perception" as signless. He does not perceive the name "perception" as having a wish; he does not perceive the name "perception" as wishless. He does not perceive the name "perception" as conditioned.
He does not perceive perception as being unconditioned; he does not perceive perception as arising; he does not perceive perception as ceasing.

Thus he correctly observes: he does not observe that perception or name is affliction; he does not observe that perception or name is purification; he does not observe that perception or name is secluded; he does not observe that perception or name is unsecluded; he does not observe that perception or name is wholesome; he does not observe that perception or name is unwholesome; he does not observe that perception or name is faulty.

He does not perceive perception as blameless; he does not perceive perception as tainted; he does not perceive perception as untainted. He does not perceive perception as affliction; he does not perceive perception as free from affliction. He does not perceive perception as mundane; he does not perceive perception as supramundane. He does not perceive perception as saṃsāra; he does not perceive perception as nirvāṇa.

He does not perceive that formations are permanent; he does not perceive that formations are impermanent. He does not perceive that formations are pleasant; he does not perceive that formations are painful. He does not perceive that formations are self; he does not perceive that formations are non-self. He does not perceive that formations are peaceful; he does not perceive that formations are unpeaceful.

He does not perceive that so-called formations are empty; he does not perceive that so-called formations are non-empty. He does not perceive that so-called formations have signs; he does not perceive that so-called formations are signless. He does not perceive that so-called formations are with aspiration; he does not perceive that so-called formations are without aspiration. He does not perceive that so-called formations are conditioned; he does not perceive that so-called formations are unconditioned.

He does not perceive that what are called "formations" are subject to arising; he does not perceive that what are called "formations" are subject to cessation; he does not perceive that what are called "formations" are defilements; he does not perceive that what are called "formations" are purifications; he does not perceive that what are called "formations" are secluded; he does not perceive that what are called "formations" are not secluded; he does not perceive that what are called "formations" are wholesome.

He does not perceive that formations are unwholesome; he does not perceive that formations are blameworthy; he does not perceive that formations are blameless; he does not perceive that formations are with outflows; he does not perceive that formations are without outflows; he does not perceive that formations are afflictions; he does not perceive that formations are free from afflictions.

He does not perceive that so-called formations are mundane; he does not perceive that so-called formations are supramundane; he does not perceive that so-called formations are saṃsāra; he does not perceive that so-called formations are nirvāṇa.

One does not perceive consciousness as permanent; one does not perceive consciousness as impermanent. One does not perceive consciousness as pleasant; one does not perceive consciousness as painful. One does not perceive consciousness as self; one does not perceive consciousness as non-self. One does not perceive consciousness as peaceful; one does not perceive consciousness as unpeaceful.

He does not perceive that what is called "consciousness" is empty; he does not perceive that what is called "consciousness" is non-empty. He does not perceive that what is called "consciousness" has signs; he does not perceive that what is called "consciousness" is signless. He does not perceive that what is called "consciousness" is conditioned; he does not...

He correctly perceives that consciousness is called "wishless. He does not perceive that consciousness is called "conditioned. He does not perceive that consciousness is called "unconditioned. He does not perceive that consciousness is called "arising. He does not perceive that consciousness is called "cessation. He does not perceive that consciousness is called "defilement. He does not perceive that consciousness is called "purification."

He does not perceive that which is called "consciousness" as secluded; he does not perceive that which is called "consciousness" as non-secluded. He does not perceive that which is called "consciousness" as wholesome; he does not perceive that which is called "consciousness" as unwholesome. He does not perceive that which is called "consciousness" as faulty; he does not perceive that which is called "consciousness" as faultless. He does not perceive that which is called "consciousness" as with-outflows.

He does not perceive consciousness as being untainted; he does not perceive consciousness as being affliction; he does not perceive consciousness as being free from affliction; he does not perceive consciousness as being mundane; he does not perceive consciousness as being supramundane; he does not perceive consciousness as being saṃsāra; he does not perceive consciousness as being nirvāṇa.

One does not perceive the eye as permanent; one does not perceive the eye as impermanent. One does not perceive the eye as pleasant; one does not perceive the eye as painful. One does not perceive the eye as self; one does not perceive the eye as non-self. One does not perceive the eye as peaceful; one does not perceive the eye as unpeaceful.
He does not perceive that what is called "the eye" is empty, nor does he perceive that what is called "the eye" is non-empty.

He does not perceive that which is called "eye" as having signs; he does not perceive that which is called "eye" as being signless. He does not perceive that which is called "eye" as being with aspiration; he does not perceive that which is called "eye" as being without aspiration. He does not perceive that which is called "eye" as conditioned; he does not perceive that which is called "eye" as unconditioned. He does not perceive that which is called "eye" as arising; he does not perceive that which is called "eye" as ceasing.

He does not perceive the eye as defilement; he does not perceive the eye as purification; he does not perceive the eye as secluded; he does not perceive the eye as non-secluded; he does not perceive the eye as wholesome; he does not perceive the eye as unwholesome; he does not perceive the eye as faulty.

He does not perceive the eye as being faultless; he does not perceive the eye as being with outflows (*sāśrava*); he does not perceive the eye as being without outflows (*anāśrava*). He does not perceive the eye as being affliction (*saṃkleśa*); he does not perceive the eye as being free from affliction (*niḥkleśa*). He does not perceive the eye as being mundane (*laukika*); he does not perceive the eye as being supramundane (*lokottara*).
He does not perceive the eye as being *saṃsāra*; he does not perceive the eye as being *nirvāṇa*.

One does not perceive form as permanent; one does not perceive form as impermanent. One does not perceive form as pleasant; one does not perceive form as painful. One does not perceive form as self; one does not perceive form as non-self. One does not perceive form as peaceful; one does not perceive form as unpeaceful.
He does not perceive that form is empty; he does not perceive that form is non-empty; he does not perceive that form has signs; nor does he perceive form...

He correctly perceives that form is not name; he correctly perceives that form is not designated as "wished for"; he correctly perceives that form is not designated as "not wished for"; he correctly perceives that form is not conditioned; he correctly perceives that form is not unconditioned; he correctly perceives that form is not arising; he correctly perceives that form is not cessation; he correctly perceives that form is not defilement.

He does not perceive form as purification; he does not perceive form as secluded; he does not perceive form as non-secluded; he does not perceive form as wholesome; he does not perceive form as unwholesome; he does not perceive form as faulty; he does not perceive form as faultless; he does not perceive form as with outflows.

He does not perceive form as being untainted; he does not perceive form as being defilement; he does not perceive form as being free from defilement; he does not perceive form as being mundane; nor does he perceive form as being supramundane; he does not perceive form as being saṃsāra; nor does he perceive form as being nirvāṇa.

One does not perceive eye-consciousness as permanent; one does not perceive eye-consciousness as impermanent. One does not perceive eye-consciousness as pleasant; one does not perceive eye-consciousness as painful. One does not perceive eye-consciousness as self; one does not perceive eye-consciousness as non-self. One does not perceive eye-consciousness as peaceful.

One does not perceive that what is called eye-consciousness is non-peaceful; one does not perceive that what is called eye-consciousness is empty; one does not perceive that what is called eye-consciousness is non-empty.

Thus he observes: he observes that what is called "eye-consciousness" is not a sign; he observes that what is called "eye-consciousness" is not signless; he observes that what is called "eye-consciousness" is not something with a wish; he observes that what is called "eye-consciousness" is not wishless; he observes that what is called "eye-consciousness" is not conditioned; he observes that what is called "eye-consciousness" is not unconditioned.

He does not perceive eye-consciousness as defilement; he does not perceive eye-consciousness as purification; he does not perceive eye-consciousness as arising; he does not perceive eye-consciousness as ceasing; he does not perceive eye-consciousness as secluded; he does not perceive eye-consciousness as non-secluded.

He does not perceive eye-consciousness as being wholesome; he does not perceive eye-consciousness as being unwholesome; he does not perceive eye-consciousness as being blameworthy; he does not perceive eye-consciousness as being blameless; he does not perceive eye-consciousness as being with outflows; he does not perceive eye-consciousness as being without outflows.

One does not perceive eye-consciousness as being defilement; one does not perceive eye-consciousness as being free from defilement. One does not perceive eye-consciousness as being mundane; one does not perceive eye-consciousness as being supramundane. One does not perceive eye-consciousness as being saṃsāra; one does not perceive eye-consciousness as being nirvāṇa.

One does not perceive that what is called eye-contact is permanent; one does not perceive that what is called eye-contact is impermanent; one does not perceive that what is called eye-contact is pleasant; one does not perceive that what is called eye-contact is painful. Not...

One does not perceive that what is called eye-contact is the self; one does not perceive that what is called eye-contact is not the self. One does not perceive that what is called eye-contact is peaceful; one does not perceive that what is called eye-contact is not peaceful. One does not perceive that what is called eye-contact is empty; one does not perceive that what is called eye-contact is not empty. One does not perceive that what is called eye-contact is a sign.

He does not perceive that what is called "eye-contact" is signless; he does not perceive that what is called "eye-contact" is with aspiration; he does not perceive that what is called "eye-contact" is without aspiration; he does not perceive that what is called "eye-contact" is conditioned; he does not perceive that what is called "eye-contact" is unconditioned; he does not perceive that what is called "eye-contact" is defilement.

He does not perceive that what is called eye-contact is purification; he does not perceive that what is called eye-contact is arising; he does not perceive that what is called eye-contact is cessation; he does not perceive that what is called eye-contact is secluded; he does not perceive that what is called eye-contact is not secluded; he does not perceive that what is called eye-contact is wholesome.

He does not perceive that what is called eye-contact is unwholesome; he does not perceive that what is called eye-contact is blameworthy; he does not perceive that what is called eye-contact is blameless; he does not perceive that what is called eye-contact is with outflows; he does not perceive that what is called eye-contact is without outflows; he does not perceive that what is called eye-contact is defilement.

He does not perceive that what is called eye-contact is "without affliction"; he does not perceive that what is called eye-contact is "worldly"; he does not perceive that what is called eye-contact is "supramundane"; he does not perceive that what is called eye-contact is "saṃsāra"; he does not perceive that what is called eye-contact is "nirvāṇa."

Furthermore, whatever feeling—whether pleasant or painful—that arises conditioned by eye-consciousness-contact, he regards it as neither permanent nor impermanent; he regards it as neither pleasant nor painful; he regards it as neither self nor non-self; he regards it as neither peaceful nor unpeaceful.

He does not perceive it as empty; he does not perceive it as non-empty. He does not perceive it as having signs; he does not perceive it as signless. He does not perceive it as having a wish; he does not perceive it as wishless. He does not perceive it as conditioned; he does not perceive it as unconditioned. He does not perceive it as defilement; he does not perceive it as purification. He does not perceive it as arising.

He does not perceive it as cessation; he does not perceive it as secluded; he does not perceive it as non-secluded; he does not perceive it as wholesome; he does not perceive it as unwholesome; he does not perceive it as faulty; he does not perceive it as faultless; he does not perceive it as with outflows; he does not perceive it as without outflows; he does not perceive it as affliction; he does not perceive it as freedom from affliction.

He does not perceive it as mundane; he does not perceive it as supramundane. He does not perceive it as saṃsāra; he does not perceive it as nirvāṇa. He does not perceive that which is called "the ear" as permanent; he does not perceive that which is called "the ear" as impermanent. He does not perceive that which is called "the ear" as pleasant; he does not perceive that which is called "the ear" as painful. He does not perceive that which is called "the ear" as self; he does not perceive that which is called "the ear" as non-self. He does not perceive that which is called "the ear"...

He perceives that the ear is peaceful; he does not perceive that the ear is not peaceful. He does not perceive that the ear is empty; he does not perceive that the ear is not empty. He does not perceive that the ear has signs; he does not perceive that the ear is signless. He does not perceive that the ear is with aspiration; he does not perceive that the ear is without aspiration.

One does not perceive the ear as conditioned; one does not perceive the ear as unconditioned. One does not perceive the ear as defilement; one does not perceive the ear as purification. One does not perceive the ear as arising; one does not perceive the ear as cessation. One does not perceive the ear as secluded.

He does not perceive that what is called "the ear" is non-discriminated; he does not perceive that what is called "the ear" is wholesome; he does not perceive that what is called "the ear" is unwholesome; he does not perceive that what is called "the ear" is faulty; he does not perceive that what is called "the ear" is faultless; he does not perceive that what is called "the ear" is with-outflows; he does not perceive that what is called "the ear" is without-outflows.

He does not perceive the ear as being defilement; he does not perceive the ear as being free from defilement. He does not perceive the ear as being mundane; he does not perceive the ear as being supramundane. He does not perceive the ear as being saṃsāra; he does not perceive the ear as being nirvāṇa.

One does not perceive that what is called "sound" is permanent; one does not perceive that what is called "sound" is impermanent. One does not perceive that what is called "sound" is pleasure; one does not perceive that what is called "sound" is suffering. One does not perceive that what is called "sound" is self; one does not perceive that what is called "sound" is non-self. One does not perceive that what is called "sound"...

He perceives that what is called "sound" is quiescent; he does not perceive that what is called "sound" is non-quiescent. He does not perceive that what is called "sound" is empty; he does not perceive that what is called "sound" is non-empty. He does not perceive that what is called "sound" has signs; he does not perceive that what is called "sound" is signless. He does not perceive that what is called "sound" is with aspiration; he does not perceive that what is called "sound" is without aspiration.

He does not perceive that "sound" is conditioned; he does not perceive that "sound" is unconditioned. He does not perceive that "sound" is defilement; he does not perceive that "sound" is purification. He does not perceive that "sound" is arising; he does not perceive that "sound" is cessation. He does not perceive that "sound" is secluded; he does not perceive that "sound" is non-secluded.

He does not perceive that what is called "sound" is wholesome; he does not perceive that what is called "sound" is unwholesome. He does not perceive body-consciousness as "wishful"; he does not perceive body-consciousness as "wishless."
One does not perceive that which is called body-consciousness as conditioned, nor does one perceive that which is called body-consciousness as unconditioned.

He does not perceive body-consciousness as defilement; he does not perceive body-consciousness as purification. He does not perceive body-consciousness as arising; he does not perceive body-consciousness as secluded. He does not perceive body-consciousness as non-secluded; he does not perceive body-consciousness as wholesome; he does not perceive body-consciousness as unwholesome.

He does not perceive body-consciousness as being with fault; he does not perceive body-consciousness as being faultless. He does not perceive body-consciousness as being with outflows; he does not perceive body-consciousness as being without outflows. He does not perceive body-consciousness as being defiled; he does not perceive body-consciousness as being undefiled. He does not perceive body-consciousness as being worldly.

He does not perceive that what is called body-consciousness is supramundane; he does not perceive that what is called body-consciousness is saṃsāra; he does not perceive that what is called body-consciousness is nirvāṇa.

One does not perceive the so-called body-contact as permanent; one does not perceive the so-called body-contact as impermanent. One does not perceive the so-called body-contact as pleasant; one does not perceive the so-called body-contact as painful. One does not perceive the so-called body-contact as self; one does not perceive the so-called body-contact as non-self. One does not perceive the so-called body-contact as peaceful.

He does not perceive the so-called body-contact as "unpeaceful"; he does not perceive the so-called body-contact as "empty"; he does not perceive the so-called body-contact as "non-empty"; he does not perceive the so-called body-contact as "characteristic. He does not...

He correctly perceives that what is called body-contact is signless; he does not perceive that what is called body-contact is with-vow; he does not perceive that what is called body-contact is without-vow; he does not perceive that what is called body-contact is conditioned; he does not perceive that what is called body-contact is unconditioned; he does not perceive that what is called body-contact is affliction.

He does not perceive body-contact as purification; he does not perceive body-contact as arising; he does not perceive body-contact as cessation; he does not perceive body-contact as secluded; he does not perceive body-contact as non-secluded; he does not perceive body-contact as wholesome.

He does not perceive bodily contact as unwholesome; he does not perceive bodily contact as blameworthy; he does not perceive bodily contact as blameless; he does not perceive bodily contact as with outflows; he does not perceive bodily contact as without outflows; he does not perceive bodily contact as affliction.

He does not perceive body-contact as being "without affliction"; he does not perceive body-contact as being "worldly"; he does not perceive body-contact as being "supramundane"; he does not perceive body-contact as being "saṃsāra"; and he does not perceive body-contact as being "nirvāṇa."

Furthermore, whatever feeling—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—arises conditioned by the body, the tangible object, and body-consciousness, he regards that as "not permanent," yet he does not regard it as "impermanent"; he does not regard it as "pleasure," nor does he regard it as "suffering"; he regards it as "not-self."

He does not perceive it as "not-self"; he does not perceive it as "peaceful," nor does he perceive it as "not peaceful. He does not perceive it as "empty," nor does he perceive it as "not empty. He does not perceive it as "signless," nor does he perceive it as "not signless. He does not perceive it as "wishless," nor does he perceive it as "not wishless. He does not perceive it as "conditioned," nor does he perceive it as "unconditioned."

He does not perceive it as affliction; he does not perceive it as purification; he does not perceive it as arising; he does not perceive it as cessation; he does not perceive it as secluded; he does not perceive it as wholesome; he does not perceive it as unwholesome; he does not perceive it as faulty; he does not perceive it as faultless; he does not perceive it as with outflows; he does not perceive it as without outflows.

He does not perceive it as defilement; he does not perceive it as freedom from defilement. He does not perceive it as mundane; he does not perceive it as supramundane. He does not perceive it as saṃsāra; he does not perceive it as nirvāṇa.

One does not perceive the mind as permanent; one does not perceive the mind as impermanent. One does not perceive the mind as pleasant; one does not perceive the mind as painful. One does not perceive the mind as self; one does not perceive the mind as non-self. One does not perceive the mind as peaceful; one does not perceive the mind as unpeaceful. One does not perceive the mind as empty.

He does not perceive that which is called "mind" as non-empty; he does not perceive that which is called "mind" as having signs; he does not perceive that which is called "mind" as signless; he does not perceive that which is called "mind" as being conditioned by vows.

He does not perceive that what is called "mind" is wishless; he does not perceive that what is called "mind" is conditioned; he does not perceive that what is called "mind" is unconditioned; he does not perceive that what is called "mind" is affliction; he does not perceive that what is called "mind" is purification; he does not perceive that what is called "mind" is arising; he does not perceive that what is called "mind" is cessation.

He does not perceive that which is called "mind" as secluded; he does not perceive that which is called "mind" as non-secluded. He does not perceive that which is called "mind" as wholesome; he does not perceive that which is called "mind" as unwholesome. He does not perceive that which is called "mind" as faulty; he does not perceive that which is called "mind" as faultless. He does not perceive that which is called "mind" as with outflows; he does not perceive that which is called "mind" as without outflows.

He does not perceive that which is called "mind" as defilement; he does not perceive that which is called "mind" as freedom from defilement. He does not perceive that which is called "mind" as mundane; he does not perceive that which is called "mind" as supramundane. He does not perceive that which is called "mind" as saṃsāra; he does not perceive that which is called "mind" as nirvāṇa.

He does not perceive phenomena as being permanent; he does not perceive phenomena as being impermanent. He does not perceive phenomena as being pleasant; he does not perceive phenomena as being painful. He does not perceive phenomena as being self; he does not perceive phenomena as being non-self. He does not perceive phenomena as being peaceful; he does not perceive phenomena as being unpeaceful.

He does not perceive phenomena as being empty; he does not perceive phenomena as being non-empty. He does not perceive phenomena as having signs; he does not perceive phenomena as being signless. He does not perceive phenomena as being with aspiration.

Thus he perceives: he does not perceive phenomena as being called "wishless"; he does not perceive phenomena as being called "conditioned"; he does not perceive phenomena as being called "unconditioned"; he does not perceive phenomena as being called "defilements"; he does not perceive phenomena as being called "purifications"; he does not perceive phenomena as being called "arising"; he does not perceive phenomena as being called "cessation."

He does not perceive that phenomena are distinct from names; he does not perceive that phenomena are not distinct from names. He does not perceive that phenomena are wholesome; he does not perceive that phenomena are unwholesome. He does not perceive that phenomena are faulty; he does not perceive that phenomena are faultless. He does not perceive that phenomena are with outflows.

He does not perceive phenomena as being "outflows" (āsrava); he does not perceive phenomena as being "afflictions" (saṃkleśa); he does not perceive phenomena as being "free from afflictions" (niḥkleśa). He does not perceive phenomena as being "worldly" (laukika); he does not perceive phenomena as being "supramundane" (lokottara). He does not perceive phenomena as being "saṃsāra"; he does not perceive phenomena as being "nirvāṇa."

One does not perceive mental consciousness as permanent; one does not perceive mental consciousness as impermanent. One does not perceive mental consciousness as pleasant; one does not perceive mental consciousness as painful. One does not perceive mental consciousness as self; one does not perceive mental consciousness as non-self. One does not perceive mental consciousness as peaceful.

He does not perceive mental consciousness as being non-peaceful; he does not perceive mental consciousness as being empty; he does not perceive mental consciousness as being non-empty; he does not perceive mental consciousness as having signs.

Thus he observes: he does not observe that mental consciousness is called "signless"; he does not observe that mental consciousness is called "wishless"; he does not observe that mental consciousness is called "non-wishless"; he does not observe that mental consciousness is called "conditioned"; he does not observe that mental consciousness is called "unconditioned"; he does not observe that mental consciousness is called "defilement."

He does not perceive mental consciousness as purification; he does not perceive mental consciousness as arising; he does not perceive mental consciousness as cessation; he does not perceive mental consciousness as secluded; he does not perceive mental consciousness as non-secluded; he does not perceive mental consciousness as wholesome; he does not perceive mental consciousness as unwholesome.

He does not perceive mental consciousness as being faulty; he does not perceive mental consciousness as being faultless. He does not perceive mental consciousness as being with outflows; he does not perceive mental consciousness as being without outflows. He does not perceive mental consciousness as being affliction; he does not perceive mental consciousness as being free from affliction. He does not perceive mental consciousness as being mundane.

He does not perceive mental consciousness as supramundane; he does not perceive mental consciousness as saṃsāra; he does not perceive mental consciousness as nirvāṇa. He does not perceive mental contact as permanent; he does not perceive mental contact as impermanent; he does not perceive mental contact as pleasure; he does not perceive mental contact as suffering; [he does not perceive] mental contact...

He does not perceive mental contact as "self"; he does not perceive mental contact as "not-self. He does not perceive mental contact as "peaceful"; he does not perceive mental contact as "unpeaceful. He does not perceive mental contact as "empty"; he does not perceive mental contact as "non-empty. He does not perceive mental contact as "characteristic."

He does not perceive mental contact as being "signless"; he does not perceive mental contact as being "wishless"; he does not perceive mental contact as being "non-wishless"; he does not perceive mental contact as being "conditioned"; he does not perceive mental contact as being "unconditioned"; he does not perceive mental contact as being "defiled."

He does not perceive mental contact as purification; he does not perceive mental contact as arising; he does not perceive mental contact as cessation; he does not perceive mental contact as secluded; he does not perceive mental contact as non-secluded; he does not perceive mental contact as wholesome.

He does not perceive mental contact as unwholesome; he does not perceive mental contact as faulty; he does not perceive mental contact as faultless; he does not perceive mental contact as with-outflows; he does not perceive mental contact as without-outflows; he does not perceive mental contact as defilement.

He does not perceive mental contact as being "without affliction"; he does not perceive mental contact as being "worldly"; he does not perceive mental contact as being "supramundane"; he does not perceive mental contact as being "saṃsāra"; he does not perceive mental contact as being "nirvāṇa."

Furthermore, regarding that mind which arises conditioned by mental phenomena, mental consciousness, and mental contact—whether it be a feeling of pleasure, pain, or neither-pain-nor-pleasure—he likewise regards it as not permanent; he does not regard it as impermanent; he does not regard it as pleasant; he does not regard it as painful; he does not regard it as self; he does not regard it as non-self; and he does not regard it as peaceful.

He does not perceive it as "unpeaceful"; he does not perceive it as "empty," nor does he perceive it as "not empty. He does not perceive it as "sign-bearing," nor does he perceive it as "signless. He does not perceive it as "with aspiration," nor does he perceive it as "without aspiration. He does not perceive it as "conditioned," nor does he perceive it as "unconditioned. He does not perceive it as "defilement," nor does he perceive it as "purification."

He does not perceive it as arising; he does not perceive it as ceasing; he does not perceive it as secluded; he does not perceive it as non-secluded; he does not perceive it as wholesome; he does not perceive it as unwholesome; he does not perceive it as faulty; he does not perceive it as faultless; he does not perceive it as with-outflows; he does not perceive it as without-outflows; he does not perceive it as defilement.

He does not perceive it as "free from affliction"; he does not perceive it as "worldly"; he does not perceive it as "supramundane"; he does not perceive it as "saṃsāra"; he does not perceive it as "nirvāṇa. For what reason? Because when a bodhisattva mahāsattva courses in the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive that perfection of wisdom, nor that bodhisattva, nor that name "bodhisattva," within the conditioned realm (*saṃskṛtadhātu*); nor does he perceive them within the unconditioned realm (*asaṃskṛtadhātu*). For what reason?

For this reason, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not perceive the name "perfection of wisdom"; he does not perceive a "bodhisattva"; he does not perceive the name "bodhisattva"; he does not perceive a "Buddha"; he does not perceive the name "Buddha. He does not practice the perfection of wisdom for the sake of cultivating the right efforts, nor does he perceive the perfection of wisdom, nor does he perceive the name "perfection of wisdom."
He does not perceive a bodhisattva; he does not perceive the name "bodhisattva. He does not perceive a Buddha; he does not perceive the name "Buddha.

He practices the perfection of wisdom for the sake of cultivating the bases of psychic power, yet he does not perceive the perfection of wisdom, nor does he perceive the name "perfection of wisdom. He does not perceive a bodhisattva; he does not perceive the name "bodhisattva. He does not perceive a Buddha; he does not perceive the name "Buddha."

He does not practice the perfection of wisdom for the sake of cultivating the sense faculties; nor does he perceive the perfection of wisdom, nor does he perceive a bodhisattva, nor does he perceive the name "bodhisattva," nor does he perceive a Buddha, nor does he perceive the name "Buddha."

He practices the perfection of wisdom for the sake of cultivating internal emptiness; yet he does not perceive the perfection of wisdom, nor does he perceive the name "perfection of wisdom. He does not perceive a bodhisattva, nor does he perceive the name "bodhisattva. He does not perceive a Buddha, nor does he perceive the name "Buddha."

By means of the cultivation of external emptiness, he courses in the perfection of wisdom; yet he does not perceive the perfection of wisdom, nor does he perceive the name "perfection of wisdom. He does not perceive a bodhisattva, nor does he perceive the name "bodhisattva. He does not perceive a Buddha, nor does he perceive the name "Buddha."

He practices the perfection of wisdom for the sake of cultivating the emptiness of the internal and external; yet he does not perceive the perfection of wisdom, nor does he perceive the name "perfection of wisdom. He does not perceive a bodhisattva, nor does he perceive the name "bodhisattva. He does not perceive a Buddha, nor does he perceive the name "Buddha."

He practices the perfection of wisdom for the sake of cultivating the emptiness of emptiness; yet he does not perceive the perfection of wisdom, nor does he perceive the name "perfection of wisdom. He does not perceive a bodhisattva, nor does he perceive the name "bodhisattva. He does not perceive a Buddha, nor does he perceive the name "Buddha."

He courses in the perfection of wisdom for the sake of cultivating great emptiness; yet he does not perceive the perfection of wisdom, nor does he perceive the name "perfection of wisdom. He does not perceive a bodhisattva, nor does he perceive the name "bodhisattva. He does not perceive a Buddha, nor does he perceive the name "Buddha."

He practices the perfection of wisdom for the sake of cultivating the emptiness of the ultimate truth; yet he does not perceive the perfection of wisdom, nor does he perceive the name "perfection of wisdom. He does not perceive the bodhisattva, nor does he perceive the name "bodhisattva. He does not perceive the Buddha, nor does he perceive the name "Buddha."

He practices the perfection of wisdom for the sake of cultivating the emptiness of conditioned phenomena; yet he does not perceive the perfection of wisdom, nor does he perceive the name "perfection of wisdom. He does not perceive a Buddha, nor does he perceive the name "Buddha."

He practices the perfection of wisdom for the sake of cultivating absolute emptiness; yet he does not perceive the perfection of wisdom, nor does he perceive the name "perfection of wisdom. He does not perceive a bodhisattva, nor does he perceive the name "bodhisattva. He does not perceive a Buddha, nor does he perceive the name "Buddha."

One practices the perfection of wisdom for the sake of cultivating the emptiness that is without beginning or end; yet one does not perceive the perfection of wisdom, nor does one perceive the bodhisattva, nor does one perceive the name "bodhisattva," nor does one perceive the Buddha, nor does one perceive the name "Buddha."

One practices the perfection of wisdom for the sake of cultivating the emptiness of non-dispersal; yet one does not perceive the perfection of wisdom, nor does one perceive the name "perfection of wisdom. One does not perceive a bodhisattva, nor does one perceive the name "bodhisattva. One does not perceive a Buddha, nor does one perceive the name "Buddha."

One practices the perfection of wisdom for the sake of cultivating the emptiness of intrinsic nature; yet one does not perceive the perfection of wisdom, nor does one perceive the name "perfection of wisdom. One does not perceive a bodhisattva, nor does one perceive the name "bodhisattva. One does not perceive a Buddha, nor does one perceive the name "Buddha."

One practices in the perfection of wisdom for the sake of cultivating the emptiness of all phenomena; yet one does not perceive the perfection of wisdom, nor does one perceive the name "perfection of wisdom. One does not perceive the bodhisattva, nor does one perceive the name "bodhisattva. One does not perceive the Buddha, nor does one perceive the name "Buddha."

One practices the perfection of wisdom for the sake of cultivating the emptiness of specific characteristics; yet one does not perceive the perfection of wisdom, nor does one perceive the name "perfection of wisdom. One does not perceive a bodhisattva, nor does one perceive the name "bodhisattva. One does not perceive a Buddha, nor does one perceive the name "Buddha.

One practices the perfection of wisdom for the sake of cultivating the emptiness of non-apprehension; yet one does not perceive the perfection of wisdom, nor does one perceive the name "perfection of wisdom."
He does not perceive a bodhisattva; he does not perceive the name "bodhisattva. He does not perceive a Buddha; he does not perceive the name "Buddha.

He practices the perfection of wisdom for the sake of cultivating the emptiness of non-existence, yet he does not perceive the perfection of wisdom; he does not perceive the name "perfection of wisdom. He does not perceive a bodhisattva; he does not perceive the name "bodhisattva. He does not perceive a Buddha; he does not perceive the name "Buddha."

One practices in the perfection of wisdom for the sake of cultivating the emptiness of intrinsic nature; yet one does not perceive the perfection of wisdom, nor does one perceive the name "perfection of wisdom. One does not perceive a bodhisattva, nor does one perceive the name "bodhisattva. One does not perceive a Buddha, nor does one perceive the name "Buddha."

He courses in the perfection of wisdom for the sake of cultivating the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence; yet he does not perceive the perfection of wisdom, nor does he perceive the name "perfection of wisdom. He does not perceive a bodhisattva, nor does he perceive the name "bodhisattva. He does not perceive a Buddha, nor does he perceive the name "Buddha."

He practices the perfection of wisdom for the sake of cultivating the foundations of mindfulness; yet he does not perceive the perfection of wisdom, nor does he perceive the name "perfection of wisdom. He does not perceive a bodhisattva, nor does he perceive the name "bodhisattva. He does not perceive a Buddha, nor does he perceive the name "Buddha."

He practices the perfection of wisdom for the sake of cultivating the noble truths; yet he does not perceive the perfection of wisdom, nor does he perceive the name "perfection of wisdom. He does not perceive a bodhisattva, nor does he perceive the name "bodhisattva. He does not perceive a Buddha, nor does he perceive the name "Buddha."

He practices the perfection of wisdom for the sake of cultivating meditative absorption; yet he does not perceive the perfection of wisdom, nor does he perceive the name "perfection of wisdom. He does not perceive a bodhisattva, nor does he perceive the name "bodhisattva. He does not perceive a Buddha, nor does he perceive the name "Buddha."

He practices the perfection of wisdom for the sake of cultivating the immeasurables, yet he does not perceive the perfection of wisdom; he does not perceive the name "perfection of wisdom. He does not perceive a bodhisattva; he does not perceive the name "bodhisattva. He does not perceive a Buddha; he does not perceive the name "Buddha."

He practices the perfection of wisdom for the sake of cultivating the formless attainments; yet he does not perceive the perfection of wisdom, nor does he perceive the name "perfection of wisdom. He does not perceive the bodhisattva, nor does he perceive the name "bodhisattva. He does not perceive the Buddha, nor does he perceive the name "Buddha."

He practices the perfection of wisdom for the sake of cultivating the eight liberations; yet he does not perceive the perfection of wisdom, nor does he perceive the name "perfection of wisdom. He does not perceive a bodhisattva, nor does he perceive the name "bodhisattva. He does not perceive a Buddha, nor does he perceive the name "Buddha."

One practices the perfection of wisdom for the sake of cultivating the nine successive meditative attainments; yet one does not perceive the perfection of wisdom, nor does one perceive the name "perfection of wisdom. One does not perceive the bodhisattva, nor does one perceive the name "bodhisattva. One does not perceive the Buddha, nor does one perceive the name "Buddha."

One practices the perfection of wisdom for the sake of cultivating the liberation door of emptiness; yet one does not perceive the perfection of wisdom, nor does one perceive the name "perfection of wisdom.
One does not perceive the bodhisattva, nor does one perceive the name "bodhisattva. One does not perceive the Buddha, nor does one perceive the name "Buddha."

He courses in the perfection of wisdom for the sake of cultivating the signless liberation; yet he does not perceive the perfection of wisdom, nor does he perceive the name "perfection of wisdom. He does not perceive the bodhisattva, nor does he perceive the name "bodhisattva. He does not perceive the Buddha, nor does he perceive the name "Buddha."

He practices the perfection of wisdom for the sake of cultivating the liberation of wishlessness; yet he does not perceive the perfection of wisdom, nor does he perceive the name "perfection of wisdom. He does not perceive a bodhisattva, nor does he perceive the name "bodhisattva. He does not perceive a Buddha, nor does he perceive the name "Buddha."

He practices the perfection of wisdom for the sake of cultivating the superknowledges; yet he does not perceive the perfection of wisdom, nor does he perceive the name "perfection of wisdom. He does not perceive the bodhisattva, nor does he perceive the name "bodhisattva. He does not perceive the Buddha, nor does he perceive the name "Buddha."

He courses in the perfection of wisdom for the sake of cultivating meditative concentration; yet he does not perceive the perfection of wisdom, nor does he perceive the name "perfection of wisdom. He does not perceive a bodhisattva, nor does he perceive the name "bodhisattva. He does not perceive a Buddha, nor does he perceive the name "Buddha. He perceives neither the Buddha nor the name "Buddha."

One practices in the perfection of wisdom for the sake of cultivating the gateways of dhāraṇī; yet one does not perceive the perfection of wisdom, nor does one perceive the name "perfection of wisdom. One does not perceive a bodhisattva, nor does one perceive the name "bodhisattva. One does not perceive a Buddha, nor does one perceive the name "Buddha."

One practices the perfection of wisdom for the sake of cultivating the ten powers of a Tathāgata; yet one does not perceive the perfection of wisdom, nor does one perceive the name "perfection of wisdom. One does not perceive the bodhisattva, nor does one perceive the name "bodhisattva. One does not perceive the Buddha, nor does one perceive the name "Buddha."

He practices the perfection of wisdom for the sake of cultivating the four grounds of self-confidence; yet he does not perceive the perfection of wisdom, nor does he perceive the name "perfection of wisdom. He does not perceive the bodhisattva, nor does he perceive the name "bodhisattva. He does not perceive the Buddha, nor does he perceive the name "Buddha."

He practices the perfection of wisdom for the sake of cultivating the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), yet he does not perceive the perfection of wisdom; he does not perceive the name "perfection of wisdom"; he does not perceive a bodhisattva; he does not perceive the name "bodhisattva"; he does not perceive a Buddha; and he does not perceive the name "Buddha."

One practices the perfection of wisdom for the sake of cultivating the unique qualities of a Buddha; yet one does not perceive the perfection of wisdom, nor does one perceive the name "perfection of wisdom. One does not perceive the bodhisattva, nor does one perceive the name "bodhisattva. One does not perceive the Buddha, nor does one perceive the name "Buddha," except for the mental engagement with the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*).

When that bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he thoroughly penetrates the dharma-characteristic of phenomena. And that which is the dharma-characteristic of phenomena neither becomes defiled nor purified. In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom must understand the designation of phenomena as a mere name and convention. Having understood the designation of phenomena as a mere name and convention, he will not adhere to form, nor...

He will not adhere to feeling; he will not adhere to volitional formations; he will not adhere to consciousness. He will not adhere to the eye; he will not adhere to forms; he will not adhere to eye-consciousness; he will not adhere to eye-contact.

Furthermore, whatever feeling—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that arises conditioned by eye-consciousness and eye-contact, that too will not be adhered to. One will not adhere to the ear; one will not adhere to sound; one will not adhere to ear-consciousness; one will not adhere to ear-contact.

Furthermore, whatever feeling—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—arises conditioned by the ear, sounds, ear-consciousness, and ear-contact, that too will not be adhered to. One will not adhere to the nose; one will not adhere to odors; one will not adhere to nose-consciousness; one will not adhere to nose-contact.

Furthermore, whatever feeling—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—arises conditioned by the nose, odors, olfactory consciousness, and olfactory contact, that too will not be adhered to. One will not adhere to the tongue; one will not adhere to tastes; one will not adhere to gustatory consciousness; and one will not adhere to gustatory contact.

Furthermore, whatever feeling—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-pleasant-nor-painful—arises conditioned by the tongue, tastes, tongue-consciousness, and tongue-contact, that too will not be adhered to. One will not adhere to the body; one will not adhere to tangible objects; one will not adhere to body-consciousness; and one will not adhere to body-contact.

Furthermore, whatever feeling—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—arises conditioned by the body, the tangible, body-consciousness, and body-contact, that too will not be adhered to; the mind will not be adhered to; phenomena will not be adhered to; mind-consciousness will not be adhered to; and mind-contact will not be adhered to.

Furthermore, whatever feeling—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—arises conditioned by the contact of the mind with mental phenomena and mental consciousness, that too will not be adhered to.

One will not be attached to the conditioned realm; one will not be attached to the unconditioned realm. One will not be attached to the perfection of generosity; one will not be attached to the perfection of ethical discipline; one will not be attached to the perfection of patience; one will not be attached to the perfection of vigor; one will not be attached to the perfection of meditative concentration; one will not be attached to the perfection of wisdom. Nor will one be attached even to their ultimate characteristics.

One will not be attached to the body of awakening; one will not be attached to the fleshly eye; one will not be attached to the divine eye; one will not be attached to the wisdom eye; one will not be attached to the Dharma eye; one will not be attached to the Buddha eye; one will not be attached to the perfection of the superknowledges; one will not be attached to internal emptiness; one will not be attached to external emptiness; one will not be attached to internal-and-external emptiness.

One will not be attached to the emptiness of emptiness; one will not be attached to great emptiness; one will not be attached to the emptiness of the ultimate truth; one will not be attached to the emptiness of the conditioned; one will not be attached to the emptiness of the unconditioned; one will not be attached to absolute emptiness; one will not be attached to the emptiness of that which has no beginning or end; one will not be attached to the emptiness of non-dispersal; one will not be attached to the emptiness of intrinsic nature.

One will not be attached to the emptiness of all phenomena; one will not be attached to the emptiness of specific characteristics; one will not be attached to the emptiness of non-apprehension; one will not be attached to the emptiness of non-existence; one will not be attached to the emptiness of intrinsic nature; one will not be attached to the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence. One will not be attached to the applications of mindfulness; one will not be attached to the right efforts; one will not be attached to the bases of psychic power.
One will not be attached to the faculties; one will not be attached to the powers; one will not be attached to the factors of enlightenment.

One will not be attached to the noble eightfold path; one will not be attached to the noble truths; one will not be attached to the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*); one will not be attached to the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*); one will not be attached to the formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*); one will not be attached to the eight liberations (*vimokṣa*); one will not be attached to the nine successive dwellings (*anupūrvavihāra*); one will not be attached to emptiness (*śūnyatā*); one will not be attached to the signless (*ānimitta*); and one will not be attached to the wishless (*apraṇihita*).

One will not be attached to the superknowledges; one will not be attached to the meditative concentrations; one will not be attached to the gateways of mnemonic formulas; one will not be attached to the ten powers of a Tathāgata; one will not be attached to the four grounds of self-confidence; one will not be attached to the realm of phenomena; one will not be attached to the four analytical knowledges; one will not be attached to great loving-kindness; and one will not be attached to great compassion.

One will not be attached to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; one will not be attached to suchness; one will not be attached to the limit of reality; one will not be attached to the realm of phenomena; one will not be attached to the ripening of sentient beings; one will not be attached to the purification of the buddha-field; one will not be attached to skill in means. Why is that? Because all those phenomena do not exist—that which one might be attached to, that by which one might be attached, or that wherein one might be attached.

In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who, being unattached to all phenomena, courses in the perfection of wisdom, increases in the perfection of generosity; he increases in the perfection of ethical discipline; he increases in the perfection of patience; he increases in the perfection of vigor; he increases in the perfection of meditative concentration; and he increases in the perfection of wisdom.

He enters the fixed course of the bodhisattvas, he ascends the stage of non-retrogression, and having perfected the superknowledges, he travels from buddhafield to buddhafield, maturing sentient beings and honoring, respecting, revering, and worshiping the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, for the sake of purifying the buddhafield.

In order to behold the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, and having seen those Blessed Ones, whatever roots of merit they may desire by which to honor, revere, respect, and worship those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones—those very roots of merit will manifest for them. By means of those very roots of merit, they will appear in the presence of those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, and in the presence of those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, they will hear the Dharma.

And that Dharma as it has been heard shall never be interrupted until he awakens to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; he shall also attain the gateways of dhāraṇīs and the gateways of samādhis.

The Blessed One said: "What do you think, Subhūti? Is that which is the suchness of birth the Bodhisattva? He replied: "No indeed, Blessed One. The Blessed One said: "What do you think, Subhūti? He replied: "No indeed, Blessed One. The Blessed One said:

"What do you think, Subhūti? Is there such a thing as the 'suchness of birth' in a bodhisattva? He replied, "Certainly not, Blessed One. The Blessed One said, "What do you think, Subhūti? Is a bodhisattva [defined by] the 'suchness of non-birth'? He replied, "Certainly not, Blessed One."

The Blessed One said: "What do you think, Subhūti? Is that which is the suchness of aging and death the Bodhisattva? He replied: "No indeed, Blessed One. Is a bodhisattva the suchness of non-old-age and non-death? He replied, "Certainly not, Blessed One. The Blessed One said, "What do you think, Subhūti? Do you speak thus because you perceive a specific purpose?"

"A bodhisattva is not form. "A bodhisattva is not elsewhere than form. "A bodhisattva is not in form. "Form is not in a bodhisattva. "A bodhisattva is not formless. "Feeling is not a bodhisattva. "Bodhisattva" is not a designation; nor is there a bodhisattva apart from designation; nor is there a bodhisattva within designation; nor is designation within the bodhisattva; nor is the bodhisattva without designation. "A bodhisattva does not exist apart from consciousness; a bodhisattva does not exist in consciousness; nor is a bodhisattva devoid of consciousness."

The eye is not the bodhisattva; the bodhisattva is not other than the eye; the bodhisattva is not in the eye; the eye is not in the bodhisattva; the bodhisattva is not one who lacks the eye. The Blessed One said: "Excellent, excellent, Subhūti! By not apprehending the designation of form as permanent, by not apprehending the designation of form as impermanent, by not apprehending the designation of feeling as permanent, by not apprehending the designation of feeling as impermanent, by not apprehending the designation of perception as permanent, by not apprehending the designation of perception as impermanent, by not apprehending the designation of formations as permanent, by not apprehending the designation of formations as impermanent, [and] by not apprehending the designation of consciousness as permanent.

By means of non-apprehension, there is the non-apprehension of the designation "consciousness is impermanent"; by means of non-apprehension, the designation "form is pleasure"; by means of non-apprehension, the designation "form is suffering"; by means of non-apprehension, the designation "feeling is pleasure"; and by means of non-apprehension, the designation "feeling is suffering."

By not apprehending the designation of the sign of perception; by not apprehending the designation of the sign of perception; by not apprehending the designation of the sign of volitional formations; by not apprehending the designation of the sign of volitional formations; by not apprehending the designation of the sign of consciousness; by not apprehending the designation of the sign of consciousness; by not apprehending the designation of the excellence of form.

The designation of form as wishless is through non-apprehension; the designation of feeling as wishless is through non-apprehension; the designation of perception as wishless is through non-apprehension; the designation of mental formations as wishless is through non-apprehension; and the designation of consciousness as wishless is through non-apprehension.
Not perceiving [them], one should train in the perfection of wisdom by means of the designation "wishless consciousness" while not perceiving it.

Furthermore, Subhūti, as for what you said: "I do not perceive any dharma, namely, a 'bodhisattva'"; Subhūti, a dharma does not perceive the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). The perception-element (*saṃjñādhātu*) does not perceive the dharma-realm; the dharma-realm does not perceive the perception-element. The formation-element (*saṃskāradhātu*) does not perceive the dharma-realm; the dharma-realm does not perceive the formation-element.

The consciousness element does not perceive the phenomena element; the phenomena element does not perceive the consciousness element. The eye element does not perceive the phenomena element; the phenomena element does not perceive the eye element. The ear element does not perceive the phenomena element; the phenomena element does not perceive the ear element. The nose element does not perceive the phenomena element.

The dharma-element does not perceive the nose-element; the tongue-element does not perceive the dharma-element; the dharma-element does not perceive the tongue-element; the body-element does not perceive the dharma-element; the dharma-element does not perceive the body-element; the mind-element does not perceive the dharma-element; and the dharma-element does not perceive the mind-element.

Subhūti, the conditioned realm does not perceive the unconditioned realm, nor does the unconditioned realm perceive the conditioned realm; furthermore, there is no unconditioned apart from the conditioned realm.

It is possible to designate [the unconditioned]; however, apart from the unconditioned, the conditioned realm cannot be designated. In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in the perfection of wisdom does not perceive any dharma whatsoever. Not perceiving them, he is not startled, he is not terrified, and he does not fall into terror. Nor does his mind sink down with regard to any dharma, nor does his mind become regretful.

For what reason? Because, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices in the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive form; he does not perceive feeling; he does not perceive perception; he does not perceive mental formations; he does not perceive consciousness. He does not perceive the eye; he does not perceive the ear; he does not perceive the nose; he does not perceive the tongue; he does not perceive the body.

One does not perceive the mind; one does not perceive form; one does not perceive sound; one does not perceive odor; one does not perceive taste; one does not perceive tangibles; one does not perceive mental phenomena. One does not perceive the earth element; one does not perceive the water element; one does not perceive the fire element; one does not perceive the wind element; one does not perceive the space element.

He does not perceive the element of consciousness; he does not perceive ignorance; he does not perceive volitional formations; he does not perceive consciousness; he does not perceive name-and-form; he does not perceive the six sense bases; he does not perceive contact; he does not perceive feeling; he does not perceive craving; he does not perceive grasping; he does not perceive becoming; he does not perceive birth.

He does not perceive aging and death; he does not perceive passion; he does not perceive hatred; he does not perceive delusion; he does not perceive a self; he does not perceive a sentient being; he does not perceive a living soul; he does not perceive a person.

One does not perceive a nourisher; one does not perceive a person; one does not perceive a human being; one does not perceive a youth; one does not perceive an agent; one does not perceive an instigator; one does not perceive an experiencer; one does not perceive a feeler; one does not perceive a knower; one does not perceive a seer; one does not perceive the realm of desire; one does not perceive the realm of form.

He does not perceive the formless realm; he does not perceive the mind of a śrāvaka; he does not perceive the mind of a pratyekabuddha; he does not perceive the mind of awakening (bodhicitta). He does not perceive the dharmas of a śrāvaka; he does not perceive a pratyekabuddha; he does not perceive the dharmas of a pratyekabuddha. He does not perceive a bodhisattva; he does not perceive the dharmas of a bodhisattva. He does not perceive a Buddha.

He does not perceive the Buddha-qualities; he does not perceive awakening; indeed, he does not perceive any phenomena whatsoever, whether mundane or supramundane. Since he does not perceive any phenomena, he is not terrified and does not fall into terror.

He asked: "For what reason, Blessed One, does the mind of a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom not sink or become despondent regarding all phenomena? The Blessed One replied: "It is because, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not apprehend and does not perceive mental states or mental factors."

"For this reason, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva courses in the perfection of wisdom, his mind does not shrink back nor does it become despondent regarding all phenomena. Subhūti asked: "How is it, Blessed One, that the mind of a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not fall into terror? The Blessed One replied: "It is because, Subhūti,"

The bodhisattva mahāsattva does not apprehend, nor does he perceive, the mind and the mind-element. It is in this way, Subhūti, that the mind of a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not fall into terror. Thus, Subhūti, should a bodhisattva mahāsattva course in the perfection of wisdom.

Furthermore, Subhūti, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while coursing in the perfection of wisdom, does not apprehend that perfection of wisdom, does not apprehend that bodhisattva, and does not apprehend even the name "bodhisattva"—this indeed is the instruction for a bodhisattva; this is the teaching.
This concludes the second chapter of the *Śatasāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā*.
Now begins the third chapter.

Then the venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to fully understand form (*rūpa*) should train in the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
