If, Blessed One, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom without skill in means practices [thinking] that the right efforts are peaceful or are not peaceful, he practices with signs.

If, Blessed One, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of wisdom without skill in means, practices thinking that the right efforts are either secluded or not secluded, he is practicing with signs.

If, Blessed One, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom without skill in means practices thinking that the bases of psychic power are permanent or impermanent, he practices in signs. If, Blessed One, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom without skill in means practices thinking that the bases of psychic power are pleasant or painful, he practices in signs.

If, Blessed One, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom without skill in means practices with the thought that the bases of psychic power are "self" or "non-self," he practices with signs. If, Blessed One, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom without skill in means practices with the thought that the bases of psychic power are "peaceful" or "not peaceful"...

Thus he courses in a sign; he courses in a sign, Blessed One, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while coursing in the perfection of wisdom through a lack of skill in means, courses [thinking] that the bases of psychic power are secluded or that they are not secluded.

If, Blessed One, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom without skill in means practices with the thought that the faculties are permanent or impermanent, he practices with signs. If, Blessed One, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom without skill in means practices with the thought that the faculties are pleasant or painful, he practices with signs.

If, Blessed One, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom without skill in means practices [thinking] that the faculties are self or that they are non-self, he practices with signs. If, Blessed One, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom without skill in means practices [thinking] that the faculties are calm or that they are not calm, he practices with signs.

Blessed One, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of wisdom without skill in means, practices with the thought that the sense faculties are either secluded or not secluded, he practices with signs.

If, Blessed One, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of wisdom without skill in means, practices with the thought that the powers are permanent or impermanent, he practices in signs. If, Blessed One, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of wisdom without skill in means, practices with the thought that the powers are pleasant or painful, he practices in signs.

If, Blessed One, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom through a lack of skill in means practices with the thought that the powers are self or that they are non-self, he practices in signs. If, Blessed One, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom through a lack of skill in means practices with the thought that the powers are peaceful or that they are not peaceful...

He courses in a sign. Blessed One, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while coursing in the perfection of wisdom through a lack of skill in means, courses with the thought that the powers are either secluded or not secluded, he courses in a sign.

If, Blessed One, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom without skill in means practices [thinking] that the factors of enlightenment are permanent or impermanent, he practices in signs. If, Blessed One, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom without skill in means practices [thinking] that the factors of enlightenment are pleasant or painful, he practices in signs.

If, Blessed One, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom without skill in means practices [thinking] that the factors of awakening are self or are non-self, he practices with signs. If, Blessed One, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom without skill in means practices [thinking] that the factors of awakening are peaceful or are not peaceful, he practices with signs.

If, Blessed One, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom without skill in means practices thinking that the factors of awakening are either secluded or not secluded, he practices with signs.

If, Blessed One, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom without skill in means practices [thinking] that the noble eightfold path is permanent or impermanent, he practices with signs. If, Blessed One, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom without skill in means practices [thinking] that the noble eightfold path is pleasure or suffering, he practices with signs.

If, Blessed One, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom without skill in means practices the noble eightfold path as "self" or as "non-self," he practices with signs. If, Blessed One, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom without skill in means [practices] the noble eightfold path as "peaceful"...

If he courses in "not calm," he courses in a sign. Blessed One, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva, lacking skill in means, while coursing in the perfection of wisdom, courses in the thought that the noble eightfold path is "secluded" or "not secluded," he courses in a sign.

If, Blessed One, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom without skill in means practices with the thought that the noble truths are permanent or impermanent, he practices in signs. If, Blessed One, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom without skill in means practices with the thought that the noble truths are pleasant or painful, he practices in signs.

If, Blessed One, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom without skill in means practices [thinking] that the noble truths are self or that they are non-self, he practices in signs. If, Blessed One, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom without skill in means practices [thinking] that the noble truths are peaceful or that they are not peaceful, he practices in signs.

If, Blessed One, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom without skill in means practices [thinking] that the noble truths are either secluded or not secluded, he practices in signs.

If, Blessed One, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom without skill in means practices with the thought that the meditative absorptions are permanent or impermanent, he practices with signs. If, Blessed One, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom without skill in means practices with the thought that the meditative absorptions are pleasant or painful, he practices with signs.

If, Blessed One, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom without skill in means practices [thinking] that the meditative concentrations are self or are non-self, he practices with signs. If, Blessed One, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom without skill in means...

If he practices thinking, "The meditative absorptions (dhyānas) are peaceful" or "they are not peaceful," he practices with regard to a sign (nimitta). Blessed One, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) without skillful means, practices thinking, "The meditative absorptions are secluded" or "they are not secluded," he practices with regard to a sign.

If, Blessed One, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom without skill in means practices [thinking] that the immeasurables are permanent or impermanent, he practices with signs. If, Blessed One, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom without skill in means practices [thinking] that the immeasurables are pleasant or painful, he practices with signs.

If, Blessed One, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom without skill in means practices by regarding the immeasurables as either self or non-self, he practices in signs. If, Blessed One, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom without skill in means practices by regarding the immeasurables as either peaceful or not peaceful, he practices in signs.

If, Blessed One, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom without skill in means practices [thinking] that the immeasurables are either secluded or not secluded, he practices with signs. If, Blessed One, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom without skill in means practices [regarding] the formless attainments as either permanent or impermanent, as pleasant or painful, as self or non-self, as peaceful or not peaceful, as secluded or not secluded, he practices with signs.

Blessed One, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of wisdom without skillful means, practices with the notion that the liberations are permanent or impermanent, pleasant or painful, self or non-self, peaceful or not peaceful, and secluded or not secluded, he practices with signs.

Blessed One, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of wisdom without skillful means, practices by regarding the nine successive attainments of meditative dwelling as permanent or impermanent, as pleasant or painful, as having a self or selfless, as peaceful or unpeaceful, or as secluded or not secluded, he practices with signs.

Blessed One, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while practicing the perfection of wisdom without skill in means, practices by regarding the gateways to liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—as permanent or impermanent, as pleasant or painful, as having a self or being selfless, as peaceful or not peaceful, and as secluded or not secluded, he is practicing with signs.

If, Blessed One, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom without skill in means practices with the notion that the superknowledges are permanent or impermanent, pleasant or painful, self or non-self, peaceful or not peaceful, secluded or not secluded, he practices with signs.

If, Blessed One, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom without skill in means practices with the notion that meditative concentrations are permanent or impermanent, pleasant or painful...
If he courses with the thought that they are "with self" or "without self," "peaceful" or "not peaceful," "secluded" or "not secluded," he courses in a sign.

Blessed One, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while coursing in the perfection of wisdom through a lack of skill in means, courses with the thought that the gateways of dhāraṇī are "permanent" or "impermanent," "pleasant" or "painful," "with self" or "without self," "peaceful" or "not peaceful," "secluded" or "not secluded," he courses in a sign.

Blessed One, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of wisdom without skill in means, practices by regarding the ten powers of a Tathāgata as permanent or impermanent, as pleasant or painful, as having a self or selfless, as peaceful or unpeaceful, or as secluded or not secluded, he practices with signs.

If, Blessed One, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of wisdom without skill in means, practices with the notion that the grounds of self-confidence are permanent or impermanent, pleasant or painful, self or non-self, peaceful or not peaceful, secluded or not secluded, he practices with signs.

If, Blessed One, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom without skill in means should course in [the notion that] the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) are permanent or impermanent, pleasant or painful, self or non-self, peaceful or not peaceful, secluded or not secluded, he courses in a sign (*nimitta*).
If, Blessed One, a bodhisattva mahāsattva [practices] the perfection of wisdom without skill in means...

If one practices with the thought that great compassion is permanent or impermanent, pleasant or painful, self or non-self, peaceful or unpeaceful, or secluded or not secluded, one is practicing with signs.

If, Blessed One, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom through a lack of skill in means practices with the thought that the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha are permanent or impermanent, he practices in signs. If, Blessed One, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom through a lack of skill in means practices with the thought that the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha are pleasant or painful, he practices in signs.

If, Blessed One, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom without skill in means practices with the thought that the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha are "self" or "non-self," he practices in signs. If, Blessed One, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom without skill in means practices with the thought that the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha are "peaceful" or "not peaceful," he practices in signs.

If, Blessed One, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom without skill in means practices thinking that the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha are "secluded" or "not secluded," he practices with signs.

If, Blessed One, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom without skill in means thinks, "I am practicing the perfection of wisdom," and perceives this, then this bodhisattva mahāsattva is practicing with signs; he is practicing in a sign. If, Blessed One, a bodhisattva mahāsattva thinks, "He who practices in such a way is practicing the perfection of wisdom," [then he too is practicing with signs].
"If he cultivates the perfection of wisdom while dwelling upon signs, he is practicing in this way; it should be known that this is not the skillful means of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Then, venerable Śāradvatīputra said this to venerable Subhūti: "How, venerable sir..."

“Subhūti, this should be understood as the lack of skill in means on the part of a bodhisattva mahāsattva. Subhūti said, “For indeed, venerable Śāradvatīputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he stabilizes form, perceives it, and resolves upon it. By stabilizing, perceiving, and resolving upon form, he courses in the formative activity of form.”

He is not liberated from birth, old age, death, sorrow, affliction, pain, dejection, and despair; I say that he is not liberated from great suffering. If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while practicing the perfection of wisdom, presides over sensation, perceives it, and resolves upon it—if, while presiding over, perceiving, and resolving upon sensation, he courses in the formative activity (*abhisaṃskāra*) of sensation—[he is not liberated].

He is not liberated from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, dejection, and despair; I say that he is not liberated from great suffering. If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while practicing the perfection of wisdom, fixes his attention on perception, perceives it, or becomes intent upon it—if, fixing his attention on perception, perceiving it, and becoming intent upon it, he courses in the formative activity of perception—[he does not escape].

He is not liberated from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, dejection, and despair; he is not liberated from great suffering—so I say. If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while practicing the perfection of wisdom, presides over, perceives, and is intent upon conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), then by presiding over, perceiving, and being intent upon conditioned phenomena, he courses in the formative activity of conditioned phenomena.

He is not liberated from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, dejection, and despair; I say that he is not liberated from great suffering. This is if a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while practicing the perfection of wisdom, stabilizes consciousness, perceives it, and becomes intent upon it. By stabilizing, perceiving, and becoming intent upon consciousness, he courses in the formative activity (*abhisaṃskāra*) of consciousness. He does not [course in the perfection of wisdom].
One is liberated from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, dejection, and despair; yet I say that one is not liberated from great suffering.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while practicing the perfection of wisdom, fixates upon the eye, perceives it, and is convinced of it, then by so fixating, perceiving, and being convinced, he courses in the formative activity of the eye. I declare that he is not liberated from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, depression, and despair; he is not liberated from great suffering.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while practicing the perfection of wisdom, presides over the ear, perceives it, and is intent upon it—if, while presiding over, perceiving, and being intent upon the ear, he courses in the formative activity of the ear—then I say that he is not liberated from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, dejection, and despair; he is not liberated from great suffering.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while practicing the perfection of wisdom, exerts himself over the nose—exerting himself, perceiving it, and resolving upon it—he courses in the formative activity of the nose. I declare that he is not liberated from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, depression, and despair; he is not liberated from great suffering. If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while practicing the perfection of wisdom, exerts himself over the tongue...

He perceives and resolves upon it. By presiding over the tongue, perceiving it, and resolving upon it, he courses in the formative activity (*abhisaṃskāra*) of the tongue. He is not liberated from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, dejection, and despair; I say that he is not liberated from great suffering. If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while coursing in the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), presides over the body, perceives it, and resolves upon it—by presiding over the body, perceiving it, and resolving upon it—he courses in the formative activity of the body.

He is not liberated from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, dejection, and despair; I say that he is not liberated from great suffering. This is because if a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while practicing the perfection of wisdom, fixes his mind upon it, perceives it, and resolves upon it—by thus fixing his mind, perceiving it, and resolving upon it—he courses in the mental formation of the mind.
He is not liberated from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, dejection, and despair; I say that he is not liberated from great suffering.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while practicing the perfection of wisdom, becomes fixated on form, perceives it, and is convinced of it; by becoming fixated on form, perceiving it, and being convinced of it, he courses in the formative activity of form. I declare that he is not liberated from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair; he is not liberated from great suffering.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while practicing the perfection of wisdom, fixates upon sound, perceives it, and becomes attached to it—fixating upon, perceiving, and becoming attached to that sound—he courses in the formative activity of sound. I declare that he is not liberated from birth, aging, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair; he is not liberated from great suffering.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while practicing the perfection of wisdom, consecrates a fragrance, perceives it, and resolves upon it—consecrating, perceiving, and resolving upon that fragrance—he courses in the formative activity of fragrance. I declare that he is not liberated from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair; he is not liberated from great suffering.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while practicing the perfection of wisdom, exerts his will toward taste, perceives it, and becomes intent upon it—exerting his will toward taste, perceiving it, and becoming intent upon it—

He courses in the formative activity of sensation (*vedanā*). He is not liberated from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, dejection, and despair; I say that he is not liberated from great suffering. If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while coursing in the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), presides over contact (*sparśa*), perceives it, and resolves upon it—presiding over contact, perceiving it, and resolving upon it—he courses in the formative activity of contact.

He is not liberated from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, depression, and despair; I say that he is not liberated from great suffering. This is so if a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while practicing the perfection of wisdom, exerts himself over phenomena, perceives them, and becomes attached to them. By exerting himself over phenomena, perceiving them, and becoming attached to them, he courses in the formative activity of phenomena.
He is not liberated from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, dejection, and despair; I say that he is not liberated from great suffering.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while practicing the perfection of wisdom, presides over, perceives, and becomes intent upon eye-consciousness—presiding over, perceiving, and becoming intent upon eye-consciousness—he courses in the formative activity of eye-consciousness. I declare that he is not liberated from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, depression, and despair; he is not liberated from great suffering.
This applies likewise to ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, and mind-consciousness.

He presides over them, perceives them, and resolves upon them. While thus presiding over, perceiving, and resolving upon them, he courses in their formative activity (*abhisaṃskāra*). He is not liberated from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, dejection, and despair; he is not liberated from great suffering—this I declare.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while practicing the perfection of wisdom, presides over, perceives, and becomes intent upon feeling born of eye-contact—presiding over, perceiving, and becoming intent upon that feeling born of eye-contact—he courses in the formative activity of feeling born of eye-contact.

He is not liberated from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, dejection, and despair; I say that he is not liberated from great suffering. This is if a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while practicing the perfection of wisdom, presides over, perceives, and becomes intent upon the feeling born of ear-contact, the feeling born of nose-contact, the feeling born of tongue-contact, the feeling born of body-contact, and the feeling born of mind-contact.

Presiding over these, perceiving them, and being intent upon them, he courses in their formative activity; he is not fully liberated from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, dejection, and despair, nor is he fully liberated from great suffering—thus I say.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while practicing the perfection of wisdom, courses in the formative activity of ignorance—abiding in ignorance, perceiving it, and being intent upon it—he courses in the formative activity of ignorance. I declare that he is not liberated from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, depression, and despair; he is not liberated from great suffering.
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while practicing the perfection of wisdom, [courses in] formative activity...

He presides over name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, clinging, becoming, birth, and old age and death; he perceives them and resolves upon them. Presiding over these, perceiving them, and resolving upon them, he courses in their formative activity. He is not liberated from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair; he is not liberated from great suffering—so I say.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while practicing the perfection of wisdom, exerts himself toward, perceives, and resolves upon the perfection of giving, the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditative concentration, and the perfection of wisdom—then by so exerting himself, perceiving, and resolving, he courses in the formative activity (*abhisaṃskāra*) of those perfections.
I declare that he is not liberated from birth, aging, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, depression, and despair; he is not liberated from great suffering.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while practicing the perfection of wisdom, dwells upon internal emptiness, perceives it, and resolves upon it—then by dwelling, perceiving, and resolving upon internal emptiness, he courses in the formative activity (*abhisaṃskāra*) of internal emptiness. I declare that he is not liberated from birth, aging, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, dejection, and despair; he is not liberated from great suffering.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while practicing the perfection of wisdom, [contemplates] external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, the emptiness of that which has no beginning or end, the emptiness of non-dispersal, essential emptiness, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of specific characteristics, the emptiness of non-apprehension, the emptiness of non-existence, and the emptiness of intrinsic nature...

He presides over the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence; he perceives it and resolves upon it. While thus presiding, perceiving, and resolving, he courses in conditioned activity. I say that he is not liberated from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, depression, and despair; he is not liberated from great suffering.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while practicing the perfection of wisdom, dwells upon, perceives, and resolves upon the four foundations of mindfulness, then by dwelling upon, perceiving, and resolving upon the four foundations of mindfulness, he courses in the formative activity of the four foundations of mindfulness.
I declare that he is not liberated from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, depression, and despair; he is not liberated from great suffering.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while practicing the perfection of wisdom, presides over, perceives, and resolves upon the four right efforts, then by presiding over, perceiving, and resolving upon them, he courses in the formative activity of the four right efforts. I declare that he is not liberated from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, depression, and despair; he is not liberated from great suffering.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while practicing the perfection of wisdom, presides over the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*), perceives them, and resolves upon them—presiding over, perceiving, and resolving upon those bases of psychic power—he courses in the formative activity of the bases of psychic power. I declare that he is not liberated from birth, aging, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair; he is not liberated from great suffering.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while practicing the perfection of wisdom, presides over the five faculties, perceives them, and resolves upon them—presiding over, perceiving, and resolving upon those five faculties—he courses in the formative activity of the faculties. I declare that he is not liberated from birth, aging, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, depression, and despair; he is not liberated from great suffering.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while practicing the perfection of wisdom, exerts himself toward, perceives, and resolves upon the five powers, then by exerting himself toward, perceiving, and resolving upon the five powers, he courses in the formative activity of those five powers. I declare that he is not liberated from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, depression, and despair; he is not liberated from great suffering.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while practicing the perfection of wisdom, presides over the seven factors of awakening, perceives them, and resolves upon them—if, while presiding over, perceiving, and resolving upon those factors of awakening, he courses in the formative activity of the factors of awakening—he is not liberated from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, depression, and despair; he is not liberated from great suffering—so I say.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while practicing the perfection of wisdom, fixes his attention upon, perceives, and resolves upon the noble eightfold path, then by fixing his attention upon, perceiving, and resolving upon the noble eightfold path, he courses in the formative activity of the noble eightfold path. I declare that he is not liberated from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, depression, and despair; he is not liberated from great suffering.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while practicing the perfection of wisdom, exerts himself toward the noble truths, perceives them, and resolves upon them—if, while exerting himself toward, perceiving, and resolving upon the noble truths, he courses in the formative activity (*abhisaṃskāra*) of the noble truths—then I say that he is not liberated from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, dejection, and despair; he is not liberated from great suffering.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while practicing the perfection of wisdom, presides over the four meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), perceives them, and resolves upon them—then by presiding over, perceiving, and resolving upon those meditative concentrations, he courses in the formative activity (*abhisaṃskāra*) of the concentrations. I declare that he is not liberated from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, depression, and despair; he is not liberated from great suffering.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while practicing the perfection of wisdom, presides over, perceives, and resolves upon the four immeasurables, then by presiding over, perceiving, and resolving upon those four immeasurables, he courses in the formative activity of the immeasurables. I declare that he is not liberated from birth, aging, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, depression, and despair; he is not liberated from great suffering.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while practicing the perfection of wisdom, dwells upon, perceives, and resolves upon the four formless attainments, then by dwelling upon, perceiving, and resolving upon those formless attainments, he courses in the formative activity of the formless attainments. I declare that he is not liberated from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair; he is not liberated from great suffering.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while practicing the perfection of wisdom, presides over, perceives, and resolves upon the eight liberations, then by presiding over, perceiving, and resolving upon these dharmas of liberation, he courses in the formative activity of those dharmas of liberation. I say that he is not liberated from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, depression, and despair; he is not liberated from great suffering.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while practicing the perfection of wisdom, dwells upon, perceives, and resolves upon the gateways to liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—he, dwelling upon, perceiving, and resolving upon them, courses in their formative activity. I declare that he is not liberated from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, dejection, and despair; he is not liberated from great suffering.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while practicing the perfection of wisdom, presides over, perceives, and resolves upon the six superknowledges (*ṣaḍabhijñā*), then by presiding over, perceiving, and resolving upon those superknowledges, he courses in the formative activity (*abhisaṃskāra*) of the superknowledges. I say that he is not liberated from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, dejection, and despair; he is not liberated from great suffering.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while practicing the perfection of wisdom, presides over, perceives, and resolves upon the five eyes—presiding over, perceiving, and resolving upon those five eyes—he courses in the formative activity of the five eyes. I declare that he is not liberated from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, dejection, and despair; he is not liberated from great suffering.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while practicing the perfection of wisdom, presides over, perceives, and is resolved upon the gateways of dhāraṇī—presiding over, perceiving, and being resolved upon those gateways of dhāraṇī—he courses in the formative activity of the gateways of dhāraṇī. I declare that he is not liberated from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair; he is not liberated from great suffering.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while practicing the perfection of wisdom, presides over, perceives, and resolves upon the ten powers of a Tathāgata, then by presiding over, perceiving, and resolving upon those ten powers of a Tathāgata, he courses in the formative activity of the ten powers of a Tathāgata. I declare that he is not liberated from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, depression, and despair; he is not liberated from great suffering.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while practicing the perfection of wisdom, presides over, perceives, and is resolved upon the four grounds of self-confidence (*vaiśāradya*), then by presiding over, perceiving, and being resolved upon those grounds of self-confidence, he courses in the formative activity (*abhisaṃskāra*) of the grounds of self-confidence. I declare that he is not liberated from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, dejection, and despair; he is not liberated from great suffering.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while practicing the perfection of wisdom, presides over, perceives, and resolves upon the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), then by presiding over, perceiving, and resolving upon those analytical knowledges, he courses in the formative activity (*abhisaṃskāra*) of the analytical knowledges. I declare that he is not liberated from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, dejection, and despair; he is not liberated from great suffering.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while practicing the perfection of wisdom, exerts himself toward, perceives, and resolves upon the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha, then by so exerting, perceiving, and resolving, he courses in the formative activity of those eighteen unique qualities of a buddha. I declare that he is not liberated from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, depression, and despair; he is not liberated from great suffering.

Furthermore, Venerable Śāradvatīputra, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva is incapable of realizing the level of a śrāvaka or the level of a pratyekabuddha, how much less could he realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening? Such a thing is impossible. Thus, Venerable Śāradvatīputra, it should be understood that a bodhisattva mahāsattva who courses in the perfection of wisdom is lacking in skillful means. Śāradvatīputra said:
"How, venerable Subhūti, should a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in the perfection of wisdom be known as skillful in means?"

Subhūti said: "Venerable Śāradvatīputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices in the perfection of wisdom, he does not practice with respect to form; he does not practice with respect to the sign of form. He does not practice thinking 'form is permanent,' nor does he practice thinking 'form is impermanent. He does not practice thinking 'form is happiness,' nor does he practice thinking 'form is suffering. He does not practice thinking 'form is self,' nor does he practice thinking 'form is non-self. He does not practice thinking 'form is peace.'"

One does not practice with the thought that form is unpeaceful; one does not practice with the thought that form is empty; one does not practice with the thought that form is non-empty; one does not practice with the thought that form has signs; one does not practice with the thought that form is signless; one does not practice with the thought that form is wishful; one does not practice with the thought that form is wishless; one does not practice with the thought that form is secluded; one does not practice with the thought that form is not secluded.

He does not course in feeling; he does not course in the sign of feeling. He does not course in the notion that "feeling is permanent," nor does he course in the notion that "feeling is impermanent. He does not course in the notion that "feeling is pleasant," nor does he course in the notion that "feeling is painful. He does not course in the notion that "feeling is self," nor does he course in the notion that "feeling is non-self. He does not course in the notion that "feeling is peaceful," nor does he course in the notion that "feeling is unpeaceful. He does not course in the notion that "feeling is empty," nor does he course in the notion that "feeling is non-empty. He does not course in the notion that "feeling is a sign."

He does not course in the notion that "feeling has a sign"; he does not course in the notion that "feeling is with aspiration," nor does he course in the notion that "feeling is without aspiration"; he does not course in the notion that "feeling is secluded," nor does he course in the notion that "feeling is not secluded.

He does not course in perception; he does not course in the sign of perception; he does not course in the notion that "perception is permanent," nor does he course in the notion that "perception is impermanent"; he does not course in the notion that "perception is pleasant," nor does he course in the notion that "perception is painful"; he does not course in the notion that "perception is self."

He does not course in the thought that perception is the self; he does not course in the thought that perception is peaceful; he does not course in the thought that perception is not peaceful. He does not course in the thought that perception is empty; he does not course in the thought that perception is not empty. He does not course in the thought that perception has signs; he does not course in the thought that perception is signless. He does not course in the thought that perception is with aspiration; he does not course in the thought that perception is without aspiration. He does not course in the thought that perception is secluded; he does not course in the thought that perception is not secluded.

He does not course in the formative forces (*saṃskāra*); he does not course in the sign of the formative forces. He does not course [with the thought] that "the formative forces are permanent"; he does not course [with the thought] that "the formative forces are impermanent. He does not course [with the thought] that "the formative forces are pleasant"; he does not course [with the thought] that "the formative forces are painful. He does not course [with the thought] that "the formative forces are self"; he does not course [with the thought] that "the formative forces are non-self. He does not course [with the thought] that "the formative forces are peaceful"; he does not course [with the thought] that "the formative forces are not peaceful. He does not course [with the thought] that "the formative forces are empty."

He does not course in the notion that formations are non-empty; he does not course in the notion that formations have signs; he does not course in the notion that formations are signless; he does not course in the notion that formations are with wish; he does not course in the notion that formations are wishless; he does not course in the notion that formations are secluded; he does not course in the notion that formations are not secluded.

One does not course in consciousness; one does not course in the sign of consciousness. One does not course [with the thought] that "consciousness is pleasure," nor does one course [with the thought] that "consciousness is suffering. One does not course [with the thought] that "consciousness is peaceful," nor does one course [with the thought] that "consciousness is unpeaceful. One does not course [with the thought] that "consciousness is empty."

He does not course in the notion that consciousness is non-empty; he does not course in the notion that consciousness has signs; he does not course in the notion that consciousness is signless; he does not course in the notion that consciousness is with aspiration; he does not course in the notion that consciousness is without aspiration; he does not course in the notion that consciousness is secluded; he does not course in the notion that consciousness is not secluded.

One does not course in the eye; one does not course in the sign of the eye. He does not course in the ear; he does not course in the signs of the ear. He does not course [thinking] "the ear is permanent"; he does not course [thinking] "the ear is impermanent. He does not course [thinking] "the body is peaceful"; he does not course [thinking] "the body is unpeaceful. He practices with the thought that "it is not empty. He practices by taking the body as a sign; he does not practice by taking the body as signless. He does not course in form; he does not course in the sign of form. He does not course [thinking] "form is permanent," nor does he course [thinking] "form is impermanent. He does not course in sound; he does not course in the sign of sound. He does not course [with the thought] "sound is permanent"; he does not course [with the thought] "sound is impermanent. He does not course in phenomena; he does not course in the signs of phenomena. He does not course with the thought that "dharmas are not empty"; he does not course with the thought that "dharmas have signs"; he does not course with the thought that "dharmas are signless"; he does not course with the thought that "dharmas are wishful"; he does not course with the thought that "dharmas are wishless"; he does not course with the thought that "dharmas are secluded"; he does not course with the thought that "dharmas are not secluded."

One does not course in the eye-element; one does not course in the sign of the eye-element. That which is the emptiness of the body is not that body; the body is not other than emptiness.

Emptiness is not other than the body; emptiness itself is the body, and the body itself is emptiness. That which is the emptiness of the mind is not that mind; nor is the mind other than emptiness, nor is emptiness other than the mind. Emptiness itself is the mind, and the mind itself is emptiness.

That which is the emptiness of form is not form; nor is form apart from emptiness, nor is emptiness apart from form. Emptiness itself is form; form itself is emptiness. That which is the emptiness of sound is not sound; nor is sound apart from emptiness, nor is emptiness apart from sound. Emptiness itself is sound; sound itself is emptiness. That which is the emptiness of odor is not odor; nor is odor apart from emptiness.

Emptiness is not other than odor; emptiness itself is odor, and odor itself is emptiness. That which is the emptiness of taste is not that taste; nor is taste other than emptiness, nor is emptiness other than taste. Emptiness itself is taste, and taste itself is emptiness. That which is the emptiness of touch is not that touch; nor is touch other than emptiness, nor is emptiness other than touch. Emptiness itself is touch, and touch itself is emptiness.

That which is the emptiness of phenomena is not those phenomena; nor are phenomena apart from emptiness, nor is emptiness apart from phenomena. Emptiness itself is phenomena; phenomena themselves are emptiness.

That which is the emptiness of the eye-element is not the eye-element; nor is the eye-element elsewhere than in emptiness, nor is emptiness elsewhere than in the eye-element. Emptiness itself is the eye-element, and the eye-element itself is emptiness. That which is the emptiness of the form-element is not the form-element; nor is the form-element elsewhere than in emptiness, nor is emptiness elsewhere than in the form-element. Emptiness itself is the form-element, and the form-element itself is emptiness.

That which is the emptiness of the eye-consciousness element is not the eye-consciousness element; nor is the eye-consciousness element elsewhere than in emptiness, nor is emptiness elsewhere than in the eye-consciousness element. Emptiness itself is the eye-consciousness element.

The eye-consciousness element itself is emptiness. That which is the emptiness of the ear element is not the ear element; nor is the ear element elsewhere than in emptiness, nor is emptiness elsewhere than in the ear element. Emptiness itself is the ear element; the ear element itself is emptiness. That which is the emptiness of the sound element is not the sound element; nor is the sound element elsewhere than in emptiness, nor is emptiness elsewhere than in the sound element. Emptiness itself is the sound element.

The sound-element itself is emptiness; that which is the emptiness of the ear-consciousness-element is not that ear-consciousness-element, nor is the ear-consciousness-element elsewhere than in emptiness, nor is emptiness elsewhere than in the ear-consciousness-element. Emptiness itself is the ear-consciousness-element, and the ear-consciousness-element itself is emptiness. That which is the emptiness of the nose-element is not that nose-element, nor is the nose-element elsewhere than in emptiness, nor is emptiness elsewhere than in the nose-element.

Emptiness itself is the nose-element; the nose-element itself is emptiness. That which is the emptiness of the odor-element is not that odor-element, nor is there an odor-element apart from emptiness, nor is there emptiness apart from the odor-element. Emptiness itself is the odor-element; the odor-element itself is emptiness. That which is the emptiness of the nose-consciousness-element is not that nose-consciousness-element, nor is there a nose-consciousness-element apart from emptiness.

The emptiness of the nose-consciousness element is not other than the nose-consciousness element; the nose-consciousness element is itself emptiness, and emptiness is itself the nose-consciousness element. That which is the emptiness of the tongue element is not that tongue element; nor is the tongue element other than emptiness, and emptiness is not other than the tongue element. The tongue element is itself emptiness, and emptiness is itself the tongue element. That which is the emptiness of the taste element is not that taste element; nor is the taste element other than emptiness.

Emptiness is not other than the taste-element; emptiness itself is the taste-element, and the taste-element itself is emptiness. That which is the emptiness of the tongue-consciousness-element is not that tongue-consciousness-element, nor is it other than emptiness.

The tongue-consciousness element; there is no emptiness apart from the tongue-consciousness element, and the tongue-consciousness element itself is emptiness, and emptiness itself is the tongue-consciousness element. That which is the emptiness of the body element is not that body element; nor is the body element apart from emptiness, and emptiness is not apart from the body element. Emptiness itself is the body element, and the body element itself is emptiness. That which is the emptiness of the contact element is not that contact element.
Nor is the element of contact other than emptiness; nor is emptiness other than the element of contact. Emptiness itself is the element of contact; the element of contact itself is emptiness.

That which is the emptiness of the body-consciousness element is not that body-consciousness element; nor is the body-consciousness element elsewhere than in emptiness, nor is emptiness elsewhere than in the body-consciousness element. Emptiness itself is the body-consciousness element; the body-consciousness element itself is emptiness. That which is the emptiness of the mind element is not that mind element; nor is the mind element elsewhere than in emptiness, nor is emptiness elsewhere than in the mind element. Emptiness itself is the mind element; the mind element itself is emptiness.

That which is the emptiness of the dharma-realm is not the dharma-realm; nor is the dharma-realm apart from emptiness, nor is emptiness apart from the dharma-realm. Emptiness itself is the dharma-realm; the dharma-realm itself is emptiness. That which is the emptiness of the mental-consciousness-element is not the mental-consciousness-element; nor is the mental-consciousness-element apart from emptiness, nor is emptiness apart from the mental-consciousness-element. Emptiness itself is the mental-consciousness-element; the mental-consciousness-element itself is emptiness.

That which is the emptiness of the earth element is not the earth element; nor is the earth element elsewhere than in emptiness, nor is emptiness elsewhere than in the earth element. Emptiness itself is the earth element; the earth element itself is emptiness. That which is the emptiness of the water element is not the water element; nor is the water element elsewhere than in emptiness, nor is [emptiness] elsewhere than in the water element.

Emptiness: emptiness itself is the water element; the water element itself is emptiness. That which is the emptiness of the fire element is not that fire element; nor is the fire element elsewhere than in emptiness, nor is emptiness elsewhere than in the fire element. Emptiness itself is the fire element; the fire element itself is emptiness. That which is the emptiness of the air element is not that air element; nor is the air element elsewhere than in emptiness, nor is emptiness elsewhere than in the air element. Emptiness itself is the air element.

The wind element itself is emptiness. That which is the emptiness of the space element is not the space element; nor is the space element apart from emptiness, nor is emptiness apart from the space element. Emptiness itself is the space element; the space element itself is emptiness.

That which is the emptiness of the element of consciousness is not that element of consciousness; nor is the element of consciousness elsewhere than in emptiness, nor is emptiness elsewhere than in the element of consciousness. Emptiness itself is the element of consciousness, and the element of consciousness itself is emptiness. That which is the emptiness of ignorance is not that ignorance; nor is ignorance elsewhere than in emptiness, nor is emptiness elsewhere than in ignorance. Ignorance itself is conditioned, and ignorance itself is emptiness. That which is the emptiness of volitional formations is not those volitional formations.

And conditioned phenomena are not other than emptiness; emptiness is not other than conditioned phenomena. Emptiness itself is the conditioned phenomena; the conditioned phenomena themselves are emptiness. That which is the emptiness of consciousness is not that consciousness; and consciousness is not other than emptiness; emptiness is not other than consciousness. Emptiness itself is consciousness; consciousness itself is emptiness.

That which is the emptiness of name-and-form is not that name-and-form; nor is name-and-form apart from emptiness, nor is emptiness apart from name-and-form. Emptiness itself is name-and-form; name-and-form itself is emptiness. That which is the emptiness of the six sense-bases is not those six sense-bases; nor are the six sense-bases apart from emptiness, nor is emptiness apart from the six sense-bases. Emptiness itself is the six sense-bases; the six sense-bases themselves are emptiness. That which is the emptiness of contact is not that...

Contact: contact is not other than emptiness, nor is emptiness other than contact; emptiness itself is contact, and contact itself is emptiness. That which is the emptiness of feeling is not that feeling; nor is feeling other than emptiness, nor is emptiness other than feeling; emptiness itself is feeling, and feeling itself is emptiness. That which is the emptiness of craving is not that craving; nor is craving other than emptiness, nor is emptiness other than craving.

Emptiness itself is craving; craving itself is emptiness. That which is the emptiness of grasping is not grasping, nor is grasping apart from emptiness, nor is emptiness apart from grasping. Emptiness itself is grasping; grasping itself is emptiness. That which is the emptiness of existence is not existence, nor is existence apart from emptiness, nor is emptiness apart from existence. Emptiness itself is existence; existence itself is emptiness. That which is the emptiness of birth is not birth.

There is no birth apart from emptiness, nor is there emptiness apart from birth; emptiness itself is birth, and birth itself is emptiness. That which is the emptiness of old age and death is not old age and death; there is no old age and death apart from emptiness, nor is there emptiness apart from old age and death; emptiness itself is old age and death, and old age and death itself is emptiness.

That which is the emptiness of the perfection of generosity is not the perfection of generosity; nor is the perfection of generosity apart from emptiness, nor is emptiness apart from the perfection of generosity. Emptiness itself is the perfection of generosity; the perfection of generosity itself is emptiness. That which is the emptiness of the perfection of ethical discipline is not the perfection of ethical discipline; nor is the perfection of ethical discipline apart from emptiness, nor is emptiness apart from the perfection of ethical discipline. Emptiness itself...

The perfection of ethical discipline; the perfection of ethical discipline itself is emptiness. That which is the emptiness of the perfection of patience is not the perfection of patience, nor is the perfection of patience apart from emptiness, nor is emptiness apart from the perfection of patience; emptiness itself is the perfection of patience, and the perfection of patience itself is emptiness. That which is the emptiness of the perfection of vigor is not the perfection of vigor, nor is the perfection of vigor apart from emptiness, nor is emptiness apart from the perfection of vigor.

Emptiness itself is the perfection of vigor; the perfection of vigor itself is emptiness. That which is the emptiness of the perfection of meditation is not the perfection of meditation, nor is the perfection of meditation apart from emptiness; there is no emptiness apart from the perfection of meditation. Emptiness itself is the perfection of meditation; the perfection of meditation itself is emptiness. That which is the emptiness of the perfection of wisdom is not the perfection of wisdom, nor is the perfection of wisdom apart from emptiness.
Emptiness is not other than the perfection of wisdom; emptiness itself is the perfection of wisdom, and the perfection of wisdom itself is emptiness.

That which is the emptiness of internal emptiness is not that internal emptiness; nor is internal emptiness apart from emptiness, nor is emptiness apart from internal emptiness. Emptiness itself is internal emptiness; internal emptiness itself is emptiness. That which is the emptiness of external emptiness is not that external emptiness; nor is external emptiness apart from emptiness, nor is emptiness apart from external emptiness.

Emptiness itself is external emptiness; external emptiness itself is emptiness. That which is the emptiness of internal-external emptiness is not that internal-external emptiness, nor is internal-external emptiness apart from emptiness, nor is emptiness apart from internal-external emptiness. Emptiness itself is internal-external emptiness.

The emptiness of the internal and external is itself emptiness. That which is the emptiness of the emptiness of emptiness is not [merely] the emptiness of emptiness; nor is the emptiness of emptiness apart from emptiness, nor is emptiness apart from the emptiness of emptiness. Emptiness itself is the emptiness of emptiness, and the emptiness of emptiness itself is emptiness. That which is the emptiness of the great emptiness is not [merely] the great emptiness; nor is the great emptiness apart from emptiness, nor is emptiness apart from the great emptiness.

Emptiness itself is great emptiness; great emptiness itself is emptiness. That which is the emptiness of the emptiness of ultimate reality is not that [separate] emptiness of ultimate reality; nor is the emptiness of ultimate reality elsewhere than in emptiness. Emptiness itself is the emptiness of ultimate reality; the emptiness of ultimate reality itself is emptiness. That which is the emptiness of the emptiness of conditioned phenomena is not that [separate] emptiness of conditioned phenomena; nor is the emptiness of conditioned phenomena elsewhere than in emptiness.

Emptiness is not other than the emptiness of the conditioned; emptiness itself is the emptiness of the conditioned, and the emptiness of the conditioned itself is emptiness. That which is the emptiness of the emptiness of the unconditioned is not that emptiness of the unconditioned; nor is the emptiness of the unconditioned other than emptiness, nor is emptiness other than the emptiness of the unconditioned. Emptiness itself is the emptiness of the unconditioned, and the emptiness of the unconditioned itself is emptiness. That which is the emptiness of the emptiness of the absolute is not that absolute emptiness.

Nor is absolute emptiness other than emptiness; nor is emptiness other than absolute emptiness. Emptiness itself is absolute emptiness; absolute emptiness itself is emptiness. The emptiness of the emptiness of the beginningless and endless is not that emptiness of the beginningless and endless. Nor is the emptiness of the beginningless and endless other than emptiness; nor is emptiness other than the emptiness of the beginningless and endless. Emptiness itself is the emptiness of the beginningless and endless. The emptiness of the emptiness of non-dispersal is not that emptiness of non-dispersal.

Nor is non-dispersal emptiness other than emptiness; nor is emptiness other than non-dispersal emptiness. Emptiness itself is non-dispersal emptiness; non-dispersal emptiness itself is emptiness. That which is the emptiness of the emptiness of intrinsic nature is not that intrinsic nature; nor is intrinsic nature emptiness other than emptiness; nor is emptiness intrinsic nature other than intrinsic nature emptiness. Emptiness itself is intrinsic nature emptiness; intrinsic nature emptiness itself is emptiness. That which is the emptiness of the emptiness of all phenomena is not that [intrinsic] emptiness of all phenomena.

The emptiness of all phenomena is not other than emptiness; emptiness is not other than the emptiness of all phenomena. Emptiness itself is the emptiness of all phenomena, and the emptiness of all phenomena itself is emptiness. That which is the emptiness of the emptiness of specific characteristics is not that emptiness of specific characteristics; nor is the emptiness of specific characteristics other than emptiness, nor is emptiness other than the emptiness of specific characteristics. Emptiness itself is the emptiness of specific characteristics.

The emptiness of specific characteristics is itself emptiness. That which is the emptiness of the emptiness of non-apprehension is not that emptiness of non-apprehension; nor is the emptiness of non-apprehension found apart from emptiness, nor is emptiness found apart from the emptiness of non-apprehension. Emptiness itself is the emptiness of non-apprehension, and the emptiness of non-apprehension itself is emptiness. That which is the emptiness of the emptiness of non-existence is not that emptiness of non-existence; nor is the emptiness of non-existence found apart from emptiness.

Emptiness is not other than the emptiness of non-existence; emptiness itself is the emptiness of non-existence, and the emptiness of non-existence itself is emptiness. That which is the emptiness of the emptiness of intrinsic nature is not [itself] the emptiness of intrinsic nature, nor is the emptiness of intrinsic nature other than emptiness, nor is emptiness other than the emptiness of intrinsic nature. Emptiness itself is the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of intrinsic nature itself is emptiness. That which is the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence is not [itself] the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence.

Emptiness is not other than the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence; the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence is not other than emptiness. Emptiness itself is the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence; the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence itself is emptiness.

That which is the emptiness of the four foundations of mindfulness is not those foundations of mindfulness; nor are the foundations of mindfulness apart from emptiness, nor is emptiness apart from the foundations of mindfulness. Emptiness itself is the foundations of mindfulness, and the foundations of mindfulness themselves are emptiness. That which is the emptiness of the four right efforts is not those right efforts; nor are the right efforts apart from emptiness, nor is emptiness apart from the right efforts.

Emptiness itself is the right efforts; the right efforts themselves are emptiness. That which is the emptiness of the four bases of psychic power is not those bases of psychic power, nor are the bases of psychic power apart from emptiness, nor is emptiness apart from the bases of psychic power. Emptiness itself is the bases of psychic power; the bases of psychic power themselves are emptiness. That which is the emptiness of the five faculties is not those faculties, nor are the faculties apart from emptiness, nor is emptiness apart from the faculties.

Emptiness itself is the faculties; the faculties themselves are emptiness. That which is the emptiness of the five powers is not those powers, nor are the powers elsewhere than in emptiness, nor is emptiness elsewhere than in the powers. Emptiness itself is the powers; the powers themselves are emptiness. That which is the emptiness of the seven factors of awakening is not those factors of awakening, nor are the factors of awakening elsewhere than in emptiness, nor is emptiness elsewhere than in the factors of awakening. Emptiness itself is the factors of awakening; the factors of awakening themselves are emptiness.

That which is the emptiness of the noble eightfold path is not the noble eightfold path; nor is the noble eightfold path apart from emptiness, nor is emptiness apart from the noble eightfold path. Emptiness itself is the noble eightfold path; the noble eightfold path itself is emptiness. That which is the emptiness of the four noble truths is not those noble truths; nor are the noble truths apart from emptiness, nor is emptiness apart from the noble truths. Emptiness itself is the noble truths; the noble truths themselves are emptiness. That which is the emptiness of the four meditative absorptions...

Emptiness is not those meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*); nor is emptiness apart from the meditative absorptions. Emptiness is not apart from the meditative absorptions; emptiness itself is the meditative absorptions, and the meditative absorptions themselves are emptiness. That which is the emptiness of the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*) is not those immeasurables; nor are the immeasurables apart from emptiness. Emptiness is not apart from the immeasurables; emptiness itself is the immeasurables, and the immeasurables themselves are emptiness.

That which is the emptiness of the four formless attainments is not those formless attainments; nor are the formless attainments apart from emptiness, nor is emptiness apart from the formless attainments. Emptiness itself is the formless attainments; the formless attainments themselves are emptiness. That which is the emptiness of the eight liberations is not those liberations; nor are the liberations apart from emptiness, nor is emptiness apart from the liberations. Emptiness itself is the liberations.

The liberations themselves are emptiness. That which is the emptiness of the nine successive meditative attainments is not those successive meditative attainments; yet the successive meditative attainments do not exist apart from emptiness, nor does emptiness exist apart from the successive meditative attainments. Emptiness itself is the successive meditative attainments, and the successive meditative attainments themselves are emptiness.

The emptiness that is the emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness of the doors of liberation is not those doors of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; nor are the doors of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—apart from emptiness. Nor is emptiness apart from the doors of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness. Emptiness itself is the doors of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; the doors of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—are themselves emptiness.

That which is the emptiness of the five superknowledges is not those superknowledges; nor are the superknowledges elsewhere than in emptiness, nor is emptiness elsewhere than in the superknowledges. Emptiness itself is the superknowledges; the superknowledges themselves are emptiness. That which is the [emptiness] of the meditative concentrations...

Emptiness is not those meditative absorptions; nor are the meditative absorptions elsewhere than emptiness. Emptiness is not elsewhere than the meditative absorptions. Emptiness itself is the meditative absorptions; the meditative absorptions themselves are emptiness. That which is the emptiness of the gateways of mnemonic formulas (*dhāraṇīmukha*) is not those gateways of mnemonic formulas; nor are the gateways of mnemonic formulas elsewhere than emptiness. Emptiness is not elsewhere than the gateways of mnemonic formulas. Emptiness itself is the gateways of mnemonic formulas; the gateways of mnemonic formulas themselves are emptiness.

That which is the emptiness of the ten powers of a Tathāgata is not those ten powers of a Tathāgata; nor are the powers of a Tathāgata apart from emptiness, nor is emptiness apart from the powers of a Tathāgata. Emptiness itself is the powers of a Tathāgata, and the powers of a Tathāgata themselves are emptiness. That which is the emptiness of the four grounds of self-confidence is not those grounds of self-confidence; nor are the grounds of self-confidence apart from emptiness, nor is emptiness apart from the grounds of self-confidence.

Emptiness itself is the grounds of self-confidence; the grounds of self-confidence themselves are emptiness. That which is the emptiness of the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) is not those analytical knowledges, nor are the analytical knowledges apart from emptiness, nor is emptiness apart from the analytical knowledges. Emptiness itself is the analytical knowledges; the analytical knowledges themselves are emptiness. That which is the emptiness of great loving-kindness (*mahāmaitrī*) is not that great loving-kindness, nor is great loving-kindness apart from emptiness.

Emptiness is not other than great loving-kindness; emptiness itself is great loving-kindness, and great loving-kindness itself is emptiness. That which is the emptiness of great compassion is not that great compassion; yet great compassion is not other than emptiness, nor is emptiness other than great compassion. Emptiness itself is great compassion, and great compassion itself is emptiness. That which is the emptiness of the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha is not those unique qualities of a Buddha.

The unique qualities of a Buddha (āveṇikabuddhadharma) are not other than emptiness, nor is emptiness other than the unique qualities of a Buddha. Emptiness itself is the unique qualities of a Buddha; the unique qualities of a Buddha themselves are emptiness.

That which is the emptiness of omniscience is not that omniscience; nor is omniscience apart from emptiness, nor is emptiness apart from omniscience. Emptiness itself is omniscience; omniscience itself is emptiness. That which is the emptiness of the knowledge of the aspects of the path is not that knowledge of the aspects of the path; nor is the knowledge of the aspects of the path apart from emptiness, nor is emptiness apart from the knowledge of the aspects of the path. Emptiness itself is the knowledge of the aspects of the path.

The knowledge of the aspects of the path itself is emptiness; that which is the emptiness of the knowledge of all aspects is not that knowledge of all aspects, nor is the knowledge of all aspects elsewhere than in emptiness, nor is emptiness elsewhere than in the knowledge of all aspects. Emptiness itself is the knowledge of all aspects; the knowledge of all aspects itself is emptiness.

In this way, venerable Śāradvatīputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom should be known as skillful in means. Indeed, venerable Śāradvatīputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom in this manner is capable of awakening to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. Furthermore, that bodhisattva mahāsattva does not apprehend "I am practicing the perfection of wisdom," nor does he apprehend "I am not practicing."

“I am practicing,” he does not approach; “I am not practicing,” he does not approach; “I am both practicing and not practicing,” he does not approach; Śāradvatīputra said: “For what reason, venerable Subhūti, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while practicing in the perfection of wisdom, not approach ‘I am practicing,’ nor approach ‘I am not practicing,’ nor approach ‘I am both practicing and not practicing,’ nor even approach ‘I am neither practicing nor not practicing’? Subhūti replied:

For in this way, venerable Śāradvatīputra, no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is apprehended in the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*). Why is that? Because the perfection of wisdom has non-existence as its intrinsic nature. By this method, venerable Śāradvatīputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not approach [the thought], "I am practicing in the perfection of wisdom," nor does he approach [the thought], "I am not practicing."

He does not approach the thought, "I am practicing" or "I am not practicing"; nor does he even approach the thought, "I am neither practicing nor not practicing. Why is that? Because by him all phenomena have been understood as having non-existence as their intrinsic nature, and thus they are not grasped. If, while practicing in this way in the perfection of wisdom, the mind of the bodhisattva mahāsattva does not sink down, does not become dejected, does not tremble, does not become terrified, and does not fall into a state of panic—
"Venerable Śāradvatīputra, it should be known that this bodhisattva mahāsattva is drawing near to all-aspect omniscience."

Furthermore, that very omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*) is non-dual and indivisible, based on the fact that all phenomena have the nature of non-existence. This is the samādhi of Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas called "the non-arising of all phenomena" (*sarvadharmanutpāda*); it is vast, preeminent, immeasurably fixed, and cannot be surpassed by any Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas. Abiding in this samādhi, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva will swiftly awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

He asked: "Furthermore, Venerable Subhūti, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwelling by means of this very samādhi quickly awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, or rather by other samādhis as well? Subhūti replied: "Venerable Śāradvatīputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwelling by means of other samādhis as well quickly awakens to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."

[Śāriputra] asked: "Furthermore, Venerable Subhūti, by dwelling in which other samādhis does a bodhisattva mahāsattva quickly awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment? Subhūti replied: "There is a samādhi called Śūraṅgama; by dwelling in that samādhi, a bodhisattva mahāsattva quickly awakens to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."

There is a samādhi called "Lion’s Play," by dwelling in which samādhi a bodhisattva mahāsattva quickly awakens to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. There is a samādhi called "Beautiful Moon," by dwelling in which samādhi a bodhisattva mahāsattva quickly awakens to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. There is a samādhi called "Moon Banner Crest," by dwelling in which samādhi a bodhisattva mahāsattva quickly awakens to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

There is a samādhi called "Arising of All Dharmas," by dwelling in which samādhi a bodhisattva mahāsattva quickly awakens to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. There is a samādhi called "Seal of All Dharmas," by dwelling in which samādhi a bodhisattva mahāsattva quickly awakens to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

There is a samādhi called "Beholding the Summit," by dwelling in which samādhi a bodhisattva mahāsattva quickly awakens to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. There is a samādhi called "Determined in the Dharmadhātu," by dwelling in which samādhi a bodhisattva mahāsattva quickly awakens to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

There is a samādhi called "Fixed Banner and Sign," by dwelling in which samādhi a bodhisattva mahāsattva quickly awakens to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. There is a samādhi called "Vajra," by dwelling in which samādhi a bodhisattva mahāsattva quickly awakens to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

There is a samādhi called the Seal of Entry into All Dharmas; dwelling in this samādhi, a bodhisattva mahāsattva quickly awakens to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. There is a samādhi called the Emission of Rays; dwelling in this samādhi, a bodhisattva mahāsattva quickly awakens to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

There is a samādhi called the Array of Power (*balavyūha*), by dwelling in which samādhi a bodhisattva mahāsattva quickly awakens to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. There is a samādhi called the Emergent (*samudgata*), by dwelling in which samādhi a bodhisattva mahāsattva quickly awakens to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. There is [a samādhi called] the Entrance into the Certainty of Etymology (*niruktiniyatapraveśa*).

There is a samādhi called "Name," by dwelling in which samādhi a bodhisattva mahāsattva quickly awakens to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. There is a samādhi called "Entry into Designations," by dwelling in which samādhi a bodhisattva mahāsattva quickly awakens to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

There is a samādhi called "Surveying the Directions," by dwelling in which samādhi a bodhisattva mahāsattva quickly awakens to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
