In the non-appearance of the emptiness of that which is without beginning or end, no footing is found. In the non-apprehension of the emptiness of that which is without beginning or end, no footing is found. Subhūti, in the non-arising of the emptiness of non-dispersal, no footing is found. In the non-affliction and non-purification of the emptiness of non-apprehension, no footing is found. In the non-conditioning of the emptiness of non-apprehension, no footing is found. In the non-manifestation of the emptiness of non-apprehension, no footing is found. In the non-apprehension of the emptiness of non-apprehension, no footing is found. In the non-affliction and non-purification of the emptiness of non-existence, no track is found. In the lack of volitional formation of the emptiness of non-existence, no track is found. In the non-appearance of the emptiness of non-existence, no track is found. In the non-apprehension of the emptiness of non-existence, no track is found. In the emptiness of intrinsic nature, no footing is found for affliction or purification; in the emptiness of intrinsic nature, no footing is found for volitional formation; in the emptiness of intrinsic nature, no footing is found for manifestation; in the emptiness of intrinsic nature, no footing is found for non-apprehension. In the non-cessation of the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence, no footing is found. In the non-ceasing of the bases of psychic power, no footprint is found; in the non-affliction and non-purification of the bases of psychic power, no footprint is found; in the non-conditioning of the bases of psychic power, no footprint is found; in the non-appearance of the bases of psychic power, no footprint is found; in the non-apprehension of the bases of psychic power, no footprint is found.

There is no footing for the factors of enlightenment in their lack of volitional formation; there is no footing for the factors of enlightenment in their non-appearance; there is no footing for the factors of enlightenment in their non-apprehension. Subhūti, there is no footing for the noble eightfold path in its non-arising; there is no footing for the noble eightfold path in its non-cessation; there is no footing for the noble eightfold path in its lack of affliction and lack of purification; there is no footing for the noble eightfold path in its lack of volitional formation.

Of the immeasurables...

In the non-apprehension of the superknowledges, no footing is found. Subhūti, in the non-arising of the meditative concentrations (*samādhi*), no footing is found. In the non-cessation of the meditative concentrations, no footing is found. In the non-affliction and non-purification of the meditative concentrations, no footing is found.

In the non-conditioning of meditative concentrations, no footing is found; in the non-appearance of meditative concentrations, no footing is found; in the non-apprehension of meditative concentrations, no footing is found. In the non-appearance of the gateways of dhāraṇī, no track is found; in the non-apprehension of the gateways of dhāraṇī, no track is found. Subhūti, it is just as if, for example, in the absolute purity of the powers of a Tathāgata, no sign or basis is found; in the absolute purity of the grounds of self-confidence, no sign or basis is found; in the absolute purity of the analytical knowledges, no sign or basis is found; in the absolute purity of great loving-kindness, no sign or basis is found; and in the absolute purity of great compassion, no sign or basis is found.

No footprint is found, because of the non-existence of a living being (*sattva*). In the same way, Subhūti, for a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), no referent for the term "bodhisattva" is found. Just as, Subhūti, no footprint is found when life is utterly pure, because of the non-existence of a living being, even so, Subhūti, for a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in the perfection of wisdom, no referent for the term "bodhisattva" is found.

Just as, Subhūti, in the knowledge and vision of liberation of a Tathāgata, Arhat, perfectly awakened Buddha, no trace is found.

Subhūti, it is just as, for example, no trace of the radiance of the gods of Immeasurable Light (Apramāṇābha) can be found; even so, Subhūti, for a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom, no referent for the term "bodhisattva" [can be found].

In the same way, Subhūti, for a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in the perfection of wisdom, the referent of the term "bodhisattva" does not exist. Why is that? Because awakening, the bodhisattva, and the referent of the term "bodhisattva"—all these phenomena are nowhere conjoined or fully joined; they are formless, invisible, non-obstructive, and characterized by a single characteristic (or, alternatively, non-obstructive and of one characteristic).

That is to say, they are without characteristics (*alakṣaṇa*). Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should train in the non-existence of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-asadbhūtatā*); and all phenomena must be fully realized by the bodhisattva mahāsattva. Subhūti asked: "Blessed One, what are all phenomena? Blessed One, how should a bodhisattva mahāsattva train in their non-existence? And how should a bodhisattva mahāsattva realize all phenomena? The Blessed One said:

Subhūti, all phenomena are said to be wholesome and unwholesome, unconditioned and conditioned, worldly and supramundane, with outflows and without outflows, conditioned and unconditioned, blameworthy and blameless, and common and uncommon. Subhūti, these are called wholesome phenomena. A bodhisattva mahāsattva should train in the non-existence of all these phenomena.
Subhūti, these are all the phenomena that must be fully understood by a bodhisattva mahāsattva.

[Subhūti] asked: "Blessed One, what are the mundane wholesome dharmas? The Blessed One replied: "Subhūti, the mundane wholesome dharmas are said to be: reverence for one's mother, reverence for one's father, proper conduct toward śramaṇas, proper conduct toward brahmins, and honoring the elders of the family; the basis of meritorious action consisting of giving, the basis of meritorious action consisting of ethical discipline, the basis of meritorious action consisting of cultivation; that which is accompanied by the practice of healing and medicinal treatment; the ten paths of wholesome action; and the nine mundane perceptions."

Namely: the perception of a bloated corpse, the perception of a discolored corpse, the perception of a festering corpse, the perception of a bloody corpse, the perception of a mangled corpse, the perception of a gnawed corpse, the perception of a scattered corpse, the perception of a mutilated corpse, the perception of a burned corpse, the perception of a skeleton; the four worldly dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, the five superknowledges, and the ten worldly recollections.

Namely: recollection of the Buddha, recollection of the Dharma, recollection of the Saṅgha, recollection of ethical discipline, recollection of relinquishment, recollection of inhalation and exhalation, recollection directed toward the body, recollection of world-weariness, and recollection of death. These, Subhūti, are called the wholesome worldly dharmas. Subhūti asked: "Blessed One, what are the unwholesome worldly dharmas? The Blessed One replied: "The ten unwholesome paths of action. Namely, Subhūti, the taking of life is an unwholesome worldly dharma."

Subhūti, taking what is not given is an unwholesome worldly dharma. Subhūti, sexual misconduct is an unwholesome worldly dharma. Subhūti, false speech is an unwholesome worldly dharma. Subhūti, harsh speech is an unwholesome worldly dharma. Subhūti, covetousness is an unwholesome worldly dharma. Subhūti, ill will is an unwholesome worldly dharma. Subhūti, wrong view is an unwholesome worldly dharma.

Anger, enmity, hypocrisy, malice, harmfulness, envy, avarice, pride, and false conceit—these, Subhūti, are called the unwholesome worldly dharmas. [Subhūti] asked: "Blessed One, what are the indeterminate dharmas? The Blessed One said:

Indeterminate bodily action, indeterminate vocal action, indeterminate mental action; indeterminate great elements; indeterminate five faculties; indeterminate six sense bases; indeterminate four formless attainments; indeterminate aggregates; indeterminate elements; indeterminate bases; and all retribution—these are called indeterminate phenomena. He said:

“Blessed One, what are mundane dharmas? The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, mundane dharmas are said to be the five aggregates, the twelve sense bases, the eighteen elements, the ten paths of wholesome action, the four meditative absorptions, the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, and the five superknowledges. Furthermore, setting aside supramundane dharmas, whatever other dharmas there are—these are called mundane dharmas. He asked:

“Blessed One, what are the supramundane dharmas? The Blessed One replied, “Subhūti, the supramundane dharmas are said to be: the four foundations of mindfulness; the four immeasurables; the four bases of psychic power; the five faculties; the five powers; the seven factors of enlightenment; the noble eightfold path; the gateways to liberation that are emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; and the faculty of ‘I shall come to know the unknown,’ as well as the faculty of knowledge.”

The faculty of one who has already known; concentration with investigation; concentration with both applied thought and investigation; concentration without applied thought and without investigation; knowledge, liberation, clear comprehension, and appropriate mental attention; the eight liberations. What are the eight? One possessing form sees forms—this is the first liberation. Perceiving internal form, one sees external forms—this is the second liberation. Being liberated from the notion of beauty—this is the third liberation.

Through the complete surmounting of perceptions of form, by the disappearance of perceptions of resistance, and by non-attention to perceptions of diversity, [thinking] "space is infinite," one attains and dwells in the sphere of infinite space; this is the fourth [dhyāna].

Liberation: by completely transcending the sphere of infinite space, thinking "consciousness is infinite," he dwells having attained the sphere of infinite consciousness; this is the fifth liberation. By completely transcending the sphere of infinite consciousness, thinking "there is nothing whatsoever," he dwells having attained the sphere of nothingness; this is the sixth liberation.

By completely transcending the sphere of nothingness, he dwells having attained the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; this is the seventh liberation. By completely transcending the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, he dwells having attained the cessation of perception and feeling; this is the eighth liberation. These are the eight liberations.

The nine successive attainments of meditative dwelling. What are the nine? Being secluded from sensual desires and secluded from evil, unwholesome states, he, with applied thought and sustained thought, enters and dwells in the first dhyāna, which is born of seclusion and characterized by joy and happiness. With the subsiding of applied and sustained thought, through internal tranquility and the unification of the mind, he, without applied thought and without sustained thought, enters and dwells in the second dhyāna, which is born of concentration and characterized by joy and happiness.

Through detachment from joy, he dwells in equanimity, mindful and clearly comprehending; and he experiences happiness with the body, of which the Noble Ones say: "He dwells in happiness, possessing equanimity and mindfulness. Thus, having attained the third dhyāna, he dwells therein.

Through the abandoning of pleasure and the abandoning of pain, and through the previous disappearance of mental joy and mental grief, he enters and dwells in the fourth dhyāna, which is neither-painful-nor-pleasant and possesses purity of equanimity and mindfulness. Through the complete transcendence of perceptions of form, by the disappearance of perceptions of sensory resistance, by not attending to perceptions of diversity, [thinking] "space is infinite," he enters and dwells in the sphere of infinite space.

Having completely transcended the sphere of infinite space, thinking "consciousness is infinite," he attains and dwells in the sphere of infinite consciousness. Having completely transcended the sphere of infinite consciousness...

Thinking "there is nothing," he attains and dwells in the sphere of nothingness (*ākiñcanyāyatana*). By completely transcending the sphere of nothingness, he attains and dwells in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*). By completely transcending the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, he attains and dwells in the cessation of perception and feeling (*saṃjñāvedayitanirodha*). These are the nine successive attainments of meditative dwelling (*anupūrvavihārasamāpatti*).

Internal emptiness, external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, the emptiness of the ultimate truth, the emptiness of the conditioned, the emptiness of the unconditioned, absolute emptiness, the emptiness of that which has no beginning or end, the emptiness of non-dispersal, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of specific characteristics, the emptiness of non-apprehension, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of self-nature, and the emptiness of the self-nature of non-existence.
The ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha—these are called supramundane dharmas.

The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, 'contaminated phenomena' refers to the five aggregates, the twelve sense bases, the eighteen elements, the four meditative absorptions, the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, and the five superknowledges. These are called contaminated phenomena. The Blessed One said: "The four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, and the five powers."

The seven factors of enlightenment; the noble eightfold path; the four noble truths; the four meditative absorptions; the eight liberations; the nine successive attainments of meditative dwelling; the gateways to liberation consisting of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; the ten powers of a Tathāgata; the four grounds of self-confidence; the four analytical knowledges; great loving-kindness; great compassion; and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha—these are so called.

[The question: "What are the untainted (*anāsrava*) phenomena? [Subhūti] asked: "Lord, what are the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) phenomena? The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, the conditioned phenomena are said to be the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), and the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*). Also, whatever other phenomena there may be that are included within the conditioned realms; furthermore, the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), the four right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*), the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*), the five faculties (*indriya*), the five powers (*bala*), and the seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*)."

The noble eightfold path; the four noble truths; the four dhyānas; the four immeasurables; the four formless attainments; the eight liberations; the nine successive meditative attainments; the gateways to liberation consisting of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; the five superknowledges; the six perfections; all the emptinesses; all the samādhis; all the gateways of dhāraṇī; the ten powers of a Tathāgata; and the four fearlessnesses.
The four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha—these are called conditioned phenomena.

He asked: "Blessed One, what are the unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*)? The Blessed One replied: "The unconditioned phenomena are said to be that which has no arising, no passing away, and no alteration of duration; the destruction of passion, the destruction of hatred, and the destruction of delusion; suchness (*tathatā*), non-falsity, non-other-suchness, the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), the stability of phenomena (*dharma-sthititā*), the fixed order of phenomena (*dharma-niyāmatā*), the inconceivable realm, and the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*). This is called the unconditioned phenomenon. He asked:

“Blessed One, what are the common dharmas? The Blessed One replied: “The four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, and the five supernormal powers—these are called the dharmas common to ordinary persons. [The interlocutor] asked: “Blessed One, what are the uncommon [dharmas]? The Blessed One replied: “The four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the noble eightfold path.”

The four noble truths; the eight liberations; the nine successive meditative attainments; emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—all samādhis; all doors of dhāraṇī; the ten powers of a Tathāgata; the four grounds of self-confidence; the four analytical knowledges; great loving-kindness; great compassion; and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha—these are called the uncommon dharmas.

In this regard, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom should not become attached to any phenomena by following their emptiness of intrinsic characteristics. By means of non-conceptualization and through the application of non-duality toward all phenomena, all phenomena are to be realized, based upon the state of being without conceptualization or discursive thought. Then, the venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One:

"Furthermore, Blessed One, regarding that which is called 'bodhisattva mahāsattva,' for what reason, Blessed One, is a bodhisattva called a 'mahāsattva'? The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, because he will bring about the leadership of the great mass of beings destined for certainty, for that reason a bodhisattva is called a 'mahāsattva'. He asked: "Blessed One, by what measure is the mass of beings destined for certainty, such that a bodhisattva mahāsattva will bring them to the state of being unheard [of the Dharma]? (i.e., will cause them to hear it).

The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, the 'multitude of great beings' refers to the one of the lineage (*gotrabhū*), the eighth-rank practitioner (*aṣṭamaka*), the stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*), the once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*), the arhat, the pratyekabuddha, and the bodhisattva mahāsattva from the first production of the thought of awakening up to the bodhisattva mahāsattva established on the stage of non-retrogression (*avaivarttyabhūmi*). Subhūti, this is called the 'multitude of great beings' destined for certainty. It is for such [beings] that the bodhisattva mahāsattva shall cause [this teaching] to be heard."

In this regard, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having generated a mind like a diamond (*vajropamacitta*), should cause a great mass of beings who are not yet fixed [in the path] to hear what they have not heard before. Subhūti asked: "Blessed One, what is this generation of a mind like a diamond? The Blessed One replied: "In this case, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva generates such a thought: 'I must don the armor within the immeasurable cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*) for the sake of all sentient beings.'"

I must become one who gives away all my possessions; I must generate a mind of equanimity toward all sentient beings; I must lead all sentient beings to final nirvana through the three vehicles. Even after leading all sentient beings to final nirvana, not a single sentient being has been led to final nirvana; I must realize the non-arising and non-ceasing of all phenomena. With an undistracted mind directed toward the knowledge of all aspects, I must practice the six perfections.

"I must train in the perfection of the penetration of phenomena that follows everywhere; I must awaken to the single, fixed accomplishment of phenomena; and I must train in phenomena for the sake of awakening to immeasurable accomplishments. Subhūti, this is the diamond-like production of the thought of enlightenment of a bodhisattva mahāsattva, abiding in which a bodhisattva mahāsattva will cause a great mass of beings who are destined to hear what they have not heard before, and that by way of non-apprehension.

Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives rise to this thought: "As many beings as there are who experience painful sensations—whether they be in the hells, or among the animals, or in the world of Yama—for their sake I shall experience those painful sensations. In that regard, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should give rise to such a mind.

For the sake of each and every sentient being, may I undergo that suffering of the hells for hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of eons, until that sentient being has been led to final nirvana in the realm of nirvana without remainder. In this very way, by means of skillful means, may I undergo that suffering of the hells for the sake of all sentient beings, until all sentient beings have been led to final nirvana in the realm of nirvana without remainder.

"Afterwards, having planted roots of merit for my own sake and having accumulated many preparations for awakening over hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of eons, may I fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. Subhūti, this is the diamond-like production of the thought of awakening of a bodhisattva mahāsattva; established in which, the bodhisattva mahāsattva will bring about the state of leadership for the great mass of beings who are destined for liberation, and that by way of non-apprehension.

Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should always and constantly possess a noble mind (*udāracitta*), by means of which noble mind he will bring about the state of preeminence among all sentient beings. In this regard, the noble-mindedness of a bodhisattva mahāsattva is as follows: prior to the initial production of the thought of awakening, he does not give rise to a mind of passion, he does not give rise to a mind of hatred, he does not give rise to a mind of delusion, and he does not give rise to a mind of harmfulness.

He does not give rise to a mind of violence; he does not give rise to the mind of a śrāvaka; he does not give rise to the mind of a pratyekabuddha. This is the magnanimity of mind of a bodhisattva mahāsattva, by which he should bring about the state of preeminence among all sentient beings. And by that magnanimity of mind, he should not be conceited.

Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva must possess an unshakable mind. In this regard, the unshakable state of mind of a bodhisattva mahāsattva is as follows: it is that mental engagement associated with the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), and by means of that, there is no conceit. This is the unshakable state of mind of a bodhisattva mahāsattva, by which he will bring about the state of being the foremost among all sentient beings, and that too through the yoga of non-apprehension (*anupalambha*).

Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should generate a mind of benefit and happiness toward all sentient beings. In this regard, the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s mind of benefit and happiness consists in being a protection for all sentient beings, in not abandoning any sentient beings, and in being patient with them. This, Subhūti, is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s mind of benefit and happiness by which he will bring about the state of preeminence among all sentient beings, and that too through the yoga of non-apprehension.

Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should be one who constantly and perpetually desires the Dharma; he should be one who delights in the Dharma, who rejoices in the Dharma, and who is devoted to the practice of finding delight in the Dharma. In this regard, what is the Dharma? That which is non-attachment toward all phenomena—this is called the Dharma. In this regard, what is the desire for the Dharma? That which is the longing and aspiration for the Dharma—this is called the desire for the Dharma. In this regard, what is delight in the Dharma? That which is delight and intense joy in this Dharma—this is called delight in the Dharma.

In that regard, what is delighting in the Dharma? It is the perception of the qualities and benefits of the Dharma; this is called delighting in the Dharma. In that regard, what is application to the practice of delighting in the Dharma? It is the cultivation and frequent practice of that very Dharma; this is called application to the practice of delighting in the Dharma. Thus indeed, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom should bring about leadership over the great mass of sentient beings, and that by way of non-apprehension.

Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom, having stood in internal emptiness, having stood in external emptiness, having stood in internal and external emptiness, having stood in the emptiness of emptiness, having stood in great emptiness, having stood in the emptiness of the ultimate truth, having stood in the emptiness of the conditioned, having stood in the emptiness of the unconditioned, having stood in absolute emptiness, and having stood in the emptiness of that which has neither beginning nor end—

Abiding in the emptiness of non-dispersal, abiding in the emptiness of intrinsic nature, abiding in the emptiness of all phenomena, abiding in the emptiness of specific characteristics, abiding in the emptiness of the unapprehendable, abiding in the emptiness of non-existence, abiding in the emptiness of self-nature, and abiding in the emptiness of the self-nature of non-existence, one should bring about the state of being foremost for the great mass of beings who are destined for certainty.

Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom, having stood in the foundations of mindfulness, having stood in the right efforts, having stood in the bases of psychic power, having stood in the faculties, having stood in the powers, having stood in the factors of enlightenment, having stood in the noble eightfold path, and having stood in the other truths—read: having stood in the noble truths—[should train].

Having abided in the meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), having abided in the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), having abided in the formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*), having abided in the liberations (*vimokṣa*), having abided in the successive dwellings and attainments (*anupūrvavihārasamāpatti*), having abided in the gateways to liberation consisting of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness (*śūnyatānimittāpraṇihitavimokṣamukha*), having abided in the meditative absorptions (*samādhi*), having abided in the gateways of mnemonic formulas (*dhāraṇīmukha*), having abided in the powers of a Tathāgata (*tathāgatabala*), having abided in the grounds of self-confidence (*vaiśāradya*), having abided in the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), having abided in great loving-kindness (*mahāmaitrī*), having abided in great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), and having abided in the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (*aṣṭādaśāveṇikabuddhadharma*).
One should bring about the state of preeminence for a great mass of beings who are established [in the path], and that by way of non-apprehension.

Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom, having stood in the Śūraṅgama samādhi, having stood in the Ratnamudrā samādhi, having stood in the Siṃhavikrīḍita samādhi, having stood in the Sucandra samādhi, having stood in the Candradhvaja samādhi, having stood in the Sarvadharmodgata samādhi, having stood in the Sarvadharmamudrā samādhi, having stood in the Vilokitamūrdhan samādhi, [should abide] in the Dharmadhātuniyata [samādhi].

Having abided in the *niyatadhvajaketu* concentration, having abided in the *vajropama* concentration, having abided in the *sarvadharmapraveśamudrā* concentration, having abided in the *samādhirājasupratiṣṭhita* concentration, having abided in the *balavyūha* concentration, having abided in the *samudgata* concentration, having abided in the *niruktiniyatapraveśa* concentration, having abided in the *adhivacanasampraveśa* concentration, having abided in the *digvilokita* concentration, and having abided in the *ādhāramudrā* concentration.

Having remained in the concentration of non-forgetfulness, having remained in the concentration of the ocean-seal of the convergence of all phenomena, having remained in the concentration of the pervasion of space, having remained in the concentration of the vajra-mandala, having remained in the concentration of the crest-ornament on the tip of a banner, having remained in the concentration of Indra’s banner, having remained in the concentration of following the stream, having remained in the concentration of the lion’s sport, and having remained in the concentration of the end of manifestation.

Having remained in the *raṇajaha* concentration, having remained in the *vairocana* concentration, having remained in the *animeṣa* concentration, having remained in the *aniketasthita* concentration, having remained in the *niśceta* concentration, having remained in the *vimalapradīpa* concentration, having remained in the *anantaprabha* concentration, having remained in the *prabhākara* concentration, having remained in the *samantāvabhāsa* concentration, having remained in the *śuddhāvabhāsa* concentration, and having remained in the *vimalaprabha* concentration, [he remained] in the *ratikara* concentration.

Abiding in the lightning-lamp concentration, abiding in the inexhaustible concentration, abiding in the invincible concentration, abiding in the delight-in-radiance concentration, abiding in the concentration that has gone beyond destruction, abiding in the irreproachable concentration, abiding in the colorless concentration, abiding in the sun-lamp concentration, abiding in the moon-pure concentration, abiding in the wisdom-lamp concentration, abiding in the pure-appearance concentration, abiding in the light-making concentration, [he dwelt] in the form of action.

Having abided in the concentration, having abided in the concentration of the Banner of Knowledge, having abided in the diamond-like concentration, having abided in the concentration of the stability of mind, having abided in the concentration of universal light, having abided in the well-established concentration, having abided in the concentration of the peak of jewels, having abided in the concentration of the seal of the sublime Dharma, having abided in the concentration of the assembly of all phenomena, having abided in the concentration that abandons delight, and having abided in the concentration of the emergence of Dharma; having abided in the concentration of scattering—

Abiding in the samādhi of the differentiation of the words of all dharmas, abiding in the samādhi of the manifestation of equal syllables, abiding in the samādhi free from syllables, abiding in the samādhi that cuts through obscurations, abiding in the samādhi of non-transformation, abiding in the samādhi of non-modality, abiding in the samādhi of entering the certainty of names, abiding in the samādhi of wandering without a dwelling, abiding in the samādhi free from darkness, abiding in the samādhi possessed of conduct, [abide] in the immovable.

Abiding in the concentration that has transcended sense objects, abiding in the concentration that has gathered all virtues, abiding in the concentration of established non-conceptuality, abiding in the concentration of pure blossoming beauty, [and] abiding in that which possesses the factors of enlightenment.

Having abided in the samādhi of infinite eloquence, having abided in the samādhi of the peerless and equal, having abided in the samādhi that transcends all phenomena, having abided in the samādhi that effects discernment, having abided in the samādhi that dispels doubt, having abided in the samādhi of non-reproach, having abided in the samādhi of the single array, having abided in the samādhi of the manifestation of forms, having abided in the samādhi of the single form, having abided in the samādhi of the non-occurrence of forms, [he dwelt] in the state where all existence and power have been removed through the absence of malice.

Abiding in the concentration on entering the sounds of conventions; abiding in the concentration on the syllables of vocal resonance; abiding in the concentration on the blazing torch; abiding in the concentration on the purification of marks; abiding in the concentration on the uncharacterizable; abiding in the concentration endowed with the excellence of all aspects; abiding in the concentration of non-relishing for any pleasure or pain; abiding in the concentration on the casket of the senses; and abiding in the concentration of the intellect of retention.

Abiding in the concentration that swallows up both rightness and wrongness; abiding in the concentration that thoroughly pacifies the cessation of all anger; abiding in the concentration of non-conformity and non-opposition; abiding in the concentration called Sāravatī; abiding in the concentration of the stainless radiance of the full moon; abiding in the concentration of lightning-radiance; abiding in the concentration of the great array; abiding in the concentration of the radiance of all modes; abiding in the concentration of the equality of concentrations; [and] in the concentration joined with the method of being free from dust and stainless.

Having abided in the concentration that is the refuge of the equality of all things free from conflict; having abided in the concentration devoted to the lack of a basis or a dwelling-place; having abided in the concentration of non-conceptualization established in suchness; having abided in the concentration that thoroughly crushes the defilement of the body; having abided in the space-like concentration that destroys the defilement of speech; having abided in the space-like, unattached, liberated, and stainless concentration—then, by means of the yoga of non-apprehension, a bodhisattva, having abided here in these dharmas, should bring about the state of preeminence for the great mass of beings who are destined for liberation. Subhūti, it is by abiding in these dharmas that a bodhisattva [should act].

The Mahāsattva, practicing in the perfection of wisdom, will bring about the state of being foremost for the great mass of beings who are destined [for enlightenment]. Therefore, he is called a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva.

Then the venerable Śāradvatīputra said this to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, it occurs to me as well for what reason a bodhisattva is called a 'mahāsattva'. The Blessed One said: "Let it occur to you, Śāradvatīputra, for what reason a bodhisattva is called a 'mahāsattva'. Śāradvatīputra said: "Blessed One, he teaches the Dharma to beings for the sake of abandoning the view of a self; for the sake of abandoning the view of a being; for the sake of abandoning the view of a life-principle."

For the sake of abandoning the view of a nourisher; for the sake of abandoning the view of a person (*pudgala*); for the sake of abandoning the view of a male (*puruṣa*); for the sake of abandoning the view of a human (*manuja*); for the sake of abandoning the view of a youth (*mānava*); for the sake of abandoning the view of an agent (*kāraka*); for the sake of abandoning the view of a causer of action (*kārāpaka*); for the sake of abandoning the view of an arouser (*utthāpaka*); for the sake of abandoning the view of a causer of arousal (*samutthāpaka*); for the sake of abandoning the view of an experiencer (*vedaka*); for the sake of abandoning the view of one who causes experience (*vedayitṛka*); for the sake of abandoning the view of a knower (*jñātṛka*); for the sake of abandoning the view of a seer (*paśyaka*).

For the abandonment of the view of annihilation; for the abandonment of the view of eternalism; for the abandonment of the view of existence; for the abandonment of the view of non-existence; for the abandonment of the view of the aggregates; for the abandonment of the view of the elements; for the abandonment of the view of the sense bases; for the abandonment of the view of dependent origination; for the abandonment of the view of the truths; for the abandonment of the view of the perfections; for the abandonment of the view of emptiness; for the abandonment of the view of the foundations of mindfulness.

For the abandonment of the view of the right efforts; for the abandonment of the view of the bases of psychic power; for the abandonment of the view of the faculties; for the abandonment of the view of the powers; for the abandonment of the view of the factors of enlightenment; for the abandonment of the view of the noble eightfold path; for the abandonment of the view of the noble truths; for the abandonment of the view of the meditative absorptions; for the abandonment of the view of the immeasurables; for the abandonment of the view of the formless attainments;

for the abandonment of the view of the liberations; for the abandonment of the view of the serial attainments; [and] for the abandonment of the view of the gateways to liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.

For the sake of abandoning the view of meditative concentration; for the sake of abandoning the view of the dhāraṇī-gates; for the sake of abandoning the view of the powers of a Tathāgata; for the sake of abandoning the view of the fearlessnesses; for the sake of abandoning the view of the analytical knowledges; for the sake of abandoning the view of great loving-kindness; for the sake of abandoning the view of great compassion; for the sake of abandoning the view of the unique qualities of a Buddha, the view of maturing sentient beings, and the view of purifying the Buddha-field; and for the sake of abandoning the view of awakening.

For the sake of abandoning the view of a Buddha, for the sake of abandoning the view of turning the wheel of Dharma, and for the sake of abandoning the view of parinirvāṇa, he teaches the Dharma to sentient beings by way of non-apprehension. For that reason, he is called a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva.

Then the venerable Subhūti said this to the venerable Śāradvatīputra: "For what reason, venerable Śāradvatīputra, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva have a view of form? Does he have a view of feeling? Does he have a view of perception? Does he have a view of formations? Does he have a view of consciousness? Does he have a view of the eye? Does he have a view of the ear? Does he have a view of the nose? Does he have a view of the tongue?"

There is the view of the body; there is the view of the mind; there is the view of form; there is the view of sound; there is the view of odor; there is the view of taste; there is the view of tangibility; there is the view of mental phenomena (*dharma*); there is the view of eye-consciousness; there is the view of ear-consciousness; there is the view of nose-consciousness; there is the view of tongue-consciousness; there is the view of body-consciousness.

There arises the view of mental consciousness; there arises the view of eye-contact; there arises the view of ear-contact; there arises the view of nose-contact; there arises the view of tongue-contact; there arises the view of body-contact; there arises the view of mind-contact; there arises the view of feeling conditioned by eye-contact; there arises the view of feeling conditioned by ear-contact.

There arises the view of sensation conditioned by olfactory contact; there arises the view of sensation conditioned by gustatory contact; there arises the view of sensation conditioned by tactile contact.

There arises the view of feeling conditioned by mental contact; there arises the view of the earth element; there arises the view of the water element; there arises the view of the fire element; there arises the view of the wind element; there arises the view of the space element; there arises the view of the consciousness element; there arises the view of ignorance; there arises the view of formative forces; there arises the view of consciousness; there arises the view of name-and-form; there arises the view of the six sense bases.

There arises the view of contact; there arises the view of sensation; there arises the view of craving; there arises the view of grasping; there arises the view of existence; there arises the view of birth; there arises the view of old age and death.

There arises the view of the perfection of generosity; there arises the view of the perfection of ethical discipline; there arises the view of the perfection of patience; there arises the view of the perfection of vigor; there arises the view of the perfection of meditative concentration; there arises the view of the perfection of wisdom; there arises the view of internal emptiness; there arises the view of external emptiness; there arises the view of internal and external emptiness; there arises the view of the emptiness of emptiness; there arises the view of great emptiness.

There arises the view of ultimate emptiness; there arises the view of the emptiness of the conditioned; there arises the view of the emptiness of the unconditioned; there arises the view of absolute emptiness; there arises the view of the emptiness of that which has no beginning or end; there arises the view of the emptiness of non-dispersal; there arises the view of the emptiness of intrinsic nature; there arises the view of the emptiness of all phenomena; there arises the view of the emptiness of specific characteristics; there arises the view of the emptiness of non-existence; there arises the view of the emptiness of self-nature; and there arises the view of the emptiness of the self-nature of non-existence.

There arises the vision of the foundations of mindfulness; there arises the vision of the right efforts; there arises the vision of the bases of psychic power; there arises the vision of the faculties; there arises the vision of the powers; there arises the vision of the factors of enlightenment; there arises the vision of the noble eightfold path; there arises the vision of the noble truths.

He possesses the vision of meditative absorption; he possesses the vision of the immeasurables; he possesses the vision of the formless attainments; he possesses the vision of the liberations; he possesses the vision of the successive dwellings and attainments; he possesses the vision of the gateways to liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; he possesses the vision of the superknowledges; he possesses the vision of meditative concentrations; he possesses the vision of the gateways to the dhāraṇīs; he possesses the vision of the powers of a Tathāgata; and he possesses the vision of the fearlessnesses.

There arises the vision of the analytical knowledges; there arises the vision of great loving-kindness; there arises the vision of great compassion; there arises the vision of the unique qualities of a Buddha; there arises the vision of purifying the Buddha-field; there arises the vision of awakening; there arises the vision of the Buddha; there arises the vision of the Dharma; there arises the vision of turning the wheel of the Dharma; there arises the vision of final nirvāṇa.

He said: "In this case, venerable Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in the perfection of wisdom, through a lack of skill in means, perceives form and generates a view by way of apprehension; he perceives feeling and generates a view by way of apprehension; he perceives perception and generates a view by way of apprehension; he perceives mental formations and generates a view by way of apprehension."

Having perceived consciousness, one gives rise to a view by way of apprehension; having perceived the eye, one gives rise to a view by way of apprehension; having perceived the ear, one gives rise to a view by way of apprehension; having perceived the nose, one gives rise to a view by way of apprehension; having perceived the tongue, one gives rise to a view by way of apprehension; having perceived the body, one gives rise to a view by way of apprehension.

Perceiving the mind, one gives rise to a view by means of apprehension; perceiving form, one gives rise to a view by means of apprehension; perceiving sound, one gives rise to a view by means of apprehension; perceiving odor, one gives rise to a view by means of apprehension; perceiving taste, one gives rise to a view by means of apprehension; perceiving tangibles, one gives rise to a view by means of apprehension;
perceiving phenomena, one gives rise to a view by means of apprehension.

Having perceived visual consciousness, one gives rise to views through the mode of apprehension; having perceived auditory consciousness, one gives rise to views through the mode of apprehension; having perceived olfactory consciousness, one gives rise to views through the mode of apprehension; having perceived gustatory consciousness, one gives rise to views through the mode of apprehension; having perceived tactile consciousness, one gives rise to views through the mode of apprehension.

Apprehending my own consciousness, one gives rise to a view by means of apprehension; apprehending visual contact, one gives rise to a view by means of apprehension; apprehending auditory contact, one gives rise to a view by means of apprehension; apprehending olfactory contact, one gives rise to a view by means of apprehension; apprehending gustatory contact, one gives rise to a view by means of apprehension.

Perceiving bodily contact, one gives rise to a view by means of apprehension; perceiving mental contact, one gives rise to a view by means of apprehension; perceiving the earth element, one gives rise to a view by means of apprehension; perceiving the water element, one gives rise to a view by means of apprehension; perceiving the fire element, one gives rise to a view by means of apprehension.

Perceiving the wind element, one gives rise to a view by means of apprehension; perceiving the space element, one gives rise to a view by means of apprehension; perceiving the consciousness element, one gives rise to a view by means of apprehension; perceiving ignorance, one gives rise to a view by means of apprehension; perceiving formative forces, one gives rise to a view by means of apprehension; perceiving consciousness, one gives rise to a view by means of apprehension.

Having apprehended name-and-form, one gives rise to views by way of apprehension; having apprehended the six sense bases, one gives rise to views by way of apprehension; having apprehended contact, one gives rise to views by way of apprehension; having apprehended feeling, one gives rise to views by way of apprehension; having apprehended craving, one gives rise to views by way of apprehension; having apprehended grasping, one gives rise to views by way of apprehension.

Perceiving existence, one gives rise to a view by means of apprehension; perceiving birth, one gives rise to a view by means of apprehension; perceiving aging and death, one gives rise to a view by means of apprehension.

Perceiving the perfection of generosity, one gives rise to a view by way of apprehension; perceiving the perfection of ethical discipline, one gives rise to a view by way of apprehension; perceiving the perfection of patience, one gives rise to a view by way of apprehension; perceiving the perfection of vigor, one gives rise to a view by way of apprehension; perceiving the perfection of meditative concentration, one gives rise to a view by way of apprehension;
perceiving the perfection of wisdom, one gives rise to a view by way of apprehension.

Having apprehended internal emptiness, one gives rise to a view by way of apprehension; having apprehended external emptiness, one gives rise to a view by way of apprehension; having apprehended internal-and-external emptiness, one gives rise to a view by way of apprehension; having apprehended the emptiness of emptiness, one gives rise to a view.

By way of apprehension, having apprehended great emptiness, he gives rise to a view by way of apprehension; having apprehended ultimate emptiness, he gives rise to a view by way of apprehension; having apprehended conditioned emptiness, he gives rise to a view by way of apprehension; having apprehended unconditioned emptiness, he gives rise to a view by way of apprehension; having apprehended absolute emptiness, he gives rise to a view by way of apprehension.

Having apprehended the emptiness of that which is without beginning or end, one gives rise to a view by way of apprehension; having apprehended the emptiness of non-dispersal, one gives rise to a view by way of apprehension; having apprehended the emptiness of intrinsic nature, one gives rise to a view by way of apprehension; having apprehended the emptiness of all phenomena, one gives rise to a view by way of apprehension; having apprehended the emptiness of specific characteristics, one gives rise to a view by way of apprehension.

Having apprehended the emptiness of non-apprehension, one gives rise to a view by means of apprehension; having apprehended the emptiness of non-existence, one gives rise to a view by means of apprehension; having apprehended the emptiness of intrinsic nature, one gives rise to a view by means of apprehension; having apprehended the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence, one gives rise to a view by means of apprehension.

Having apprehended the foundations of mindfulness, one generates a view by way of apprehension; having apprehended the right efforts, one generates a view by way of apprehension; having apprehended the bases of psychic power, one generates a view...

One generates [a view] by way of apprehension; having apprehended the faculties, one generates a view by way of apprehension; having apprehended the powers, one generates a view by way of apprehension; having apprehended the factors of enlightenment, one generates a view by way of apprehension; having apprehended the noble eightfold path, one generates a view by way of apprehension; having apprehended the noble truths, one generates a view by way of apprehension.

Having apprehended the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*), one gives rise to a view by way of apprehension. Having apprehended the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), one gives rise to a view by way of apprehension. Having apprehended the formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*), one gives rise to a view by way of apprehension. Having apprehended the liberations (*vimokṣa*), one gives rise to a view by way of apprehension. Having apprehended the serial attainments (*anupūrvavihārasamāpatti*), one gives rise to a view by way of non-apprehension.

Having apprehended the gateways to liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—one gives rise to a view through the application of apprehension. Having apprehended the superknowledges, one gives rise to a view through the application of apprehension. Having apprehended the meditative concentrations, one gives rise to a view through the application of apprehension. Having apprehended the gateways to the dhāraṇīs, one gives rise to a view through the application of apprehension. Having apprehended the powers of a Tathāgata, one gives rise to a view through the application of apprehension.

Having apprehended the grounds of self-confidence (*vaiśāradya*), one produces a view by way of apprehension; having apprehended the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), one produces a view by way of apprehension; having apprehended great loving-kindness (*mahāmaitrī*), one produces a view by way of apprehension; having apprehended great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), one produces a view by way of apprehension; having apprehended the unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇikabuddhadharma*), one produces a view by way of apprehension.

Perceiving the ripening of sentient beings, one generates a view by way of apprehension; perceiving the purification of the Buddha-field, one generates a view by way of apprehension; perceiving awakening, one generates a view by way of apprehension; perceiving the Buddha, one generates a view by way of apprehension; perceiving the Dharma, one generates a view by way of apprehension.
Perceiving the turning of the wheel of Dharma, one gives rise to a view by means of apprehension; perceiving parinirvāṇa, one gives rise to a view by means of apprehension.

For this reason, Venerable Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva comes to have a view of form; he comes to have a view of feeling; he comes to have a view of perception; he comes to have a view of mental formations; he comes to have a view of consciousness. For this reason, he comes to have a view of the eye; he comes to have a view of the ear; he comes to have a view of the nose; he comes to have a view of the tongue; he comes to have a view of the body; he comes to have a view of the mind.

For this reason, there is the vision of forms; there is the vision of sounds; there is the vision of odors; there is the vision of tastes; there is the vision of tangibles; there is the vision of phenomena. For this reason, there is the vision of eye-consciousness; there is the vision of ear-consciousness; there is the vision of nose-consciousness; there is the vision of tongue-consciousness; there is the vision of body-consciousness; there is the vision of mind-consciousness.

For this reason, there arises the view of eye-contact; there arise the views of ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, and mind-contact. For this reason, there arises the view of feeling conditioned by eye-contact.

There arises the view of feeling conditioned by auditory contact, the view of feeling conditioned by olfactory contact, the view of feeling conditioned by gustatory contact, the view of feeling conditioned by tactile contact, and the view of feeling conditioned by mental contact.

For this reason, there arises the view of the earth element; there arise the views of the water element, the fire element, the wind element, the space element, and the consciousness element. For this reason, there arises the view of ignorance; there arise the views of volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, existence, birth, and old age and death.

For this reason, there arises the view of the perfection of giving; there arise the views of the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditative concentration, and the perfection of wisdom.
For this reason, there arises the view of internal emptiness and the view of external emptiness.

There arises the view of internal-and-external emptiness, the view of the emptiness of emptiness, the view of great emptiness, the view of ultimate emptiness, the view of conditioned emptiness, the view of unconditioned emptiness, the view of absolute emptiness, the view of the emptiness of that which is without beginning or end, the view of the emptiness of non-dispersal, the view of the emptiness of intrinsic nature, the view of the emptiness of all phenomena, the view of the emptiness of specific characteristics, the view of the emptiness of non-apprehension, the view of the emptiness of non-existence, the view of the emptiness of self-nature,
and the view of the emptiness of the self-nature of non-existence.

For this reason, there arises the vision of the foundations of mindfulness; the vision of the right efforts; the vision of the bases of psychic power; the vision of the faculties; the vision of the powers; the vision of the factors of enlightenment; the vision of the noble eightfold path; the vision of the noble truths; the vision of the meditative absorptions; the vision of the immeasurables; the vision of the formless attainments; the vision of the liberations; the vision of the successive dwellings; the vision of the gateways to liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; the vision of the superknowledges; the vision of the concentrations; and the vision of the gateways to the dhāraṇīs.

It becomes the vision of the powers of a Tathāgata, the vision of fearlessness, the vision of the analytical knowledges, the vision of great loving-kindness, the vision of great compassion, the vision of the unique qualities of a Buddha, the vision of the maturation of sentient beings, the vision of the purification of the Buddha-field, the vision of awakening, the vision of the Buddha, the vision of the Dharma, the vision of turning the wheel of the Dharma, and the vision of parinirvāṇa.

In that regard, the bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of wisdom, teaches the Dharma through skillful means for the sake of abandoning these views, by way of non-apprehension. Then the venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, it occurs to me as well as to what purpose the term 'bodhisattva mahāsattva' is used. The Blessed One said: "Let it occur to you, Subhūti. Subhūti said:

Furthermore, although the Blessed One’s thought of awakening is an unequaled thought, an uncommon thought not shared by any of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, he is nonetheless unattached even to that thought; for that reason, he is called a bodhisattva mahāsattva. Why is that? Because that thought of omniscience is untainted (*anāśrava*) and unconditioned (*aparyāpanna*); and since that thought of omniscience is untainted and unconditioned within the triple world, he is unattached even to that thought by virtue of its emptiness of intrinsic nature (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*). Therefore, he is reckoned as a bodhisattva mahāsattva.

Then the Venerable Śāradvatīputra said this to the Venerable Subhūti: "Venerable Subhūti, what is that unequalled mind, that uncommon mind of a bodhisattva mahāsattva, which is not shared with any śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas? Subhūti replied: "In this regard, Venerable Śāradvatīputra, from the first production of the thought of awakening onwards, a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not perceive the arising or the cessation of any dharma whatsoever."

There is neither decrease nor increase, neither going nor coming, neither affliction nor purification. Venerable Śāradvatīputra, where there is no arising and no cessation, no decrease and no increase, no going and no coming, no affliction and no purification—therein there is no thought of a śrāvaka, no thought of a pratyekabuddha, no thought of a pratyekabuddha-bodhisattva, no thought of awakening, and no thought of a perfectly awakened Buddha. This, venerable Śāradvatīputra, is the [nature] of a bodhisattva.

"The mind of the Mahāsattva is an unequaled mind, a mind not shared with any Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas. [Śāriputra] said: "Venerable Subhūti, regarding what you have said—that even that mind of omniscience, which is untainted and unconditioned, is still 'attached' by means of that mind—"

For indeed, Venerable Subhūti, form is unattached, and feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also unattached; the eye is unattached, the ear is unattached, the nose is unattached, the tongue is unattached, the body is unattached, and the mind is also unattached. Form is unattached, sound is unattached, odor is unattached, taste is unattached, tangibles are unattached, and mental phenomena are also unattached.

Eye-consciousness is also unattached; ear-consciousness is also unattached; nose-consciousness is also unattached; tongue-consciousness is also unattached; body-consciousness is also unattached; and mind-consciousness is also unattached. Eye-contact is also unattached; ear-contact is also unattached; nose-contact is also unattached; tongue-contact is also unattached; body-contact is also unattached; and mind-contact is also unattached.
Feeling conditioned by eye-contact is unattached; feeling conditioned by ear-contact is unattached;

feeling conditioned by nose-contact is unattached; feeling conditioned by tongue-contact is unattached; feeling conditioned by body-contact is unattached; feeling conditioned by mind-contact is also unattached.

The earth element is unattached; the water element is unattached; the fire element is unattached; the wind element is unattached; the space element is unattached; the consciousness element is unattached. Ignorance is unattached; the formative forces are unattached; consciousness is unattached; name-and-form is unattached; the six sense bases are unattached; contact is unattached; feeling is unattached; craving is unattached; grasping is unattached.

Existence is also unattached; birth is also unattached; aging and death are also unattached; the perfection of generosity is also unattached; the perfection of ethical discipline is also unattached; the perfection of patience is also unattached; the perfection of vigor is also unattached; the perfection of meditative concentration is also unattached; and the perfection of wisdom is also unattached.

Inner emptiness is also unattached; outer emptiness is also unattached; inner-and-outer emptiness is also unattached; the emptiness of emptiness is also unattached; great emptiness is also unattached; the emptiness of the ultimate truth is also unattached; the emptiness of the conditioned is also unattached; the emptiness of the unconditioned is also unattached; absolute emptiness is also unattached; the emptiness of that which has no beginning or end is also unattached; the emptiness of non-dispersal is also unattached; and the emptiness of intrinsic nature is also unattached.

The emptiness of all phenomena is also unattached; the emptiness of specific characteristics is also unattached; the emptiness of non-apprehension is also unattached; the emptiness of non-existence is also unattached; the emptiness of intrinsic nature is also unattached; the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence is also unattached. The applications of mindfulness are also unattached; the right efforts are also unattached; the bases of psychic power are also unattached; the faculties are also unattached; the powers are also unattached; the factors of enlightenment are also unattached; the noble eightfold path is also unattached; and the noble truths are also unattached.

The meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) are also unattached; the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*) are also unattached; the formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*) are also unattached; the liberations (*vimokṣa*) are also unattached; the serial attainments (*anupūrvavihārasamāpatti*) are also unattached; the gateways to liberation consisting of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness (*śūnyatānimittāpraṇihita-vimokṣamukha*) are also unattached; the superknowledges (*abhijñā*) are also unattached; the concentrations (*samādhi*) are also unattached; the gateways of mnemonic formulas (*dhāraṇīmukha*) are also unattached; the powers of a Tathāgata (*tathāgatabala*) are also unattached; and the grounds of self-confidence (*vaiśāradya*) are also unattached.

The analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) are also unattached; great loving-kindness (*mahāmaitrī*) is also unattached; great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) is also unattached; the unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇikabuddhadharma*) are also unattached; omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) is also unattached; the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*) is also unattached; and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) is also unattached.

Subhūti said: "It is so, Venerable Śāradvatīputra. Form also is unattached; feeling also is unattached; perception also is unattached; mental formations also are unattached; consciousness also is unattached. The eye also is unattached; the ear also is unattached; the nose is unattached; the tongue also is unattached; the body also is unattached; the mind also is unattached. Form also is unattached; sound also is unattached; odor also is unattached; taste also is unattached."

Contact, too, is unattached; mental phenomena, too, are unattached. Eye-consciousness, too, is unattached; ear-consciousness, too, is unattached; nose-consciousness, too, is unattached; tongue-consciousness, too, is unattached; body-consciousness, too, is unattached; mind-consciousness, too, is unattached. Eye-contact, too, is unattached; ear-contact, too, is unattached; nose-contact, too, is unattached; tongue-contact, too, is unattached.

Contact of the body is also unattached; contact of the mind is also unattached. Feeling conditioned by visual contact is also unattached; feeling conditioned by auditory contact is also unattached; feeling conditioned by olfactory contact is also unattached; feeling conditioned by gustatory contact is also unattached; feeling conditioned by tactile contact is also unattached; feeling conditioned by mental contact is also unattached.

The earth element is unattached; the water element is unattached; the fire element is unattached; the wind element is unattached; the space element is unattached; the consciousness element is unattached. Ignorance is unattached; the formative forces are unattached; consciousness is unattached; name-and-form is unattached.

The six sense bases are also unattached; contact is also unattached; feeling is also unattached; craving is also unattached; grasping is also unattached; becoming is also unattached; birth is also unattached; aging and death are also unattached. The perfection of generosity is also unattached; the perfection of ethical discipline is also unattached; the perfection of patience is also unattached; the perfection of vigor is also unattached; the perfection of meditation is also unattached; the perfection of wisdom is also unattached.

Internal emptiness is also unattached; external emptiness is also unattached; internal-external emptiness is also unattached; the emptiness of emptiness is also unattached; great emptiness is also unattached; the emptiness of the ultimate truth is also unattached; the emptiness of the conditioned is also unattached; the emptiness of the unconditioned is also unattached; absolute emptiness is also unattached; the emptiness of that which has no beginning or end is also unattached; the emptiness of non-dispersal is also unattached; the emptiness of intrinsic nature is also unattached.

The emptiness of all phenomena is also unattached; the emptiness of specific characteristics is also unattached; the emptiness of non-apprehension is also unattached; the emptiness of non-existence is also unattached; the emptiness of intrinsic nature is also unattached; and the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence is also unattached.

The foundations of mindfulness are also unattached; the right efforts are also unattached; the bases of psychic power are also unattached; the faculties are also unattached; the powers are also unattached; the factors of enlightenment are also unattached; the noble eightfold path is also unattached; the noble truths are also unattached; the meditative absorptions are also unattached; the immeasurables are also unattached; the formless attainments are also unattached; and the liberations are also unattached.

The successive attainments of the meditative dwellings (*anupūrvavihārasamāpatti*) are also unattached; the gateways to liberation (*vimokṣamukha*) of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness are also unattached; the superknowledges (*abhijñā*) are also unattached; the concentrations (*samādhi*) are also unattached; the gateways to the mnemonic formulas (*dhāraṇīmukha*) are also unattached; the powers of a Tathāgata (*tathāgatabala*) are also unattached; the grounds of self-confidence (*vaiśāradya*) are also unattached; the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) are also unattached; great loving-kindness (*mahāmaitrī*) is also unattached; great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) is also unattached; and the unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇikabuddhadharma*) [are also unattached].
Even omniscience is unattached; even the knowledge of the aspects of the path is unattached; even the knowledge of all aspects is unattached.

He said: "As for what the Venerable Subhūti has said—that even that mind of omniscience is untainted (*anāsrava*) and unconditioned (*aparyāpanna*)—in this regard, Venerable Subhūti, even the minds of foolish ordinary people (*bālapṛthagjana*) are untainted and unconditioned by virtue of the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*). Likewise, the minds of Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and even the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, are untainted and unconditioned by virtue of the emptiness of intrinsic nature. Subhūti said:

Venerable Śāradvatīputra, even the minds of foolish common people are untainted and unconditioned, by virtue of their natural emptiness. Even the minds of the śrāvakas are untainted and unconditioned, by virtue of their natural emptiness. Even the minds of the pratyekabuddhas are untainted and unconditioned, by virtue of their natural emptiness. Even the minds of the Blessed Buddhas are untainted and unconditioned, by virtue of their natural emptiness.

"Indeed, venerable Subhūti, form also is outflow-free and unconditioned, by virtue of its emptiness of intrinsic nature; feeling also is outflow-free and unconditioned, by virtue of its emptiness of intrinsic nature; perception also is outflow-free and unconditioned, by virtue of its emptiness of intrinsic nature; volitional formations also are outflow-free and unconditioned, by virtue of their emptiness of intrinsic nature; and consciousness also is outflow-free and unconditioned, by virtue of its emptiness of intrinsic nature."

The eye, too, is untainted and unconditioned, by virtue of its emptiness of intrinsic nature; the ear, too, is untainted and unconditioned, by virtue of its emptiness of intrinsic nature; the nose, too, is untainted and unconditioned, by virtue of its emptiness of intrinsic nature; the tongue, too, is untainted and unconditioned, by virtue of its emptiness of intrinsic nature; the body, too, is untainted and unconditioned, by virtue of its emptiness of intrinsic nature.

The mind, too, is untainted and unconditioned, by virtue of its natural emptiness; form, too, is untainted and unconditioned, by virtue of its natural emptiness; sound, too, is untainted and unconditioned, by virtue of its natural emptiness.

By virtue of their intrinsic emptiness, odor is also untainted and non-included; by virtue of their intrinsic emptiness, taste is also untainted and non-included; by virtue of their intrinsic emptiness, touch is also untainted and non-included; by virtue of their intrinsic emptiness, mental phenomena are also untainted and non-included; and by virtue of their intrinsic emptiness, visual consciousness is also untainted and non-included.

Ear-consciousness, too, is untainted and non-included, by virtue of its emptiness of intrinsic nature; nose-consciousness, too, is untainted and non-included, by virtue of its emptiness of intrinsic nature; tongue-consciousness, too, is untainted and non-included, by virtue of its emptiness of intrinsic nature; body-consciousness, too, is untainted and non-included, by virtue of its emptiness of intrinsic nature; and mind-consciousness, too, is untainted and non-included, by virtue of its emptiness of intrinsic nature.

Eye-contact as well is untainted and unconditioned, by virtue of its emptiness of intrinsic nature; ear-contact as well is untainted and unconditioned, by virtue of its emptiness of intrinsic nature; nose-contact as well is untainted and unconditioned, by virtue of its emptiness of intrinsic nature; tongue-contact as well is untainted and unconditioned, by virtue of its emptiness of intrinsic nature; body-contact as well is untainted and unconditioned, by virtue of its emptiness of intrinsic nature.

Mental contact as well is untainted and unconditioned, by virtue of its emptiness of intrinsic nature. Feeling born of visual contact is also untainted and unconditioned, by virtue of its emptiness of intrinsic nature. Feeling born of auditory contact is also untainted and unconditioned, by virtue of its emptiness of intrinsic nature. Feeling born of olfactory contact is also untainted and unconditioned, by virtue of its emptiness of intrinsic nature.

Feeling born of tongue-contact is also untainted and unconditioned, by virtue of its emptiness of intrinsic nature; feeling born of body-contact is also untainted and unconditioned, by virtue of its emptiness of intrinsic nature; feeling born of mind-contact is also untainted and unconditioned, by virtue of its emptiness of intrinsic nature;
even the earth element is untainted and unconditioned, by virtue of its emptiness of intrinsic nature.

The water element is also untainted and unconditioned, by virtue of its natural emptiness; the fire element is also untainted and unconditioned, by virtue of its natural emptiness; the wind element is also untainted and unconditioned, by virtue of its natural emptiness; the space element is also untainted and unconditioned, by virtue of its natural emptiness; and the consciousness element is also untainted and unconditioned, by virtue of its natural emptiness.

Ignorance (*avidyā*) is also untainted (*anāsrava*) and unconditioned (*aparyāpanna*), by virtue of its emptiness of intrinsic nature (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*). Formative forces (*saṃskāra*) are also untainted and unconditioned, by virtue of their emptiness of intrinsic nature. Consciousness (*vijñāna*) is also untainted and unconditioned, by virtue of its emptiness of intrinsic nature. Name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) is also untainted and unconditioned, by virtue of its emptiness of intrinsic nature. The six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) are also untainted and unconditioned, by virtue of their emptiness of intrinsic nature.
