The non-applications of mindfulness are also unattached to the applications of mindfulness; the non-right-exertions are also unattached to the right-exertions; the non-bases of psychic power are also unattached to the bases of psychic power; the non-faculties are also unattached to the faculties; the non-powers are also unattached to the powers; the non-factors of enlightenment are also unattached to the factors of enlightenment; the non-noble eightfold path is also unattached to the noble eightfold path; and the non-noble truths are also unattached to the noble truths.

The higher meditations (*adhyāna*) are also unattached to the meditations; the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*) are also unattached to the immeasurables; the formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*) are also unattached to the formless attainments; the liberations (*vimokṣa*) are also unattached to the liberations; the serial attainments (*anupūrvavihārasamāpatti*) are also unattached to the serial attainments; and the gateways to liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—are also [unattached] to the gateways to liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.

They are unattached; even those who lack the superknowledges (*abhijñā*) are unattached to the superknowledges; even those who lack meditative concentrations (*samādhi*) are unattached to the meditative concentrations; even the gateways of mnemonic formulas (*dhāraṇīmukha*) are unattached to the gateways of mnemonic formulas; even those who lack the powers of a Tathāgata (*tathāgatabala*) are unattached to the powers of a Tathāgata; even those who lack the grounds of self-confidence (*vaiśāradya*) are unattached to the grounds of self-confidence; even those who lack the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) are unattached to the analytical knowledges; even those who lack great loving-kindness (*mahāmaitrī*) are unattached to great loving-kindness; even those who lack great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) are unattached to great compassion.

The non-exclusive buddha-qualities are also unattached to the non-exclusive buddha-qualities; even non-omniscience is unattached to omniscience; even the knowledge of the aspects of what is not the path is unattached to the knowledge of the aspects of the path; and even the non-knowledge of all aspects is unattached to the knowledge of all aspects.

"In this way indeed, venerable Śāradvatīputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in the perfection of wisdom does not conceive of nor adhere even to that thought of awakening—the thought which is equal to the unequaled—by means of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas. Because of the yoga of non-apprehension of all phenomena, he is called a 'bodhisattva mahāsattva. Then, the venerable Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra said this to the Blessed One:"

“It occurs to me as well, Blessed One, by what noble quality a bodhisattva is called a ‘mahāsattva. The Blessed One said, “Let it occur to you, Pūrṇa. Pūrṇa said, “Indeed, Blessed One, that being is connected with the great beings; that being, Blessed One, has set out upon the Mahāyāna; that being, Blessed One, has mounted the Mahāyāna. For that reason, he is called a bodhisattva mahāsattva.”

Then the venerable Śāradvatīputra said to the venerable Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra: "To what extent, venerable Pūrṇa, is a bodhisattva mahāsattva said to be 'connected with the lineage of mahāsattvas'? Pūrṇa replied: "In this case, venerable Śāradvatīputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not give a gift while abiding in the perfection of generosity for the sake of limited beings; rather, practicing the perfection of generosity for the sake of all beings, he gives a gift—not for limited beings."

Having established himself in the perfection of ethical discipline for the sake of all beings, he guards his morality; yet he does not guard his morality merely for the sake of limited beings. Having established himself in the perfection of patience for the sake of all beings, he cultivates patience; yet he does not cultivate patience merely for the sake of limited beings. Having established himself in the perfection of vigor for the sake of all beings, he exerts vigor; yet he does not exert vigor merely for the sake of limited beings.

Rather, for the sake of all sentient beings, while practicing the perfection of vigor, he exerts vigor; he does not, for the sake of limited beings, abide in the perfection of meditative concentration and produce meditative concentrations. Rather, for the sake of all sentient beings, while practicing the perfection of meditative concentration, he produces meditative concentrations. He does not, for the sake of limited beings, abide in the perfection of wisdom and cultivate wisdom.
Rather, for the sake of all sentient beings, while practicing the perfection of wisdom, he cultivates wisdom.

A bodhisattva mahāsattva does not don the armor by way of delimiting sentient beings, thinking: "I shall lead this many sentient beings to final nirvana in the realm of nirvana without remainder; I shall not lead this many sentient beings to final nirvana; I shall establish this many sentient beings in awakening; I shall not establish this many sentient beings in awakening. Rather, on the contrary, the bodhisattva mahāsattva dons the great armor for the sake of all sentient beings.

And he thinks thus: "I myself shall fulfill the perfection of generosity, and I shall establish all sentient beings in the perfection of generosity. I myself shall fulfill the perfection of ethical discipline, and I shall establish all sentient beings in the perfection of ethical discipline. I myself shall fulfill the perfection of patience, and I shall establish all sentient beings in the perfection of patience. I myself..."

I shall fulfill the perfection of vigor and I shall establish all sentient beings in the perfection of vigor. I myself shall fulfill the perfection of meditation and I shall establish all sentient beings in the perfection of meditation. I myself shall fulfill the perfection of wisdom and I shall establish all sentient beings in the perfection of wisdom.

I myself shall fulfill internal emptiness, and I shall establish all sentient beings in internal emptiness; I myself shall fulfill external emptiness, and I shall establish all sentient beings in external emptiness; I myself shall fulfill internal-and-external emptiness, and I shall establish all sentient beings in internal-and-external emptiness.

And I myself shall fulfill the emptiness of emptiness, and I shall establish all sentient beings in the emptiness of emptiness; and I myself shall fulfill the great emptiness, and I shall establish all sentient beings in the great emptiness; and I myself shall fulfill the emptiness of the ultimate truth, and I shall establish all sentient beings in the emptiness of the ultimate truth; and I myself shall fulfill the emptiness of the conditioned.

I shall establish all sentient beings in the emptiness of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta-śūnyatā*), and I myself shall fulfill the emptiness of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta-śūnyatā*). I shall establish all sentient beings in the emptiness of the unconditioned, and I myself shall fulfill the ultimate emptiness (*atyanta-śūnyatā*). I shall establish all sentient beings in the ultimate emptiness, and I myself shall fulfill the emptiness of that which has no beginning or end (*anavarāgra-śūnyatā*). I shall establish all sentient beings in the emptiness of that which has no beginning or end.
I myself shall fulfill the emptiness of non-dispersal, and I shall establish all sentient beings in the emptiness of non-dispersal; and I myself [shall fulfill] the emptiness of intrinsic nature...

I shall fulfill [this]; and I shall establish all sentient beings in the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*). And I myself shall fulfill the emptiness of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-śūnyatā*), and I shall establish all sentient beings in the emptiness of all phenomena. And I myself shall fulfill the emptiness of specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*), and I shall establish all sentient beings in the emptiness of specific characteristics. And I myself shall fulfill the emptiness of non-apprehension (*anupalambha-śūnyatā*).

I shall establish all sentient beings in the emptiness of non-apprehension; and I myself shall fulfill the emptiness of non-existence, and I shall establish all sentient beings in the emptiness of non-existence. I myself shall fulfill the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and I shall establish all sentient beings in the emptiness of intrinsic nature. I myself shall fulfill the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence, and I shall establish all sentient beings in the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence.

I myself shall abide in the four foundations of mindfulness, and I shall establish others in the four foundations of mindfulness. I myself shall abide in the four right efforts, and I shall establish others in the four right efforts. I myself shall abide in the four bases of psychic power, and I shall establish others in the four bases of psychic power. I myself shall abide in the five faculties.

I shall establish others in the five faculties; I myself shall abide in the five powers and I shall establish others in the five powers; I myself shall abide in the seven factors of enlightenment and I shall establish others in the seven factors of enlightenment; I myself shall abide in the noble eightfold path and I shall establish others in the noble eightfold path; I myself shall abide in the noble truths.

I will establish others in the noble truths; I myself will abide in the meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), and I will establish others in the meditative concentrations. I myself will abide in the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), and I will establish others in the immeasurables. I myself will abide in the formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*), and I will establish others in the formless attainments. I myself will abide in the eight liberations (*vimokṣa*), and I will establish others in the eight liberations. I myself will abide in the nine successive meditative attainments (*anupūrvavihārasamāpatti*).

I shall establish others in the nine successive meditative attainments (*anupūrvavihārasamāpatti*), and I myself shall abide in the gateways to liberation (*vimokṣamukha*) of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; I shall also establish others in the gateways to liberation of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness. I myself shall abide in the superknowledges (*abhijñā*), and I shall establish others in the superknowledges; I myself shall abide in the meditative concentrations (*samādhi*), and I shall establish others in the meditative concentrations.

I myself shall abide in the gateways of dhāraṇī, and I shall establish others in the gateways of dhāraṇī. I myself shall abide in the powers of a Tathāgata, and I shall establish others in the powers of a Tathāgata. I myself shall abide in the grounds of self-confidence, and I shall establish others in the grounds of self-confidence. I myself shall abide in the analytical knowledges, and I shall establish others in the analytical knowledges. I myself shall abide in great loving-kindness.

"I shall establish others in great loving-kindness; I myself shall abide in great compassion, and I shall establish others in great compassion; I myself shall abide in the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, and I shall establish others in the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
To this extent, Venerable Śāradvatīputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva is said to have donned the great armor.

Furthermore, venerable Śāradvatīputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom gives a gift, he does so with mental engagements associated with the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), not with those associated with the disciples or solitary buddhas. Having made that root of merit common to all sentient beings, he dedicates it toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment. This is the armor of the perfection of generosity for a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom.

Furthermore, Venerable Śāradvatīputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives a gift, he dedicates it to the stage [of awakening] through mental engagements associated with the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), and not through those associated with the disciples or solitary buddhas. This is the armor of the perfection of ethical discipline for a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom while giving a gift.

Furthermore, Venerable Śāradvatīputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives a gift while attending with mental orientations associated with the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), that which is his endurance, delight, and acceptance toward those phenomena—this is the armor of the perfection of patience for a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom while giving a gift.

Furthermore, venerable Śāradvatīputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives a gift with mental attentions associated with the knowledge of all aspects, there is an indefatigability of vigor (*vīryāsraṃsanatā*).

This is the armor of the perfection of vigor of a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom while giving gifts. Furthermore, Venerable Śāradvatīputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives a gift, that one-pointedness of mind—namely, mental engagements associated with the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) and the non-provisioning of space for the arising of thoughts associated with the disciples or solitary buddhas—is based upon having a single object of focus.

This is the armor of the perfection of meditative concentration belonging to a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom while giving a gift. Furthermore, Venerable Śāradvatīputra, for a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom while giving a gift, there is the presence of the perception of being created by illusion—through mental engagements associated with the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), even when there is no perception of being created by pride.
He exists; yet he does not perceive the gift, nor does he perceive the giver, nor the recipient.

This is the armor of the perfection of wisdom for a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom while giving gifts. Venerable Śāradvatīputra, it is when a bodhisattva mahāsattva, through mental engagements associated with the knowledge of all aspects, does not take those perfections as signs and does not apprehend them. In this way, indeed, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom should be understood as being equipped with the great armor.

Furthermore, venerable Śāradvatīputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of ethical discipline gives a gift with mental orientations associated with the knowledge of all aspects, and having made that common to all sentient beings, dedicates it toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by means of the yoga of non-apprehension—this is the perfection of generosity of a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of ethical discipline.

Furthermore, Venerable Śāradvatīputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of ethical discipline with mental engagements associated with the knowledge of all aspects, his lack of longing for the levels of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas—let alone the levels of ordinary persons—is the perfection of ethical discipline of that bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of ethical discipline.

Furthermore, Venerable Śāradvatīputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of ethical discipline, that which is the endurance, the proclamation, and the acceptance of those phenomena through mental engagements associated with the knowledge of all aspects—this is the perfection of patience of a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of ethical discipline.

Furthermore, Venerable Śāradvatīputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*), that state of non-laxity in vigor and non-depressed vigor through mental attentions associated with the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) is the perfection of vigor (*vīryapāramitā*) of that bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*). Furthermore, Venerable Śāradvatīputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of ethical discipline, [through] mental attentions associated with the knowledge of all aspects...

For one who dwells with mental attentions, that which is the non-admission of the minds of Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, and the dedication of those roots of virtue—shared in common with all sentient beings—toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment: this is the perfection of meditation for a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practicing the perfection of ethical discipline.

Furthermore, venerable Śāradvatīputra, for a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom, there arises—through mental engagements associated with the knowledge of all aspects, and not through those associated with the disciples or solitary buddhas—the perception that all phenomena are like illusions. And by means of that morality, he does not conceive pride, nor does he apprehend that morality, because of its essential emptiness (*prakṛtiśūnyatā*).

And having made that root of merit common to all sentient beings, he dedicates it toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment. This is the perfection of wisdom of a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of ethical discipline. In this way indeed, venerable Śāradvatīputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of ethical discipline embraces the six perfections. Therefore, he is said to be "armed with the great armor."

Furthermore, Venerable Śāradvatīputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of patience gives a gift, he does so with mental attentions associated with the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), not with those associated with the disciples or solitary buddhas; and having made that root of merit common to all sentient beings, he dedicates it toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

This is the perfection of generosity of a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of patience. Furthermore, venerable Śāradvatīputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of patience observes ethical discipline, he does so with mental attentions associated with the knowledge of all aspects, and not with those associated with the disciples or solitary buddhas.

And having made that root of merit common to all sentient beings, he dedicates it toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment; this is the perfection of ethical discipline of a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of patience. Furthermore, Venerable Śāradvatīputra, for a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of patience, it is the endurance, the proclamation, and the acceptance of mental attentions associated with the knowledge of all aspects.

This is the perfection of patience for one practicing the perfection of patience. Furthermore, Venerable Śāradvatīputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of patience, that one-pointedness of mind which is associated with the mental engagements connected to the knowledge of all aspects, and not associated with those connected to the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas—this is the perfection of meditative concentration for one practicing the perfection of patience.

Furthermore, venerable Śāradvatīputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of patience, through mental attentions associated with the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) and not those associated with the disciples or solitary buddhas, the perception of all sentient beings as being like illusions (*māyākṛta*) becomes present before him. And he reflects upon that patience in such a way that he does not apprehend that patience. This is the perfection of wisdom for one practicing the perfection of patience.
In this way indeed, venerable Śāradvatīputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of patience embraces all six perfections; therefore, he is said to be "armed with the great armor."

Furthermore, venerable Śāradvatīputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of vigor gives a gift, he does so with mental orientations associated with the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), not with those associated with the disciples or solitary buddhas. Having made that root of merit common to all sentient beings, he dedicates it toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. This is the perfection of generosity of a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of vigor. Furthermore...

Furthermore, Venerable Śāradvatīputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of vigor guards morality with mental engagements associated with the knowledge of all aspects, and not with those associated with the disciples or solitary buddhas, and having made that root of merit common to all sentient beings, dedicates it toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment—this is the perfection of morality for one practicing the perfection of vigor.

Furthermore, Venerable Śāradvatīputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of vigor, his endurance, proclamation, and acceptance of those phenomena—accomplished through mental attentions associated with the knowledge of all aspects, and not through mental attentions associated with śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas—this is the perfection of patience for one practicing the perfection of vigor.

Furthermore, venerable Śāradvatīputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of vigor, his non-laxity and grasping at vigor for the sake of all sentient beings—accompanied by mental attentions associated with the knowledge of all aspects, and not associated with the levels of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas—is the perfection of vigor for one practicing the perfection of vigor.

Furthermore, venerable Śāradvatīputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of vigor, his mental attention is associated with the knowledge of all aspects and not associated with the level of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas; this is the perfection of meditative concentration for one practicing the perfection of vigor.

Furthermore, venerable Śāradvatīputra, for a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of vigor and wisdom, there is that one-pointedness of mind associated with the mental engagements of omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*), not those associated with the disciples or solitary buddhas; it is that which brings about the presence of the perception of all phenomena as being like illusions. And by means of that vigor, he does not conceive of it, nor does he apprehend that vigor.

And having made that root of virtue common to all sentient beings, he dedicates it toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment; this is the perfection of wisdom for one practicing the perfection of vigor. In this way, indeed, O Venerable Śāradvatīputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of vigor encompasses all six perfections. Therefore, he is said to be "armed with the great armor."

Furthermore, Venerable Śāradvatīputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of meditative concentration gives a gift, he does so with mental engagements associated with the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), not with those associated with the disciples or solitary buddhas. Having made all that merit common to all sentient beings, he dedicates it toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. This is the perfection of generosity of a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of meditative concentration.

Furthermore, venerable Śāradvatīputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of meditative concentration observes ethical discipline, he does so with mental attentions associated with the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), not with those associated with the disciples or solitary buddhas; and having made that root of virtue common to all sentient beings, he dedicates it toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment—this is the perfection of ethical discipline for one practicing the perfection of meditative concentration.

Furthermore, venerable Śāradvatīputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of meditative concentration cultivates patience. With mental attentions associated with the knowledge of all aspects, and not those associated with the disciples or solitary buddhas, he shares that root of merit with all sentient beings and dedicates it toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening. This is the perfection of patience for one practicing the perfection of meditative concentration.

Furthermore, venerable Śāradvatīputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of meditative concentration, his state of non-laxity in vigor—through mental engagements associated with the knowledge of all aspects, and not through those associated with śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas—and having made that root of virtue common to all sentient beings, he dedicates it toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment: this is the perfection of vigor for one practicing the perfection of meditative concentration.

Furthermore, venerable Śāradvatīputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of meditative concentration, that one-pointedness of mind within mental attentions associated with the knowledge of all aspects—which does not allow any opportunity for mental attentions associated with śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, by virtue of having a single object of focus—and which, having made that root of merit common to all sentient beings, dedicates it toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment: this is the perfection of meditative concentration for one practicing the perfection of meditative concentration.

Furthermore, venerable Śāradvatīputra, for a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*), the perception that all phenomena are like illusions (*māyākṛta*) is present. By means of that meditative concentration, he does not conceive of himself [as an agent], nor does he apprehend the meditative concentration. Having made those roots of virtue common to all sentient beings, he dedicates them toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment; this is the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) for one practicing the perfection of meditative concentration.
In this way indeed, venerable Śāradvatīputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of meditation embraces all six perfections; therefore, he is said to be "armed with the great armor."

Furthermore, venerable Śāradvatīputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he gives a gift purified in its three spheres (*trimandala-pariśuddha*), with mental orientations associated with the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) and not associated with the vehicles of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas. Having made that root of merit common to all sentient beings, he dedicates it toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; this is the perfection of wisdom of the bodhisattva mahāsattva.

[This is] the perfection of giving for one who practices. Furthermore, venerable Śāradvatīputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, guarding morality with mental attentions associated with the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) and not with those associated with the disciples or solitary buddhas, he makes that root of virtue common to all sentient beings and dedicates it toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment; this is [the practice] of one practicing the perfection of wisdom.

The Perfection of Ethical Discipline (*śīlapāramitā*). Furthermore, Venerable Śāradvatīputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), there is his endurance, proclamation, and acceptance of those phenomena; through mental attentions associated with the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) and not associated with the levels of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, he shares that root of virtue with all sentient beings and dedicates it toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment—this is the perfection of patience (*kṣāntipāramitā*) for one practicing the perfection of wisdom.

Furthermore, venerable Śāradvatīputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, his non-laxity of vigor consists of mental attentions associated with the knowledge of all aspects, rather than those associated with the level of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas. And having made that root of virtue common to all sentient beings, he dedicates it toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment; this is the perfection of vigor for one practicing the perfection of wisdom.

Furthermore, venerable Śāradvatīputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, that one-pointedness of mind associated with the mental engagements connected to the knowledge of all aspects—and not those associated with the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas—and having made that root of virtue common to all sentient beings, dedicates it toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening: this is the perfection of meditation for one practicing the perfection of wisdom.
Furthermore, venerable Śāradvatīputra, for a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom, the perception that all phenomena are like illusions is present.

Through mental engagements associated with the knowledge of all aspects, and not those associated with the disciples or solitary buddhas, he makes that root of virtue common to all sentient beings and dedicates it toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment; this is the perfection of wisdom for one practicing the perfection of wisdom.

Venerable Śāradvatīputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva, with a mind associated with the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*), does not take these perfections as signs (*nimitta*)—neither as sentient beings nor as awakening—and does not apprehend them, this is the great armor of the six perfections for a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
Thus indeed, Venerable Śāradvatīputra, by abiding in each individual perfection, a bodhisattva mahāsattva fulfills all six perfections.

Furthermore, venerable Śāradvatīputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not enter the meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), or the formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*); yet he does not conceal the meditative concentrations, the immeasurables, and the formless attainments. He is not captivated by those meditative concentrations, the immeasurables, and the formless attainments, nor is he reborn through the power of the meditative concentrations, the immeasurables, and the formless attainments.

Venerable Śāradvatīputra, this is the perfection of wisdom of a bodhisattva mahāsattva accompanied by skill in means. Furthermore, Venerable Śāradvatīputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva enters into the meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), and the formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*) through the vision of seclusion and the vision of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; yet he is not reborn under their influence, nor does he realize the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).

And [he surpasses] all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas. This is the great armor of skillful means for a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom. In this way indeed, venerable Śāradvatīputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva is said to be "armed with the great armor."

Venerable Śāradvatīputra, for a bodhisattva mahāsattva who has thus donned the armor, the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, in world systems in the eastern direction as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā, utter words of exultation; they proclaim his name, raise their voices, and cause their sound to be heard.

In that world-system, this bodhisattva mahāsattva, having donned the great armor, matures sentient beings and purifies a buddha-field, and sports with supernatural powers. In world-systems in the southern direction as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā, the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, utter a cry of exultation, proclaim his name, raise their voices, and cause their sound to be heard: "This one, in that [world-system]..."

In this world-system, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, clad in the great armor, brings sentient beings to maturity, purifies a Buddha-field, and sports with supernatural powers. He asked: "To what extent, venerable Pūrṇa, is a bodhisattva mahāsattva said to have set out in the Great Vehicle? And what is the Great Vehicle of the bodhisattva mahāsattva? Pūrṇa replied: "In this regard, venerable Śāradvatīputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the six perfections. While practicing the perfection of giving, he is secluded from sensual desires."

Secluded from evil, unwholesome states, he enters and dwells in the first dhyāna, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought, and possesses the joy and happiness born of seclusion. With the subsiding of applied and sustained thought, through internal tranquility and the unification of the mind, he enters and dwells in the second dhyāna, which is without applied or sustained thought, and possesses the joy and happiness born of concentration. Through detachment from joy, he dwells in equanimity.

Possessing mindfulness and clear comprehension, he experiences happiness with the body; that which the Noble Ones describe as "dwelling in equanimity, mindful, and happy," he attains and dwells in this third dhyāna, free from joy. And through the abandoning of pleasure and the abandoning of pain, and with the prior disappearance of mental gladness and dejection, he attains and dwells in the fourth dhyāna, which is neither-painful-nor-pleasant and characterized by the purity of equanimity and mindfulness.

With a mind accompanied by loving-kindness—vast, exalted, non-dual, immeasurable, free from enmity, unassailable, without rival, perfected, and well-cultivated—he dwells having resolved upon pervading the ten directions throughout the world that is bounded by the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu) and extends to the limits of the realm of space (ākāśadhātu).

With a mind accompanied by compassion—vast, exalted, non-dual, immeasurable, free from enmity, free from malice, without rival, perfected, and well-cultivated—he dwells having resolved upon and pervaded the ten directions throughout the world that is bounded by the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*) and reaches to the limits of the realm of space (*ākāśadhātu*).

With a mind accompanied by sympathetic joy—vast, exalted, non-dual, immeasurable, free from enmity, free from malice, without rival, perfected, and well-cultivated—he dwells having resolved upon and pervaded the ten directions throughout the world that is bounded by the realm of phenomena and reaches to the limits of the realm of space.

With a mind accompanied by equanimity—vast, exalted, non-dual, immeasurable, free from enmity, free from ill-will, undisturbed, perfected, and well-cultivated—he dwells pervading the ten directions within this world that is bounded by the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*) and terminates in the realm of space (*ākāśadhātu*), by way of non-apprehension. Having completely transcended all perceptions of form...

Having practiced the disappearance of perceptions of diversity through mental attention to the cessation of perceptions, he attains and dwells in the sphere of infinite space. By completely transcending the sphere of infinite space, thinking "consciousness is infinite," he attains and dwells in the sphere of infinite consciousness. By completely transcending the sphere of infinite consciousness, thinking "there is nothing at all," he attains and dwells in the sphere of nothingness.

Having completely transcended the sphere of nothingness, he dwells having attained the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception by means of the yoga of non-apprehension. This is the meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) of the bodhisattva mahāsattva.

When the bodhisattva mahāsattva enters into and emerges from these meditative concentrations, these immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), and these formless attainments (*ārūpya*) through their aspects, forms, signs, and marks, and dedicates them toward omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*), this is the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*) of the bodhisattva mahāsattva.

Through detachment from joy, he dwells in equanimity; mindful and clearly comprehending, he experiences happiness with the body. That which the Noble Ones describe as "dwelling in happiness with equanimity and mindfulness," he attains and dwells in that third dhyāna, free from joy.

Through the abandoning of pleasure and the abandoning of pain, and through the prior disappearance of mental joy and dejection, he dwells having attained the fourth dhyāna, which is neither painful nor pleasant and is purified by equanimity and mindfulness. Having pervaded the ten directions and resolved upon them, he dwells there. Through the complete transcendence of perceptions of form, through the disappearance of perceptions [of sensory resistance], and through non-attention to perceptions of diversity, thinking "space is infinite," he attains and dwells in the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*).

By completely transcending the sphere of infinite space, thinking "consciousness is infinite," he attains and dwells in the sphere of infinite consciousness. Practicing the perfection of wisdom, he, secluded from sensual desires and secluded from evil, unwholesome states, enters and dwells in the first dhyāna, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought, and possesses the joy and happiness born of seclusion. Through the abandoning of both pleasure and pain...

Entering into meditative absorption and emerging from it, he dedicates [the merit] toward omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*); this is the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) of the bodhisattva mahāsattva. It is in this way, venerable Śāradvatīputra, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva is said to have set out upon the Great Vehicle (*mahāyāna*).

Furthermore, venerable Śāradvatīputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells having resolved upon and pervaded the ten directions with a mind accompanied by loving-kindness—vast, exalted, non-dual, immeasurable, free from enmity, unassailable, without malice, fulfilled, and well-cultivated—extending through the world as far as the limit of the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu) and reaching to the end of the realm of space (ākāśadhātu).

With the fading away of rapture, he dwells in equanimity; mindful and clearly comprehending, he experiences bliss with the body—that of which the Noble Ones say, "He dwells in bliss who is equanimous and mindful"—and thus he enters and dwells in the third dhyāna, which is devoid of rapture.

He dwells; through the abandoning of pleasure and the abandoning of pain, and with the prior disappearance of mental joy and dejection, he enters and dwells in the fourth dhyāna, which is neither painful nor pleasant and is purified by equanimity and mindfulness. Through the complete transcending of perceptions of form, by the disappearance of perceptions of resistance, and by not attending to perceptions of diversity, thinking "space is infinite," he enters and dwells in the sphere of infinite space.

Furthermore, that bodhisattva mahāsattva, with a mind associated with the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) and preceded by great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), for the sake of abandoning the afflictions (*kleśa*), explains, teaches, illuminates, elucidates, and clarifies to others the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*), the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), and the formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*). He instructs them regarding their distinctions, their traditional enumeration, their disadvantages (*ādīnava*), and the way of escape (*niḥsaraṇa*). This is the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*) of the bodhisattva mahāsattva.

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva, by means of those very mental attentions associated with the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), enters into and emerges from the meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), and the formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*), and allows no opportunity for other thoughts to arise—namely, thoughts of the disciples (*śrāvaka*) or thoughts of the solitary buddhas (*pratyekabuddha*)—this is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s supreme perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*).

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in the meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), and the formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*) through mental attentions associated with the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), it occurs to him thus:

"I shall teach the Dharma for the sake of exhausting the afflictions of all sentient beings"—the endurance, appreciation, investigation, and realization of those mental attentions, as well as the higher meditative cultivation, this is the perfection of patience (*kṣāntipāramitā*) of the bodhisattva mahāsattva; when the bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in the meditations, the immeasurables, and the formless attainments associated with the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*).

And when, for the sake of all sentient beings, one does not slacken in vigor regarding the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), this is the perfection of vigor (*vīryapāramitā*) of the bodhisattva mahāsattva. When a bodhisattva mahāsattva, through mental engagements associated with the knowledge of all aspects, enters into and emerges from the meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), liberations (*vimokṣa*), and attainments (*samāpatti*) of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), and does not dedicate [the merit] to the level of a śrāvaka or the level of a pratyekabuddha—this is the [perfection of concentration] of the bodhisattva mahāsattva.

The perfection of meditation: when a bodhisattva mahāsattva, through mental attentions associated with the knowledge of all aspects, [cultivates] those factors of the first dhyāna, the factors of the second dhyāna, the factors of the third dhyāna, and the factors of the fourth dhyāna.

Not contemplating loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, equanimity, the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception by way of the aspect of impermanence, the aspect of suffering, the aspect of selflessness, the aspect of non-peace, the aspect of emptiness, the aspect of signlessness, or the aspect of wishlessness, he does not apprehend those meditative concentrations, immeasurables, or formless attainments; nor does he conceive himself by means of them. This is the perfection of wisdom of the bodhisattva mahāsattva.

Venerable Śāradvatīputra, this is the Mahāyāna of a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom. Furthermore, Venerable Śāradvatīputra, the Mahāyāna of a bodhisattva mahāsattva consists in that he cultivates the four foundations of mindfulness in all their aspects; he cultivates the four right efforts in all their aspects; [he cultivates] the four... in all their aspects.

He cultivates the bases of psychic power; he cultivates the five faculties in all their aspects; he cultivates the five powers in all their aspects; he cultivates the seven factors of enlightenment in all their aspects; he cultivates the noble eightfold path in all its aspects; he cultivates the noble truths in all their aspects; he cultivates the meditative absorptions in all their aspects; he cultivates the immeasurables in all their aspects; he cultivates the formless attainments in all their aspects.

He cultivates the liberations in all their aspects; he cultivates the meditative attainments of the successive dwellings in all their aspects; he cultivates the gateways to liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—in all their aspects; he cultivates the superknowledges in all their aspects; he cultivates meditative concentration in all its aspects; he cultivates the gateways to the dhāraṇīs in all their aspects; he cultivates the powers of a Tathāgata in all their aspects; he cultivates the grounds of self-confidence in all their aspects.

He cultivates the analytical knowledges in all their aspects; he cultivates great loving-kindness in all its aspects; he cultivates great compassion in all its aspects; he cultivates the unique qualities of a Buddha in all their aspects; he cultivates omniscience in all its aspects; he cultivates the knowledge of the aspects of the path in all its aspects; he cultivates the knowledge of all aspects in all its aspects. Venerable Śāradvatīputra, this is the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva mahāsattva.

Furthermore, venerable Śāradvatīputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva enters the concentration of loving-kindness (*maitrī-samādhi*) and resolves: "I must protect all sentient beings. He enters the concentration of compassion (*karuṇā-samādhi*) and directs pity and compassion toward sentient beings. He enters the concentration of sympathetic joy (*muditā-samādhi*) and resolves toward sentient beings: "I shall establish myself in this very way. He also enters the concentration of equanimity (*upekṣā-samādhi*).

And this determination to bring about the exhaustion of the outflows (*āsravakṣayaṇatā*) among sentient beings is the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*) of a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*). When a bodhisattva mahāsattva enters into and emerges from the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*), the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), the aspects (*ākāra*), the characteristics (*liṅga*), and the signs (*nimitta*), and does not dedicate [the merit] toward the level of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, but rather toward all-aspect omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*), this is the ungrasping perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*) of a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in the immeasurables.

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells unmixed with those meditative concentrations, immeasurables, and formless attainments, and does not desire these two levels—the level of the śrāvaka or the level of the pratyekabuddha—but rather only the knowledge of all aspects (sarvākārajñatā) is acceptable and pleasing to him, this is the perfection of patience of that bodhisattva mahāsattva while practicing within the immeasurables.

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells with thoughts associated with the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), never laying down the burden, for the sake of abandoning unwholesome dharmas and for the perfection of wholesome dharmas—this is the perfection of vigor (*vīryapāramitā*) of the bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*). When the bodhisattva mahāsattva enters into these meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*) and these formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*).

He is not reborn by the power of the meditative absorptions, the immeasurables, or the formless attainments; he does not relish them, nor is he captivated by them. This is the perfection of vigor of a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the immeasurables.

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva, through mental attentions associated with the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), enters into and emerges from those meditative concentrations, immeasurables, and formless attainments, and examines them by way of the aspect of impermanence, the aspect of suffering, the aspect of selflessness, the aspect of non-peace, the aspect of emptiness, the aspect of signlessness, and the aspect of wishlessness, yet does not fall into the level of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas—this is the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) of the bodhisattva mahāsattva.

This, venerable Śāradvatīputra, is the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva mahāsattva. Furthermore, venerable Śāradvatīputra, the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva mahāsattva is that knowledge which pertains to internal emptiness, yet not by way of non-apprehension; that knowledge which pertains to external emptiness, yet not by way of non-apprehension; that knowledge which pertains to internal-and-external emptiness, yet not by way of non-apprehension; and that knowledge which pertains to the emptiness of emptiness, yet not by way of non-apprehension.

That which is knowledge of the great emptiness, yet not by way of non-apprehension; that which is knowledge of the ultimate emptiness, yet not by way of non-apprehension; that which is knowledge of the conditioned emptiness, yet not by way of non-apprehension; that which is knowledge of the unconditioned emptiness, yet not by way of non-apprehension; that which is knowledge of the absolute emptiness, yet not by way of non-apprehension; that which is knowledge of the emptiness of that which is without beginning or end, yet not by way of non-apprehension.

That knowledge which pertains to the emptiness of non-dispersal (*anavakāra-śūnyatā*), yet not by way of non-apprehension; that knowledge which pertains to the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*), yet not by way of non-apprehension; that knowledge which pertains to the emptiness of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-śūnyatā*), yet not by way of non-apprehension; that knowledge which pertains to the emptiness of specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*), yet not by way of non-apprehension; that knowledge which pertains to the emptiness of non-apprehension (*anupalambha-śūnyatā*), yet not by way of non-apprehension; that knowledge which pertains to the emptiness of non-existence (*abhāva-śūnyatā*), yet not by way of non-apprehension.

The knowledge that, within the emptiness of intrinsic nature, there is no apprehension by way of non-apprehension; the knowledge that, within the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence, there is no apprehension by way of non-apprehension—this is the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva mahāsattva.

Furthermore, Venerable Śāradvatīputra, the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva mahāsattva is this: the knowledge that the mind is concentrated and is not differentiated with respect to all phenomena. This is the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva mahāsattva.

Neither does the cognition that "it is permanent" arise, nor does the cognition that "it is impermanent" arise; neither does the cognition that "it is pleasant" arise, nor does the cognition that "it is painful" arise; neither does the cognition that "it is self" arise, nor does the cognition that "it is non-self" arise; neither does the cognition that "it is pure" arise, nor does the cognition that "it is impure" arise. This is the Mahāyāna of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, and it is by way of non-apprehension (*anupalambha-yogena*).

Furthermore, venerable Śāradvatīputra, the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva mahāsattva is that knowledge which operates in the past time, operates in the future time, and operates in the present time; yet this knowledge of his regarding the three times is the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva mahāsattva through the application of non-apprehension.

Furthermore, Venerable Śāradvatīputra, the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva mahāsattva is that wherein knowledge does not operate in the desire realm, nor in the form realm, nor does knowledge operate in the formless realm; and yet, his knowledge functions within the desire, form, and formless realms—this too is the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva mahāsattva, and it is by way of non-apprehension.

Furthermore, venerable Śāradvatīputra, the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva mahāsattva is that wherein knowledge does not operate at all with respect to worldly things, nor with respect to supramundane things; it does not operate with respect to things with outflows (*sāśrava*) nor things without outflows (*anāśrava*); it does not operate with respect to conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) nor unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*).

Furthermore, O Venerable Śāradvatīputra, there is no knowledge of his regarding worldly or supramundane phenomena, nor regarding phenomena with outflows or without outflows, nor regarding conditioned or unconditioned phenomena; this, O Venerable Śāradvatīputra, is the Mahāyāna of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, and that is by way of non-apprehension. He said:

"To what extent, venerable Pūrṇa, is a bodhisattva mahāsattva said to be 'mounted upon the Great Vehicle'? Pūrṇa replied: "Venerable Śāradvatīputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he mounts the perfection of giving. Yet he does not apprehend the gift, nor the perfection of giving, nor the bodhisattva, nor the recipient, nor those mental attentions."

In this way, indeed, a bodhisattva mahāsattva is said to be "mounted upon the Great Vehicle" by means of the yoga of non-apprehension. Here, venerable Śāradvatīputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom [fulfills] the perfection of ethical discipline...

He ascends; yet he does not perceive morality, nor the perfection of morality, nor the bodhisattva, nor those mental orientations. In this way, indeed, a bodhisattva mahāsattva is said to have "ascended the perfection of morality" by means of non-apprehension. Here, venerable Śāradvatīputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in the perfection of wisdom ascends the perfection of patience.

He does not perceive patience, nor the perfection of patience, nor the bodhisattva, nor those mental engagements; in this way, indeed, a bodhisattva mahāsattva is said to have mounted the perfection of patience by means of non-apprehension. Here, venerable Śāradvatīputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in the perfection of wisdom mounts the perfection of vigor.

He does not perceive energy, nor the perfection of energy, nor the bodhisattva, nor those mental engagements; it is in this way that a bodhisattva mahāsattva is said to have mounted the perfection of energy, by means of non-apprehension. Here, venerable Śāradvatīputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in the perfection of wisdom mounts the perfection of meditation.

He does not perceive meditation, nor the perfection of meditation, nor the bodhisattva, nor those mental engagements; it is in this way, indeed, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva is said to have ascended to the perfection of meditation through the yoga of non-perception. Here, venerable Śāradvatīputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in the perfection of wisdom ascends to the perfection of wisdom; he does not perceive even wholesome dharmas.

He does not perceive any phenomenon that is unwholesome, nor mundane, nor supramundane, nor conditioned, nor unconditioned, nor with outflows, nor without outflows; nor does he perceive wisdom, nor the perfection of wisdom, nor the bodhisattva, nor those mental attentions. It is in this way, indeed, through the yoga of non-perception, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva is said to have mounted the perfection of wisdom.

Furthermore, Venerable Śāradvatīputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva cultivates internal emptiness with undistracted mental orientations associated with the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), for the purpose of cultivating and eliminating [conceptualization], and that by way of non-apprehension (*anupalambha*). With undistracted mental orientations associated with the knowledge of all aspects, he cultivates external emptiness, for the purpose of cultivating and eliminating [conceptualization], and that by way of non-apprehension.

With unadulterated mental attentions associated with the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), he cultivates internal and external emptiness (*adhyātmabahirdhā-śūnyatā*) for the purpose of cultivating and deconstructing [conceptualization], and that by way of non-apprehension (*anupalambha-yoga*). With unadulterated mental attentions associated with the knowledge of all aspects, he cultivates the emptiness of emptiness (*śūnyatā-śūnyatā*) for the purpose of cultivating and deconstructing [conceptualization], and that by way of non-apprehension.

With mental attentions that are unadulterated and associated with the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), he cultivates the great emptiness (*mahāśūnyatā*) for the purpose of cultivation and non-cultivation, and that by way of non-apprehension (*anupalambha*). With mental attentions that are unadulterated and associated with the knowledge of all aspects, he cultivates the ultimate emptiness (*paramārthaśūnyatā*) for the purpose of cultivation and non-cultivation, and that by way of non-apprehension.

With mental attentions that are unmixed and associated with the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), he cultivates the emptiness of the conditioned (*saṃskṛtaśūnyatā*) for the purpose of cultivating and then transcending cultivation; and he does so through the yoga of non-apprehension (*anupalambha*). With mental attentions that are unmixed and associated with the knowledge of all aspects, he cultivates the emptiness of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛtaśūnyatā*) for the purpose of cultivating and then transcending cultivation; and he does so through the yoga of non-apprehension.

With unadulterated mental attentions associated with the knowledge of all aspects, he cultivates absolute emptiness for the purpose of cultivating and deconstructing cultivation, and that by way of non-apprehension. With unadulterated mental attentions associated with the knowledge of all aspects, he cultivates the emptiness of that which is without beginning or end for the purpose of cultivating and deconstructing cultivation, and that by way of non-apprehension.

With unadulterated mental attentions associated with the knowledge of all aspects, he cultivates the emptiness of non-dispersal for the purpose of cultivation and the elimination of what is to be cultivated, and that by means of non-apprehension—with unadulterated mental attentions associated with the knowledge of all aspects.

By means of mental attentions (*manasikāra*), he cultivates the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*) for the purpose of cultivation and non-cultivation, and that by way of non-apprehension (*anupalambha-yoga*). By means of unmixed mental attentions associated with the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), he cultivates the emptiness of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-śūnyatā*) for the purpose of cultivation and non-cultivation, and that by way of non-apprehension. By means of unmixed mental attentions associated with the knowledge of all aspects, he cultivates the emptiness of specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*) for the purpose of cultivation and non-cultivation.

And that is by way of non-apprehension. With mental attentions associated with the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) that are unadulterated, he cultivates the emptiness of non-apprehension for the purpose of cultivating and eliminating [conceptualization], and that is by way of non-apprehension. With mental attentions associated with the knowledge of all aspects that are unadulterated, he cultivates the emptiness of non-existence for the purpose of cultivating and eliminating [conceptualization], and that is by way of non-apprehension.

With mental attentions that are unadulterated and associated with the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), he cultivates the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*) for the purpose of cultivating and dispelling [conceptualization], and that by way of non-apprehension (*anupalambha-yoga*). With mental attentions that are unadulterated and associated with the knowledge of all aspects, he cultivates the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence (*abhāva-svabhāva-śūnyatā*) for the purpose of cultivating and dispelling [conceptualization], and that by way of non-apprehension.

Furthermore, venerable Śāradvatīputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva cultivates the four applications of mindfulness with undistracted mental attentions associated with the knowledge of all aspects, for the purpose of cultivation and thorough cultivation, and by means of the yoga of non-apprehension. With undistracted mental attentions associated with the knowledge of all aspects, he cultivates the four right efforts for the purpose of cultivation and thorough cultivation, and by means of the yoga of non-apprehension.

With unadulterated mental attentions associated with the knowledge of all aspects, he cultivates the four bases of psychic power for the purpose of cultivation and non-cultivation, and that by way of non-apprehension. With unadulterated mental attentions associated with the knowledge of all aspects, he cultivates the five faculties for the purpose of cultivation and non-cultivation.

And that is by way of non-apprehension. With mental engagements associated with the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) that are unadulterated, he cultivates the five powers for the purpose of cultivation and elimination; and that is by way of non-apprehension. With mental engagements associated with the knowledge of all aspects that are unadulterated, he cultivates the seven factors of enlightenment for the purpose of cultivation and elimination; and that is by way of non-apprehension.

With mental engagements associated with the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) that are unadulterated, he cultivates the noble eightfold path for the purpose of cultivation and non-cultivation, and that by way of non-apprehension (*anupalambha*). With mental engagements associated with the knowledge of all aspects that are unadulterated, he cultivates the noble truths for the purpose of cultivation and non-cultivation, and that by way of non-apprehension.

He cultivates the four dhyānas with mental applications associated with the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) that are unmixed [with other thoughts], and that by way of non-apprehension (*anupalambha*). He cultivates the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*) with mental applications associated with the knowledge of all aspects that are unmixed, for the purpose of cultivation and the elimination [of afflictions], and that by way of non-apprehension. He cultivates the four formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*) with mental applications associated with the knowledge of all aspects that are unmixed.

For the purpose of cultivating and then transcending [them], and by means of non-apprehension, he cultivates the eight liberations with mental attentions associated with the knowledge of all aspects that are unadulterated—for the purpose of cultivating and then transcending them, and by means of non-apprehension. For the purpose of cultivating and then transcending them, and by means of non-apprehension, he cultivates the nine successive attainments of meditative dwelling with mental attentions associated with the knowledge of all aspects that are unadulterated—for the purpose of cultivating and then transcending them, and by means of non-apprehension.

With mental attentions associated with the knowledge of all aspects that are unadulterated, he cultivates the doors of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—for the purpose of cultivation and non-cultivation, and that by way of non-apprehension. With mental attentions associated with the knowledge of all aspects that are unadulterated, he cultivates the superknowledges for the purpose of cultivation and non-cultivation, and that by way of non-apprehension. [He does so] with mental attentions associated with the knowledge of all aspects that are unadulterated.

He cultivates the concentrations for the purpose of cultivation and non-cultivation, and that by way of non-apprehension. With undistracted mental attentions associated with the knowledge of all aspects, he cultivates the gateways of mnemonic formulas for the purpose of cultivation and non-cultivation, and that by way of non-apprehension. With undistracted mental attentions associated with the knowledge of all aspects, he cultivates the powers of a Tathāgata for the purpose of cultivation and non-cultivation, and that by way of non-apprehension.

With mental attentions associated with the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) that are unadulterated, he cultivates the four grounds of self-confidence (*vaiśāradya*), in the sense of cultivation and non-cultivation, and by means of the yoga of non-apprehension (*anupalambha*). With mental attentions associated with the knowledge of all aspects that are unadulterated, he cultivates the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), in the sense of cultivation and non-cultivation, and by means of the yoga of non-apprehension.

Unmixed with other mental engagements, he cultivates great loving-kindness (*mahāmaitrī*) through mental engagements associated with the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), for the purpose of cultivation and non-cultivation, and that by way of non-apprehension (*anupalambha*). Unmixed with other mental engagements, he cultivates great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) through mental engagements associated with the knowledge of all aspects, for the purpose of cultivation and non-cultivation, and that by way of non-apprehension.

Unmixed with mental engagements associated with anything other than the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), he cultivates the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇikabuddhadharma*) for the purpose of cultivation and non-cultivation, and that by way of non-apprehension (*anupalambha*). It is in this way, O Venerable Śāradvatīputra, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva is said to have "embarked upon the Great Vehicle."

Furthermore, venerable Śāradvatīputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva understands thus: "This which is called 'bodhisattva' is a mere conventional designation, based on the non-apprehensibility of a bodhisattva. This which is called 'form' is a mere name, based on the non-apprehensibility of form. This which is called 'feeling' is a mere name, based on the non-apprehensibility of feeling. This which is called 'perception' is a mere name, based on the non-apprehensibility of perception."

This is a mere name, namely, the formative forces (saṃskāra), based on the non-apprehensibility of the formative forces; this is a mere name, namely, consciousness (vijñāna), based on the non-apprehensibility of consciousness.

Based on [this], it is a mere name, namely "eye," based on the non-apprehensibility of the eye; it is a mere name, namely "ear," based on the non-apprehensibility of the ear; it is a mere name, namely "nose," based on the non-apprehensibility of the nose; it is a mere name, namely "tongue," based on the non-apprehensibility of the tongue; it is a mere name, namely "body," based on the non-apprehensibility of the body.

This is mere name, namely the mind, based on the non-apprehension of the mind. This is mere name, namely form, based on the non-apprehension of form. This is mere name, namely sound, based on the non-apprehension of sound. This is mere name, namely odor, based on the non-apprehension of odor. This is mere name, namely taste, based on the non-apprehension of taste.
This which is called "contact" is a mere name, based on the non-apprehensibility of contact; this which is called "phenomena" is a mere name, based on the non-apprehensibility of phenomena.

This which is called eye-consciousness is a mere name, based on the non-apprehensibility of eye-consciousness; this which is called ear-consciousness is a mere name, based on the non-apprehensibility of ear-consciousness; this which is called nose-consciousness is a mere name, based on the non-apprehensibility of nose-consciousness; this which is called tongue-consciousness is a mere name, based on the non-apprehensibility of tongue-consciousness.

This which is called body-consciousness is a mere name, based on the non-apprehensibility of body-consciousness. This which is called mind-consciousness is a mere name, based on the non-apprehensibility of mind-consciousness. This which is called eye-contact is a mere name, based on the non-apprehensibility of eye-contact. This which is called ear-contact is a mere name, based on the non-apprehensibility of ear-contact.

This so-called "olfactory contact" is a mere name, based on the non-apprehensibility of olfactory contact. This so-called "gustatory contact" is a mere name, based on the non-apprehensibility of gustatory contact. This so-called "tactile contact" is a mere name.

Based on the non-apprehension of bodily contact, this which is called "mental contact" is a mere name, based on the non-apprehension of mental contact. This which is called "feeling born of eye-contact" is a mere name, based on the non-apprehension of feeling born of eye-contact. This which is called "feeling born of ear-contact" is a mere name, based on the non-apprehension of feeling born of ear-contact.

This is a mere name, namely, feeling born of nose-contact, based on the non-apprehensibility of feeling born of nose-contact. This is a mere name, namely, feeling born of tongue-contact, based on the non-apprehensibility of feeling born of tongue-contact. This is a mere name, namely, feeling born of body-contact, based on the non-apprehensibility of feeling born of body-contact.
This is a mere name, namely, feeling born of mind-contact, based on the non-apprehensibility of feeling born of mind-contact.

This is merely a name, namely the earth element, based on the non-apprehensibility of the earth element. This is merely a name, namely the water element, based on the non-apprehensibility of the water element. This is merely a name, namely the fire element, based on the non-apprehensibility of the fire element. This is merely a name, namely the air element, based on the non-apprehensibility of the air element. This is merely a name, namely the space element, based on the non-apprehensibility of the space element.

This is merely a name, namely, the element of consciousness, based on the non-apprehensibility of the element of consciousness. This is merely a name, namely, ignorance, based on the non-apprehensibility of ignorance. This is merely a name, namely, the formative forces, based on the non-apprehensibility of the formative forces. This is merely a name, namely, consciousness, based on the non-apprehensibility of consciousness. This is merely a name, namely, name-and-form, based on the non-apprehensibility of name-and-form.

This which is called the six sense bases is merely a name, based on the non-apprehensibility of the six sense bases. This which is called contact is merely a name, based on the non-apprehensibility of contact. This which is called feeling is merely a name, based on the non-apprehensibility of feeling. This which is called craving is merely a name, based on the non-apprehensibility of craving.

This is merely a name, namely grasping, based on the non-apprehensibility of grasping; this is merely a name, namely existence, based on the non-apprehensibility of existence; this is merely a name, namely birth, based on the non-apprehensibility of birth; this is merely a name, namely aging and death, based on the non-apprehensibility of aging and death.

This so-called "perfection of generosity" is a mere name, based on the non-apprehensibility of the perfection of generosity. This so-called "perfection of ethical discipline" is a mere name, based on the non-apprehensibility of the perfection of ethical discipline. This so-called "perfection of patience" is a mere name, based on the non-apprehensibility of the perfection of patience. This so-called "perfection of vigor" is a mere name, based on the non-apprehensibility of the perfection of vigor.

This so-called perfection of meditation is a mere name, based on the non-apprehensibility of the perfection of meditation; this so-called perfection of wisdom is a mere name, based on the non-apprehensibility of the perfection of wisdom.

This is merely a name, namely internal emptiness, based on the non-apprehensibility of internal emptiness. This is merely a name, namely external emptiness, based on the non-apprehensibility of external emptiness. This is merely a name, namely internal-and-external emptiness, based on the non-apprehensibility of internal-and-external emptiness. This is merely a name, namely the emptiness of emptiness, based on the non-apprehensibility of the emptiness of emptiness.

This is merely a name, namely "great emptiness," based on the non-apprehensibility of great emptiness. This is merely a name, namely "emptiness of the ultimate," based on the non-apprehensibility of the emptiness of the ultimate. This is merely a name, namely "emptiness of the conditioned," based on the non-apprehensibility of the emptiness of the conditioned. This is merely a name, namely "emptiness of the unconditioned," based on the non-apprehensibility of the emptiness of the unconditioned.

This is a mere name, namely "absolute emptiness," based on the non-apprehensibility of absolute emptiness. This is a mere name, namely "emptiness without beginning or end," based on the non-apprehensibility of emptiness without beginning or end.

This is merely a name, namely, the emptiness of non-dispersal, based on the non-apprehensibility of the emptiness of non-dispersal. This is merely a name, namely, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, based on the non-apprehensibility of the emptiness of intrinsic nature. This is merely a name, namely, the emptiness of all phenomena, based on the non-apprehensibility of the emptiness of all phenomena. This is merely a name, namely, the emptiness of specific characteristics, based on the non-apprehensibility of the emptiness of specific characteristics.

This is merely a name, namely, the emptiness of non-apprehension, based on the non-apprehensibility of the emptiness of non-apprehension. This is merely a name, namely, the emptiness of non-existence, based on the non-apprehensibility of the emptiness of non-existence. This is merely a name, namely, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, based on the non-apprehensibility of the emptiness of intrinsic nature. This is merely a name, namely, the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence, based on the non-apprehensibility of the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence.

This is merely a name, namely the four foundations of mindfulness, based on the non-apprehensibility of the four foundations of mindfulness. This is merely a name, namely the four right efforts, based on the non-apprehensibility of the four right efforts. This is merely a name, namely the four bases of psychic power, based on the non-apprehensibility of the four bases of psychic power. This is merely a name, namely the five faculties, based on the non-apprehensibility of the faculties.

This is merely a name, namely the five powers, based on the non-apprehensibility of the powers. This is merely a name, namely the seven factors of enlightenment, based on the non-apprehensibility of the factors of enlightenment. This is merely a name, namely the noble eightfold path, based on the non-apprehensibility of the noble eightfold path. This is merely a name, namely the noble truths, based on the non-apprehensibility of the noble truths. This is merely a name, namely the meditative concentrations, based on the non-apprehensibility of the meditative concentrations.

These are merely names, namely the immeasurables, based on the non-apprehensibility of the immeasurables; these are merely names, namely the formless attainments, based on the non-apprehensibility of the formless attainments; these are merely names, namely the eight liberations, based on the non-apprehensibility of the liberations; these are merely names, namely the serial meditative attainments.

Based on the non-apprehensibility of the successive attainments of the meditative dwellings, these are merely names, namely: the gateways to liberation of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; based on the non-apprehensibility of the gateways to liberation of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, these are merely names. Based on the non-apprehensibility of the superknowledges, these are merely names, namely: the superknowledges; based on the non-apprehensibility of the superknowledges, these are merely names. Based on the non-apprehensibility of the concentrations, these are merely names, namely: the concentrations.

These so-called "gateways of dhāraṇī" are mere names, based on the non-apprehensibility of the gateways of dhāraṇī. These so-called "ten powers of a Tathāgata" are mere names, based on the non-apprehensibility of the powers of a Tathāgata. These so-called "four grounds of self-confidence" are mere names, based on the non-apprehensibility of the grounds of self-confidence. These so-called "four analytical knowledges" are mere names, based on the non-apprehensibility of the analytical knowledges.

This is a mere name, namely "great loving-kindness," on account of the non-apprehensibility of great loving-kindness. This is a mere name, namely "great compassion," on account of the non-apprehensibility of great compassion. This is a mere name, namely "the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha," on account of the non-apprehensibility of the unique qualities of a Buddha. This is a mere name, namely "suchness," on account of the non-apprehensibility of suchness.

This is merely a name, namely "suchness," based on the non-apprehensibility of suchness. This is merely a name, namely "the nature of phenomena" (*dharmatā*), based on the non-apprehensibility of the nature of phenomena. This is merely a name, namely "the realm of phenomena" (*dharmadhātu*), based on the non-apprehensibility of the realm of phenomena. This is merely a name, namely "the stability of phenomena" (*dharma-sthititā*), based on the non-apprehensibility of the stability of phenomena.

This is a mere name, namely the fixed nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), based on the non-apprehensibility of the fixed nature of phenomena. This is a mere name, namely the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), based on the non-apprehensibility of the limit of reality. This is a mere name, namely awakening (*bodhi*), based on the non-apprehensibility of awakening. This is a mere name, namely a Buddha, based on the non-apprehensibility of a Buddha.
It is in this way, venerable Śāradvatīputra, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva is said to have mounted the Great Vehicle.

Furthermore, venerable Śāradvatīputra, from the first production of the thought of awakening, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having fully perfected all the superknowledges (*abhijñā*), brings sentient beings to maturity and travels from buddhafield to buddhafield.

For the sake of honoring, respecting, revering, and worshiping the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, he who is a reciter hears from those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, the method for the worship and honor of those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones; that is to say, the very Bodhisattva Vehicle. Having mounted that Bodhisattva Vehicle, he travels from Buddha-field to Buddha-field and purifies the Buddha-fields.

He brings sentient beings to maturity, yet the notion of a "Buddha-field" does not arise for him.
