Abiding on the stage of non-duality, he intentionally assumes whatever form of body he is able to take in order to accomplish the welfare of mortals. He is never separated from that vehicle until he attains the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*).

Having attained omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*), he turns the wheel of Dharma, which cannot be turned by Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas, nor by the world of gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas, humans, or non-humans. When he has fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, in world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges in the eastern direction, proclaim his praise and utter his glory.

They proclaim this sound: "In that world-system, this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, having mounted the Great Vehicle, the Unsurpassed Vehicle, the Preeminent Vehicle, has attained all-aspect omniscience; having attained all-aspect omniscience, he turns the wheel of Dharma. In world-systems in the southern direction as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges, the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, speak his praise, utter his renown, and proclaim this sound.

In that world-system, this bodhisattva mahāsattva, having mounted the Great Vehicle, the Unsurpassed Vehicle, the Preeminent Vehicle, has attained all-aspect omniscience; and having attained all-aspect omniscience, [he turns] the wheel of Dharma.

He causes [them] to turn. In world-systems in the western direction as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā, the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, speak his praise, proclaim his fame, and cause his renown to be heard: "In such-and-such a world-system, this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, having mounted the Great Vehicle, the Unsurpassed Vehicle, the Preeminent Vehicle, has attained all-aspect omniscience; having attained all-aspect omniscience, he turns the wheel of Dharma."

In the northern direction, in world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā, the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, speak his praise, proclaim his fame, and cause his renown to be heard: "In that world-system, this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva has mounted the Great Vehicle, the Unsurpassed Vehicle, the Preeminent Vehicle, and has attained all-aspect omniscience; having attained all-aspect omniscience, he turns the wheel of Dharma."

In the southeastern direction, in world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā, the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, speak his praise, proclaim his fame, and cause his renown to be heard: "In that world-system, this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva has mounted the Great Vehicle, the Unsurpassed Vehicle, the Preeminent Vehicle, and has attained all-aspect omniscience; having attained all-aspect omniscience, he turns the wheel of Dharma."

In the southwestern direction, in world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges, the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, speak his praise, proclaim his fame, and cause his renown to resound: "In that world-system, this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, having mounted the Great Vehicle, the Unsurpassed Vehicle, the Preeminent Vehicle, has attained all-aspect omniscience; having attained all-aspect omniscience, he turns the wheel of Dharma."

In the northwestern direction, in world systems as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā, the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, speak his praise, proclaim his fame, and cause his renown to be heard: "In that world system, this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, having mounted the Great Vehicle, the Unsurpassed Vehicle, the Preeminent Vehicle, has attained all-aspect omniscience; having attained all-aspect omniscience, he turns the wheel of Dharma.
In the northeastern direction, in [world systems] as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā...

In the world-systems, the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, speak his praise, proclaim his fame, and cause his renown to resound: "In such-and-such a world-system, the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, speak his praise, proclaim his fame, and cause his renown to resound; in that very world-system, this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, having mounted the Great Vehicle, the Unsurpassed Vehicle, the Preeminent Vehicle, has attained all-aspect omniscience."

Having attained the knowledge of all modes, he turns the wheel of Dharma; in world systems in the downward direction as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges, the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, speak his praise, proclaim his fame, and cause his voice to resound.

"In that world-system, this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, having mounted the Great Vehicle, the Unsurpassed Vehicle, the Preeminent Vehicle, has attained all-aspect omniscience; having attained all-aspect omniscience, he turns the wheel of Dharma. In the world-systems above, as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges, the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, speak his praise, proclaim his fame, and cause his renown to resound."

"In that world-system, this bodhisattva mahāsattva has mounted the Great Vehicle, the supreme vehicle, and attained all-aspect omniscience; having attained all-aspect omniscience, he turns the wheel of Dharma. It is in this way, venerable Śāradvatīputra, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva is said to have 'mounted the Great Vehicle.'"

Then the venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, it is said, 'one who has donned the great armor, one who has donned the great armor. To what extent, Blessed One, is a bodhisattva mahāsattva said to have donned the great armor? When this was said, the Blessed One said this to the venerable Subhūti: "In this case, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva has donned the armor of the Great Vehicle."

That is to say, having donned the armor of the perfection of generosity, having donned the armor of the perfection of ethical discipline, having donned the armor of the perfection of patience, having donned the armor of the perfection of vigor, having donned the armor of the perfection of meditative concentration, and having donned the armor of the perfection of wisdom.

Having donned the armor; having donned the armor of internal emptiness, having donned the armor of external emptiness, having donned the armor of internal and external emptiness, having donned the armor of the emptiness of emptiness, having donned the armor of great emptiness, having donned the armor of the emptiness of the ultimate truth, having donned the armor of the emptiness of the conditioned, having donned the armor of the emptiness of the unconditioned, having donned the armor of absolute emptiness, having donned the armor of the emptiness of that which has no beginning or end...

Having donned the armor of the emptiness of non-dispersal, having donned the armor of the emptiness of intrinsic nature, having donned the armor of the emptiness of all phenomena, having donned the armor of the emptiness of specific characteristics, having donned the armor of the emptiness of the non-apprehendable, having donned the armor of the emptiness of non-existence, having donned the armor of the emptiness of self-nature, having donned the armor of the emptiness of self-nature, and having donned the armor of the emptiness of the self-nature of non-existence;

Having donned the armor of the foundations of mindfulness, having donned the armor of the right efforts, having donned the armor of the bases of psychic power, having donned the armor of the faculties, having donned the armor of the powers, having donned the armor of the factors of enlightenment, having donned the armor of the noble eightfold path, having donned the armor of the noble truths, having donned the armor of the meditative absorptions, having donned the armor of the immeasurables, having donned the armor of the formless attainments, and having donned the armor of the liberations.

Having donned the armor of the meditative attainments of the successive dwellings; having donned the armor of the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; having donned the armor of meditative concentration; having donned the armor of the superknowledges; having donned the armor of the gateways of mnemonic formulas; having donned the armor of the powers of a Tathāgata; having donned the armor of the grounds of self-confidence; having donned the armor of the analytical knowledges; having donned the armor of great loving-kindness; and having donned the armor of great compassion.

Having donned the armor of the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, having donned the armor of the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), and having donned the armor of the body of a Buddha, he pervaded this triple-thousandfold world system with his radiance. He pervaded worlds in the eastern direction, as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges, with his radiance; he pervaded worlds in the southern direction, as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges, with his radiance; [he pervaded] worlds in the western direction, as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges...

He irradiates world-systems with his light; he irradiates world-systems in the northern direction, as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges, with his light; he irradiates world-systems in the southeastern direction, as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges, with his light; he irradiates world-systems in the southwestern direction, as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges, with his light; he irradiates world-systems in the northwestern direction, as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges, with his light.

In the northeastern direction, he radiates light that pervades world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā; in the downward direction, he radiates light that pervades world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā; in the upward direction, he radiates light that pervades world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā. Having caused this trichiliocosm, the great trichiliocosm, to tremble in six ways, he causes world-systems in the eastern direction as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā to tremble in six ways.

In the southern direction, he causes world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges to tremble in six ways; in the western direction, he causes world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges to tremble in six ways; in the northern direction, he causes world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges to tremble in six ways; and in the southeastern direction, he causes world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges to tremble in six ways.

In the south-western direction, he causes world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā to tremble in six ways; in the north-western direction, he causes world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā to tremble in six ways; in the north-eastern direction, he causes world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā to tremble in six ways; in the downward direction, he causes world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā to tremble in six ways;
and in the upward direction, he causes world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā to tremble in six ways.

Having extinguished all the masses of fire belonging to the hell-beings within this trichiliocosm, he utters the words, "Homage to that Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha! and causes that sound to resound. Then the beings in the hells obtain the happiness and mental joy of that sound of the Buddha; through that happiness and mental joy, they emerge from those hells.

Having emerged from those hells, they are reborn wherever the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, reside, dwell, maintain themselves, and teach the Dharma in various world-systems. Having pacified the suffering of the animal realm for beings in the animal realm within this great trichiliocosm, he utters the words, "Homage to that Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha," and proclaims this sound.

Then those beings born as animals, having heard that sound of "Buddha," obtain happiness and mental well-being; through that happiness and mental well-being, they emerge from those animal births. Having emerged from those animal births, they are reborn wherever Buddhas, Blessed Ones, reside, remain, maintain themselves, and teach the Dharma in various Buddha-fields.

Then, having pacified the suffering of the world of Yama for the beings belonging to that realm within this trichiliocosm, he utters the sound: "Homage to that Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha! He makes the proclamation heard. Then, those beings of the world of Yama, having heard that sound of the Buddha, obtain happiness and gladness; through that happiness and gladness, they emerge from that world of Yama.

Then, having emerged from the world of Yama, he is reborn in whichever Buddha-fields the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, reside, remain, and maintain themselves, and where they teach the Dharma. In the eastern direction, in world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges, he extinguishes every mass of fire belonging to the hells.

Having extinguished [the fire], he utters the words "Homage to that Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha" and causes the sound to resound; then those beings in the hells, having heard that sound of the Buddha, obtain happiness and gladness, and by means of that happiness and gladness, they emerge from those hells.

Then, having emerged from the hells, he is reborn in whichever Buddha-fields the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, reside, dwell, maintain themselves, and teach the Dharma. In those very places, he arises. Having extinguished the entire mass of fire belonging to the hell-beings in world-systems in the southern direction as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā, he utters the words, "Homage to that Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha," and makes this sound resound.

Then those beings in the hells, having heard that sound of the Buddha, obtain happiness and gladness. By means of that happiness and gladness, they emerge from those hells. Having emerged from those hells, they are reborn wherever the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, reside, dwell, and maintain themselves, and where they teach the Dharma; they are reborn in those very places.

In the western direction, having extinguished all the masses of fire belonging to those in the hells throughout world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā, he utters the words, "Homage to that Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha! and causes this sound to resound. Then, those sentient beings in the hells, hearing that sound of the Buddha, obtain happiness and mental well-being; through that happiness and mental well-being, they emerge from those hells.

Then, having emerged from the hells, he is reborn in whichever Buddha-fields the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, reside, remain, and maintain themselves, and where they teach the Dharma. Having extinguished the entire mass of fire belonging to the hell-beings in world-systems in the northern direction as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges, he utters the words and proclaims the sound: "Homage to that Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha!"

Then those beings in the hells, having heard that sound of the Buddha, obtain happiness and mental well-being. By means of that happiness and mental well-being, they emerge from those hells. Having emerged from those hells, they are reborn in whichever buddha-fields the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, reside, remain, and maintain themselves, and where they teach the Dharma. In those very places they take birth.

In the eastern direction, he extinguishes all the masses of fire belonging to the hells in as many world-systems as there are grains of sand in the river Ganges; he utters the words "Homage to that Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha" and makes this sound heard. Then those beings in the hells, having heard that sound of the Buddha, obtain happiness and mental gladness; through that happiness and mental gladness, they emerge from those hells.

Then, having emerged from the hells, he is reborn in whichever Buddha-fields the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, reside, remain, and maintain themselves, and where they teach the Dharma. In those very places, he arises; and in world-systems in the south-western direction as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges, he extinguishes every mass of fire belonging to the hell-beings and utters this sound: "Homage to that Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha!"

He causes a proclamation to be heard. Then those beings in the hells, having heard that sound of the Buddha, obtain happiness and gladness. By means of that happiness and gladness, they emerge from those hells. Having emerged from those hells, they are reborn in whichever buddha-fields the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, reside, dwell, and maintain themselves, and where they teach the Dharma. In those very places they take birth.

In the northwestern direction, having extinguished all the masses of fire belonging to the hells in world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā, he utters the words, "Homage to that Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha," and makes this sound heard. Then those beings in the hells, hearing that sound of the Buddha, obtain happiness and gladness; and by means of that happiness and gladness, they emerge from those hells.
Then, having emerged from the hells, wherever the Blessed Buddhas abide, dwell, and maintain themselves, and [teach] the Dharma...

They teach the Dharma there, and beings are reborn in those very places. In the northeastern direction, having extinguished all the masses of fire belonging to the hells in world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges, he utters the words, "Homage to that Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha," and causes this sound to resound. Then, upon hearing that sound of the Buddha, those beings in the hells obtain happiness and mental well-being.

And by means of that happiness and mental gladness, they emerge from those hells. Having emerged from those hells, they are reborn in whichever Buddha-fields the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, reside, remain, maintain themselves, and teach the Dharma. In those very places they take birth.

Having extinguished all the masses of fire belonging to the hell-beings in world systems as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges in the direction below, he utters the sound: "Homage to that Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha! and causes his voice to be heard. Then those beings in the hells, having heard that sound of the Buddha, obtain happiness and gladness; and by means of that happiness and gladness, they emerge from those hells.

Then, having emerged from the hells, he is reborn in whichever Buddha-fields the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, reside, remain, maintain themselves, and teach the Dharma. Having extinguished all the masses of hell-fire in world-systems in the upward direction as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges, he utters the words, "Homage to that Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha," and makes this sound heard.

Then those beings in the hells, having heard that sound of the Buddha, obtain happiness and mental well-being; by means of that happiness and mental well-being, they emerge from those hells. Having emerged from the hells, they are reborn in whichever Buddha-fields the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, reside, dwell, maintain themselves, and teach the Dharma.
In that way, he [perceives] in the eastern direction as many world-systems as there are grains of sand in the river Ganges.

Having pacified the suffering of the animal realm and the world of Yama for those beings reborn therein, he utters the words, "Homage to that Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksambuddha," and makes his voice heard. Then, those beings reborn in the animal realm and the world of Yama, upon hearing that sound of the Buddha, obtain happiness and mental ease; and by means of that happiness and mental ease, they emerge from those realms of animals and the world of Yama.

Having emerged from those animal births and the world of Yama, they are reborn wherever the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, reside, remain, and maintain themselves, and where they teach the Dharma—in those very places they take birth.

In the southern direction, having pacified the suffering of the animal realm and the world of Yama for those beings born in world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā, he utters the sound: "Homage to that Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha! and makes this proclamation heard. Then, those beings born in the animal realm and the world of Yama, upon hearing that sound of the Buddha, obtain happiness and gladness.

By means of that happiness and mental gladness, they emerge from those animal births and worlds of Yama. Having emerged from those animal births and worlds of Yama, they are reborn wherever the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, reside, remain, maintain themselves, and teach the Dharma in various Buddha-fields.

In the western direction, having pacified the suffering of the animal realm and the world of Yama for those beings reborn there in world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā, he utters the sound, "Homage to that Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha! and makes his voice heard. Then, those beings reborn in the animal realm and the world of Yama, upon hearing that sound of the Buddha, obtain happiness and mental well-being.

And by means of that happiness and mental gladness, they emerge from those animal births and the world of Yama; having emerged from those animal births and the world of Yama, they go to whichever Buddha-fields the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, reside, remain, and maintain themselves.

They teach the Dharma and are reborn in those very places. In the northern direction, in world systems as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges, he pacifies the suffering of the animal realm and the world of Yama for those beings born in the animal realm, and utters the words: "Homage to that Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha! He causes this sound to resound.

Then those beings who have been reborn in the animal realm or the world of Yama, upon hearing that sound of the Buddha, obtain happiness and gladness; and by means of that happiness and gladness, they emerge from those animal realms and worlds of Yama. Having emerged from those animal realms and worlds of Yama, they are reborn wherever the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, reside, dwell, maintain themselves, and teach the Dharma in various Buddha-fields.

In the southeastern direction, having pacified the suffering of the animal realm and the world of Yama for those beings reborn there in as many world-systems as there are grains of sand in the river Gaṅgā, he utters the words, "Homage to that Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha," and makes this sound heard. Then, those beings reborn in the animal realm and the world of Yama, upon hearing that sound of the Buddha, obtain happiness and mental well-being.

By means of that happiness and mental gladness, they emerge from those animal births and the worlds of Yama. Having emerged from those animal births and the worlds of Yama, they are reborn wherever Buddhas, Blessed Ones, reside, remain, live on, and teach the Dharma in various Buddha-fields.

In the southwestern direction, having pacified the suffering of the animal realm and the world of Yama for those beings reborn therein in as many world-systems as there are grains of sand in the river Gaṅgā, he utters the sound: "Homage to that Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha! and makes his voice heard. Then, those beings reborn in the animal realm and the world of Yama, having heard that sound of the Buddha, obtain happiness and gladness; by means of that happiness and gladness, from those realms of animals and the world of Yama—
They emerge from those animal births and the world of Yama; having emerged, they are reborn wherever the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, reside, dwell, maintain themselves, and teach the Dharma.

In the northwestern direction, having pacified the suffering of the animal realm and the world of Yama for those beings born in world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā, he utters the words, "Homage to that Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha," and proclaims this sound. Then, those beings born in the animal realm and the world of Yama, having heard that sound of the Buddha, obtain happiness and gladness.

By means of that happiness and mental gladness, they emerge from those animal births and the worlds of Yama. Having emerged from those animal births and the worlds of Yama, they are reborn wherever there are Buddhas, Blessed Ones, who reside, remain, and maintain themselves, and who teach the Dharma in those various Buddha-fields.

In the northeastern direction, having pacified the suffering of the animal realm and the world of Yama for those beings reborn therein across world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā, he utters the sound: "Homage to that Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha! and makes his voice heard. Then, those beings reborn in the animal realm and the world of Yama, upon hearing that sound of the Buddha, attain happiness and gladness.

By means of that pleasure and mental joy, they emerge from those animal births and the world of Yama. Having emerged from those animal births and the world of Yama, they are reborn in whichever Buddha-fields the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, reside, remain, maintain themselves, and teach the Dharma. In those very places they take birth.

Having pacified the suffering of the animal realm and the world of Yama for those beings reborn therein within world-systems in the downward direction as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges, he utters the sound: "Homage to that Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha! and makes his voice heard. Then those beings reborn in the animal realm and the world of Yama [hear] him...

Upon hearing the word "Buddha," they obtain happiness and mental well-being. By means of that happiness and mental well-being, they emerge from those states of animal rebirth and the world of Yama. Having emerged from those states of animal rebirth and the world of Yama, they are reborn wherever the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, reside, remain, maintain themselves, and teach the Dharma in various Buddha-fields.

In the direction above, in world systems as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā, he pacifies the suffering of the animal realm and the world of Yama for those beings reborn there; he utters the sound, "Homage to that Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha! and makes his voice heard. Then, those beings reborn in the animal realm and the world of Yama, having heard that sound of the Buddha, obtain happiness and gladness.

By means of that pleasure and mental ease, they emerge from those animal births and the worlds of Yama; having emerged from those animal births and the worlds of Yama, they are reborn wherever the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, reside, dwell, and maintain themselves.

Subhūti, it is just as if, for example, a skilled illusionist or an apprentice of an illusionist were to manifest at a great crossroads before a vast crowd of people the hells, the animal realm, and the world of Yama; and having manifested those illusory beings, he were to proclaim the sound of "Buddha," proclaim the sound of "Dharma," and proclaim the sound of "Saṅgha. Then, by that sound of Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha, those manifested beings [would be moved] from those hells.

"Would they emerge from the animal realm and the world of Yama? What do you think, Subhūti? Would any sentient being have been delivered from the hells, the animal realm, or the world of Yama by that magician or the magician’s apprentice? Subhūti replied, "Certainly not, Blessed One. The Blessed One said, "In the same way, Subhūti, even if a bodhisattva mahāsattva were to deliver immeasurable and incalculable sentient beings from the animal realm and the miserable states throughout the worlds in the ten directions, not a single sentient being would have been delivered from the hells."

It is so. For what reason? Subhūti, this is the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) based upon the illusory nature of all phenomena. Indeed, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva is called one who has "donned the great armor."

Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, established in the perfection of generosity and donning the great armor, miraculously creates this trichiliocosm made of lapis lazuli. Having miraculously created it as being made of lapis lazuli, he miraculously creates an array of a universal monarch (*cakravartin-vyūha*). Having miraculously created the array of a universal monarch, he gives it to those who lack it; he gives drink to those who desire drink; he gives vehicles to those who desire vehicles.

He gives clothing to those who need clothing; he gives flowers to those who need flowers; he gives garlands to those who need garlands; he gives perfumes to those who need perfumes; he gives ointments to those who need ointments; he gives beds and seats to those who need beds and seats; he gives shelter to those who need shelter; he gives the means of livelihood to those who need the means of livelihood; he gives requisites to those who need requisites.

He gives medicinal requisites for the sick to those who need medicinal requisites for the sick; he gives jewels, pearls, lapis lazuli, conch shells, crystals, coral, silver, and gold to those who need jewels, pearls, lapis lazuli, conch shells, crystals, coral, silver, and gold; indeed, he gives various kinds of human requisites.
Having given food to those seeking food, drink to those seeking drink, vehicles to those seeking vehicles, clothing to those seeking clothing, and flowers to those seeking flowers.

Garlands to those seeking garlands, perfumes to those seeking perfumes, ointments to those worthy of ointments, beds and seats to those seeking beds and seats, shelter to those seeking shelter, means of livelihood to those seeking a livelihood, requisites to those seeking requisites, and medicinal provisions for the sick to those in need of them.

To those who require medicinal requisites for the sick, he gives gems, pearls, lapis lazuli, conch shells, crystals, coral, silver, and gold; and to those who require pearls, lapis lazuli, conch shells, crystals, coral, silver, and gold, having given these, and even having given various other human requisites, he teaches the Dharma to those beings—namely, this very teaching of the Dharma associated with the six perfections.

Furthermore, those beings, having heard that teaching of the Dharma, shall never again be separated from the six perfections until they fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Subhūti, it is just as if, for example, a skilled magician or a magician’s apprentice were to create at a great crossroads, before a vast multitude of people, a great illusory crowd; and having created it, he were to give food to those seeking food, drink to those seeking drink, clothing to those seeking clothing, flowers to those seeking flowers, garlands to those seeking garlands, perfumes to those seeking perfumes, and ointments to those seeking ointments.

One should give bedding to those who need bedding, a dwelling to those who need a dwelling, a livelihood to those who need a livelihood, requisites to those who need requisites, and medicinal provisions for the sick to those who need medicinal provisions for the sick; [as well as] gems, pearls, lapis lazuli, conch shells, crystals, coral, silver, and gold.

He would give gems, pearls, lapis lazuli, conch shells, crystals, coral, silver, and gold to those seeking them; indeed, he would give any and all human requisites. What do you think, Subhūti? Would anything at all have been given by that magician or the magician’s apprentice to any sentient being? Subhūti replied, "Certainly not, Blessed One. The Blessed One said, "In the very same way, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having manifested the array of a universal monarch, gives food to those seeking food, drink..."

By giving a vehicle to those who desire a vehicle; by giving clothing to those who desire clothing; by giving flowers to those who desire flowers; by giving garlands to those who desire garlands; by giving incense to those who desire incense; by giving ointment to those who desire ointment; by giving bedding and seating to those who desire bedding and seating; by giving a shelter to those who desire a shelter; by giving the means of livelihood to those who desire the means of livelihood; and by giving utensils.

When giving requisites for the sick to those who need them; when giving medicinal supplies and comforts for the sick to those who need them; when giving gems, pearls, lapis lazuli, conch shells, crystals, coral, silver, and gold to those who need gems, pearls, lapis lazuli, conch shells, crystals, coral, silver, and gold; and when giving various other human requisites—none of this constitutes anything truly given to any sentient being.

For what reason? Subhūti, this is the nature of phenomena, based on the illusory nature of all things. It is in this way, Subhūti, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva is said to be "girded with the great armor. Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, established in the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*), through the intentional assumption of rebirth, is born into the family of a universal monarch (*cakravartin*). Remaining there in the conduct of a universal monarch, he establishes sentient beings in the ten paths of wholesome action.

And he [dwells] in the four dhyānas, the immeasurables, the four formless attainments, the five supernormal knowledges, the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, and the seven factors of enlightenment.

He establishes them in the noble eightfold path, in the gateways to liberation of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, in the nine successive meditative attainments, in the four noble beings, in all samādhis, in all dhāraṇī-gateways, in the ten powers of a Tathāgata, in the four fearlessnesses, in the four analytical knowledges, in great loving-kindness, in great compassion, and in the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha. They...

Sentient beings are never deprived of such teaching of the Dharma until they fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. Subhūti, it is just as if, for example, a skilled illusionist or an apprentice of an illusionist were to manifest a great multitude of people before a vast crowd at a crossroads, and then establish those beings in the ten paths of wholesome action, in the four meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), and the four formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*).

In the five superknowledges, the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, the noble eightfold path, the gateways to liberation of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, the nine successive meditative attainments, the four noble truths, all meditative concentrations, all gateways to dhāraṇī, the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four grounds of self-confidence, and the four [fearless assurances]...

One would establish them in the analytical knowledges, in great loving-kindness, in great compassion, and in the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha. What do you think, Subhūti, has any sentient being been established by that illusionist or his apprentice in the ten paths of wholesome action?

In the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, the five superknowledges, the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, the noble eightfold path, and the gateways to liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.

He is established in the nine successive meditative attainments (*anupūrvavihārasamāpatti*), the four noble truths, all samādhis, all dhāraṇī-doors, the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha. Subhūti said: "Certainly not, Blessed One.
"In the same way, Subhūti, even after a bodhisattva mahāsattva has established immeasurable and incalculable beings in the ten paths of wholesome action..."

In the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, the five superknowledges, the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, the noble eightfold path, the gateways to liberation of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, the eight liberations, the nine successive meditative attainments, the four noble truths, and all samādhis.

No sentient being whatsoever has been established in the gateways of all dhāraṇīs, in the ten powers of a Tathāgata, in the four grounds of self-confidence, in the four analytical knowledges, in great loving-kindness, in great compassion, or in the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha. For what reason? Subhūti, this is the very nature of phenomena, based on the illusory nature of phenomena. It is in this way, Subhūti, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva is said to have "donned the great armor."

Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, abiding in the perfection of patience, enjoins all sentient beings to the perfection of patience and establishes them therein. And how, Subhūti, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, abiding in the perfection of patience, enjoin all sentient beings to the perfection of patience and establish them therein?

In this regard, Subhūti, from the first production of the thought of awakening, a bodhisattva mahāsattva dons this very armor: "Even if all sentient beings were to strike me with clods of earth, sticks, or weapons, I must not give rise to even a single thought accompanied by agitation. Furthermore, I shall establish all sentient beings in such patience as this."

Subhūti, it is just as if, for example, a skilled illusionist or an illusionist’s apprentice were to manifest a great multitude of people before a vast crowd at a major crossroads, and then urge them toward and establish them in the perfection of patience. What do you think, Subhūti, would that illusionist or illusionist’s apprentice [have done anything real]?

“Could it be that some sentient being has been established in the perfection of patience? He replied, “No indeed, Blessed One. The Blessed One said, “In the same way, Subhūti, although a bodhisattva mahāsattva has established immeasurable and incalculable sentient beings in the perfection of patience, not a single sentient being has been established in the perfection of patience. Why is that? Because, Subhūti, this is the nature of phenomena, based on the illusory nature of all phenomena.”
In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva is said to be "one who has donned the great armor.

Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, abiding in the perfection of vigor, encourages, introduces, and establishes sentient beings in the perfection of vigor. And how, Subhūti, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, abiding in the perfection of vigor, encourage, introduce, and establish all sentient beings in the perfection of vigor?

In this regard, Subhūti, by means of a thought of mind associated with the knowledge of all aspects, a bodhisattva mahāsattva encourages, introduces, and establishes all sentient beings in physical and mental vigor.

Subhūti, it is just as if, for example, a skilled illusionist or an illusionist’s apprentice were to create a great multitude of people before a vast crowd at a major crossroads, and then establish them in physical and mental vigor. What do you think, Subhūti? Would that illusionist or illusionist’s apprentice have established that great multitude of people created by him in physical and mental vigor?

He would establish them therein. What do you think, Subhūti? Would any sentient being have been established by that illusionist or the illusionist’s apprentice in physical or mental vigor? He replied: "No indeed, Blessed One. "In the same way, Subhūti, by a bodhisattva mahāsattva, immeasurable and incalculable [beings...]"

Having established beings in physical and mental vigor, not a single being is actually established in physical and mental vigor. Why is that? Subhūti, this is the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), based on the fact that all phenomena have the nature of an illusion (māyā). It is in this way that a bodhisattva mahāsattva is said to be "one who has donned the great armor."

Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, abiding in the perfection of meditative concentration, encourages all sentient beings toward the perfection of meditative concentration, leads them into it, and establishes them therein. And how, Subhūti, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, abiding in the perfection of meditative concentration, encourage all sentient beings toward the perfection of meditative concentration, lead them into it, and establish them therein?

In this regard, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, abiding in the equality of all phenomena, does not perceive the distraction of any phenomenon whatsoever; thus he becomes established in the perfection of meditative concentration. In that very same way, he encourages beings toward the perfection of meditative concentration, settles them in it, and establishes them therein.

And those whom they have thus encouraged never become separated from the perfection of meditative concentration until they fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. Subhūti, it is just as if, for example, a skilled illusionist or an illusionist’s apprentice were to manifest a great multitude of people before a vast crowd at a crossroads and establish them in the perfection of meditative concentration.

"What do you think, Subhūti? Would any sentient being have been established in the perfection of meditative concentration by that illusionist or his apprentice? Subhūti replied, "Certainly not, Blessed One. The Blessed One said, "In the same way, Subhūti, although a bodhisattva mahāsattva establishes all sentient beings in the perfection of meditative concentration, no sentient being has actually been established in the perfection of meditative concentration. Why is that? Because, Subhūti, this is the nature of phenomena, based upon the illusory nature of phenomena."
In this way indeed, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva is said to have donned the great armor.

Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, abiding in the perfection of wisdom, encourages all sentient beings toward the perfection of wisdom, settles them in it, and establishes them in it. And how, Subhūti, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, abiding in the perfection of wisdom, encourage all sentient beings toward the perfection of wisdom, settle them in it, and establish them in it?

He said: "Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in the perfection of wisdom perceives neither the arising nor the cessation, neither defilement nor purification, nor this shore nor the further shore of any dharma—thus indeed, Subhūti, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva become established in the perfection of wisdom. In that very same way, he encourages all sentient beings toward the perfection of wisdom, leads them into it, and establishes them therein."

"Subhūti, it is just as if, for example, a skilled illusionist or an illusionist’s apprentice were to create a great multitude of people before a vast crowd at a crossroads and then encourage them, establish them, and settle them in the perfection of wisdom. What do you think, Subhūti? Would any being at all have been encouraged, established, or settled in the perfection of wisdom by that illusionist or his apprentice? Subhūti replied:

"Certainly not, Blessed One. The Blessed One said: "In the same way, Subhūti, although a bodhisattva mahāsattva establishes all sentient beings in the perfection of wisdom, not a single sentient being has been established in the perfection of wisdom. Why is that? Because this is the nature of phenomena, Subhūti, based on the illusory nature of phenomena. It is in this sense, Subhūti, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva is said to be 'one who has donned the great armor.'"

Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having donned the great armor, goes to world-systems in the eastern direction as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā; there he himself abides in the perfection of generosity, and likewise he encourages, introduces, and establishes all those beings in those world-systems in the perfection of generosity, just as he himself abides in the perfection of ethical discipline.

In the same way, he encourages, introduces, and establishes all those beings who are in those world-systems in the perfection of ethical discipline; just as he himself abides in the perfection of patience, so too does he encourage, introduce, and establish all those beings who are in those world-systems in the perfection of patience; just as he himself abides in the perfection of vigor.

In the very same way, he encourages, introduces, and establishes all those beings who are in those world-systems in the perfection of vigor; just as he himself abides in the perfection of meditative concentration, so too does he encourage, introduce, and establish all those beings who are in those world-systems in the perfection of meditative concentration; just as he himself abides in the perfection of wisdom.

In the same way, he encourages, introduces, and establishes all those beings who are in those world-systems in the perfection of wisdom; that is to say, having heard that very Dharma of the six perfections, those beings shall never be separated from the six perfections until they fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Having gone to world systems in the southern direction as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges, just as he himself abides in the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*), so too does he exhort, introduce, and establish all those sentient beings in those world systems in the perfection of generosity; and just as he himself abides in the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*), so too does he [establish them] there.

In all world-systems, he encourages, introduces, and establishes all those beings in the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*). Just as he himself abides in the perfection of patience (*kṣāntipāramitā*), so too does he encourage, introduce, and establish all those beings in those world-systems in the perfection of patience. Just as he himself abides in the perfection of vigor (*vīryapāramitā*).

In the same way, he encourages, introduces, and establishes all those beings who are in those world-systems in the perfection of vigor; just as he himself abides in the perfection of meditation, so too does he encourage, introduce, and establish all those beings who are in those world-systems in the perfection of meditation; just as he himself abides in the perfection of wisdom.

In the same way, he encourages, introduces, and establishes all those beings who are in those world-systems in the perfection of wisdom; he teaches the Dharma, namely these very six perfections. Having heard that Dharma, those beings never become separated from the six perfections until they fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Having gone to world-systems in the western direction as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā, just as he himself abides in the perfection of generosity, so too does he cause all those beings in those world-systems to take up, enter, and be established in the perfection of generosity; and just as he himself abides in the perfection of ethical discipline...

In the same way, he encourages, introduces, and establishes all those beings who are in those world-systems in the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*). Just as he himself abides in the perfection of patience (*kṣāntipāramitā*), so too does he encourage all those beings who are in those world-systems in the perfection of patience. Just as he himself abides in the perfection of vigor (*vīryapāramitā*), so too does he [encourage] all those beings who are in those world-systems in the perfection of vigor.

He encourages, introduces, and establishes [beings] in it; just as he himself abides in the perfection of meditation (*dhyānapāramitā*), so too does he encourage, introduce, and establish all those beings who are in those world-systems in the perfection of meditation. Just as he himself abides in the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), so too does he encourage, introduce, and establish all those beings who are in those world-systems in the perfection of wisdom.

He teaches the Dharma, namely these very six perfections; having heard that Dharma, those beings never become separated from the six perfections until they fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Having gone to world-systems in the northern direction as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges, just as he himself abides in the perfection of generosity, so too does he cause all those beings in those world-systems to undertake the perfection of generosity. Just as he himself abides in the perfection of ethical discipline, so too does he cause all those beings in those world-systems to undertake, enter into, and be established in the perfection of ethical discipline.

Just as he himself abides in the perfection of patience, so too does he exhort, establish, and settle all those beings in those world-systems in the perfection of ethical discipline. Just as he himself abides in the perfection of vigor, so too does he exhort, establish, and settle all those beings in those world-systems in the perfection of vigor.

Just as he himself abides in the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*), so too does he encourage all those beings in those world-systems to undertake the perfection of meditative concentration. Just as he himself abides in the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), so too does he encourage all those beings in those world-systems to undertake the perfection of wisdom; he establishes them, settles them, and teaches the Dharma.

Namely, those very six perfections; having heard that Dharma, those beings shall never be separated from the six perfections until they fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Having gone to world-systems in the southeastern direction as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā, just as he himself abides in the perfection of giving, so too does he exhort, establish, and settle all those sentient beings in those world-systems in the perfection of giving; and just as he himself abides in the perfection of ethical discipline.

In the same way, he encourages, introduces, and establishes all those beings who are in those world-systems in the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*). Just as he himself abides in the perfection of patience (*kṣāntipāramitā*), so too does he encourage, introduce, and establish all those beings who are in those world-systems in the perfection of patience. Just as he himself abides in the perfection of vigor (*vīryapāramitā*).

In the same way, he encourages, introduces, and establishes all those beings who are in those world-systems in the perfection of vigor; just as he himself abides in the perfection of meditation, so too does he encourage, introduce, and establish all those beings who are in those world-systems in the perfection of meditation; and just as he himself abides in the perfection of wisdom.

In the same way, he encourages, introduces, and establishes all those beings in those world-systems in the perfection of wisdom; and he teaches the Dharma, namely these very six perfections. Having heard that Dharma, those beings never become separated from the six perfections until they fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Having gone to world-systems in the south-western direction as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā, he abides in those world-systems in the very same manner as he himself abides in the perfection of generosity.

He encourages, introduces, and establishes all those beings in the perfection of generosity. Just as he himself abides in the perfection of ethical discipline, so too does he encourage, introduce, and establish all those beings in those world-systems in the perfection of ethical discipline. Just as he himself abides in the perfection of patience...

In the very same way, he encourages, introduces, and establishes all those beings who are in those world-systems in the perfection of patience; just as he himself abides in the perfection of vigor, so too he encourages, introduces, and establishes all those beings who are in those world-systems in the perfection of vigor; just as he himself abides in the perfection of meditative concentration...

In the same way, he encourages, introduces, and establishes all those beings who are in those world-systems in the perfection of meditation (*dhyānapāramitā*). Just as he himself abides in the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), so too does he encourage, introduce, and establish all those beings who are in those world-systems in the perfection of wisdom; and he teaches the Dharma, namely, these very six perfections.
Having heard that Dharma, those beings never become separated from the six perfections until they fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Having gone to world-systems in the northwestern direction as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges, just as he himself abides in the perfection of generosity, so too does he cause all those beings in those world-systems to take up, enter into, and be established in the perfection of generosity; and just as he himself abides in the perfection of ethical discipline.

In the same way, he encourages, introduces, and establishes all those beings in those world-systems in the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*), just as he himself abides in the perfection of patience (*kṣāntipāramitā*).

In the same way, he encourages, introduces, and establishes all those beings who are in those world-systems in the perfection of patience; just as he himself abides in the perfection of vigor, so too does he encourage, introduce, and establish all those beings who are in those world-systems in the perfection of vigor; just as he himself abides in the perfection of meditation.

In the same way, he encourages, introduces, and establishes all those beings who are in those world-systems in the perfection of meditation (*dhyānapāramitā*). Just as he himself abides in the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), so too does he encourage, introduce, and establish all those beings who are in those world-systems in the perfection of wisdom; and he teaches the Dharma, namely, these very six perfections.
Having heard that Dharma, those beings never become separated from the six perfections until they fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Having gone to world-systems in the northeastern direction as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā, just as he himself abides in the perfection of generosity, even so he causes all those beings in those world-systems to take up, enter, and be established in the perfection of generosity. Just as he himself abides in the perfection of ethical discipline...

In the same way, he encourages, introduces, and establishes all those beings who are in those world-systems in the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*). Just as he himself abides in the perfection of patience (*kṣāntipāramitā*), so too does he encourage, introduce, and establish all those beings who are in those world-systems in the perfection of patience. Just as he himself abides in the perfection of vigor (*vīryapāramitā*).

In the same way, he encourages all those beings who are in those world-systems toward the perfection of vigor; just as he himself abides in the perfection of meditation, so too does he encourage, lead, and establish all those beings who are in those world-systems in the perfection of meditation. Just as he himself abides in the perfection of wisdom, so too does he encourage, lead, and establish all those beings who are in those world-systems in the perfection of wisdom.

And he teaches the Dharma, namely these very six perfections; having heard that Dharma, those beings never become separated from the six perfections until they fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Having gone to world systems in the downward direction as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā, just as he himself abides in the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*), so too does he exhort, introduce, and establish all those beings in those world systems in the perfection of generosity; and just as he himself abides in the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*).

In the same way, he encourages, introduces, and establishes all those beings who are in those world-systems in the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*). Just as he himself abides in the perfection of patience (*kṣāntipāramitā*), so too does he encourage, introduce, and establish all those beings who are in those world-systems in the perfection of patience. Just as he himself abides in the perfection of vigor (*vīryapāramitā*).

In the same way, he encourages, introduces, and establishes all those beings who are in those world-systems in the perfection of vigor; just as he himself abides in the perfection of meditation, so too does he encourage, introduce, and establish all those beings who are in those world-systems in the perfection of meditation; just as he himself abides in the perfection of wisdom.

In the very same way, he encourages, introduces, and establishes all those beings who are in those world-systems in the perfection of wisdom; and he teaches the Dharma, namely these six perfections. Having heard that Dharma, those beings never become separated from the six perfections until they awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Having gone to world-systems in the upward direction as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā, just as he himself abides in the perfection of generosity, so too does he cause all those beings in those world-systems to take up, enter into, and be established in the perfection of generosity; and just as he himself abides in the perfection of ethical discipline...

In the same way, he encourages, introduces, and establishes all those beings who are in those world-systems in the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*). Just as he himself abides in the perfection of patience (*kṣāntipāramitā*), so too does he encourage, introduce, and establish all those beings who are in those world-systems in the perfection of patience. Just as he himself abides in the perfection of vigor (*vīryapāramitā*), [so too does he do the same for them].

In the same way, he encourages, introduces, and establishes all those beings in those world-systems in the perfection of vigor; just as he himself abides in the perfection of meditative concentration, so too does he encourage, introduce, and establish all those beings in those world-systems in the perfection of meditative concentration; just as he himself abides in the perfection of wisdom.

In the same way, he encourages, introduces, and establishes all those beings in those world-systems in the perfection of wisdom; and he teaches the Dharma, namely these very six perfections. Having heard that Dharma, those beings never become separated from the six perfections until they fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Subhūti, it is just as if, for example, a skilled illusionist or an apprentice of an illusionist were to manifest a great multitude of people before a vast crowd at a major crossroads.

Having manifested them, he would cause them to undertake, lead them into, and establish them in the six perfections. What do you think, Subhūti? Would any sentient being at all have been caused to undertake, led into, or established in the six perfections by that illusionist or the illusionist’s apprentice? He replied, "Certainly not, Blessed One. The Blessed One said, "In the same way, by a bodhisattva mahāsattva in the world-systems of the eastern direction, as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges..."

In the southern direction, in world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges; in the western direction, in world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges; in the northern direction, in world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges; in the northeastern direction, in world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges; in the southeastern direction, in world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges; and in the southwestern direction, in world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges.

In the northwestern direction, in world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges; in the downward direction, in world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges; and in the upward direction, in world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges—all those sentient beings are established in the six perfections. For what reason? Subhūti, this is the nature of phenomena, based on the illusory nature of phenomena.
It is in this way, Subhūti, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva is said to be "one who has donned the great armor."

Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having donned the great armor and dwelling with a mind associated with the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), allows no opportunity for other thoughts to arise, such as: "I must establish this many beings in the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*); I must not establish that many. Or: "I must establish this many beings in the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*); I must not establish that many."

"I must establish this many beings in the perfection of patience; these many I must not establish. I must establish this many beings in the perfection of vigor; these many I must not establish. I must establish this many beings in the perfection of meditation; these many I must not establish. I must establish this many beings in the perfection of wisdom; these many I must not establish."

"I must establish this many sentient beings in internal emptiness; these many I must not establish therein. I must establish this many sentient beings in external emptiness; these many I must not establish therein. I must establish this many sentient beings in internal-and-external emptiness; these many I must not establish therein. I must establish this many sentient beings in the emptiness of emptiness."

"So many beings should not be established [in this]; so many beings should by me be established in the great emptiness; so many should not be established. So many beings should by me be established in the ultimate emptiness; so many should not be established. So many beings should by me be established in the conditioned emptiness; so many should not be established."

"I must establish this many sentient beings in the emptiness of the unconditioned; this many I must not establish. I must establish this many sentient beings in the emptiness of the ultimate; this many I must not establish. I must establish this many sentient beings in the emptiness of that which has no beginning or end; this many I must not establish. I must establish this many sentient beings in the emptiness of non-dispersal."
"This many beings should not be established; this many beings by me [should be established] in the emptiness of intrinsic nature."

"So many should be established; so many should not be established. So many sentient beings should be established by me in the emptiness of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-śūnyatā*); so many should not be established. So many sentient beings should be established by me in the emptiness of specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*); so many should not be established. So many sentient beings should be established by me in the emptiness of non-apprehensibility (*anupalambha-śūnyatā*); so many should not be established."

"I must establish this many sentient beings in the emptiness of non-existence; these many I must not establish [therein]. I must establish this many sentient beings in the emptiness of intrinsic nature; these many I must not establish [therein]. I must establish this many sentient beings in the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence; these many I must not establish [therein]."

"I must establish this many beings in the four foundations of mindfulness; these many I must not establish therein. I must establish this many beings in the four right efforts; these many I must not establish therein. I must establish this many beings in the four bases of psychic power; these many I must not establish therein. I must establish this many beings in the five faculties."

"So many should not be established [in this]; so many beings should be established by me in the five powers; so many should not be established. So many beings should be established by me in the seven factors of enlightenment; so many should not be established. So many beings should be established by me in the noble eightfold path; so many should not be established."

"I must establish this many sentient beings in the noble truths; these many I must not establish. I must establish this many sentient beings in the four meditative absorptions; these many I must not establish."

"I must establish this many sentient beings in the four immeasurables; these many I must not establish. I must establish this many sentient beings in the liberations; these many I must not establish. I must establish this many sentient beings in the nine successive meditative attainments; these many I must not establish."

"I must establish this many beings in the liberations of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; these many I must not establish therein. I must establish this many beings in the five superknowledges; these many I must not establish therein. I must establish this many beings in all samādhis; these many I must not establish therein. I must establish this many beings in all the gateways of dhāraṇīs."

"This many beings should not be established [in these qualities]; this many beings should by me be established in the ten powers of a Tathāgata; this many should not be established. This many beings should by me be established in the four grounds of self-confidence; this many should not be established. This many beings should by me be established in the four analytical knowledges; this many should not be established."

"I must establish this many sentient beings in great loving-kindness; I must not establish that many. I must establish this many sentient beings in great compassion; I must not establish that many. I must establish this many sentient beings in the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; I must not establish that many. I must establish this many sentient beings in the fruit of stream-entry."

"So many [beings] should not be established [in this]; so many beings should by me be established in the fruit of a once-returner; so many should not be established; so many beings should by me be established in the fruit of a non-returner."

"This many beings should not be established [in this state]; this many beings should by me be established in arhatship; this many should not be established. This many beings should by me be established in pratyekabodhi; this many should not be established. This many beings should by me be established in the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*); this many should not be established. This many beings should by me be established in the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*); this many should not be established."

Moreover, it occurs to him: "I must establish immeasurable and incalculable beings in the perfection of generosity; I must establish them in the perfection of ethical discipline; I must establish them in the perfection of patience; I must establish them in the perfection of vigor; I must establish them in the perfection of meditative concentration; I must establish them in the perfection of wisdom; and I must establish them in internal emptiness."

They should be established in external emptiness; they should be established in internal-external emptiness; they should be established in the emptiness of emptiness; they should be established in great emptiness; they should be established in ultimate emptiness; they should be established in conditioned emptiness; they should be established in unconditioned emptiness; they should be established in absolute emptiness.

They should be established in the emptiness of that which has no beginning or end; they should be established in the emptiness of non-dispersal; they should be established in the emptiness of intrinsic nature; they should be established in the emptiness of all phenomena; they should be established in the emptiness of specific characteristics; they should be established in the emptiness of non-apprehension; they should be established in the emptiness of non-existence; they should be established in the emptiness of self-nature.
They should be established in the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence; they should be established in the four foundations of mindfulness; in the four...

They should be established in the right efforts; they should be established in the four bases of psychic power; they should be established in the five faculties; they should be established in the five powers; they should be established in the seven factors of enlightenment; they should be established in the noble eightfold path; they should be established in the four noble truths; they should be established in the four meditative absorptions.

They should be established in the four immeasurables; they should be established in the four formless attainments; they should be established in the eight liberations; they should be established in the nine successive meditative attainments; they should be established in the gateways to liberation that are emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; they should be established in the five superknowledges; and they should be established in all meditative concentrations.

They should be established in all the gateways of dhāraṇīs; they should be established in the ten powers of a Tathāgata; they should be established in the four grounds of self-confidence; they should be established in the four analytical knowledges; they should be established in great loving-kindness; they should be established in great compassion; they should be established in the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; and they should be established in the fruit of stream-entry.

They should be established in the fruit of once-returning; they should be established in the fruit of non-returning; they should be established in arhatship; they should be established in pratyekabuddha-enlightenment; they should be established in the knowledge of the aspects of the path; they should be established in the knowledge of all aspects.

Subhūti, it is just as if, for example, a skilled illusionist or an illusionist’s apprentice were to create a great mass of people at a major crossroads before a vast crowd of people, and then form this thought: "I must establish these immeasurable and incalculable beings in the six perfections; I must establish them in the eighteen kinds of emptiness."

They should be established in the four foundations of mindfulness; they should be established in the four right efforts; they should be established in the four bases of psychic power; they should be established in the five faculties; they should be established in the five powers; they should be established in the seven factors of enlightenment; they should be established in the noble eightfold path; and they should be established in the four noble truths.

They should be established in the four meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*); they should be established in the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*); they should be established in the four formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*); they should be established in the eight liberations (*vimokṣa*); they should be established in the nine successive dwellings in attainment (*anupūrvavihārasamāpatti*); they should be established in the gateways to liberation consisting of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness (*śūnyatānimittāpraṇihita-vimokṣamukha*); and they should be established in the five superknowledges (*abhijñā*).

They should be established in all samādhis; they should be established in all dhāraṇī-gates; they should be established in the ten powers of a Tathāgata; they should be established in the four grounds of self-confidence; they should be established in the four analytical knowledges; they should be established in great loving-kindness; they should be established in great compassion; and they should be established in the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.

They should be established in the fruit of stream-entry; they should be established in the fruit of once-returning; they should be established in the fruit of non-returning; they should be established in arhatship; they should be established in pratyekabuddha-enlightenment; they should be established in the knowledge of the aspects of the path; they should be established in the knowledge of all aspects.

What do you think, Subhūti? Would any sentient being have been established by that illusionist or the illusionist’s apprentice in the six perfections? Would they have been established in the eighteen kinds of emptiness? Or in the four foundations of mindfulness?

He would be established; he would be established in the four right efforts; he would be established in the four bases of psychic power; he would be established in the five faculties; he would be established in the five powers; he would be established in the seven factors of enlightenment; he would be established in the noble eightfold path; he would be established in the four noble truths.

He would be established in the four dhyānas; he would be established in the four immeasurables; he would be established in the four formless attainments; he would be established in the eight liberations; he would be established in the nine successive meditative attainments; he would be established in the gateways to liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; and he would be established in the five superknowledges.

He shall be established in all samādhis; he shall be established in the gateways of all dhāraṇīs; he shall be established in the ten powers of a Tathāgata; he shall be established in the four fearlessnesses; he shall be established in the four analytical knowledges; he shall be established in great loving-kindness; he shall be established in great compassion; and he shall be established in the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.

He would be established in the fruit of stream-entry; he would be established in the fruit of once-returning; he would be established in the fruit of non-returning; he would be established in arhatship; he would be established in pratyekabuddha-enlightenment; he would be established in the knowledge of the aspects of the path; he would be established in the knowledge of all aspects.

He said, "Certainly not, Blessed One. The Blessed One said, "In just this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having generated the thought for the sake of establishing immeasurable and incalculable sentient beings in the six perfections, and for the sake of establishing them in the eighteen kinds of emptiness..."

Having generated the thought, having generated the thought for the sake of establishing [beings] in the four foundations of mindfulness; having generated the thought for the sake of establishing them in the four right efforts; having generated the thought for the sake of establishing them in the four bases of psychic power; having generated the thought for the sake of establishing them in the five faculties; having generated the thought for the sake of establishing them in the five powers; having generated the thought for the sake of establishing them in the seven factors of awakening.

Having generated the thought for the sake of establishing [beings] in the noble eightfold path; having generated the thought for the sake of establishing them in the noble truths; having generated the thought for the sake of establishing them in the four meditative absorptions; having generated the thought for the sake of establishing them in the four immeasurables; having generated the thought for the sake of establishing them in the formless attainments; having generated the thought for the sake of establishing them in the eight liberations.

Having generated the thought for the sake of establishing [beings] in the nine successive meditative attainments (*anupūrva-vihāra-samāpatti*); having generated the thought for the sake of establishing them in the gateways to liberation (*vimokṣa-mukha*) of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; having generated the thought for the sake of establishing them in the five superknowledges (*abhijñā*); having generated the thought for the sake of establishing them in all meditative concentrations (*samādhi*); having generated the thought for the sake of establishing them in all gateways of mnemonic formulas (*dhāraṇī-mukha*); having generated the thought for the sake of establishing them in the ten powers of a Tathāgata (*tathāgata-bala*).

Having generated the thought for the sake of establishing [beings] in the four grounds of self-confidence; having generated the thought for the sake of establishing them in the four analytical knowledges; having generated the thought for the sake of establishing them in great loving-kindness; having generated the thought for the sake of establishing them in great compassion; having generated the thought for the sake of establishing them in the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; and having generated the thought for the sake of establishing them in the fruit of stream-entry.

Having generated the mind for establishing [beings] in the fruit of once-returning; having generated the mind for establishing them in the fruit of non-returning; having generated the mind for establishing them in arhatship; having generated the mind for establishing them in pratyekabuddha-enlightenment; having generated the mind for establishing them in the knowledge of the aspects of the path; having generated the mind for establishing them in the knowledge of all aspects.

It is not for the sake of any sentient being that the thought [of awakening] has been generated. Why is that? Subhūti, this is the nature of phenomena (dharmatā): that they arise with the nature of an illusion. It is in this way, Subhūti, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva is said to be "armed with the great armor."

Subhūti said: "O Blessed One, as I understand the meaning of what you have taught, this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva should indeed be known as one who has donned the armor of non-armoring, by virtue of the emptiness of intrinsic characteristics. Why is that?
