The concentration called "beyond syllables," the concentration called "severing the veil of objects," the concentration called "unchanging," the concentration called "light-maker," the concentration called "entry into the certainty of names," the concentration called "wandering without a home," the concentration called "free from darkness," the concentration called "possessing conduct," the concentration called "the powerless," the concentration called "crossed over the realm of sense-objects," the concentration called "accumulation of all virtues," and the concentration called "steadfast mind."

The concentration named Purity of Auspicious Blossoming; the concentration named Possessing the Factors of Enlightenment; the concentration named Infinite Eloquence; the concentration named Peerless Equality.

The concentration named "Transcending All Phenomena"; the concentration named "Effecting Delimitation"; the concentration named "Dispelling Doubt"; the concentration named "Without Basis"; the concentration named "Single Array"; the concentration named "Manifestation of Aspects"; the concentration named "Single Aspect"; the concentration named "Non-Relishing of All Pleasure and Pain"; the concentration named "Endowed with the Excellence of All Aspects"; and the concentration named "Non-Admission of Aspects."

The concentration named "Having transcended the depths of all existences through penetration," the concentration named "Entry into conventional sounds," the concentration named "Liberated from the syllables of vocal sound," the concentration named "Blazing Torch," the concentration named "Purification of Characteristics," the concentration named "Uncharacterized," the concentration named "Endowed with the Excellence of All Aspects," the concentration named "Non-attachment to All Pleasure and Pain," and the concentration named "Inexhaustible Casket."

The concentration named Dhāraṇīmati; the concentration named Samyaktvamithyātvasaṃpraśama; the concentration named Sarvarodhanirodhasaṃpraśamana; the concentration named Anurodhāpratirodha; the concentration named Visaraprabha; the concentration named Sāravatī; the concentration named Paripūrṇacandravimala; the concentration named Vidyutprabha; the concentration named Mahāvyūha; and the concentration named Sarvalokaprabhākara.

The concentration called "equality of concentration"; the concentration called "unassociated with dust and free from passion"; the concentration called "convergence of non-affliction and death"; the concentration called "convergence of all things into non-affliction and death"; the concentration called "delighting in the signless and the objectless"; the concentration called "mindless and abiding in suchness"; the concentration called "thoroughly crushing the defilement of the body"; the concentration called "like the sky, destroying the defilement of speech"; and the concentration called "unattached, liberated like space, and unstained."
The seventh chapter of the Prajñāpāramitā in One Hundred Thousand Lines.

Now begins the eighth chapter. In this regard, what is the concentration called "Heroic Progress" (śūraṅgama)? That concentration which experiences the range of all concentrations is called the concentration named "Heroic Progress. In this regard, what is the concentration called "Jewel Seal" (ratnamudra)? That concentration by which all concentrations are sealed is called the concentration named "Jewel Seal. In this regard, what is the concentration called "Lion’s Play" (siṃhavikrīḍita)?
Abiding in which concentration one sports with all concentrations—this is called the concentration named "Lion’s Sport."

In that regard, what is the concentration called "Beautiful Moon"? That concentration in which, having remained, one illuminates all concentrations—this is called the concentration named "Beautiful Moon. In that regard, what is the concentration called "Moon-Flag Banner"? That concentration which holds the banner of all concentrations—this is called the concentration named "Moon-Flag Banner. In that regard, what is the concentration called "Surpassing All Phenomena"?

The meditative concentration in which, having remained, one emerges preeminent through all meditative concentrations is called the "Samādhi of the Emergence of All Dharmas. In that regard, what is the meditative concentration called "Beholding the Summit"? The meditative concentration in which, having remained, one beholds the summit of all meditative concentrations is called the "Samādhi of Beholding the Summit. In that regard, what is the meditative concentration called "Fixed in the Dharmadhātu"?

The concentration in which, having remained, one attains certainty regarding the *dharmadhātu* is called the concentration named "Certainty in the *Dharmadhātu*. In that regard, what is the concentration named "Banner of Certainty"? The concentration in which, having remained, one holds the certain banner of all concentrations is called the concentration named "Banner of Certainty. In that regard, what is...

The concentration called "Vajra": when one is established in this concentration, one is not broken; this is called the concentration named Vajra. In that regard, what is the concentration called "Seal of Entry into All Dharmas"? When one abides in this concentration, one enters the seal of all dharmas; this is called the concentration named Seal of Entry into All Dharmas. In that regard, what is the concentration called "Well-Established King of Concentrations"?

Abiding in which concentration, one becomes firmly established through the excellent establishment in all concentrations—this is called the concentration named "Well-Established King of Concentrations. In that regard, what is the concentration named "Emission of Rays"? Abiding in which concentration, one emits rays from all concentrations—this is called the concentration named "Emission of Rays. In that regard, what is the concentration named "Array of Powers"?

Abiding in which concentration one effects the array of power for all concentrations—this is called the concentration named "Array of Power" (*balavyūha*). In that regard, what is the concentration named "Exalted" (*samudgata*)? Abiding in which concentration all concentrations arise together—this is called the concentration named "Exalted. In that regard, what is the concentration named "Entry into the Certainty of Etymology" (*niruktiniyatapraveśa*)?

The concentration in which, having remained, one enters into the etymological explanations and designations of all concentrations is called the concentration named "Entry into the Certainty of Etymology. In that regard, what is the concentration named "Thorough Entry into Designation"? It is the concentration in which, having remained, one enters into the designations of all concentrations; this is called the concentration named "Thorough Entry into Designation. In that regard, what is the concentration named "Surveying the Directions"?

Abiding in that concentration, one surveys the directions of all concentrations; this is called the concentration named "Surveying the Directions" (*digvilokita*). In that regard, what is the concentration named "Seal of the Support" (*ādhāramudra*)? Abiding in that concentration, one holds the seal of all concentrations; this is called the concentration named "Seal of the Support. In that regard, what is [the concentration] named "Non-forgetfulness" (*asaṃpramoṣa*)?

Concentration: that concentration in which, having remained, one's concentrations do not become confused. This is called the concentration named "Non-forgetfulness. In that regard, what is the concentration named "Ocean-Seal of the Convergence of All Dharmas"? That concentration in which, for one who remains therein, all concentrations reach a state of inclusion and convergence. This is called the concentration named "Ocean-Seal of the Convergence of All Dharmas."

In that regard, what is the concentration called "pervading space"? It is the concentration in which, having remained, one pervades all concentrations by means of the pervasion of space. This is called the concentration named "pervading space. In that regard, what is the concentration called "diamond-mandala"? It is the concentration in which, having remained, one maintains the mandalas of all concentrations. This is called the concentration named "diamond-mandala. In that regard, what is the concentration called "abandoning strife"?

The concentration in which, having remained, one dries up all the stains of the afflictions (*kleśa*) is called the concentration named "Abandoning Strife" (*raṇajaha*). In that regard, what is the concentration named "Illumination" (*vairocana*)? The concentration in which, having remained, one illuminates, heats, and shines forth all concentrations is called the concentration named "Illumination. In that regard, what is the concentration named "Not Seeking" (*aneṣa*)? The concentration in which, having remained, one does not seek any phenomenon (*dharma*) whatsoever.

This is called the concentration named "Non-Desire. In that regard, what is the concentration named "Abiding Without Abode"? It is the concentration in which, having remained, one does not perceive any phenomenon as abiding in an abode; this is called the concentration named "Abiding Without Abode. In that regard, what is the concentration named "Mindless"? It is the concentration in which, for one who has remained therein, neither the mind nor mental factors proceed; this is called the concentration named "Mindless."

In that regard, what is the concentration called "Stainless Lamp"? Abiding in which concentration one makes a stainless lamp for all concentrations—this is called the concentration named "Stainless Lamp. In that regard, what is the concentration called "Endless Radiance"?

The concentration in which, having remained, one produces infinite radiance is called the "Infinite Radiance" (*anantaprabha*) concentration. In that regard, what is the concentration called "Light-Maker" (*prabhākara*)? It is that concentration through the simultaneous attainment of which one produces the radiance of all concentrations; this is called the "Light-Maker" concentration. In that regard, what is the concentration called "Universal Illumination" (*samantāvabhāsa*)? It is that concentration through the simultaneous attainment of which one illuminates the gateways of all concentrations.

This is called the samādhi named Universal Illumination (*samantāvabhāsa*). In that regard, what is the samādhi named Pure Essence (*śuddhasāra*)? When one abides in this samādhi, one attains the universal purity of all samādhis; this is called the samādhi named Pure Essence. In that regard, what is the samādhi named Stainless Radiance (*vimalaprabha*)? When one abides in this samādhi, one removes the defilement of all samādhis and causes all samādhis to be reflected therein.

This is called the samādhi named Vimalaprabha (Stainless Light). In that regard, what is the samādhi named Ratikara (Delight-Maker)? It is that samādhi, abiding in which one experiences the delight of all samādhis; this is called the samādhi named Ratikara. In that regard, what is the samādhi named Vidyutpradīpa (Lightning-Lamp)? It is that samādhi, abiding in which one acts as a lamp for all samādhis; this is called the samādhi named Vidyutpradīpa.

In that regard, what is the concentration called "Inexhaustible" (*akṣaya*)? It is the concentration in which, having remained, one perceives neither the exhaustion nor the non-exhaustion of all concentrations. This is called the concentration named "Inexhaustible. In that regard, what is the concentration called "Radiant" (*tejovatī*)? It is the concentration in which, having remained, one causes all concentrations to blaze with splendor and majesty. This is called the concentration named "Radiant. In that regard, what is the concentration called "Free from Exhaustion" (*kṣayāpagata*)?

Abiding in which concentration, one does not perceive any concentrations as subject to exhaustion; and one perceives them in such a way that one does not perceive even an atom. This is called the concentration named "Free from Exhaustion. In that regard, what is the concentration named "Immovable"?

Concentration (*samādhi*): Abiding in which concentration one does not move, does not conceive, does not flow, and does not proliferate regarding all concentrations—that is called the concentration named "The Immovable" (*aniñja*). In that regard, what is the concentration named "The Non-retrogressive" (*avivarta*)? Abiding in which concentration one does not perceive the retrogression of any concentrations—this is called the concentration named "The Non-retrogressive. In that regard, what is the concentration named "The Sun-Lamp" (*sūryapradīpa*)?

The meditative concentration in which, having remained, one illuminates the gateway of all meditative concentrations is called the "Sun-Lamp" (*sūryapradīpa*) samādhi. In that regard, what is the meditative concentration called "Stainless Moon" (*candravimala*)? The meditative concentration in which, having remained, one renders all meditative concentrations free from darkness is called the "Stainless Moon" samādhi. In that regard, what is the meditative concentration called "Pure Radiance" (*śuddhapratibhāsa*)?

The concentration in which, having remained, one attains the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) of all concentrations is called the concentration named "Pure Radiance" (*śuddhapratibhāsa*). In that regard, what is the concentration named "Light-Maker" (*ālokakara*)? The concentration in which, having remained, one produces light for the gateways of all concentrations is called the concentration named "Light-Maker. In that regard, what is the concentration named "Form-Maker" (*kārākāra*)?

Abiding in which concentration one performs the activity that serves as the cause for all concentrations—this is called the concentration named "The Performer of Action" (*kārākāra*). In that regard, what is the concentration named "The Banner of Knowledge" (*jñānaketu*)? Abiding in which concentration one perceives the banner of knowledge of all concentrations—this is called the concentration named "The Banner of Knowledge. In that regard, what is the concentration named "Like a Vajra" (*vajropama*)? Abiding in which concentration one effects the penetration of all concentrations.

That in which one does not even perceive concentration—this is called the concentration named "diamond-like" (*vajropama*). In that regard, what is the concentration named "abiding of the mind"? It is that concentration in which, having remained, one's mind does not waver, does not turn back, and does not tremble.

He encounters no affliction, nor does the thought "this is my mind" occur to him; this is called the meditative concentration named *cittasthiti* (abiding of the mind). In that regard, what is the meditative concentration named *samantāloka* (universal light)? It is that concentration in which, having remained, one perceives light on all sides; this is called the meditative concentration named *samantāloka*. In that regard, what is the meditative concentration named *supratiṣṭhita* (well-established)? It is that concentration in which, having remained, one becomes well-established in all meditative concentrations.

This is called the samādhi named "Well-Established. In that regard, what is the samādhi named "Jewel-Crest" (*ratnakoṭi*)? When one abides in this samādhi, all samādhis are seen from every side like a crest of jewels; this is called the samādhi named "Jewel-Crest. In that regard, what is the samādhi named "Seal of the Excellent Dharma" (*varadharmamudra*)? When one abides in this samādhi, all samādhis become sealed, by virtue of being sealed with the seal of the "seal of the unsealed crest."

This is called the samādhi named "Seal of the Supreme Dharma" (*varadharmanmudrā*). In that regard, what is the samādhi named "Equanimity of All Dharmas" (*sarvadharmasamatā*)? It is that samādhi in which, having remained, one does not perceive any dharma as being apart from equanimity. This is called the samādhi named "Equanimity of All Dharmas. In that regard, what is the samādhi named "Abandoning Delight" (*ratijaha*)? It is that samādhi in which, having remained, one abandons delight in all samādhis and in all dharmas.

This is called the concentration named "Abandoning Delight. In that regard, what is the concentration named "Arising of Dharmas"? It is the concentration in which, having remained, one rises above all concentrations by means of the darkness-removing nature of all dharmas; this is called the concentration named "Arising of Dharmas. In that regard, what is the concentration named "Scattering"? It is the concentration in which, having remained, one scatters all dharmas by means of all concentrations; this is called the concentration named "Scattering."

In that regard, what is the concentration called "the differentiation of the words of all phenomena"? It is that concentration in which, having remained, one differentiates the words of all concentrations and all phenomena; this is called the "differentiation of the words of all phenomena."

This is the samādhi called "Equal Letter. In that regard, what is the samādhi called "Equal Letter Aspect"? It is the samādhi in which, having remained, one attains the state of equal letters regarding all samādhis; this is called the samādhi called "Equal Letter Aspect. In that regard, what is the samādhi called "Free from Letters"? It is the samādhi in which, having remained, one does not perceive even a single letter of any samādhi; this is called the samādhi called "Free from Letters."

In that regard, what is the concentration called "the severance of objective referents"? It is that concentration wherein, by abiding in it, there occurs the severance of the objective referents of all concentrations; this is called the concentration called "the severance of objective referents. In that regard, what is the concentration called "the unchanging"? It is that concentration wherein, by abiding in it, one does not perceive any changes in all phenomena; this is called the concentration called "the unchanging. In that regard, what is the concentration called "the non-manifestation"?

That concentration in which, having remained, one does not perceive even the mode of all phenomena—this is called the concentration named "Modeless. In that regard, what is the concentration named "Wandering Without Abode"? That concentration in which, having remained, one does not perceive the abode of any concentrations—this is called the concentration named "Wandering Without Abode. In that regard, what is the concentration named "Free from Obscurity"?

The concentration in which, having remained, one purifies the darkness of all phenomena is called the concentration named "Free from Darkness. In that regard, what is the concentration named "Possessing Conduct"? The concentration in which, having remained, one perceives the movement of all concentrations is called the concentration named "Possessing Conduct. In that regard, what is the concentration named "Immovable"? The concentration in which, having remained, one perceives all concentrations as immovable.

This is called the concentration named "the immovable. In that regard, what is the concentration named "crossing over the objective sphere"? It is that concentration, by abiding in which one transcends the objective sphere of all concentrations. This is called...

The concentration named "Transcending Objects. In that regard, what is the concentration named "Attaining the Accumulation of All Qualities"? It is that concentration by remaining in which one attains the accumulation of qualities of all phenomena and all concentrations; this is called the concentration named "Attaining the Accumulation of All Qualities. In that regard, what is the concentration named "Stable Mind"? It is that concentration in which, for one who is established, the mind does not engage with any concentrations.

This is called the samādhi named "Stable Mind. In that regard, what is the samādhi named "Purity of Blooming Flowers"? It is the samādhi in which, having remained, one attains the purity of blooming flowers of all samādhis; this is called the samādhi named "Purity of Blooming Flowers. In that regard, what is the samādhi named "Possessing the Factors of Enlightenment"? It is the samādhi in which, having remained, one attains the seven factors of enlightenment of all samādhis.

This is called the concentration named "Possessing the Factors of Enlightenment. In that regard, what is the concentration named "Infinite Eloquence"? It is that concentration in which, having remained, one attains infinity within all concentrations; this is called the concentration named "Infinite Eloquence. In that regard, what is the concentration named "Unequaled Equality"? It is that concentration in which, having remained, one attains the state of unequaled equality within all concentrations; this is called the concentration named "Unequaled Equality."

In that regard, what is the concentration called "Transcending All Phenomena"? It is that concentration by remaining in which one transcends the entire triple world; this is called the concentration called "Transcending All Phenomena. In that regard, what is the concentration called "Discerning"? It is that concentration by remaining in which one perceives the discernment of all phenomena and of all concentrations; this is called the concentration called "Discerning."

In that regard, what is the concentration called "dispeller of doubt"? It is that concentration by abiding in which one attains the state of dispelling doubt regarding all concentrations and all phenomena. This is called the "dispeller of doubt."

...the concentration named [such-and-such]. In that regard, what is the concentration named "without foundation" (*niradhiṣṭhāna*)? That concentration in which, having remained, one does not perceive the location of any phenomena; this is called the concentration named "without foundation. In that regard, what is the concentration named "single array" (*ekavyūha*)? That concentration in which, having remained, one does not perceive the duality of any phenomenon; this is called the concentration named "single array."

In this regard, what is the concentration called "the production of aspects"? It is that concentration in which, having remained, one perceives the production of the aspects of all phenomena and of all concentrations. This is called the concentration called "the production of aspects. In this regard, what is the concentration called "single aspect"? It is that concentration in which, having remained, one does not perceive the aspect of any concentrations. This is called the concentration called "single aspect."

In that regard, what is the concentration called "non-entry into aspects" (*ākārānavakāra*)? It is the concentration in which, having remained, one perceives the non-duality of all concentrations. This is called the concentration named "non-entry into aspects. In that regard, what is the concentration called "penetrating all the depths of existence" (*nairvedhika-sarvabhavatalavigata*)? It is the concentration in which, having remained, one enters into the penetrating knowledge (*nairvedhika-jñāna*) of all concentrations; by entering into which, there is nothing that is not thoroughly understood.

This is called the samādhi named "penetrating all the depths of existence. In that regard, what is the samādhi named "entry into conventional sounds"? It is that samādhi in which, having abided, one enters into the conventional sounds of all samādhis; this is called the samādhi named "entry into conventional sounds. In that regard, what is the samādhi named "liberated from the syllables of vocal sound"? It is that samādhi in which, having abided, one perceives all samādhis as being liberated from the syllables of vocal sound.

This is called the concentration named "Free from Vocal Sound and Syllables. In that regard, what is the concentration named "Blazing Torch"? It is the concentration in which, having remained, one illuminates all concentrations with brilliance.

This is called the meditative concentration named "Blazing Torch. In that regard, what is the meditative concentration named "Purification of Characteristics"? It is that meditative concentration in which, for one who abides therein, the characteristics of all meditative concentrations are completely purified. This is called the meditative concentration named "Purification of Characteristics. In that regard, what is the meditative concentration named "Uncharacterized"? It is that meditative concentration in which, having abided therein, one perceives all meditative concentrations as being uncharacterized.

This is called the concentration named "The Unmarked. In that regard, what is the concentration named "Endowed with the Excellence of All Aspects"? It is the concentration in which, for one who abides therein, all concentrations become endowed with the excellence of all aspects. This is called the concentration named "Endowed with the Excellence of All Aspects. In that regard, what is the concentration named "Non-Relishing of All Pleasure and Pain"? It is the concentration in which, having abided, one does not perceive the pleasure or pain of any concentrations.

This is called the samādhi named "Rejoicing in Neither All Pleasure nor Pain. In that regard, what is the samādhi named "Inexhaustible Casket"? It is that samādhi in which, having abided, one does not perceive the exhaustion of any samādhis. This is called the samādhi named "Inexhaustible Casket. In that regard, what is the samādhi named "Mind of Retention" (Dhāraṇīmati)? It is that samādhi in which, having abided, one retains all dhāraṇīs. This is called the samādhi named "Mind of Retention."

In that regard, what is the concentration called "the total subduer of correctness and error"? It is that concentration in which, having abided, one does not perceive the correctness or error of any concentrations whatsoever. This is called the concentration called "the total subduer of correctness and error. In that regard, what is the concentration called "the pacifier of all obstructions and oppositions"? It is that concentration in which, having abided, one perceives the obstruction and opposition of all concentrations whatsoever.

This is called the samādhi named "the pacifier of all obstruction and opposition. In that regard, what is the samādhi named "non-conformity and non-opposition"? It is that samādhi wherein, having abided, [one perceives] all phenomena and all samādhis...

And one does not perceive either compliance or opposition; this is called the samādhi named "Compliance and Non-opposition. In that regard, what is the samādhi named "Stainless Radiance"? When one abides in this samādhi, one does not perceive the circle of light of any samādhis; this is called the samādhi named "Stainless Radiance. In that regard, what is the samādhi named "Possessing Essence"? When one abides in this samādhi, one perceives the essence of all samādhis.

This is called the concentration named "Possessing Essence. In that regard, what is the concentration named "Stainless Radiance of the Full Moon"? It is that concentration in which, for one who abides therein, all concentrations become completely fulfilled, just like the orb of the moon on the night of the full moon. This is called the concentration named "Stainless Radiance of the Full Moon. In that regard, what is the concentration named "Great Array"?

The concentration by abiding in which one becomes endowed with the great array of all concentrations—this is called the concentration named "Great Array. In that regard, what is the concentration named "Illuminator of All Aspects"? The concentration by abiding in which one illuminates all concentrations and all phenomena—this is called the concentration named "Illuminator of All Aspects. In that regard, what is the concentration named "Equanimity of Concentrations"?

The concentration in which, having remained, one perceives the non-distraction and one-pointedness of all concentrations is called the concentration named "Equanimity of Concentrations" (*samādhisamatā*). In that regard, what is the concentration named "Convergence of the Non-contentious and the Contentious"? It is the concentration in which, for one who remains therein, all concentrations do not become contentious; this is called the concentration named "Convergence of the Non-contentious and the Contentious. In that regard, what is the concentration named "Convergence of All That Is Non-contentious and Contentious"?

The meditative concentration by abiding in which one attains the state of being the non-contention, the refuge, and the universal convergence of all things—this is called the meditative concentration named "Non-contention, Refuge, and Universal Convergence. In that regard, what is the meditative concentration named "Delighting in the Signless and Without Support"?

The meditative concentration in which, having remained, one does not arrive at an abode for any meditative concentrations is called the concentration named "delighting in the lack of a basis. In that regard, what is the concentration named "the mind certain in its abiding in suchness"? The meditative concentration in which, having remained, one does not increase from the suchness of all meditative concentrations is called the concentration named "the mind certain in its abiding in suchness. In that regard, what is the concentration named "the crushing of the defilement of the body"?

The concentration in which, having remained, one does not perceive the body of all concentrations is called the concentration named "The Thoroughly Crushing of the Defilement of Body. In that regard, what is the concentration named "Like the Sky, Destroying the Defilement of Speech"? It is the concentration in which, having remained, one does not perceive the vocal activity of any concentrations; this is called the concentration named "Like the Sky, Destroying the Defilement of Speech. In that regard, what is the concentration named "Unstained Liberation Unattached like Space"?

Abiding in which concentration, one attains the state of all phenomena being unattached like space and free from defilement; this is called the concentration named "Unattached and Undefiled Liberation Like Space. Subhūti, this is the Great Vehicle of a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom.
The eighth chapter of the Śatasāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā.
Now begins the ninth chapter.

Furthermore, Subhūti, the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva mahāsattva consists of the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*). What are the four? They are: the foundation of mindfulness of the body, the foundation of mindfulness of feelings, the foundation of mindfulness of the mind, and the foundation of mindfulness of phenomena (*dharma*). In that regard, what is the foundation of mindfulness of the body? Here, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells contemplating the body within the internal body.

And he does not engage in discursive thoughts associated with the body, being ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and dejection regarding the world, by means of non-apprehension. He dwells contemplating the body in the external body. And he does not engage in discursive thoughts associated with the body, being ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and dejection regarding the world, by means of non-apprehension. He dwells contemplating the body in the internal and external body.

And he does not engage in discursive thoughts associated with the body, being ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and dejection regarding the world, by means of the yoga of non-apprehension.

He dwells contemplating feelings in internal feelings; yet he does not engage in discursive thoughts associated with feelings, being ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and dejection regarding the world, by means of the yoga of non-apprehension. He dwells contemplating feelings in external feelings; yet he does not engage in discursive thoughts associated with feelings, being ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and dejection regarding the world, by means of the yoga of non-apprehension.

He dwells contemplating feelings in internal and external feelings; yet he does not engage in discursive thoughts accompanied by feeling, being ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and dejection regarding the world—this by means of non-apprehension. He dwells contemplating the mind in the internal mind; yet he does not engage in discursive thoughts accompanied by the mind, being ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and dejection regarding the world—this by means of non-apprehension. He dwells contemplating the mind in the external mind.

And he does not direct discursive thoughts associated with the mind; ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and dejection regarding the world, by means of non-apprehension. He dwells contemplating the mind in the internal and external mind. And he does not direct discursive thoughts associated with the mind; ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and dejection regarding the world, by means of non-apprehension.

He dwells contemplating phenomena among internal phenomena; yet he does not engage in discursive thoughts associated with phenomena, being ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and dejection regarding the world, by means of the yoga of non-apprehension.

Subhūti, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwell observing the body within the internal body? Here, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when walking, knows "I am walking"; when standing, he knows "I am standing"; when sitting, he knows "I am sitting"; and when lying down, he knows "I am lying down. Furthermore, however his body may be positioned—whether in a refined or unrefined posture—he does not perceive it as a self.

In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells contemplating the body in the internal body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and dejection regarding the world, and that by means of non-apprehension. Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells contemplating the body in the internal body; he is not one who acts with clear comprehension when advancing or when retreating.

He acts with clear comprehension when looking ahead and looking around; he acts with clear comprehension when bending and stretching his limbs; he acts with clear comprehension when wearing his outer robe, inner robe, and bowl; he acts with clear comprehension when eating, drinking, chewing, and tasting; he acts with clear comprehension when relieving himself of the fatigue of lying down and sleep; he acts with clear comprehension when coming and going; and he acts with clear comprehension when standing and sitting.

He acts with clear comprehension while dreaming and while awake; he acts with clear comprehension in speaking and in remaining silent; he acts with clear comprehension in seclusion. In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom dwells contemplating the body within the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and dejection regarding the world, by means of the yoga of non-apprehension.

Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, breathing in mindfully, he knows: "I am breathing in mindfully"; breathing out mindfully, he knows: "I am breathing out mindfully. Breathing in long, he knows: "I am breathing in long"; breathing out long, he knows: "I am breathing out long. Breathing in short, he knows: "I am breathing in short."

Breathing out short, he discerns, "I am breathing out short. Subhūti, it is just as if a skilled turner of a lathe, or a pupil of a turner of a lathe, were to discern, "I am making a long stroke," or discern, "I am making a short stroke. In the very same way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom, breathing in mindfully, discerns, "I am breathing in mindfully."

Mindful, he breathes out; mindful, he discerns, "I am breathing out. Breathing in long, he discerns, "I am breathing in long. Breathing out long, he discerns, "I am breathing out long. Breathing in short, he discerns, "I am breathing in short."

Breathing out short, he discerns, "I am breathing out short. In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom dwells contemplating the body internally—ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and dejection regarding the world—and that by means of non-apprehension.

Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom contemplates this very body-element as it truly is: "In this body there is the earth element, the water element, the fire element, and the wind element."

Subhūti, it is just as if a skilled butcher, or a butcher’s apprentice, having slaughtered a cow with a sharp blade, were to divide it into four quarters; having divided it into four quarters, he examines them while standing or sitting. In the very same way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom examines this very body-element as it truly is.

"In this body there is the earth element, the water element, the fire element, and the air element. In this very way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom dwells observing the body within the internal body—whether standing or sitting—ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and dejection regarding the world; and that is by means of non-apprehension."

Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom contemplates this very body, from the soles of the feet upwards and from the hair of the head downwards, bounded by the nails, body hair, and skin, as full of various kinds of impurity, according to reality.

In this body there are: head-hairs, body-hairs, nails, teeth, skin, hide, flesh, sinews, blood, bones, marrow, kidneys, heart, liver, pleura, spleen, lungs, small intestines, large intestines, stomach, excrement, tears, sweat, fat, saliva, snot, pus, bile, phlegm, grease, lymph, filth, the brain,
the brain-membrane, and the eye-excrement.

Subhūti, it is just as if there were a farmer’s granary full of various kinds of grain—sesame, mustard seeds, mung beans, black gram, lentils, barley, wheat, rice, and paddy—and a man with sight, having opened it and examining it, should know: "These are sesame seeds; these are mustard seeds; these are mung beans; these are black gram; these are lentils; these are barley; these are wheat; these are rice; these are paddy."

In the same way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva [contemplates] this very body, from the soles of the feet upwards and from the hair of the head downwards, bounded by the nails, hair, and skin, as full of various kinds of impurities.

In this body there are: head-hairs, body-hairs, nails, teeth, skin, inner skin, flesh, sinews, blood, bones, marrow, kidneys, heart, liver, pleura, spleen, lungs, small intestines, large intestines, stomach, feces, tears, sweat, fat, saliva, nasal mucus, pus, bile, phlegm, grease, lymph, filth, the head, the skull, and the brain.

The eye-secretion, the ear-secretion—thus indeed, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom dwells contemplating the body within the internal body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and dejection regarding the world; and that by way of non-apprehension. Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom has gone to a cemetery and sees [the corpses].

He sees various forms cast away upon the path of the dead on the bed of corpses—corpses that have been dead for one day, or two days, or three days, or four days, or five days; bloated, or livid, or putrefied, or gnawed by animals, or bloody, or scattered about. He applies this very body to that situation: "This body, too, is of such a nature, of such a character, and it has not transcended this natural law."

In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom dwells contemplating the body in the external body—ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and dejection regarding the world—and that by means of non-apprehension.

Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom sees on a charnel ground corpses that have been dead for six nights or seven nights, bloated, being devoured by crows, hawks, ospreys, vultures, herons, jackals, dogs, or various other kinds of living creatures;

He applies this very body to that [corpse], thinking: "This body, too, is of such a nature, of such a character; it has not transcended this natural law. In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of wisdom, dwells contemplating the body in the external body—ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and dejection regarding the world—and that by means of non-apprehension.

Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom sees on a charnel ground corpses that have been devoured, dead, impure, putrid, and foul-smelling, he applies this very body to that [sight], thinking: "This body, too, is of such a nature, of such a character; it has not transcended this natural law."

In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom dwells contemplating the body in the external body—ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and dejection regarding the world—by means of the yoga of non-apprehension.

Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom sees on a charnel ground fragments of bone, still smeared with flesh and blood and bound together by sinews, he compares this very body to them: "This body, too, is of such a nature and such a character."

He has completely transcended this very nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*). In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom dwells contemplating the body in the external body—ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and dejection regarding the world—by means of non-apprehension (*anupalambha-yoga*).

Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he sees the various bones in a charnel ground—devoid of flesh, blood, and the binding of sinews, appearing like mere skeletons. He then applies this very body to that [vision], thinking: "This body, too, is of such a nature, of such a character; it has not transcended this natural law."

In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom dwells contemplating the body in the external body—ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and dejection regarding the world—and that by means of non-apprehension. Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom sees:

On the path of the dead, just as heaps of bones, freed from their binding connections, are scattered upon the earth like shells, he applies this very body to that situation: "This body, too, is of such a nature, of such a character; it has not transcended this natural law.

In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom dwells contemplating the body in the external body—ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and dejection regarding the world—by means of non-apprehension.

Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom sees bones in a cemetery scattered upon the earth in every direction and intermediate direction—foot-bones in one place, shin-bones in another, thigh-bones in another, the pelvic bone in another, the backbone in another, the rib-bones in another, the arm-bones in another, and the neck-bones in another.

With another [part], he [observes] the skull-bones of the head. He then applies this very body to that [state], thinking: "This body, too, is of such a nature, of such a character; it has not transcended this natural law. In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom dwells contemplating the body in the external body—ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and dejection regarding the world—and that by means of non-apprehension.

Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom sees bones on a charnel ground that have been there for many years, parched by the sun and wind, and withered by the heat and air;

They are white, resembling conch shells. He applies this very body to that [state], thinking: "This body, too, is of such a nature, of such a character; it has not transcended this natural law. In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom dwells contemplating the body in the external body—ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and dejection regarding the world—and that by means of non-apprehension.

Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom sees bones on a charnel ground that have been there for many years—disintegrated, blue-black, the color of pigeons, putrid, reduced to powder, and level with the dust of the earth—he applies this very body to that situation: "This body, too, is of such a nature, of such a character; it has not transcended this natural law."

In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom dwells contemplating the body in the internal body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and dejection regarding the world, by means of the yoga of non-apprehension.

He dwells contemplating the body in the external body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and dejection regarding the world, by means of the yoga of non-apprehension.

He dwells contemplating the body in the internal and external body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and dejection regarding the world, by means of non-apprehension.

He dwells contemplating feelings in internal feelings, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and dejection regarding the world, by means of non-apprehension. He dwells contemplating feelings in external feelings, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and dejection regarding the world, by means of non-apprehension.

He dwells contemplating feelings in internal and external feelings—ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and dejection regarding the world—by means of the yoga of non-apprehension. He dwells contemplating the mind in the internal mind—ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and dejection regarding the world—by means of the yoga of non-apprehension.

He dwells contemplating the mind as the mind with respect to the external mind, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world, by means of the yoga of non-apprehension. He dwells contemplating the mind as the mind with respect to both the internal and external mind, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world, by means of the yoga of non-apprehension.

He dwells contemplating phenomena among internal phenomena—ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and dejection regarding the world—by means of non-apprehension. He dwells contemplating phenomena among external phenomena—clearly comprehending and mindful, having removed covetousness and dejection regarding the world—by means of non-apprehension.

Contemplating phenomena in internal and external phenomena, he is clearly comprehending and mindful, having removed covetousness and dejection regarding the world, by means of non-apprehension. This too, Subhūti, is the Great Vehicle of the bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Furthermore, Subhūti, the Great Vehicle of the bodhisattva mahāsattva is as follows: namely, the four right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*). Which are they? Here, Subhūti, the bodhisattva...

The Mahāsattva, practicing in the perfection of wisdom, generates desire, exerts himself, arouses vigor, takes hold of the mind, and applies himself correctly so that evil, unwholesome states that have not yet arisen do not arise. He generates desire, exerts himself, arouses vigor, takes hold of the mind, and applies himself correctly so that evil, unwholesome states that have already arisen are abandoned.

He generates desire, exerts himself, arouses energy, uplifts the mind, and correctly applies himself so that wholesome states not yet arisen may arise. He generates desire, exerts himself, arouses energy, uplifts the mind, and correctly applies himself so that wholesome states already arisen may endure, increase further, not be lost, and reach fulfillment. And he does this through the application of non-apprehension (*anupalambha*).
This too, Subhūti, is the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva mahāsattva.

Furthermore, Subhūti, the Mahāyāna of a bodhisattva mahāsattva consists of the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*). What are the four? Here, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom cultivates the bases of psychic power endowed with the formative forces of abandonment and the concentration of desire; they are based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, and result in relinquishment.

He cultivates the bases of psychic power endowed with the exertions of vigor and concentration. He cultivates the bases of psychic power with a mind that relies on seclusion, relies on dispassion, relies on cessation, and results in relinquishment, being endowed with the formative forces of concentration and exertion. He cultivates the bases of psychic power relying on seclusion, relying on dispassion, relying on cessation, resulting in relinquishment, and endowed with the formative forces of concentration and exertion. He cultivates the bases of psychic power endowed with the formative forces of concentration and exertion.

It is based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, and results in relinquishment; and that is by way of non-apprehension. Subhūti, this too is the Great Vehicle of the bodhisattva mahāsattva.

Furthermore, Subhūti, the Mahāyāna of a bodhisattva mahāsattva is as follows: namely, the five faculties. What are the five? The faculty of faith, the faculty of vigor, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, and the faculty of wisdom. This too, Subhūti, is the Mahāyāna of a bodhisattva mahāsattva, and that is by way of non-apprehension.

Furthermore, Subhūti, the Mahāyāna of a bodhisattva mahāsattva is as follows: namely, the five powers. What are the five? They are the power of faith, the power of vigor, the power of mindfulness, the power of concentration, and the power of wisdom. This too, Subhūti, is the Mahāyāna of a bodhisattva mahāsattva, and that is by way of non-apprehension. Furthermore, Subhūti, the Mahāyāna of a bodhisattva mahāsattva is as follows: namely, the seven factors of enlightenment.

What are the seven factors of enlightenment? They are the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness, the factor of enlightenment of investigation of phenomena, the factor of enlightenment of energy, the factor of enlightenment of joy, the factor of enlightenment of pliancy, the factor of enlightenment of concentration, and the factor of enlightenment of equanimity. Among these, what is the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness?

In this regard, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom cultivates the factor of awakening that is mindfulness, which is based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, and results in relinquishment; and that by way of non-apprehension. What is the factor of awakening that is the investigation of phenomena? In this regard, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom cultivates the factor of awakening that is the investigation of phenomena.

It is based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, and results in relinquishment; and that is by way of non-apprehension. What is the factor of enlightenment that is energy? Here, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in the perfection of wisdom cultivates the factor of enlightenment that is energy; it is based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, and results in relinquishment; and that is by way of non-apprehension.

In that regard, what is the factor of awakening that is joy (*prītisaṃbodhyaṅga*)? Here, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing in the perfection of wisdom, cultivates the factor of awakening that is joy—relying on seclusion, relying on dispassion, relying on cessation, and culminating in relinquishment—and that by way of non-apprehension (*anupalambha*). In that regard, what is the factor of awakening that is serenity (*prasrabdhi-saṃbodhyaṅga*)?

In this regard, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in the perfection of wisdom cultivates the factor of awakening that is mindfulness; it is based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, and results in relinquishment, and that is by way of non-apprehension. In that context, what is the factor of awakening that is concentration? In this regard, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in the perfection of wisdom cultivates the factor of awakening that is concentration.

It is based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, and results in relinquishment; and that is by way of non-apprehension. In this regard, what is the factor of enlightenment of equanimity? Here, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of wisdom, cultivates the factor of enlightenment of equanimity—based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, and resulting in relinquishment—and that is by way of non-apprehension. This too, Subhūti, is the Great Vehicle of the bodhisattva mahāsattva.

Furthermore, Subhūti, the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva mahāsattva is this, namely: the noble eightfold path—right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration. In that regard, what is right view? Here, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing in the perfection of wisdom, cultivates right view.

It is based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, and results in relinquishment, and that by way of non-apprehension. In this regard, what is right intention? Here, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom cultivates right intention; it is based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, and results in relinquishment, and that by way of non-apprehension. What is right speech? Here—

Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he cultivates right speech—which is based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, and results in relinquishment—and that by way of non-apprehension. What is right action? Here, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom cultivates right action.

It is based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, and results in relinquishment; and that is by way of non-apprehension. What is right livelihood? Here, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of wisdom, cultivates right livelihood; it is based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, and results in relinquishment; and that is by way of non-apprehension. What is right effort?

In this regard, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom cultivates right effort; it is based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, and results in relinquishment, and that is by way of non-apprehension. What is right mindfulness? In this regard, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom cultivates right mindfulness.

It is based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, and results in relinquishment; and that is by way of non-apprehension. What is right concentration? Here, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing in the perfection of wisdom, cultivates right concentration—based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, and resulting in relinquishment—and that is by way of non-apprehension.
This, Subhūti, is the Great Vehicle of the bodhisattva mahāsattva.

Furthermore, Subhūti, the Mahāyāna of a bodhisattva mahāsattva consists of these three concentrations. What are the three concentrations? They are the concentration on emptiness (*śūnyatā-samādhi*), the concentration on the signless (*ānimitta-samādhi*), and the concentration on the wishless (*apraṇihita-samādhi*). Among these, what is the concentration on emptiness?

The stability of the mind of one who contemplates all phenomena as empty of their own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇaśūnya*)—which is the gate of liberation called emptiness—is called the concentration of emptiness (*śūnyatāsamādhi*). In that regard, what is the concentration of signlessness (*ānimittasamādhi*)? The stability of the mind of one who contemplates all phenomena as signless—which is the gate of liberation called signlessness—is called the signless concentration. In that regard, what is the concentration of wishlessness (*apraṇihitasamādhi*)?

"All phenomena are unconditioned"—the stability of the mind for one who does not perform such conditioning is called the liberation of wishlessness; this is known as the concentration of wishlessness. These recollections regarding the gates of liberation should be practiced by one who is not ashamed. This too, Subhūti, is the Great Vehicle of the bodhisattva mahāsattva, and that is through the application of non-apprehension.

Furthermore, Subhūti, the Mahāyāna of a bodhisattva mahāsattva consists of these eleven knowledges. What are the eleven? They are: the knowledge of suffering, the knowledge of the origin, the knowledge of cessation, the knowledge of the path, the knowledge of destruction, the knowledge of non-arising, the knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*), the subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*), conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtti-jñāna*), analytical knowledge (*paricaya-jñāna*), and knowledge according to the literal expression (*yathāruta-jñāna*). Among these, what is the knowledge of suffering? It is the knowledge of the non-arising of suffering.

In that regard, what is the knowledge of origination? It is the knowledge of the abandonment of origination. In that regard, what is the knowledge of cessation? It is the knowledge of the cessation of suffering. In that regard, what is the knowledge of the path? It is the knowledge of the noble eightfold path. In that regard, what is the knowledge of destruction? It is the knowledge of the destruction of passion, hatred, and delusion. In that regard, what is the knowledge of non-arising? It is the knowledge of non-arising regarding the Blessed One.

In that regard, what is the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*)? It is the knowledge of the non-examination and non-differentiation of the five aggregates. In that regard, what is subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*)? It is the knowledge that "the eye is impermanent," the knowledge that "the ear is impermanent," the knowledge that "the nose is impermanent," the knowledge that "the tongue is impermanent," the knowledge that "the body is impermanent," the knowledge that "the mind is impermanent," the knowledge that "form is impermanent," the knowledge that "sound is impermanent," and the knowledge that "odor is impermanent."

The knowledge that "taste is impermanent," the knowledge that "touch is impermanent," the knowledge that "phenomena are impermanent"; the knowledge that "the eye-element is impermanent," the knowledge that "the form-element is impermanent," the knowledge that "the eye-consciousness-element is impermanent"; the knowledge that "the ear-element is impermanent," the knowledge that "the sound-element is impermanent," the knowledge that "the ear-consciousness-element is impermanent"; the knowledge that "the nose-element is impermanent."

The knowledge that the odor-element is impermanent; the knowledge that the nose-consciousness-element is impermanent; the knowledge that the tongue-element is impermanent; the knowledge that the taste-element is impermanent; the knowledge that the tongue-consciousness-element is impermanent; the knowledge that the body-element is impermanent; the knowledge that the tactile-object-element is impermanent; the knowledge that the body-consciousness-element is impermanent; the knowledge that the mind-element is impermanent; and the knowledge that the mental-object-element is impermanent.

The knowledge that the element of mental consciousness is impermanent; the knowledge that the earth element is impermanent; the knowledge that the water element is impermanent; the knowledge that the fire element is impermanent; the knowledge that the wind element is impermanent; the knowledge that the space element is impermanent; the knowledge that the consciousness element is impermanent; the knowledge that ignorance is impermanent; the knowledge that volitional formations are impermanent; the knowledge that consciousness is impermanent; and the knowledge that name-and-form are impermanent.

The knowledge that the six sense bases are impermanent; the knowledge that contact is impermanent; the knowledge that feeling is impermanent; the knowledge that craving is impermanent; the knowledge that clinging is impermanent; the knowledge that becoming is impermanent; the knowledge that birth is impermanent; and the knowledge that aging and death are impermanent.

In that regard, what is conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*)? It is the knowledge of the minds of other beings and other persons by means of one's own mind. In that regard, what is knowledge through familiarity (*paricayajñāna*)? It is the knowledge of the antidote (*pratipakṣajñāna*). In that regard, what is knowledge of what has been done as it was (*yathākatajñāna*)? It is the Tathāgata’s knowledge of the omniscience of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatājñāna*). This too, Subhūti, is the Great Vehicle of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, and that is by way of non-apprehension (*anupalambha-yogena*).

Furthermore, Subhūti, the Mahāyāna of a bodhisattva mahāsattva consists of these three faculties. What are the three? They are the faculty "I shall come to know the unknown," the faculty of knowing, and the faculty of one who has known. Among these, what is the faculty "I shall come to know the unknown"?

That which, among the persons in training (*śaikṣa*), has not yet been fully realized but is being directed toward the perfect discipline, namely the faculty of faith, the faculty of energy, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, and the faculty of wisdom—this is called the faculty "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātamājñāsyāmīndriya*). In that regard, what is the faculty of knowing (*ājñendriya*)? That which, among the persons in training who have already known [the truth], consists of the faculty of faith, the faculty of energy, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, and the faculty of wisdom—this is called the faculty of knowing.

In that regard, what is the faculty of one who has already known (*ājñātāvīndriya*)? It is the faculty of faith, the faculty of energy, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, and the faculty of wisdom belonging to those individuals who are in training (*śaikṣa*), Arhats, Pratyekabuddhas, Bodhisattvas, and Tathāgatas. This is called the faculty of one who has already known. This too, Subhūti, is the Great Vehicle of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, and that is by way of non-apprehension (*anupalambha*).

Furthermore, Subhūti, the Mahāyāna of a bodhisattva mahāsattva consists of these three concentrations. What are the three? They are: concentration with applied thought and sustained thought; concentration without applied thought and with sustained thought only; and concentration without applied thought and without sustained thought. Among these, what is concentration with applied thought and sustained thought?

In this regard, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, secluded from sensual desires and secluded from evil, unwholesome states, attains and dwells in the first dhyāna, which is accompanied by applied thought (*savitarka*) and sustained thought (*savicāra*), and possesses the joy and happiness born of seclusion. This is called concentration with applied and sustained thought. In that context, what is concentration without applied thought and with only sustained thought? It is that which lies between the first dhyāna and the second dhyāna.

This is called the concentration that is without applied thought and consists of sustained thought only. In that regard, what is the concentration without sustained thought? It is the second dhyāna, the third dhyāna, the fourth dhyāna, and the attainment of the sphere of infinite space.

The attainment of the sphere of infinite consciousness, the attainment of the sphere of nothingness, the attainment of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, and the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling—this is called the concentration without applied thought and without sustained thought. This too, Subhūti, is the Great Vehicle of the bodhisattva mahāsattva, and that is by way of non-apprehension.

Furthermore, Subhūti, the Mahāyāna of a bodhisattva mahāsattva is as follows: namely, the ten recollections (*anusmṛti*). What are the ten? They are: the recollection of the Buddha, the recollection of the Dharma, the recollection of the Saṅgha, the recollection of ethical discipline (*śīla*), the recollection of relinquishment (*tyāga*), the recollection of the deities (*devatā*), the recollection of mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpāna*), the recollection of disenchantment (*udvega*), the recollection of death (*maraṇa*), and the recollection directed toward the body (*kāyagata*). This too, Subhūti, is the Mahāyāna of a bodhisattva mahāsattva, and that is by way of non-apprehension (*anupalambha-yoga*).

Furthermore, Subhūti, the Mahāyāna of a bodhisattva mahāsattva is as follows: namely, the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, the eight liberations, and the nine successive meditative attainments. In that regard, what are the four dhyānas?

In this regard, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom, secluded from sensual desires and secluded from evil, unwholesome states, enters and dwells in the first dhyāna, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought, and filled with the joy and happiness born of seclusion.

Having emerged from the state accompanied by applied and sustained thought, through internal serenity and the unification of the mind, he dwells having attained the second dhyāna, which is without applied or sustained thought, born of concentration, and characterized by joy and bliss. Through detachment from joy, he dwells in equanimity; mindful and clearly comprehending, he experiences bliss with the body.

That which the Noble Ones describe as: "Equanimous, mindful, dwelling in happiness, he attains and dwells in the third dhyāna, which is free from joy. Through the abandoning of pleasure and the abandoning of pain, and through the previous disappearance of mental ease and distress, he attains and dwells in the fourth dhyāna, which is neither painful nor pleasant and is purified by equanimity and mindfulness. And that is by way of non-apprehension. These are the four dhyānas.

In that regard, what are the four immeasurables? Here, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing in the perfection of wisdom, dwells having resolved upon and attained a mind accompanied by loving-kindness—vast, exalted, non-dual, immeasurable, free from enmity, without rival, and unassailable—pervading the ten directions throughout the world, which is supreme as the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu) and bounded by the realm of space (ākāśadhātu).

With a mind accompanied by compassion—vast, exalted, non-dual, immeasurable, free from enmity, without rival, and unassailable—he dwells having pervaded the ten directions, resolved upon them, and attained to them, throughout the world bounded by the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu) and extending to the limits of the realm of space (ākāśadhātu).

With a mind accompanied by sympathetic joy—vast, exalted, non-dual, immeasurable, free from enmity, without rival, and unassailable—he dwells having pervaded the ten directions, resolved upon them, and attained to them, throughout the world bounded by the realm of phenomena and extending to the limits of the realm of space.

With a mind accompanied by equanimity—vast, exalted, non-dual, immeasurable, free from enmity, without rival, and unassailable—he dwells pervading the ten directions, reaching as far as the world-system of the *dharmadhātu* and extending to the limits of the *ākāśadhātu*, having resolved upon and attained this through the yoga of non-apprehension. These are the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*).

What are the four formless attainments? Here, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing in the perfection of wisdom, by completely transcending all perceptions of form, by the disappearance of perceptions of sensory resistance, and by non-attention to perceptions of diversity, thinking "space is infinite," dwells having attained the sphere of infinite space.

Having completely transcended the sphere of infinite space by the thought "consciousness is infinite," he enters and dwells in the sphere of infinite consciousness. Having completely transcended the sphere of infinite consciousness, [he perceives] that there is nothing.

Having attained and dwelt in the sphere of nothingness (*ākiñcanyāyatana*), he transcends the sphere of nothingness in every respect and attains and dwells in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), by way of non-apprehension (*anupalambha*). These are the four formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*). In that regard, what are the eight liberations (*vimokṣa*)? One who possesses the perception of forms sees forms; this is the first liberation. Having the internal perception of form, one sees external forms; this is the second liberation.

He becomes intent upon emptiness; this is the third liberation. Through the complete transcendence of perceptions of form, the disappearance of perceptions of sensory resistance, and non-attention to perceptions of diversity, he dwells having attained the sphere of infinite space, thinking "space is infinite"; this is the fourth liberation. Through the complete transcendence of the sphere of infinite space, he dwells having attained the sphere of infinite consciousness, thinking "consciousness is infinite."

This is the fifth liberation. By completely transcending the sphere of infinite consciousness, thinking "there is nothing at all," he attains and dwells in the sphere of nothingness; this is the sixth liberation. By completely transcending the sphere of nothingness, he attains and dwells in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; this is the seventh liberation.

By completely transcending the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, he dwells having attained the cessation of perception and feeling; this is the eighth liberation. And that is by way of non-apprehension. These are the eight liberations.

In that regard, what are the nine successive attainments of meditative dwelling? Here, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of wisdom, secluded from sensual desires and secluded from evil, unwholesome states, attains and dwells in the first dhyāna, which is accompanied by applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*), and possesses the joy and happiness born of seclusion. Through the subsiding of applied and sustained thought, through internal tranquility and the unification of the mind, he attains and dwells in the second dhyāna, which is without applied thought and without sustained thought.

Having attained and dwelt in the second dhyāna, which is the joy and happiness born of concentration, he, through detachment from joy, dwells in equanimity; mindful and clearly comprehending, he experiences happiness with the body, of which the Noble Ones say: "He dwells in happiness, possessing equanimity and mindfulness. Thus, having attained and dwelt in the third dhyāna, which is free from joy.

Through the abandoning of pleasure and the abandoning of pain, and through the prior disappearance of mental joy and dejection, he dwells having attained the fourth dhyāna, which is neither-painful-nor-pleasant and purified by equanimity and mindfulness. Through the complete surmounting of perceptions of form, the disappearance of perceptions of sensory resistance, and non-attention to perceptions of diversity, he dwells having attained the sphere of infinite space, [perceiving] "space is infinite."

By completely transcending the sphere of infinite space, thinking "consciousness is infinite," he attains and dwells in the sphere of infinite consciousness. By completely transcending the sphere of infinite consciousness, thinking "there is nothing at all," he attains and dwells in the sphere of nothingness. By completely transcending the sphere of nothingness, he attains and dwells in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

Having completely transcended the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, he dwells having attained the cessation of perception and feeling. These are the successive attainments of meditative dwelling.

Furthermore, Subhūti, the Mahāyāna of a bodhisattva mahāsattva is as follows: namely, the ten powers of a Tathāgata. What are the ten? Here, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in the perfection of wisdom understands, in accordance with reality, what is possible as possible and what is impossible as impossible. He understands, in accordance with reality, the ripening of karma according to its basis and its cause for past, future, and present phenomena and the undertaking of actions.

He understands, as it truly is, the world of various elements as a world of many elements, and the world of many elements as a world of many elements; he understands, as it truly is, other sentient beings and other persons who possess manifold inclinations.

He understands, as it truly is, the various inclinations [of beings]. He understands, as it truly is, the knowledge of the superior and inferior faculties of other beings and other individuals. He understands, as it truly is, the path leading to all destinations. He understands, as it truly is, the basis for the defilement and purification of the faculties, powers, factors of awakening, meditative absorptions, liberations, concentrations, and attainments. He recollects his manifold past abodes; he recollects even a single birth.

He recollects even a hundred births, a thousand, ten thousand, ten million, a hundred ten-millions, a thousand ten-millions, a hundred thousand ten-millions, and even a hundred thousand times ten-million-billion births. He recollects even a single eon; he recollects up to a hundred eons, a thousand eons, a hundred thousand eons, and even many hundreds of thousands of ten-million-billion eons.

"In this place I was, with such a name, such a clan, such a birth; such was my food, such my duration of stay, and such my lifespan. Having passed away from there, I was reborn in that other place, and having passed away from there, I have been reborn here"—in this way, he recollects his manifold former abodes with their modes, details, and descriptions. With the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, he beholds sentient beings.

He perceives beings as they pass away and are reborn, having been born—whether beautiful or ugly, lowly or exalted, in a happy destination or a miserable destination—and he understands them according to their karma: "These worthy beings were possessed of misconduct of body, possessed of misconduct of speech, and possessed of misconduct of mind."

Those who revile the noble ones, holding wrong views, because of that cause and by reason of that condition, upon the dissolution of the body, are reborn in states of woe, in miserable destinies, in perdition, in the hells. But these beings, sirs, are endowed with good conduct of body, endowed with good conduct of speech, and endowed with good conduct of mind; they do not revile the noble ones and hold right views; because of that cause...

With that as their condition, after the breaking up of the body, they are reborn in a good destination, in a heavenly world among the gods. Through the destruction of the outflows (*āsrava*), having personally realized, witnessed, and attained the untainted liberation of mind (*anāsravacittavimukti*) and liberation through wisdom (*prajñāvimukti*), they dwell therein. They know: "Birth is exhausted for me; the holy life has been lived; what was to be done has been done; there is no further state of being. Subhūti, this too is the Great Vehicle of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, and that is by way of non-apprehension (*anupalambha*).

Furthermore, Subhūti, the Mahāyāna of a bodhisattva mahāsattva consists of the four grounds of self-confidence (*vaiśāradya*). What are the four? "If anyone—whether a śramaṇa, a brāhmaṇa, a deva, Māra, Brahmā, or anyone else in the world—should rightfully challenge me, who claim to be perfectly awakened, by saying: 'These dharmas have not been fully realized by you,' [I have no fear]."

I do not perceive any ground for attack here; and perceiving no such ground, I dwell having attained security, having attained fearlessness, and having attained self-confidence. I recognize my noble, preeminent position; having entered the assembly, I roar the perfect lion’s roar.

I set in motion the Brahma-wheel, which cannot be turned back by any ascetic or brahmin, by any god, Māra, or Brahmā, nor by anyone else in the world in accordance with the Dharma—[the wheel] of one who claims, "My outflows are indeed exhausted," such that no ascetic or brahmin, no god, Māra, Brahmā, or anyone else in the world can rightfully challenge him, saying, "These outflows of yours are not yet exhausted. In this regard, no ascetic or brahmin, no god, Māra, Brahmā, or anyone else in the world can challenge me in accordance with the Dharma.
