I do not perceive any ground for them at all; and not perceiving any ground therein, I dwell having attained security, having attained fearlessness, and having attained intrepidity. I claim my noble, preeminent place. Having entered the assembly, I roar the true lion’s roar. I set in motion the Brahma-wheel, which cannot be turned back by any ascetic, brahmin, deva, Māra, Brahmā, or anyone else in the world who acts in accordance with the Dharma.
Furthermore, those things which have been declared by me to be obstructive factors—those...

"It is impossible that for one who practices this, it should not suffice to reach the goal; no such situation exists. Herein, indeed, whether a śramaṇa, a brāhmaṇa, a deva, Māra, Brahmā, or anyone else in the world might challenge me with a legitimate argument—such a sign I do not perceive at all. Not perceiving any such sign therein, I dwell having attained security, having attained fearlessness, and having attained self-confidence. I claim the noble, bull-like position."

Having entered the assembly, I roar the true lion’s roar; I turn the Brahma-wheel, which cannot be turned back by any ascetic, brahmin, deva, Māra, Brahmā, or anyone else in the world in accordance with the Dharma. And as for those paths of practice that have been declared by me—noble, leading to liberation, and penetrating—leading to the complete destruction of suffering for one who practices them: it is impossible that one who practices them would not go forth to the complete destruction of suffering. This is not possible.

"In this regard, indeed, I do not perceive any ground on which a śramaṇa, a brāhmaṇa, a deva, Māra, Brahmā, or anyone else in the world could rightfully challenge me. Not perceiving any such ground, I dwell having attained security, having attained fearlessness, and having attained self-confidence. I know my own noble, preeminent place; having entered the assembly, I roar the perfect lion’s roar."

"I turn the Brahma-wheel, which cannot be turned back by any ascetic, brahmin, deva, Māra, Brahmā, or anyone else in the world in accordance with the Dharma. Subhūti, this too is the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva mahāsattva, and that is through the yoga of non-apprehension.

Furthermore, Subhūti, the Mahāyāna of a bodhisattva mahāsattva is as follows: namely, the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*). What are the four? They are the analytical knowledge of meaning (*arthapratisaṃvid*), the analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dharmapratisaṃvid*), the analytical knowledge of language (*niruktipratisaṃvid*), and the analytical knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhānapratisaṃvid*). This too, Subhūti, is the Mahāyāna of a bodhisattva mahāsattva, and that is by way of non-apprehension (*anupalambha-yogena*). Furthermore, Subhūti, the Mahāyāna of a bodhisattva mahāsattva is as follows: namely, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇikabuddhadharma*).

Which are the eighteen? From the night the Tathāgata fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment until the night he attained final nirvāṇa in the realm of nirvāṇa without remainder—having taught the path leading to the destruction of suffering to the world with its gods, Māras, and Brahmās, and to this generation with its śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, gods, humans, and asuras—in the interval between these two nights, there was no stumbling on the part of the Tathāgata, no misconduct, and no loss of mindfulness.

There is no perception of diversity; there is no unconcentrated mind; there is no equanimity lacking discernment; there is no loss of zeal, no loss of energy, no loss of mindfulness, no loss of concentration, no loss of wisdom, no loss of liberation, and no loss of the knowledge and vision of liberation. All bodily action is preceded by knowledge and follows after knowledge; all vocal action is preceded by knowledge and follows after knowledge.

All mental action is preceded by knowledge and follows after knowledge. Unimpeded and unattached knowledge and vision operate regarding the past; unimpeded and unattached knowledge and vision operate regarding the future; unimpeded and unattached knowledge and vision operate regarding the present. This too, Subhūti, is the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva mahāsattva, and that is by way of non-apprehension.

Furthermore, Subhūti, the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva mahāsattva consists of the gateways of dhāraṇī. What are these gateways of dhāraṇī? They are the equality of syllables, the equality of speech, the gateway of syllables, and the entrance into syllables. In that regard, what is the gateway of syllables and the entrance into syllables? The letter *a* is the gateway to all phenomena because they are unproduced from the very beginning. The letter *ra* is the gateway to all phenomena because they are free from dust (*rajas*).

The letter *ya* is the gateway to all phenomena (*dharmas*), because it indicates the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). The letter *ca* is the gateway to all phenomena, because neither passing away (*cyavana*) nor rebirth (*upapatti*) is perceived; indeed, all phenomena neither pass away nor are they reborn. The letter *na* is the gateway to all phenomena, because they are devoid of names (*nāma*).

By its very nature, the letter *na* is neither acquired nor lost. The letter *la* is the gateway to all phenomena (*dharmas*), because they have transcended the world and because the causes and conditions for the creeper of craving (*tṛṣṇā*) have been utterly eradicated. The letter *da* is the gateway to all phenomena, because they are defined by self-control and discipline. The letter *va* is the gateway to all phenomena, because they are free from bondage. The letter *u* is the gateway to all phenomena, because they have gone beyond both [extremes]. The letter *sa* is the gateway to all phenomena, because attachment is not perceived therein.

It is not attached and not bound. The letter *va* is the gateway to all phenomena (*dharmas*), because the remainder of what is to be expressed has been completely severed. The letter *ta* is the gateway to all phenomena, because suchness (*tathatā*) is immovable. The letter *ya* is the gateway to all phenomena, because there is non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) of them as far as they extend. The letter *sta* is the gateway to all phenomena, because a pillar (*stambha*) is unapprehendable. The letter *ka* is the gateway to all phenomena, because an agent (*kāraka*) is unapprehendable.

The syllable *sa* is the gateway to all phenomena because of the non-apprehension of their sameness; it does not deviate from the universal. The syllable *ma* is the gateway to all phenomena by virtue of the non-apprehension of the syllable *ma*. The syllable *ga* is the gateway to all phenomena because of the non-apprehension of going. The syllable *ma* is the gateway to all phenomena because of the non-apprehension of staying. The syllable *ja* is the gateway to all phenomena because of the non-apprehension of birth.

The letter Śva is the gateway to all phenomena because breath is unapprehendable. The letter Dha is the gateway to all phenomena because the dharma-realm is unapprehendable. The letter Śa is the gateway to all phenomena because calm abiding is unapprehendable. The letter Kha is the gateway to all phenomena because the equality of space is unapprehendable. The letter Kṣa is the gateway to all phenomena because destruction is unapprehendable. The letter Sta is the gateway to all phenomena because praise is unapprehendable.

The letter *ja* is the gateway to all phenomena because of the non-apprehensibility of knowledge (*jñāna*). The letter *ta* is the gateway to all phenomena because of the non-apprehensibility of measure (*māsa*). The letter *ha* is the gateway to all phenomena because of the non-apprehensibility of cause (*hetu*). The letter *bha* is the gateway to all phenomena because of the non-apprehensibility of destruction (*bhaṅga*). The letter *cha* is the gateway to all phenomena because of the non-apprehensibility of cutting (*chedana*). The letter *sma* is the gateway to all phenomena because of the non-apprehensibility of recollection (*smaraṇa*).

The syllable *hva* is the gateway to all phenomena, because invocation is unapprehendable. The syllable *a* is the gateway to all phenomena, because enthusiasm is unapprehendable. The syllable *dha* is the gateway to all phenomena, because wealth is unapprehendable. The syllable *ṭha* is the gateway to all phenomena, because the act of piercing is unapprehendable. The syllable *ṇa* is the gateway to all phenomena, because they are free from conflict.

No one goes, no one comes, no one stands, no one sits, and no one prepares for rest; there is neither conceptualization nor discursive thought. The letter *la* is the gateway to all phenomena because of the non-apprehension of results. The letter *ska* is the gateway to all phenomena because of the non-apprehension of the aggregates (*skandhas*). The letter *psa* is the gateway to all phenomena because of the non-apprehension of the letter *psa*. The letter *śca* is the gateway to all phenomena because of the non-apprehension of conduct (*caryā*).

The letter *ḍha* is the gateway to all phenomena because the letter *ḍha* is non-apprehensible. The letter *ha* is the gateway to all phenomena because the letter *ha* is non-apprehensible. This is the ultimate limit; by means of this, one neither passes away nor is one reborn. Beyond this, there is no further linguistic usage of syllables. Why is that? Because for anything whatsoever, no other name is conventionally employed by which it could be expressed, by which it could be censured, written down, seen, or spoken.

Subhūti, just as space itself, so should all phenomena be understood. This is called the entrance into the gateway of dhāraṇī; it is the entrance into the teaching of the syllables beginning with *a*. Subhūti, any bodhisattva mahāsattva who understands this skill in the syllables beginning with *a* will not be diminished by any sound; he will perfectly accomplish the equality of all phenomena and will attain skill in the knowledge of sounds.

Subhūti, whatever bodhisattva mahāsattva hears this seal of entry into the letters beginning with *a*, and having heard it, takes it up, retains it, recites it, masters it, and teaches it to others—not with a merely conventional understanding—twenty benefits are to be expected for him. What are the twenty? Namely, he will be possessed of mindfulness.

He will be wise, intelligent, steadfast, modest, possessed of insight, and endowed with eloquence; and he will attain this gateway of dhāraṇī with little difficulty. He will not become a talkative chatterer; his mind will not be dull. Having heard harsh words from another, he will not be drawn along by them; having heard rough speech, he will not be repelled by it. He will neither be haughty nor dejected; he will remain exactly as he is.

He will be skilled in sounds; he will be skilled in the aggregates (*skandha*); he will be skilled in the elements (*dhātu*); he will be skilled in the sense bases (*āyatana*). He will be skilled in the truths, skilled in dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), skilled in causes, and skilled in conditions. He will be skilled in the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), skilled in the knowledge of the superior and inferior faculties of beings, skilled in death and rebirth, skilled in the knowledge of the divine ear, skilled in the knowledge of others' minds, and skilled in the knowledge of recollecting former abodes (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti*).

He will become skilled in the knowledge of the methods of supernatural power (*ṛddhi*), skilled in the knowledge of the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣaya*), skilled in the exposition of what is possible and impossible (*sthānāsthāna*), skilled in advancing, skilled in retreating, and skilled in the modes of deportment (*īryāpatha*). He will also attain skill in the protection of those who have reached the state of exhaustion. Subhūti, this too is a gateway to the dhāraṇī for a bodhisattva mahāsattva, the entrance into the letters beginning with 'A', which is the Great Vehicle; and that is by way of non-apprehension (*anupalambha*).
The Ninth Chapter in the *Śatasāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā*.
Now begins the Tenth Chapter.

Furthermore, as Subhūti has asked: "How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva become one who has set out in the Great Vehicle? Here, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing in the six perfections, passes from stage to stage. And how, Subhūti, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing in the six perfections, pass from stage to stage?

That is to say, because of the non-transmigration of all phenomena, no phenomenon whatsoever comes or goes, transmigrates or does not transmigrate. Furthermore, he does not conceive of, does not reflect upon, does not perform the preparation for, and does not even perceive that ground which belongs to all phenomena. In this regard, what is the preparation for the grounds of a bodhisattva mahāsattva?

Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwelling on the first stage must perform ten preparations. What are the ten? They are: the preparation of the basis of benefit by means of the yoga of non-apprehension, beginning with the resolute intention; the preparation of equanimity of mind toward all beings by means of the non-apprehension of beings; and the preparation of relinquishment by means of the non-apprehension of gift, giver, and recipient.

The preparation consisting in attending upon spiritual friends is based on the non-apprehension of [any] disagreeableness; the preparation consisting in the search for the Dharma is based on the non-apprehension of all phenomena (*dharma*); the preparation consisting in frequent renunciation is based on the non-apprehension of the home; the preparation consisting in longing for the Buddha-body is based on the non-apprehension of the marks and secondary characteristics (*lakṣaṇānuvyañjana*); the preparation consisting in the exposition of the Dharma is based on the non-apprehension of distinctions;
and the preparation consisting in the eradication of pride and arrogance is based on the non-apprehension of anything marvelous.

Subhūti, based on these ten preparations—beginning with the preparation of truthful speech by way of the non-apprehensibility of speech—a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwelling in the first stage must perform these ten preparations.

Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwelling on the second stage must constantly bring eight qualities to mind and practice them accordingly. What are these eight? Namely: purity of ethical discipline; gratitude and thankfulness; being established in the power of patience; joy; experiencing gladness; non-abandonment of all sentient beings; the manifestation of great compassion; service to the gurus; and faith and reverence.
Subhūti, these eight qualities must be constantly brought to mind and practiced by a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwelling in the second stage: diligent pursuit of the perfections.

Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwelling on the third stage should abide in five qualities. What are these five? Namely: insatiability in great learning; therein, the investigation of the dharma free from attachment by not clinging to syllables; likewise, through non-conceptualization, the dedication of roots of merit for the purification of the buddha-field; and likewise, through non-conceptualization, tirelessness in the immeasurable cycle of saṃsāra.

And likewise, by way of non-differentiation, he should abide in the state of possessing a sense of shame and dread of blame; and likewise, by way of non-differentiation, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwelling on the third bhūmi should abide in these five qualities.

Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwelling on the fourth bhūmi should proceed by undertaking ten qualities, and he should also relinquish them. What are the ten? Dwelling in the forest; contentment with few desires; and the persistence in the ascetic practices (*dhuta-guṇa*) and refinement.

Not abandoning the training; loathing the qualities of sensual desire; generating a mind accompanied by [the thought of] nirvāṇa; not abandoning any sentient being; having a mind that is not dejected; and having no regard for any material thing—Subhūti, these ten dharmas should not be abandoned by a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwelling on the fourth bhūmi; rather, they should be undertaken and practiced.

Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva abiding on the fifth stage must avoid six things. What are these six? Namely: association with householders must be avoided; association with bhikṣuṇīs; stinginess regarding families; socializing in crowds; self-exaltation and disparaging others. These six things must be avoided. Furthermore, eighteen things must be avoided.

Namely, the ten unwholesome paths of action must be avoided; pride and arrogance, perversions, doubt, and the habitual tendencies of passion, hatred, and delusion—these eighteen factors must be avoided by a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwelling on the fifth stage.

Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwelling on the sixth stage must fulfill six qualities, namely the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*). There are another six qualities that must be avoided: which six? The mind of a śrāvaka must be avoided; the mind of a pratyekabuddha must be avoided; the mind of thirsting desire must be avoided; and upon seeing a beggar, one must avoid being discouraged or disheartened.

One should not be despondent; having relinquished all things, one must avoid dejection. One should not become dejected. Upon seeing a beggar, one must avoid a distracted mind; one must not cause distraction for the sake of the beggar. Subhūti, these six qualities are to be avoided by a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwelling on the sixth stage.

Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwelling on the seventh stage should not engage in twenty things. What are these twenty? Namely: one should not grasp at a self; one should not grasp at a being; one should not grasp at a soul; one should not grasp at a person; one should not grasp at annihilation; one should not grasp at permanence; and one should not form perceptions of signs.

The view of causality; attachment to the aggregates (*skandha*); attachment to the elements (*dhātu*); attachment to the sense bases (*āyatana*); attachment to the three realms (*traidhātuka*); clinging to the three realms; dwelling in the three realms; attachment to the view of relying on the Buddha; attachment to the view of relying on the Dharma; attachment to the view of relying on the Saṅgha; attachment to the view of relying on ethical discipline (*śīla*); despondency that "all phenomena are empty"; and [despondency] regarding emptiness and cessation (*nirodha*).

Subhūti, these twenty dharmas are not to be practiced; rather, those same twenty dharmas are to be fulfilled. What are the twenty? Namely: the non-rejection of emptiness; the realization of the signless; the knowledge of the wishless; the purity of the three spheres; compassion and pity toward all sentient beings; not despising those sentient beings; the vision of the equality of all dharmas; non-attachment even to that [vision]; and the penetration of the true principle.

And by that, there is non-conceptuality; the patient acceptance of non-arising (*anutpādakṣānti*); the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*); the teaching of the single principle; the eradication of conceptualization regarding all phenomena; the turning away from perceptions (*saṃjñā*); the turning away from views (*dṛṣṭi*); the turning away from afflictions (*kleśa*); the state of observing tranquility; the state of a tamed mind; unimpeded knowledge; non-deficiency; knowledge of the appropriate occasion; and going to whichever buddha-field one desires.
Subhūti, these twenty qualities are to be perfected by a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwelling on the seventh stage.
Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwelling on the eighth stage must fulfill four dharmas. What are the four? Namely:

Penetration into the minds of all sentient beings; sporting with the superknowledges (*abhijñā*); beholding the Buddha-fields; the perfect accomplishment of those Buddha-fields exactly as they have been seen; attending upon the Buddhas; and the correct contemplation of the body of a Buddha according to reality—Subhūti, these four qualities are to be fulfilled. Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwelling on the eighth stage must fulfill four further qualities.

Namely: knowledge of the superior and inferior faculties; the purification of the Buddha-field; frequent entry into the illusion-like samādhi; the production of a physical form in accordance with how the roots of virtue of sentient beings reach fulfillment; and the intentional assumption of existence. Subhūti, these four dharmas are to be perfected by a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwelling on the eighth stage.

Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwelling on the ninth stage must fulfill twelve qualities. What are these twelve? They are as follows: the undertaking of infinite vows; such that in whatever way he makes a vow, it is fulfilled for him accordingly; knowledge of the cries of gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas, and humans; knowledge of the exposition of the fulfillment of vows; and perfection in the descent into the womb.

Perfection of lineage; perfection of retinue; perfection of birth; perfection of the array of the Bodhi tree; and perfection of the fulfillment of all qualities. Subhūti, these twelve dharmas are to be fulfilled by a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwelling on the ninth stage.

"Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva abides on the tenth stage, he should be called a Tathāgata indeed. When this had been said, the venerable Subhūti addressed the Blessed One: "Blessed One, what is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s cultivation of the higher resolve and so forth? The Blessed One replied: "Subhūti, it is that which belongs to a bodhisattva mahāsattva who, through [dharmas] associated with the knowledge of all aspects..."

Through the production of thoughts of awakening, he accumulates roots of virtue. Subhūti, this is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s preparation of the resolute intention and so forth. In that regard, what is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s preparation of equanimity toward all sentient beings? It is that, through the production of thoughts associated with the knowledge of all aspects, he brings forth the noble immeasurables.

Loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity—this is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s cultivation of a mind of equality toward all sentient beings. In that regard, what is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s cultivation of relinquishment? That which gives a gift to all sentient beings without conceptual discrimination—this is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s cultivation of relinquishment. In that regard, what is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s cultivation of attending upon spiritual friends?

That is to say, those who are the spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) of the bodhisattva mahāsattva, who indeed cause him to undertake, lead him into, and establish him in omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*). The service, devotion, attendance, and obedience toward those spiritual friends—this is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s preparation consisting in the service of spiritual friends. In that regard, what is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s preparation consisting in the search for the Dharma?

That he seeks the Dharma with thoughts associated with the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), so that he does not fall to the level of a Śrāvaka or Pratyekabuddha—this is the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva’s preparation for the quest for the Dharma. In that regard, what is the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva’s constant preparation for renunciation? It is when he goes forth unconfused among the entire class of sentient beings and enters the religious life within the teaching of the Tathāgata.

And no one can create any obstacle for him; this is the constant preparation for renunciation (*naiṣkramya*) of the bodhisattva mahāsattva. In that regard, what is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s preparation consisting of longing for the Buddha-body? It is when, having seen the form of a Buddha, he is never again separated from the mental attention (*manasikāra*) directed toward the Buddha until he attains all-aspect omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*); this is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s preparation consisting of longing for the Buddha-body.

In this regard, what is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s preparation for the exposition of the Dharma? It is when a bodhisattva mahāsattva teaches the Dharma to sentient beings—whether the Tathāgata has appeared in person or has entered final nirvāṇa—proclaiming the holy life that is virtuous in the beginning, virtuous in the middle, and virtuous in the end; excellent in meaning and excellent in phrasing; solitary, complete, pure, and pristine.

Namely: the discourses (*sūtra*), songs (*geya*), prophecies (*vyākaraṇa*), verses (*gāthā*), inspired utterances (*udāna*), introductory narratives (*nidāna*), parables (*ityuktaka*), birth stories (*jātaka*), extensive teachings (*vaipulya*), marvelous events (*adbhutadharma*), legends (*avadāna*), and instructions (*upadeśa*). This is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s preparation for the exposition of the Dharma. In that regard, what is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s preparation for the eradication of pride and arrogance? It is that through the eradication of pride and arrogance, one is never reborn in lowly families.

This is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s preparation for the eradication of pride and arrogance. In that regard, what is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s preparation of truthful speech? It is this: acting exactly as one speaks. Subhūti, this is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s preparation of truthful speech. Subhūti, these are the ten preparations of a bodhisattva mahāsattva abiding in the first stage.

In that regard, what is the purification of ethical discipline (*śīla*) for a bodhisattva mahāsattva? It is as follows: it is the non-attention (*amanasikāra*) toward the minds of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas; furthermore, it is the non-attention toward those other factors that constitute immorality (*dauḥśīlya*) and those factors that act as obstacles to awakening (*bodhi*). This is the purification of ethical discipline for a bodhisattva mahāsattva. In that regard, what is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s gratitude and the performance of what has been done?

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while practicing the conduct of a bodhisattva, does not forget even a single benefit received throughout the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*), how much more so this gratitude and sense of obligation shown by a bodhisattva mahāsattva! In that regard, what is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s establishment in the power of patience? It is the state of being free from malice and thoughts of harm toward all sentient beings; this is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s establishment in the power of patience.

In that regard, what is the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva’s experience of joy and gladness? It is, namely, the ripening of all sentient beings in the three vehicles; this is the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva’s experience of joy and gladness. In that regard, what is the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva’s non-abandonment of all sentient beings? It is, namely, the protection of all sentient beings; this is the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva’s non-abandonment of all sentient beings.

In that regard, what is the manifestation of great compassion for a bodhisattva mahāsattva? It is when a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while practicing the conduct of a bodhisattva, thinks: "For the sake of even a single sentient being, I would dwell in the hells for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the river Ganges, experiencing there cutting, splitting, boiling, sweating, and roasting, until all sentient beings have been established in the knowledge of a Buddha."

In this way, up to the point that one exerts effort and remains untiring for the sake of all sentient beings—this is called the manifestation of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) in a bodhisattva mahāsattva. In that regard, what is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s service to teachers and faith-based reverence? It is the perception of teachers as the Teacher (*śāstṛ*) in their presence; this is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s service to teachers and faith-based reverence.

In that regard, what is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s diligent pursuit of the perfections? It is this: the pursuit of the perfections with undivided action for the sake of maturing all sentient beings. This is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s diligent pursuit of the perfections. In that regard, what is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s insatiability regarding extensive learning?

Thinking, "I shall retain all that has been spoken by the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, here in this world-system and throughout the world-systems in the ten directions," there arises a lack of satiety; this is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s lack of satiety regarding extensive learning. In that regard, what is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s exposition of the gift of the Dharma free from worldly motives? It is when a bodhisattva...

The Mahāsattva teaches the Dharma, and by that gift of Dharma, he does not even expect awakening as a reward. This is the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva’s exposition of the non-material gift of Dharma. In that regard, what is the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva’s planting of roots of merit for the purification of the Buddha-field? It is the dedication of those roots of merit by which, while purifying the Buddha-field, he also purifies the mental fields of others. This is the dedication of those roots of merit.

This is the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva’s engagement in the dedication of roots of merit for the purification of a Buddha-field. In that regard, what is the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva’s lack of weariness throughout immeasurable saṃsāra? It is this: for the sake of supporting the roots of merit, being supported by those roots of merit, he brings sentient beings to maturity and purifies the Buddha-field, and never experiences weariness.

Until he fulfills all-aspect-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*), this is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s state of being untiring throughout immeasurable saṃsāra. In that regard, what is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s basis for shame and modesty? It is, namely, the loathing of the mindsets of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas; this is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s basis for shame and modesty. In that regard, what is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s non-abandonment of dwelling in the forest?

That which is the transcending of the levels of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas—this is the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva’s non-abandonment of dwelling in the forest. In that regard, what is the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva’s fewness of desires? It is when the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva does not desire even awakening; this is the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva’s fewness of desires. In that regard, what is the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva’s contentment?

That which is not obtained even through the attainment of the knowledge of all aspects—this is the contentment of the bodhisattva mahāsattva. What is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s practice of the ascetic qualities and their reduction? It is this: the patient acceptance of emergence regarding profound dharmas; this is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s [practice].

It is the practice of the ascetic qualities (*dhutaguṇa*) and the reduction of worldly attachments (*saṃlekha*). In that regard, what is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s non-abandonment of training? It is that wherein there is no activity of any trainings whatsoever; this is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s [non-abandonment] of training.

Non-abandonment. In that regard, what is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s revulsion toward the qualities of sensual desire? It is the non-arising of a mind set on sensual desire; this is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s revulsion toward the qualities of sensual desire. In that regard, what is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s production of the thought of awakening accompanied by cessation? It is the non-conditioning of all phenomena (*sarvadharmāṇām anabhisaṃskāra*); this, Subhūti, is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s production of the thought of awakening accompanied by cessation.

In that regard, what is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s relinquishment of all possessions? It is the non-appropriation of internal and external phenomena; this is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s relinquishment of all possessions. In that regard, what is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s lack of mental depression? It is that his mind does not dwell in the stations of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*), and his mind does not become depressed within those stations of consciousness.

This is the non-depressed state of mind of a bodhisattva mahāsattva. In that regard, what is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s lack of regard for all things? It is the non-attention toward all things; this is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s lack of regard for all things. In that regard, what is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s avoidance of intimacy with household life? It is, namely, the transition from buddha-field to buddha-field and birth by spontaneous apparition (*upapāduka*).

Appearing as a small fish and being protected by the wind—this is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s avoidance of intimacy with householders. In that regard, what is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s avoidance of intimacy with bhikṣuṇīs? It is when he does not stand together with a bhikṣuṇī even for the duration of a finger-snap; nor, on account of that, does he give rise to a mind of longing, nor does he obtain robes on account of that. This is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s avoidance of intimacy with bhikṣuṇīs. In that regard, what is...

The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva must avoid stinginess regarding families. Here, Subhūti, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva should give rise to this thought: "I must provide a basis for happiness for all sentient beings. Since these sentient beings will become happy through their own merits alone, I should not give rise to a stingy mind in this regard. In this way, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva should avoid stinginess regarding families.

In that regard, how should a bodhisattva mahāsattva avoid places of social distraction? Wherever there might be śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas for a bodhisattva mahāsattva staying in a place of social distraction, or where there might be discourses associated with them, or where thoughts associated with them might arise—therein a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not remain.

This is the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva’s avoidance of dwelling in social circles. In that regard, what is the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva’s avoidance of self-exaltation? In that regard, how should the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva avoid malice? By not giving any opportunity for thoughts of malice or doubt to arise.

To give no opportunity to a mind of quarrel or a mind of conflict—this is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s avoidance of malice (*vyāpāda*). That which is the non-perception of internal phenomena (*dharma*)—this is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s avoidance of self-exaltation (*utkarṣaṇa*). In that regard, what is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s avoidance of disparaging others? It is, namely, the non-perception of external phenomena.

Thus is the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva’s avoidance of disparaging others. In that regard, how should a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva avoid the ten unwholesome paths of action? For these act as obstacles even to a happy rebirth, let alone to the Noble Path, and let alone to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment. In this way, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva should avoid the ten unwholesome paths of action.
In that regard, how should a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva [avoid] overweening pride?

It should be avoided. Since he perceives [all things] as equal, how much less could there be anything superior by which he might become conceited? In this way, overweening pride (*adhimāna*) should be avoided. In that regard, how should a bodhisattva mahāsattva avoid arrogance (*stambha*)? For he does not perceive any object whatsoever upon which arrogance might arise. In this manner, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should avoid arrogance.

In that regard, how should a bodhisattva mahāsattva avoid the perversions? By means of the non-apprehension of any objective entity (*vastu*); thus should a bodhisattva mahāsattva avoid the perversions. In that regard, how should a bodhisattva mahāsattva not tolerate passion, hatred, and delusion? Because he does not perceive an objective entity for those who possess passion, hatred, and delusion;
thus should a bodhisattva mahāsattva not tolerate passion, hatred, and delusion.

In that regard, which six dharmas are to be fulfilled on the sixth bhūmi? Namely, the six pāramitās: the perfection of generosity, the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditative concentration, and the perfection of wisdom—these are to be fulfilled. For it is by abiding in these six pāramitās that the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, as well as the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, have gone, and will go, to the further shore of the fivefold ocean of the knowable.

Of which fivefold [nature]? Namely: the past, the future, the present, the ineffable, and the unconditioned. In this way, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should fulfill six qualities. In that regard, how should a bodhisattva mahāsattva avoid the mind of a śrāvaka? For this is not the path to awakening. The mind of a pratyekabuddha should be avoided; for this too is not the path to awakening.

One should not give rise to a mind of thirsting desire; for this is not the path to awakening. Upon seeing a beggar, one should not give rise to a shrinking or discouraged mind; for what reason? Because this is not the path.

For the sake of awakening, all things must be relinquished; one should not become dejected. Why is that? Because this is not the path to awakening. From the first production of the thought of awakening (prathamacittotpāda) onward, one should constantly practice giving and should not have a mind of attachment. In that regard, how should a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva avoid grasping at a self? For in the ultimate sense, a self does not exist. One should also not grasp at a living being (jīva).

For in this way, a living being (*jīva*) does not exist at all; thus, one should not grasp at a person (*pudgala*), for in this way, a person does not exist at all. In that regard, how is it that a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not grasp at annihilation? For no dharma whatsoever is annihilated, because all dharmas are ultimately unapprehendable. In that regard, how is it that a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not grasp at permanence?

For what reason? Because phenomena do not arise; they are neither eternal nor subject to annihilation. In that regard, how should a bodhisattva mahāsattva not form a perception of signs? For in that way, defilement does not exist at all. In that regard, how should a bodhisattva mahāsattva not form a view of causality? For in that way, he does not perceive such a view.

In that regard, how should a bodhisattva mahāsattva not form an attachment to name-and-form? For he does not perceive that entity as real. In that regard, how should a bodhisattva mahāsattva not form an attachment to the aggregates? For the aggregates do not exist at all; thus, one should not form an attachment to the aggregates. In that regard, how should a bodhisattva mahāsattva not form an attachment to the elements?

For in this way, the elements (*dhātu*) do not exist at all; thus, one should not form an attachment to the elements. In that regard, how should a bodhisattva mahāsattva not form an attachment to the sense-bases (*āyatana*)? For in this way, the sense-bases do not exist at all; thus, one should not form an attachment to the sense-bases. In that regard, how should a bodhisattva mahāsattva...

One should not form an attachment to the three realms, for they do not exist by way of their own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Thus, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not form an attachment to the three realms. In that regard, how should a bodhisattva mahāsattva avoid forming a fixation on the three realms? Because that object does not exist and is not apprehended; thus, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not form a fixation on the three realms.

In that regard, how should a bodhisattva mahāsattva not make an abode in the three realms? Because for him that entity does not exist at all, in this way he should not make an abode in the three realms. In that regard, how should a bodhisattva mahāsattva not make a reliance on the three realms? Because for him that entity does not exist; in this way a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not make a reliance on the three realms.

In this regard, how should a bodhisattva mahāsattva avoid forming an attachment to the view of relying on a Buddha? For it is not by relying on the view of a Buddha that there is the vision of a Buddha. Thus, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not form an attachment to the view of relying on a Buddha. In this regard, how should a bodhisattva mahāsattva avoid forming an attachment to the view of relying on the Dharma? For it is not by relying on the view of the Dharma that there is the vision of the Dharma.

In this way, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not form an attachment to the view of reliance on the Dharma. In that regard, how should a bodhisattva mahāsattva avoid forming an attachment to the view of reliance on the Saṅgha? For it is not through reliance on the view of the Saṅgha that there is the vision of the Saṅgha. Thus, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not form an attachment to the view of reliance on the Saṅgha.

In that regard, how should a bodhisattva mahāsattva avoid forming an attachment to the view of relying on ethical discipline? For purity of ethical discipline does not arise from reliance on a view of ethical discipline; thus, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not form an attachment to the view of relying on ethical discipline. In that regard, how should a bodhisattva mahāsattva avoid despondency regarding the fact that all phenomena are empty? For all phenomena...

They are empty by way of their own-characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), not by way of emptiness itself. Thus, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not feel despondency regarding emptiness. In that regard, how should a bodhisattva mahāsattva not oppose it? For all phenomena are empty, and emptiness does not oppose the emptiness of emptiness. Thus, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not oppose emptiness. In that regard, how should a bodhisattva mahāsattva fulfill emptiness?

The fulfillment of the emptiness of specific characteristics is the fulfillment of emptiness for the bodhisattva mahāsattva. In that regard, what is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s realization of the signless? It is the non-attention toward all signs. In that regard, what is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s knowledge of the wishless? It is that his mind does not operate within the three realms. In that regard, what is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s purity of the three spheres?

Namely, the fulfillment of the ten paths of wholesome action. In that regard, what is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s fulfillment of pity and compassion toward sentient beings? Namely, the attainment of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*). In that regard, how should a bodhisattva mahāsattva not perceive sentient beings? Namely, through the fulfillment of loving-kindness (*maitrī*). In that regard, what is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s vision of the equality of all phenomena? Namely, non-accumulation and non-destruction.

Of all phenomena. In that regard, what is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s penetration of the true method? It is the penetration of the single method of all phenomena, which is non-penetration. In that regard, what is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s patience regarding non-arising? It is the patience regarding the non-arising, non-cessation, and non-conditioning of all phenomena. In that regard, what is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s knowledge of non-arising?

That which is the knowledge of the non-arising of name-and-form—this is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s knowledge of non-arising. In that regard, what is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s teaching on the single principle? It is the state of non-occurrence; this is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s teaching on the single principle.

In that regard, what is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s eradication of unwholesomeness? It is the non-conceptualization of all phenomena. In that regard, what is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s turning away from views? It is the turning away from views regarding the level of the śrāvaka and the level of the pratyekabuddha. In that regard, what is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s turning away from afflictions? It is the exhaustion of all afflictions along with their latencies and continuities.

In that regard, what is the stage of calm abiding and insight (*śamatha-vipaśyanā*) of the bodhisattva mahāsattva? It is namely the knowledge of the omniscience of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā-jñāna*). In that regard, what is the state of a tamed mind for the bodhisattva mahāsattva? It is that which does not become overpowered by the three realms (*traidhātuka*). In that regard, what is the state of a peaceful mind for the bodhisattva mahāsattva? It is the withdrawal of the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya*). In that regard, what is the unimpeded knowledge of the bodhisattva mahāsattva?

Namely, the attainment of the Buddha-eye. In that regard, what is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s reliance on the six sense bases through non-deficient omniscience? In that regard, what is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s going to whichever field he desires, and manifesting his own form in various circles of assemblies? In that regard, what is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s penetration into the minds of all sentient beings?

That by which, with a single mind, one comprehends the minds and mental factors of all sentient beings: therein, what is the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva’s sporting with the superknowledges (*abhijñāvikrīḍatā*)? It is that, sporting with those superknowledges, he travels from Buddha-field to Buddha-field in order to behold the Buddhas, yet he does not form the notion of a "Buddha" [regarding them]. Therein, what is the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva’s beholding of the Buddha-fields?

That while remaining in a single buddha-field, one sees immeasurable buddha-fields, yet no perception of a "buddha-field" arises for them—this is what constitutes the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s accomplishment of a buddha-field exactly as it is seen. It is that which consists in the relinquishing of the trichiliocosm great trichiliocosm world-system by one who stands upon the level of a wheel-turning monarch, the sovereign of the trichiliocosm great trichiliocosm world-system.

And [the state of] being seated. In that regard, what is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s attendance upon the Buddhas? It is the attendance upon the Dharma for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings. In that regard, what is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s contemplation of the Buddha-body as it truly is? It is the contemplation of the Dharma-body as it truly is. In that regard, what is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s knowledge of the superior and inferior faculties [of beings]?

That which consists in the thorough knowledge of the fulfillment of the faculties of all sentient beings while abiding in the ten wholesome paths of action—therein, what is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s purification of the buddha-field? It is the purification of the minds of sentient beings by means of the yoga of non-apprehension. Therein, what is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s illusion-like samādhi? It is that samādhi in which, having established himself, the bodhisattva mahāsattva performs all activities.

And his mind does not engage with any phenomenon whatsoever. In that regard, what is the constant meditative attainment of the bodhisattva mahāsattva? It is the maturation-born samādhi of the bodhisattva mahāsattva. In that regard, how does the bodhisattva mahāsattva bring about the perfection of his physical existence in such a way that the roots of virtue of his perceptions reach perfection? In whatever manner the roots of virtue of his perceptions are perfected, in that very manner he brings his physical existence to perfection.

In this regard, a bodhisattva mahāsattva intentionally assumes a physical form (ātmabhāva) in accordance with the ripening of sentient beings. In that context, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva intentionally take up a physical form? Namely, for the sake of the ripening of all sentient beings. In that context, how is it that a bodhisattva mahāsattva’s aspirations are fulfilled exactly as they have been made? Because the bodhisattva mahāsattva has brought the six perfections (pāramitā) to completion, whatever he aspires to is fulfilled accordingly.

In that regard, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva penetrate the knowledge of the gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas, and humans? Namely, by means of the analytical knowledge of etymological interpretation (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*). In that regard, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva penetrate the knowledge of teaching with perfected eloquence (*pratibhāna*)?

Namely, through the analytical knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhāna-saṃvid*). In that regard, what is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s perfection of descent into the womb (*garbhāvakrānti-saṃpat*)? Here, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva is born by spontaneous apparition (*upapāduka*) in all his births; this is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s perfection of descent into the womb. In that regard, what is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s perfection of family (*kula-saṃpat*)? It is when a bodhisattva mahāsattva is reborn into great families.

This is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s perfection of family. In that regard, what is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s perfection of birth? It is when a bodhisattva mahāsattva is born into great kṣatriya families or great brahmin families; this is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s perfection of birth. In that regard, what is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s perfection of lineage?

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva is born into that lineage from which previous bodhisattvas have arisen—that is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s perfection of lineage. In that regard, what is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s perfection of retinue? When a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having established sentient beings in awakening, becomes a retinue for bodhisattvas themselves—that is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s perfection of retinue.

In this regard, what is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s perfection of birth? It is when a bodhisattva mahāsattva, immediately upon being born, pervades incalculable world-systems with his radiance and causes them to tremble in six ways; this is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s perfection of birth. In this regard, what is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s perfection of renunciation? It is when a bodhisattva mahāsattva goes forth for the sake of the religious life.

Together with many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of beings, those beings become fixed in the three vehicles; this is the perfection of the Great Bodhisattva’s Great Departure. In that regard, what is the perfection of the Great Bodhisattva’s array of the Bodhi tree? It is when the Great Bodhisattva...

The root of the Bodhi tree is made of gold; its trunk is made of lapis lazuli; its branches are made of the seven precious gems; and its leaves and flowers are composed of every kind of jewel. The fragrant scent and the radiance of this tree pervade infinite world-systems. This is the perfection of the array of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva’s Bodhi tree. In that regard, what is the perfection of the complete fulfillment of all qualities of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva?

That which is the purification of the maturation of sentient beings and the purification of the buddha-field for a bodhisattva mahāsattva—this is the perfection of the fulfillment of all qualities of a bodhisattva mahāsattva. In that regard, how is it that a bodhisattva mahāsattva established in the tenth stage is to be called a Tathāgata? It is because for that bodhisattva mahāsattva, all the perfections (*pāramitā*) have become fully complete.

The ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, the knowledge of all aspects, the abandonment of all afflictions along with their habitual tendencies, great compassion, and all the qualities of a Buddha become fully perfected. In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva established in the tenth stage should indeed be called a Tathāgata.

In that regard, Subhūti, what are the ten stages of a bodhisattva mahāsattva? Here, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, through skill in means, practices the perfection of generosity, practices the perfection of ethical discipline, practices the perfection of patience, practices the perfection of vigor, practices the perfection of meditative concentration, and practices the perfection of wisdom.

Practicing in internal emptiness, practicing in external emptiness, practicing in internal-and-external emptiness, practicing in the emptiness of emptiness, practicing in great emptiness, practicing in the emptiness of the ultimate, practicing in the emptiness of the conditioned, practicing in the emptiness of the unconditioned, practicing in absolute emptiness, practicing in the emptiness of that which has no beginning or end, practicing in the emptiness of non-dispersal, and practicing in the emptiness of intrinsic nature.

Practicing in the emptiness of all phenomena, practicing in the emptiness of specific characteristics, practicing in the emptiness of non-apprehension, practicing in the emptiness of non-existence, practicing in the emptiness of intrinsic nature, practicing in the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence; practicing in the applications of mindfulness, practicing in the right efforts, practicing in the bases of psychic power, practicing in the faculties, practicing in the powers, practicing in the factors of enlightenment, practicing in the noble eightfold path, practicing in the noble truths, practicing in the meditative concentrations, [and] practicing in the immeasurables.

Practicing in the formless attainments, practicing in the liberations, practicing in the successive meditative dwellings, practicing in the liberations of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, practicing in the superknowledges, practicing in the gateways of dhāraṇī, practicing in the samādhis, practicing in the powers of a Tathāgata, practicing in the four grounds of self-confidence, practicing in the four analytical knowledges, practicing in great loving-kindness, practicing in great compassion, and practicing in the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.

He transcends the stage of pure insight (*śuklavipaśyanā-bhūmi*); he transcends the stage of the spiritual lineage (*gotra-bhūmi*); he transcends the stage of the eighth person (*aṣṭamaka-bhūmi*); he transcends the stage of vision (*darśana-bhūmi*); he transcends the stage of refinement (*tanu-bhūmi*); he transcends the stage of freedom from passion (*vītarāga-bhūmi*); he transcends the stage of one who has completed what was to be done (*kṛtāvi-bhūmi*); he transcends the stage of the solitary buddha (*pratyekabuddha-bhūmi*); he transcends the stage of the bodhisattva (*bodhisattva-bhūmi*). In this way, Subhūti, the bodhisattva mahāsattva transcends nine stages.

He abides on the stage of a Buddha. Subhūti, herein are the ten stages of a bodhisattva mahāsattva. In this way, Subhūti, it should be understood that a bodhisattva mahāsattva has set out in the Mahāyāna.

Furthermore, as for what Subhūti said: "From where will that vehicle depart? It will depart from the triple world (traidhātuka). It will abide in that which is omniscience (sarvākārajñatā). Moreover, that is by way of non-duality. Why is that? Because, Subhūti, both the Great Vehicle (mahāyāna) and omniscience—these two phenomena (dharma)—are neither dissociated nor conjoined; they are formless (arūpin).

They are invisible and characterized by non-obstruction. Why is that? Subhūti, it is because dharmas without characteristics do not emerge from the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu), nor will they emerge, nor have they emerged. Subhūti, he who would desire the emergence of dharmas without characteristics would desire the emergence of suchness (tathatā). Subhūti, he who would desire the emergence of non-falsity (avitathatā) would desire the emergence of suchness.

Subhūti, he who would desire the departure from phenomena that are without marks would desire the departure from the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*). Subhūti, he who would desire the departure from phenomena that are without marks would desire the departure from the inconceivable realm (*acintyadhātu*). Subhūti, he who would desire the departure from phenomena that are without marks would desire the departure from the realm of space (*ākāśadhātu*). Subhūti, he who would desire the departure from phenomena that are without marks would desire the departure from the realm of the exhaustion of passion (*rāgakṣayadhātu*).

Subhūti, whoever would seek the departure from phenomena that are without marks, he would seek the departure from the element of abandonment. Subhūti, whoever would seek the departure from phenomena that are without marks, he would seek the departure from the element of dispassion. Subhūti, whoever would seek the departure from phenomena that are without marks, he would seek the departure from the element of cessation. Subhūti, whoever would seek the departure from phenomena that are without marks, he would seek the departure from the emptiness of form.

Subhūti, he who would desire the departure from the emptiness of feeling would desire the departure from phenomena that are without marks. Subhūti, he who would desire the departure from the emptiness of perception would desire the departure from phenomena that are without marks. Subhūti, he who would desire the departure from the emptiness of volitional formations would desire the departure from phenomena that are without marks.

Subhūti, whoever would desire the departure of signless phenomena would desire the departure of the emptiness of consciousness. Why is that? Subhūti, it is because the emptiness of form does not depart from the three realms, nor does it abide in omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*). The emptiness of feeling does not depart from the three realms, nor does it abide in omniscience. It is the emptiness of perception that departs from the three realms, nor does it [abide]...

One abides in omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*). The emptiness of formative forces (*saṃskāra-śūnyatā*) does not emerge from the triple world, nor does it abide in omniscience. The emptiness of consciousness (*vijñāna-śūnyatā*) does not emerge from the triple world, nor does it abide in omniscience. Why is that? Because, Subhūti, form is empty of form; feeling is empty of feeling; perception is empty of perception; formative forces are empty of formative forces; and consciousness is empty of consciousness.

Subhūti, whoever would desire the departure of phenomena that are without marks should desire the departure from the emptiness of the eye. Subhūti, whoever would desire the departure of phenomena that are without marks should desire the departure from the emptiness of the ear. Subhūti, whoever would desire the departure of phenomena that are without marks should desire the departure from the emptiness of the nose. Subhūti, whoever would desire the departure of phenomena that are without marks should desire the departure from the emptiness of the tongue.

Subhūti, whoever would desire the departure of signless phenomena would desire the departure of the emptiness of the body; Subhūti, whoever would desire the departure of signless phenomena would desire the departure of the emptiness of the mind. Why is that? Because, Subhūti, the emptiness of the eye does not depart from the three realms, nor does it abide in the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*); the emptiness of the ear does not depart from the three realms, nor does it abide in the knowledge of all aspects.

The emptiness of the vital breath does not emerge from the three realms, nor does it abide in the knowledge of all aspects. The emptiness of the tongue does not emerge from the three realms, nor does it abide in the knowledge of all aspects. The emptiness of the body does not emerge from the three realms, nor does it abide in the knowledge of all aspects. The emptiness of the mind does not emerge from the three realms, nor does it abide in the knowledge of all aspects. Why is that? Because, Subhūti, the eye is empty of the eye.
The ear is empty of the ear; the nose is empty of the nose; the tongue is empty of the tongue; the body is empty of the body; the mind is empty of the mind.

Subhūti, whoever would desire the departure from phenomena that are without marks, he would desire the departure from the emptiness of form. Subhūti, whoever would desire the departure from phenomena that are without marks, he would desire the departure from the emptiness of sound. Subhūti, whoever would desire the departure from phenomena that are without marks, he would desire the departure from the emptiness of odor. Subhūti, whoever would desire the departure from phenomena that are without marks, he would desire the departure from the emptiness of taste.

Subhūti, whoever would desire the departure from phenomena that are without marks would desire the departure from the emptiness of contact. Subhūti, whoever would desire the departure from phenomena that are without marks would desire the departure from the emptiness of phenomena. Why is that? Because, Subhūti, the emptiness of form does not depart from the triple world, nor does it abide in omniscience. The emptiness of sound does not depart from the triple world, nor does it abide in omniscience.

The emptiness of odor does not emerge from the triple world, nor does it abide in omniscience. The emptiness of taste does not emerge from the triple world, nor does it abide in omniscience. The emptiness of tangibility does not emerge from the triple world, nor does it abide in omniscience. The emptiness of phenomena does not emerge from the triple world, nor does it abide in omniscience.

For what reason? Because, Subhūti, form is empty of form; sound is empty of sound; smell is empty of smell; taste is empty of taste; touch is empty of touch; and mental phenomena are empty of mental phenomena.

Subhūti, he who would desire the departure of signless phenomena would desire the departure of the emptiness of eye-consciousness. Subhūti, he who would desire the departure of signless phenomena would desire the departure of the emptiness of ear-consciousness. Subhūti, he who would desire the departure of signless phenomena would desire the departure of the emptiness of nose-consciousness. Subhūti, he who would desire the departure of signless phenomena would desire the departure of the emptiness of tongue-consciousness.

Subhūti, whoever would desire the departure of phenomena that are without marks, he would desire the departure of the emptiness of body-consciousness; Subhūti, whoever would desire the departure of phenomena that are without marks, he would desire the departure of the emptiness of mind-consciousness. Why is that? Because, Subhūti, the emptiness of eye-consciousness does not depart from the three realms, nor does it abide in the knowledge of all aspects.

The emptiness of ear-consciousness does not emerge from the three realms, nor does it abide in omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*). The emptiness of nose-consciousness does not emerge from the three realms, nor does it abide in omniscience. The emptiness of tongue-consciousness does not emerge from the three realms, nor does it abide in omniscience. The emptiness of body-consciousness does not emerge from the three realms, nor does it abide in omniscience.

The emptiness of mental consciousness does not emerge from the three realms, nor does it abide in the knowledge of all aspects. Why is that? Because, Subhūti, visual consciousness is empty of visual consciousness; auditory consciousness is empty of auditory consciousness; olfactory consciousness is empty of olfactory consciousness; gustatory consciousness is empty of gustatory consciousness; and tactile consciousness is empty of tactile consciousness.

Subhūti, whoever would desire the departure of phenomena that are without marks would desire the departure of the emptiness of eye-contact. Subhūti, whoever would desire the departure of phenomena that are without marks would desire the departure of the emptiness of ear-contact. Subhūti, whoever would desire the departure of phenomena that are without marks would desire the departure of the emptiness of nose-contact.

Subhūti, he who would desire the departure of signless phenomena would desire the departure of the emptiness of tongue-contact. Subhūti, he who would desire the departure of signless phenomena would desire the departure of the emptiness of body-contact.

Subhūti, whoever would desire the departure of phenomena that are without marks should desire the departure of the emptiness of mental contact. Why is that? Because, Subhūti, the emptiness of visual contact does not depart from the three realms, nor does it abide in the knowledge of all aspects. The emptiness of auditory contact does not depart from the three realms, nor does it abide in the knowledge of all aspects. The emptiness of olfactory contact does not depart from the three realms.

It does not abide in omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*). The emptiness of tongue-contact (*jihvā-saṃsparśa-śūnyatā*) does not emerge from the triple world; it does not abide in omniscience. The emptiness of body-contact (*kāya-saṃsparśa-śūnyatā*) does not emerge from the triple world; it does not abide in omniscience. The emptiness of mind-contact (*manaḥ-saṃsparśa-śūnyatā*) does not emerge from the triple world; it does not abide in omniscience.

For what reason? It is because, Subhūti, eye-contact is empty of eye-contact; ear-contact is empty of ear-contact; nose-contact is empty of nose-contact; tongue-contact is empty of tongue-contact; body-contact is empty of body-contact; and mind-contact is empty of mind-contact.

Subhūti, whoever would desire the departure of feeling conditioned by eye-contact would desire the departure of dharmas that are without marks. Subhūti, whoever would desire the departure of feeling conditioned by ear-contact would desire the departure of dharmas that are without marks. Subhūti, whoever would desire the departure of feeling conditioned by nose-contact would desire the departure of dharmas that are without marks.

Subhūti, he who would seek the departure of sensation conditioned by tongue-contact would seek the departure of phenomena that are without marks. Subhūti, he who would seek the departure of sensation conditioned by body-contact would seek the departure of phenomena that are without marks. Subhūti, he who would seek the departure of sensation conditioned by mind-contact would seek the departure of phenomena that are without marks. Why is that? Because it is not so.

Feeling conditioned by eye-contact departs from the three realms; it does not abide in omniscience. Feeling conditioned by ear-contact departs from the three realms; it does not abide in omniscience. Feeling conditioned by nose-contact departs from the three realms; it does not abide in omniscience. Feeling conditioned by tongue-contact departs from the three realms.

It does not abide in omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*). Feeling conditioned by bodily contact does not emerge from the three realms; it does not abide in omniscience. Feeling conditioned by mental contact does not emerge from the three realms; it does not abide in omniscience. For what reason? Because, Subhūti, feeling conditioned by visual contact is empty of feeling conditioned by visual contact.

Feeling conditioned by auditory contact is empty of feeling conditioned by auditory contact; feeling conditioned by olfactory contact is empty of feeling conditioned by olfactory contact; feeling conditioned by gustatory contact is empty of feeling conditioned by gustatory contact; feeling conditioned by tactile contact is empty of feeling conditioned by tactile contact; feeling conditioned by mental contact is empty of feeling conditioned by mental contact.

Subhūti, whoever would desire the departure of signless phenomena would desire the departure of a dream. Subhūti, whoever would desire the departure of signless phenomena would desire the departure of an illusion. Subhūti, whoever would desire the departure of signless phenomena would desire the departure of a mirage. Subhūti, whoever would desire the departure of signless phenomena would desire the departure of an echo.

Subhūti, whoever would desire the departure of phenomena that are without marks, he would desire the departure of a reflection. Subhūti, whoever would desire the departure of phenomena that are without marks, he would desire the departure of a magical creation of the Tathāgata. Why is that? Because, Subhūti, the intrinsic nature of a dream does not exist within the triple world.

It does not emerge; it does not abide in omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*). The intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of an illusion does not emerge from the triple world; it does not abide in omniscience. The intrinsic nature of a mirage does not emerge from the triple world; it does not abide in omniscience. The intrinsic nature of an echo does not emerge from the triple world; it does not abide in omniscience. The intrinsic nature of a reflection does not emerge from the triple world.

He does not abide in the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*). The intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of a Tathāgata’s emanation does not emerge from the triple world, nor does it abide in the knowledge of all aspects. Why is that? For, Subhūti, the intrinsic nature of a dream is empty of the intrinsic nature of a dream; the intrinsic nature of an illusion is empty of the intrinsic nature of an illusion; the intrinsic nature of a mirage is empty of the intrinsic nature of a mirage; the intrinsic nature of an echo is empty of the intrinsic nature of an echo.
The nature of an appearance is empty of the nature of an appearance; the nature of a Tathāgata’s emanation is empty of the nature of a Tathāgata’s emanation.

Subhūti, he who would desire the departure of the perfection of generosity would desire the departure of dharmas that are without marks. Subhūti, he who would desire the departure of the perfection of ethical discipline would desire the departure of dharmas that are without marks. Subhūti, he who would desire the departure of the perfection of patience would desire the departure of dharmas that are without marks.

Subhūti, he who would desire the departure of signless phenomena would desire the departure of the perfection of vigor; Subhūti, he who would desire the departure of signless phenomena would desire the departure of the perfection of meditation; Subhūti, he who would desire the departure of signless phenomena would desire the departure of the perfection of wisdom.

For what reason? Because, Subhūti, the intrinsic nature of the perfection of giving does not emerge from the triple world, nor does it abide in omniscience. That which is the intrinsic nature of the perfection of ethical discipline does not emerge from the triple world; that which is the intrinsic nature of the perfection of patience does not [emerge] from the triple world...

It does not depart; it does not abide in omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*). That which is the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the perfection of vigor (*vīryapāramitā*) does not depart from the triple world, nor does it abide in omniscience. That which is the intrinsic nature of the perfection of meditation (*dhyānapāramitā*) does not depart from the triple world, nor does it abide in omniscience. That which is the intrinsic nature of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) does not depart from the triple world, nor does it abide in omniscience.

For what reason? Because, Subhūti, the intrinsic nature of the perfection of generosity is empty of the intrinsic nature of the perfection of generosity; the intrinsic nature of the perfection of ethical discipline is empty of the intrinsic nature of the perfection of ethical discipline; the intrinsic nature of the perfection of patience is empty of the intrinsic nature of the perfection of patience; the intrinsic nature of the perfection of vigor is empty of the intrinsic nature of the perfection of vigor; the intrinsic nature of the perfection of meditation is empty of the intrinsic nature of the perfection of meditation;
and the intrinsic nature of the perfection of wisdom is empty of the intrinsic nature of the perfection of wisdom.

Subhūti, whoever would desire the departure from phenomena that are without marks, he would desire the departure from internal emptiness. Subhūti, whoever would desire the departure from phenomena that are without marks, he would desire the departure from external emptiness. Subhūti, whoever would desire the departure from phenomena that are without marks, he would desire the departure from internal and external emptiness.

Subhūti, whoever would desire the departure from the emptiness of emptiness, he would desire the departure from dharmas that are without marks. Subhūti, whoever would desire the departure from great emptiness, he would desire the departure from dharmas that are without marks. Subhūti, whoever would desire the departure from the emptiness of the ultimate truth, he would desire the departure from dharmas that are without marks.

Subhūti, whoever would desire the departure from phenomena that are without marks would desire the departure from conditioned emptiness; Subhūti, whoever would desire the departure from phenomena that are without marks would desire the departure from unconditioned emptiness; Subhūti, whoever [would desire the departure from phenomena that are without marks would desire the departure] from absolute emptiness.

Subhūti, whoever would desire the departure of phenomena that are without marks, he would desire the departure of the emptiness that is without beginning or end. Subhūti, whoever would desire the departure of phenomena that are without marks, he would desire the departure of the emptiness of non-dispersal. Subhūti, whoever would desire the departure of phenomena that are without marks, he would desire the departure of the emptiness of intrinsic nature.

Subhūti, whoever would desire the departure from phenomena that lack characteristics would desire the departure from the emptiness of all phenomena; Subhūti, whoever would desire the departure from phenomena that lack characteristics would desire the departure from the emptiness of specific characteristics; Subhūti, whoever would desire the departure from phenomena that lack characteristics would desire the departure from the emptiness of non-apprehension.

Subhūti, whoever would desire the departure of phenomena that are without marks would desire the departure of the emptiness of non-existence. Subhūti, whoever would desire the departure of phenomena that are without marks would desire the departure of the emptiness of intrinsic nature. Subhūti, whoever would desire the departure of phenomena that are without marks would desire the departure of the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence. Why is that? Because, Subhūti, internal emptiness does not depart from the triple world.

It does not abide in omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*). External emptiness (*bahirdhāśūnyatā*) does not emerge from the triple world; it does not abide in omniscience. Internal-and-external emptiness (*adhyātmabahirdhāśūnyatā*) does not emerge from the triple world; it does not abide in omniscience. The emptiness of emptiness (*śūnyatāśūnyatā*) does not emerge from the triple world; it does not abide in omniscience. Great emptiness (*mahāśūnyatā*) does not emerge from the triple world; it does not abide in omniscience.

Ultimate emptiness does not emerge from the three realms, nor does it abide in omniscience. Conditioned emptiness does not emerge from the three realms, nor does it abide in omniscience. Unconditioned emptiness does not emerge from the three realms.

It does not abide in the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*). Ultimate emptiness (*atyantaśūnyatā*) does not emerge from the three realms; it does not abide in the knowledge of all aspects. Emptiness without beginning or end (*anavarāgraśūnyatā*) does not emerge from the three realms; it does not abide in the knowledge of all aspects. Emptiness of the non-dispersed (*anavakāraśūnyatā*) does not emerge from the three realms; it does not abide in the knowledge of all aspects. Emptiness of intrinsic nature (*prakṛtiśūnyatā*) does not emerge from the three realms; it does not abide in the knowledge of all aspects.

The emptiness of all phenomena does not emerge from the triple world, nor does it abide in omniscience. The emptiness of specific characteristics does not emerge from the triple world, nor does it abide in omniscience. The emptiness of non-apprehension does not emerge from the triple world, nor does it abide in omniscience. The emptiness of non-existence does not emerge from the triple world, nor does it abide in omniscience. The emptiness of intrinsic nature does not emerge from the triple world.
It does not abide in the knowledge of all aspects; the emptiness of the nature of non-existence does not emerge from the three realms, nor does it abide in the knowledge of all aspects.

For what reason? It is because, Subhūti, internal emptiness is empty of internal emptiness; external emptiness is empty of external emptiness; internal-external emptiness is empty of internal-external emptiness; the emptiness of emptiness is empty of the emptiness of emptiness; great emptiness is empty of great emptiness; the emptiness of the ultimate is empty of the emptiness of the ultimate; and the emptiness of the conditioned is empty of the emptiness of the conditioned.

Unconditioned emptiness is empty of unconditioned emptiness; ultimate emptiness is empty of ultimate emptiness; emptiness without beginning or end is empty of emptiness without beginning or end; emptiness of non-dispersal is empty of emptiness of non-dispersal; natural emptiness is empty of natural emptiness; the emptiness of all phenomena is empty of the emptiness of all phenomena.

The emptiness of specific characteristics is empty of the emptiness of specific characteristics; the emptiness of non-apprehension is empty of the emptiness of non-apprehension; the emptiness of non-existence is empty of the emptiness of non-existence; the emptiness of intrinsic nature is empty of the emptiness of intrinsic nature; the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence is empty of the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence.

Subhūti, whoever would desire the departure of the applications of mindfulness would desire the departure of dharmas that are without marks.
